overview.text: Edvard Hagerup Grieg (1843–1907) was a Norwegian composer and pianist associated with the Romantic era. He used Norwegian folk music in his compositions, helping bring Norway’s musical traditions to wider attention and connecting his work with the development of Norwegian national identity.

Grieg’s music remains part of the standard classical repertoire worldwide. His legacy is closely linked with Bergen, where statues, cultural institutions, and a museum at his former home, Troldhaugen, commemorate him.

key_facts.text: He lived from 15 June 1843 to 4 September 1907.
Grieg Hall, the Grieg Academy, and the Edvard Grieg Kor in Bergen are named after him.
The Edvard Grieg Museum is located at Troldhaugen, his former home.

overview.text: Prague (Czech: Praha) is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic. It stands on the Vltava River and is the historical capital of Bohemia, linking the city to both the modern country and the historic Bohemian region.

Prague’s built environment includes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque architecture. Its history connects it with the Kingdom of Bohemia, the Holy Roman Empire, the Habsburg monarchy, the Protestant Reformations, and Czechoslovakia. Prague Castle, Charles Bridge, Old Town Square, and the astronomical clock are among its cultural attractions.

key_facts.text: Holy Roman Emperors Charles IV and Rudolf II were among the rulers who had Prague as a residence.
Prague’s historic center has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.
Charles University in Prague is described as the oldest university in Central Europe.
Prague served as the capital of Czechoslovakia between the World Wars and during the post-war Communist era.

overview.text: Venezuela, officially the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, is a South American country on the northern coast. Its territory includes a mainland area and Caribbean islands. It borders the Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean to the north, Colombia to the west, Brazil to the south, Guyana to the east, and Trinidad and Tobago to the northeast. Caracas is the capital and largest urban agglomeration, while most residents live in northern urban areas.

Petroleum is a central geographic and economic association: oil came to dominate Venezuela’s exports and government revenues after an earlier export economy based on commodities such as coffee and cocoa. Its modern political history includes an independence declaration in 1811, separation from Gran Colombia in 1830, and the political transformation that followed Hugo Chávez’s 1998 election and the 1999 constitution.

key_facts.text: Venezuela is divided into 23 states, the Capital District, and Federal Dependencies.
An estimated 88.4% of the population lived in urban areas in 2022, making Venezuela one of Latin America’s highly urbanized countries.
Spain colonized the territory in 1522 amid resistance from Indigenous peoples.
Venezuela is formally a federal presidential republic.

overview.text: Jhumpa Lahiri (Nilanjana Sudeshna Lahiri) is a British-American author of short stories, novels, and essays who writes in English and, more recently, Italian. Her works explore the Indian-immigrant experience in America. Her books include the short-story collection Interpreter of Maladies and the novels The Namesake and The Lowland; The Namesake was adapted into a film. After moving to Rome in 2012, Lahiri began writing in Italian and published fiction, essays, and translations.

key_facts.text: Interpreter of Maladies (1999), her debut short-story collection, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Hemingway Award.
Unaccustomed Earth won the Frank O’Connor International Short Story Award.
The Lowland was a finalist for both the Man Booker Prize and the National Book Award for Fiction.
Her Italian-language works include the 2018 novel Dove mi trovo and the 2023 collection Roman Stories.

overview.text: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni, usually called Michelangelo, was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence and active mainly in Rome from his thirties onward, he drew on classical antiquity and had a lasting influence on Western art. His versatility reflects the Renaissance ideal of the accomplished artist.

His work ranged from sculpture and fresco painting to architecture. Important examples include the Pietà and David, scenes from Genesis on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, The Last Judgment, the Laurentian Library, and work on St. Peter’s Basilica.

key_facts.text: Michelangelo sculpted both the Pietà and David before he was 30.
The Sistine Chapel ceiling contains scenes from Genesis, while The Last Judgment occupies the chapel’s altar wall.
At age 71, Michelangelo became architect of St. Peter’s Basilica and reshaped its western end and dome design.
Michelangelo was the first Western artist whose biography was published during his lifetime; three biographies appeared before his death.
Contemporaries called him Il Divino, “the divine one.” His expressive style helped inspire Mannerism, the movement between the High Renaissance and Baroque.

overview.text: The pope holds the office of Bishop of Rome and leads the worldwide Catholic Church. The office is called the papacy, while the Holy See names the jurisdiction of Rome’s bishop. The Holy See is separate from Vatican City, the independent city-state where it is headquartered; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 established this arrangement to protect its political and spiritual independence.

Catholic tradition connects the Roman office with Saint Peter, while history shows popes acting as both religious leaders and, at times, political figures. They addressed doctrinal disputes and mediated among medieval Christian monarchs; modern papal work includes ecumenism, interfaith dialogue, charity, and human-rights advocacy. The papacy’s secular authority has declined, leaving religious matters as its main focus.

key_facts.text: The pope also has titles such as Roman Pontiff, Supreme Pontiff, and Sovereign Pontiff.
Catholic tradition grounds the bishop of Rome’s primacy in Saint Peter and his apostolic role.
From the eighth century through 1870, popes also ruled the Papal States as secular heads of state.
The 1870 doctrine of papal infallibility applies to rare ex cathedra statements: formal definitions of faith or morals issued by the pope.

overview.text: Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist whose economical, understated style influenced later twentieth-century writers. Several of his works became classics of American literature, and he received the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.

His career connected literary modernism and the expatriate “Lost Generation” in 1920s Paris with firsthand experience of war and journalism. These experiences shaped major fiction about World War I and the Spanish Civil War, while his public image also became associated with adventure and bluntness.

key_facts.text: The Sun Also Rises, Hemingway’s debut novel, was published in 1926.
His World War I experiences supplied material for the 1929 novel A Farewell to Arms.
His reporting on the Spanish Civil War formed the basis for the 1940 novel For Whom the Bell Tolls.
The Old Man and the Sea appeared in 1952 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

overview.text: The Seagull is a play by Russian playwright Anton Chekhov. It belongs to a set of four works that also includes Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard. These plays favor atmosphere and partly hidden inner life over conventional action.

This theatrical approach challenges performers and audiences, and connects Chekhov with the emergence of early modernism in theatre. The play is therefore associated both with Chekhov’s major dramatic works and with a changing style of modern drama.

key_facts.text: After The Seagull’s 1896 reception, Chekhov renounced the theatre.
Konstantin Stanislavski’s Moscow Art Theatre revived the play to acclaim in 1898.
Chekhov is often grouped with Henrik Ibsen and August Strindberg as a seminal figure in early modernist theatre.
Chekhov was both a physician and a writer of plays and short stories.

overview.text: Elephants are the largest living land animals and the only surviving members of the family Elephantidae and order Proboscidea. Three living species are recognized: the African bush elephant, African forest elephant, and Asian elephant. Their distinctive features include a prehensile trunk, tusks, large ears, pillar-like legs, and tough gray skin.

These herbivores inhabit African and Asian savannahs, forests, deserts, and marshes, and are considered keystone species because they strongly affect their environments. Females generally live in family groups led by a matriarch, while males often leave after puberty. Elephants communicate through several senses, including long-distance infrasound and seismic signals.

key_facts.text: Tusks are modified incisor teeth used as weapons and as tools for moving objects and digging.
Musth is a period of increased testosterone and aggression in adult bulls that helps them compete for dominance and reproductive success.
African bush and Asian elephants are listed as endangered, while African forest elephants are listed as critically endangered.
Ivory poaching, habitat destruction, and conflicts with local people are major threats to wild elephant populations.
Elephants have been used as working animals in Asia and, historically, in warfare; they also have a major presence in human art, folklore, religion, and literature.

overview.text: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor from Syracuse in Sicily. His surviving work used infinitesimals and the method of exhaustion to prove geometric results involving circles, spheres, ellipses, parabolas, and spirals.

He applied mathematics to physical phenomena, linking the study of forces and fluids with practical machines. His work included statics and hydrostatics, the law of the lever, centers of gravity, a screw pump, compound pulleys, and defensive machines.

key_facts.text: Archimedes’ principle is the name of the law of buoyancy associated with him.
He approximated π and investigated the Archimedean spiral.
He measured the Sun’s apparent diameter and the size of the universe; he is also said to have built a planetarium demonstrating celestial movements.
Archimedes was killed during the Roman siege of Syracuse, despite orders that he not be harmed.
His work was translated into Arabic in the ninth century and Latin in the twelfth; the 1906 discovery of the Archimedes Palimpsest provided new insights into his methods.

overview.text: Pocahontas was a Powhatan woman associated with the English settlement at Jamestown, Virginia. Born Amonute and also known as Matoaka and Rebecca Rolfe, she was the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, leader of a network of tributary tribes in the Tidewater region of present-day Virginia. (p1)

English colonists captured Pocahontas during hostilities in 1613. While held, she was encouraged to convert to Christianity and was baptized Rebecca; she married the tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614. In 1616, the couple traveled to London, where English society presented her as an example intended to encourage investment in Jamestown. Her later image was romanticized, and many stories about her are fictional or contested. (p2–p4)

key_facts.text: She was held for ransom after her capture in 1613. (p2)
Her son, Thomas Rolfe, was born in January 1615. (p2)
Pocahontas died at Gravesend, England, in 1617 at age 20 or 21; the cause was unknown, and the exact location of her grave is uncertain. (p3)
Her name has been used for places, landmarks, and products in the United States, and she remains a subject of art, literature, and film. (p4)

overview.text: Atar is the Zoroastrian sacred fire associated with temple worship and ritual purity. The supplied material places fire alongside water as an agent of purity and connects the care of fire and ash with purification practices. Atar is therefore best recognized through the linked ideas of Zoroastrian worship, purity, and properly tended fire.

key_facts.text: Clean white ash plays an important role in Zoroastrian purification ceremonies.
Fire ceremonies also model the proper way to tend domestic fires.
The main fire temples are called Atash Behrams; smaller temples are known as agiaries.

overview.text: Lyndon Baines Johnson, or LBJ, was a Texas Democrat who served as John F. Kennedy’s vice president and became the 36th U.S. president after Kennedy’s assassination. He served from 1963 to 1969, following a long congressional career that included leadership in the Senate.

Johnson’s Great Society agenda expanded civil rights, health care, education, welfare, and public services, including the War on Poverty. His administration also prioritized the Apollo Moon program. In foreign policy, Johnson emphasized containing communism and escalated U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War, which contributed to declining public approval.

key_facts.text: Before becoming president, Johnson rose through Congress from House member to Senate majority whip, Democratic leader, and majority leader.
The Social Security Amendments of 1965 created Medicare and Medicaid as part of Johnson’s domestic program.
Major civil-rights laws associated with his presidency include the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Civil Rights Act of 1968.
Johnson initially sought reelection in 1968 but withdrew after disappointing results in the New Hampshire primary.

overview.text: The Boston Tea Party was a December 16, 1773 protest in Boston, Massachusetts, initiated by the Sons of Liberty during rising conflict between Great Britain and Patriots in the Thirteen Colonies. Its immediate target was the Tea Act, which allowed the East India Company to sell Chinese tea in the colonies under tax arrangements that protesters viewed as violating their rights as Englishmen—especially the principle of no taxation without representation.

That night, participants disguised as American Indians boarded the Dartmouth and dumped hundreds of chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor. Parliament answered in 1774 with the Intolerable Acts, including the closure of Boston’s port and an end to local self-government in Massachusetts. The measures prompted further colonial resistance before the Revolutionary War.

key_facts.text: The protest opposed both the Tea Act and the earlier Townshend Acts, which imposed taxes on colonial goods.
Participants threw 340 or 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor.
The Intolerable Acts led colonists to convene the First Continental Congress and coordinate resistance through the Continental Association.
The Battles of Lexington and Concord followed less than two years later and began the American Revolutionary War.

overview.text: Caves, also called caverns, are natural voids beneath Earth’s surface. They often form through rock weathering and can extend deep underground. Their scientific study is called speleology, and caves have also been observed on other rocky worlds, including Mars.

key_facts.text: Exogene caves are relatively small openings that extend only a short distance underground; rock shelters are an example.
Endogene caves extend farther underground than the width of their openings.
Recreational cave exploration may be called caving, potholing, or spelunking.

overview.text: Pizza is an Italian dish made from a flat base of leavened wheat dough, typically topped with tomato, cheese, and other ingredients. It is baked at high heat, traditionally in a wood-fired oven. [p1]

Pizza is a widely popular everyday food found in pizzerias, restaurants, delivery services, street-food settings, and grocery stores as frozen products or home-assembly kits. In Italy, restaurant pizza is traditionally served unsliced and eaten with a knife and fork, while casual versions are often cut into hand-held slices. [p3]

key_facts.text: The word pizza was first recorded in A.D. 997 in a Latin manuscript from Gaeta in southern Italy. [p2]
Raffaele Esposito is often credited with creating the modern version of pizza in Naples in the late 19th century. [p2]
Neapolitan pizza was registered by the European Union in 2009 as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed dish. [p2]
The art of making Neapolitan pizza was added to UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage in 2017. [p2]

overview.text: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English writer and major English Romantic poet. His poetry is associated with sweeping imagery, varied forms, and a complex interplay of skeptical, idealist, and materialist ideas. He also expressed radical political and social views.

A useful starting group of works includes the short poems “Ozymandias,” “Ode to the West Wind,” and “To a Skylark.” Shelley also wrote longer poems, verse dramas, prose fiction, and essays on political, social, and philosophical issues.

key_facts.text: His longer poems include Alastor, Julian and Maddalo, Adonais, and The Triumph of Life.
His verse dramas include The Cenci, Prometheus Unbound, and Hellas.
Shelley’s influence grew after his death, affecting poets such as Robert Browning, Algernon Charles Swinburne, Thomas Hardy, and W. B. Yeats.
Some of his writing was unpublished or altered during his lifetime because of the risk of prosecution for political or religious libel.
His second wife, Mary Shelley, was the author of Frankenstein.

overview.text: Oregon is a state in the Pacific Northwest and the Western United States, bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean. Its varied landscapes include volcanoes, abundant water, evergreen and mixed forests, high deserts, and semi-arid shrublands.

Indigenous nations have lived in Oregon for thousands of years. Later exploration, fur trading, joint British-American occupation, the Oregon Treaty, and territorial government preceded Oregon’s admission to the Union.

key_facts.text: The Columbia River forms much of Oregon’s northern boundary with Washington, while the Snake River marks much of its eastern boundary with Idaho.
Oregon became the 33rd U.S. state on February 14, 1859.
Mount Hood is Oregon’s highest point, and Crater Lake National Park is the state’s only national park.
Agriculture, fishing, logging, and hydroelectric power have historically supported Oregon’s economy; technology later became another major economic force.

overview.text: The Kalahari Desert is a large semiarid sandy savanna in Southern Africa. It covers about 900,000 square kilometers, making it a major regional landform rather than a small, localized desert.
Its range includes much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa. These countries are the central geographic associations for recognizing the Kalahari on a map.

key_facts.text: Landscape: sandy savanna.
Climate: semiarid, meaning it is dry but not among the most extremely arid environments.
Area: approximately 900,000 km² (350,000 sq mi).
Countries: Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa.

overview.text: Hajj (also spelled Haj or Hadj) is the annual Islamic pilgrimage to the Kaaba in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. It is one of the Five Pillars of Islam and is a required duty once in a Muslim’s life for those physically and financially able to make the journey while supporting their family. The pilgrimage expresses submission to Allah and Muslim solidarity.

Its central rites take place over five to six days in Dhu’l-Hijja, the last month of the Islamic lunar calendar, so its Gregorian dates change from year to year. Pilgrims wear ihram, circle the Kaaba, travel between Safa and Marwah, stand in vigil at Arafat, and perform symbolic stoning at three pillars.

key_facts.text: Muslim sources connect the pilgrimage tradition to Abraham; Hajj is also associated with Muhammad and the seventh century.
A major rite has pilgrims walk counter-clockwise seven times around the Kaaba and kiss the Black Stone set into its wall.
After an animal sacrifice, male pilgrims shave or trim their heads, while female pilgrims trim the ends of their hair; Eid al-Adha follows.
Umrah is a separate “lesser pilgrimage” that may be performed at other times, but it does not replace Hajj for Muslims who are able to undertake it.

overview.text: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair (Spanish: Veinte poemas de amor y una canción desesperada) is a Spanish-language poetry collection by Chilean poet Pablo Neruda. Published in June 1924, it helped establish Neruda’s fame when he was 19 and is regarded as one of the renowned Spanish-language literary works of the twentieth century. Its English-language literary history also includes a 1969 translation by poet W. S. Merwin.

key_facts.text: The collection was published in June 1924.
Its Spanish title is Veinte poemas de amor y una canción desesperada.
W. S. Merwin produced an English translation in 1969.

source.title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair

overview.text: Pennsylvania, officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, is a U.S. state in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeastern, Appalachian, and Great Lakes regions. Philadelphia is its largest city and metropolitan area, Pittsburgh anchors the second-largest, and Harrisburg is the capital between them. The state borders six U.S. states and Ontario across Lake Erie.

Its landscape is marked by the Appalachian Mountains, extensive forests, and waterfront on Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River. Founded in 1681 through William Penn’s royal land grant, Pennsylvania became an important setting of the American Revolution: Philadelphia hosted both Continental Congresses and the adoption of the Declaration of Independence.

key_facts.text: The Allegheny and Pocono mountains occupy much of northeastern Pennsylvania, while about 59% of the state is forested.
Pennsylvania has no ocean coastline, but it has waterfront along Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River.
The southeastern part of the state was part of New Sweden, a Swedish colony, from 1638 to 1655.
Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the U.S. Constitution, on December 12, 1787, after Delaware.

overview.text: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That Which Is to Come is a Christian allegory by the English nonconformist preacher John Bunyan. Its first part was first published in 1678, and the work is associated with Protestant devotional literature and wider early modern English literature.

The work has remained widely read: it has been translated into more than 200 languages, has never been out of print, and influenced writers including C. S. Lewis and Louisa May Alcott. Bunyan began writing it during imprisonment connected to restrictions on nonconformist religious services.

key_facts.text: The first part was completed in 1677; an expanded edition appeared in 1679.
The Second Part appeared in 1684, making the English work a two-part continuous narrative.
The English text has no chapter divisions.
Scholars disagree about whether Bunyan began the work during his long imprisonment from 1660 to 1672 or during a shorter imprisonment in 1675.

overview.text: “Lady Lazarus” is a poem by Sylvia Plath. It is commonly interpreted as an expression of Plath’s suicidal attempts and thoughts, and it is often discussed as an example of her writing style. The poem has also attracted substantial literary criticism since its publication.

key_facts.text: The poem was originally included in Plath’s collection Ariel.
Ariel was published in 1965.
Ariel appeared two years after Plath’s death by suicide.
“Lady Lazarus” has been the subject of extensive literary criticism.

overview.text: Polymers are substances made of very large molecules, or macromolecules, built from many repeating subunits derived from one or more kinds of smaller molecules called monomers. Polymerization links many monomers into these large molecules. Both natural and synthetic polymers are broad classes with important roles in everyday life.

Their large molecular mass gives polymers distinctive properties such as toughness, high elasticity, and viscoelasticity, and they may form amorphous or semicrystalline structures rather than crystals. Polymers also matter biologically: DNA and proteins are natural polymeric materials, while synthetic polymers include familiar plastics.

key_facts.text: Polyisoprene in latex rubber is a natural polymer; polystyrene, including Styrofoam, is a synthetic polymer.
Proteins, nucleic acids, and polysaccharides are biological macromolecules that are polymeric or contain substantial polymeric components.
Polymer science includes polymer chemistry and polymer physics and connects with biophysics and materials science and engineering.
Supramolecular polymers are an area involving polymer structures formed through non-covalent links rather than only conventional covalent bonds.

overview.text: The Count of Monte Cristo (French: Le Comte de Monte-Cristo) is an adventure novel by French writer Alexandre Dumas. It was serialized from 1844 to 1846 and published in book form in 1846; it is regarded as a classic of French and world literature.

Set in France, Italy, and Mediterranean islands during the historical years 1815–1839, the novel follows Edmond Dantès, a sailor falsely accused of treason and imprisoned in the Château d’If. After finding hidden treasure, he becomes the enigmatic Count of Monte Cristo and pursues revenge, while the story explores justice, vengeance, mercy, forgiveness, and redemption.

key_facts.text: In prison, Dantès meets Abbé Faria, who educates him and reveals the location of treasure on Monte Cristo.
Dantès targets Danglars, Fernand, and Villefort in his revenge plan; Villefort had ensured Dantès’s imprisonment.
By the conclusion, Dantès moves away from complete devotion to revenge, seeks redemption, and leaves with Haydée.
Its serialization attracted large European audiences, and the novel has remained in print while inspiring many film and television adaptations.

overview.text: Karma (Pali: kamma) is an ancient Indian concept of action or deed and its consequences. In Indian religions, it describes a cause-and-effect principle in which a person’s intentions and actions influence later outcomes: good intentions and deeds contribute to good karma, while harmful ones contribute to bad karma.

Karma is closely associated with rebirth in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism; in these traditions, present karma can affect circumstances in this life and the nature or quality of future lives. Interpretations vary: some scriptures do not link karma with rebirth, and karma should not be equated with fate or predetermination.

key_facts.text: Traditional Hindu classifications call accumulated karma from past actions across lifetimes sanchita karma; prārabdha karma is the portion currently bearing fruit.
Hindu classifications also describe āgāmi karma, generated by present actions for the future, and kriyamāṇa karma, created by current actions with immediate or later results.
Karma is not simply fate, destiny, or predetermination.

overview.text: Optical reflection is the change in direction of a light wavefront at an interface between two media so that it returns to the medium from which it came. In a mirror example, the reflection is specular, and the law of reflection says that the angle at which light arrives equals the angle at which it leaves. Reflection is a broader wave phenomenon: similar behavior occurs with sound, water waves, and electromagnetic waves beyond visible light.

key_facts.text: Reflected sound produces echoes and is used in sonar.
Reflection of very-high-frequency and higher-frequency electromagnetic waves is important for radio transmission and radar.
Special grazing mirrors can reflect hard X-rays and gamma rays at shallow angles.

overview.text: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia in West Asia and includes the smaller region of East Thrace in Southeast Europe. It has coasts on the Black, Mediterranean, and Aegean seas and land borders with countries including Greece, Bulgaria, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, and Syria.
Its physical geography includes coastal plains, a high central plateau, and mountain ranges; elevation rises toward the east.

key_facts.text: Ankara is the capital and second-largest city; Istanbul is the largest city and economic center.
Climate types range from Mediterranean and other temperate climates to semi-arid and continental.
Turkey is home to three biodiversity hotspots and is prone to frequent earthquakes.

overview.text: Finland, officially the Republic of Finland, is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. Its physical setting combines a predominantly boreal-forest landscape with more than 180,000 recorded lakes. The climate varies from humid continental in the south to boreal in the north. Its maritime setting includes the Gulf of Bothnia and Gulf of Finland.

key_facts.text: Finland shares land borders with Sweden to the northwest, Norway to the north, and Russia to the east.
The Gulf of Bothnia is west of Finland; the Gulf of Finland is south, opposite Estonia.
Helsinki is Finland’s capital and largest city.
Finnish and Swedish are Finland’s official languages.

overview.text: Portugal developed from a medieval kingdom in western Iberia. Roman rule established Lusitania in the south and Gallaecia in the north; later Germanic and Islamic powers controlled the region. Afonso Henriques proclaimed himself king in 1139, and Portugal completed its conquest of the Algarve in 1249.

Portugal became a major world power in the 15th and 16th centuries by building a vast empire during Europe’s Age of Discovery. Its later history combined imperial decline, political upheaval, and a twentieth-century transition from dictatorship to democratic reform and decolonization.

key_facts.text: Lisbon became Portugal’s capital in 1255. After defeating Castile in 1385, Portugal established an alliance with England through the Treaty of Windsor in 1386.
The 1578 Battle of Alcácer Quibir in Morocco was a major setback: King Sebastian died, and much of Portugal’s high nobility was imprisoned and later ransomed.
Portugal’s independence was interrupted by a dynastic union with Spain from 1580 to 1640; John IV led the Restoration War that began in 1640.
The monarchy fell in 1910. A military coup in 1926 installed a dictatorship; another coup in 1974 was followed by democratic reforms and independence for all Portuguese African colonies in 1975.
Portugal was a founding member of NATO, the OECD, EFTA, and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries, and joined the European Economic Community in 1986.

overview.text: Portugal, officially the Portuguese Republic, is a country in southwestern Europe whose mainland occupies the southwestern part of the Iberian Peninsula. It borders Spain to the north and east and also includes the Atlantic archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores. Lisbon is the capital and largest city. Portugal’s physical geography includes varied landscapes and regional climates, and its maritime territory is substantial.

key_facts.text: Madeira and the Azores are Portugal’s two autonomous overseas regions.
Portugal’s internal waters and territorial sea together account for two-fifths of its territory.
Portugal has one of Europe’s largest exclusive economic zones.
Portugal is divided into seven mainland regions and two autonomous overseas regions.

overview.text: Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer and statesman who became a radical Jacobin leader during the French Revolution. His political career connected arguments for expanded political rights and revolutionary virtue with support for the harsh measures of the Reign of Terror. Robespierre remains important because his career illustrates the Revolution’s tension between ideals of political reform and the repression used against its opponents, making his legacy deeply controversial.

key_facts.text: He supported voting rights for all men, access to the National Guard, the right to petition, self-defense with arms, and abolition of the Atlantic slave trade.
Robespierre was elected to the National Convention in 1792 and joined the Committee of Public Safety in July 1793.
On 9 Thermidor, accusations of revolutionary excesses culminated in his arrest with about 90 others, including Louis Antoine de Saint-Just and Georges Couthon; he was executed without trial.
Debates about his legacy focus on his actual or perceived role in repression, as well as his ideas about virtue and revolutionary violence.

overview.text: Heracles—also called Hercules in Roman tradition and known as Alcaeus or Alcides—was a Greek hero regarded as both a hero and a god. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene and the foster son of Amphitryon. A conventionally numbered set of twelve labors, ordered by his cousin Eurystheus, includes killing the Nemean Lion and Lernaean Hydra, stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides, and capturing Cerberus.

His importance extends beyond the labor stories: he was worshipped as a patron of young men and gymnasia, and festivals could honor him first as a hero and then as a god. His Roman form, Hercules, remains a frequent subject of Western art and popular culture.

key_facts.text: The myths often portray Hera as hostile to Heracles; one story says that her influence drove him mad, leading him to kill his wife Megara and their children.
According to his apotheosis story, Deianira’s poisoned garment led Heracles to burn himself atop Mount Oeta; the story ends with his ascent to Olympus and marriage to Hebe.
Heracles’ descendants were called the Heracleidae.
Roman emperors such as Commodus and Maximian identified themselves with Hercules.

overview.text: A volcano is a vent or fissure in the crust of a planet-sized object that lets hot lava, volcanic ash, and gases escape from a magma chamber below the surface.

On Earth, volcanoes commonly occur where tectonic plates diverge or converge, though they can also form at crustal rifts and hotspots. Most of Earth’s plate boundaries are underwater, so most volcanoes are underwater; major eruptions can cool the atmosphere and contribute to volcanic winters and famines.

key_facts.text: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge illustrates volcanism at a divergent boundary, while the Pacific Ring of Fire is associated with convergent boundaries.

Active volcanoes have a history of volcanism and are likely to erupt again; dormant volcanoes may erupt after a long quiet period, while extinct volcanoes are described as unable to erupt because they lack a magma source.
Hotspot volcanism can occur away from plate boundaries. The Hawaiian hotspot is an example and can produce a volcanic island chain as its tectonic plate moves.
Volcanoes also occur on Venus and Mars. A proposed broader definition includes cryovolcanism and treats “magma” as material defined for the relevant planet or moon.

overview.text: Frédéric François Chopin, born Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin, was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the early Romantic period. He wrote mainly for solo piano, creating technically demanding music that expanded the instrument’s expressive possibilities. His performances were noted for nuance and sensitivity.

His major forms include mazurkas, waltzes, nocturnes, polonaises, études, preludes, ballades, and sonatas. Polish folk music, Mozart and Schubert, and Parisian salons shaped his style. His innovations in musical style, harmony, and form influenced music during and after the late Romantic period, and his work became associated with nationalism.

key_facts.text: Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola and grew up in Warsaw. He left Poland at age 20, shortly before the November 1830 Uprising, and settled in Paris at 21.
He preferred intimate salon performances to large public appearances and gave only 30 public performances. He supported himself through composition and piano teaching.
He wrote six works for piano and orchestra, including two piano concertos. His other output includes chamber music and 19 songs set to Polish lyrics.
Chopin created the instrumental ballade as a genre: a ballade written for instruments rather than for a singer.
The Fryderyk Chopin Institute researches and promotes his life and works and hosts the International Chopin Piano Competition, devoted entirely to his music.

overview.text: Sulfur, symbol S, is the nonmetallic element with atomic number 16. At room temperature it is a bright yellow crystalline solid, and its atoms commonly form ring-shaped S₈ molecules. On Earth, sulfur usually occurs in sulfide and sulfate minerals, although native sulfur also exists.

Sulfur links mineral chemistry to industry, biology, and familiar odors. It is essential to life in sulfur-containing biological compounds, while hydrogen sulfide produces the characteristic smell of rotting eggs. Its compounds also support major chemical processes and fertilizer production.

key_facts.text: The largest commercial use of sulfur is making sulfuric acid, including for sulfate and phosphate fertilizers.
Nearly all elemental sulfur is recovered while removing sulfur-containing contaminants from natural gas and petroleum.
The amino acids cysteine and methionine, along with the vitamins biotin and thiamine, are organosulfur compounds important to life.
Disulfide bonds—S–S links—help give keratin strength and resistance to dissolving in skin, hair, and feathers.
Sulfur’s historical name “brimstone” means “burning stone.”

overview.text: Jules Gabriel Verne (1828–1905) was a French novelist, poet, and playwright. With publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel, he developed the Voyages extraordinaires, a series of adventure novels including Journey to the Center of the Earth, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, and Around the World in Eighty Days. His stories generally place adventure in the second half of the nineteenth century while engaging with the scientific knowledge and technological advances of his time.

Verne’s influence extends beyond popular adventure: his writing influenced the literary avant-garde and surrealism, and his works have been adapted for film, television, comics, theater, opera, music, and video games.

key_facts.text: Verne also wrote plays, short stories, autobiographical works, poetry, songs, and studies of science, art, and literature.

His reputation differed across language markets: he was regarded as an important author in France and much of Europe, while abridged and altered translations helped lead to his being labeled genre or children’s fiction in the Anglosphere.
He is sometimes called the “father of science fiction,” although that label is also applied to H. G. Wells and Hugo Gernsback.

overview.text: A self-portrait is a portrait an artist makes of themself. The artist may be the main subject or an important character in a larger work. Although self-portraits existed earlier, artists can be identified making them much more often from the mid-15th century onward. Better, cheaper mirrors and the spread of panel portraits helped the practice grow, while Renaissance interest in individual identity made it especially popular.
Self-portraits also had practical and social uses. They could be printed and sold, given as gifts, or kept in a portrait painter’s studio as evidence of the artist’s skill for prospective clients.

key_facts.text: Jan van Eyck’s Portrait of a Man in a Turban, dated 1433, may be the earliest known panel self-portrait.
By the Baroque period, most artists with established reputations had made at least drawings of themselves.
Rembrandt produced an unusually large number of self-portraits in both paintings and prints.
Self-portraits could avoid the need to arrange for another model.

overview.text: New York is a state in the Northeastern United States. It borders Canada to the north and reaches both the Atlantic Ocean and the Great Lakes. Albany is the state capital. Its landscape ranges from major lakes and river valleys to the Adirondack and Catskill Mountains.

The state is often divided geographically into Downstate and Upstate. Downstate includes New York City, Long Island, and the lower Hudson Valley; Upstate extends from the Great Lakes toward Lake Champlain and includes much of the state’s mountainous and inland lake country.

key_facts.text: Western New York borders Lakes Ontario and Erie and is part of the Great Lakes region.
The Finger Lakes are a prominent landmark between Central and Western New York; Syracuse anchors Central New York.
The east–west Mohawk River Valley meets the north–south Hudson River valley near Albany.
The Southern Tier lies along the Pennsylvania border on the Allegheny Plateau, part of the northern Appalachian region.
New York’s nickname, the “Empire State,” arose during its nineteenth-century political, cultural, and economic rise.

overview.text: New York City, often shortened to NYC, is the most populous city in the United States. It lies at the southern tip of New York State on New York Harbor and consists of five boroughs.

The city is the geographic and demographic center of the New York metropolitan area and the broader Northeast megalopolis. It is also a global center for finance, culture, media, the arts, and diplomacy, including as the headquarters of the United Nations.

key_facts.text: The five boroughs are Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island; each corresponds to a county.
Dutch colonists established New Amsterdam on Manhattan in the 1620s. After English control began in 1664, the settlement was renamed New York.
New York City served as the national capital of the United States from 1785 to 1790.
The modern five-borough city was formed through consolidation in 1898.
Wall Street anchors Manhattan’s Financial District, while New York City is home to the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.

overview.text: New Orleans is a consolidated city-parish on the Mississippi River in Louisiana and a major port and commercial hub for the Gulf Coast. Founded by French colonists in 1718, it became part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.

The city is associated with distinctive music, Creole cuisine, Mardi Gras, and the French Quarter. That historic district is known for French and Spanish Creole architecture and Bourbon Street nightlife.

key_facts.text: New Orleans is also commonly called NOLA and The Big Easy; the city is coextensive with Orleans Parish.
New Orleans was once the territorial capital of French Louisiana before joining the United States.
Its low elevation, poor natural drainage, heavy rainfall, and proximity to several bodies of water make the city vulnerable to flooding; levees and drainage pumps help protect it.
Hurricane Katrina severely affected New Orleans in August 2005, flooding more than 80% of the city and displacing thousands of residents.

overview.text: Ragnarök is a foretold sequence of events in Norse mythology, centered on a great battle in which many major figures—including Odin, Thor, Týr, Freyr, Heimdall, and Loki—die. Catastrophic natural disasters follow, including the burning and submersion of the world.

Ragnarök also leads to renewal: after the destruction, the world rises again, cleansed and fertile. Surviving and returning gods meet, and two human survivors, Líf and Lífþrasir, repopulate it. The event is known mainly from the 13th-century Poetic Edda and Prose Edda; the Poetic Edda was compiled from earlier traditional sources.

key_facts.text: A variant form, Ragnarøkkr, appears in the Prose Edda and one poem of the Poetic Edda; it means “Twilight of the Gods.”
The Poetic Edda was compiled in the 13th century from earlier traditional sources.
The Prose Edda was written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson.
Richard Wagner’s 1876 opera title Götterdämmerung helped popularize the “Twilight of the Gods” wording.

overview.text: Birds, class Aves, are warm-blooded vertebrates recognized by feathers, beaks, hard-shelled eggs, high metabolism, and lightweight skeletons. They are the only known living dinosaurs: birds evolved from earlier theropods, and their primitive avialan relatives include Archaeopteryx. Their closest living relatives are crocodilians.

Many species communicate with visual signals, calls, and songs and show social behaviors such as flocking, cooperative breeding, and predator mobbing. Birds also have important human connections: they provide food and materials, appear in culture, and attract birdwatchers, while human activity has caused extinctions and threatens additional species.

key_facts.text: Wings are modified forelimbs, but some birds—including penguins, ratites, and various island species—have evolved to lose flight.
The scientific study of birds is called ornithology.
Birds reproduce by laying fertilized eggs, usually in nests; parents commonly incubate the eggs and care for young after hatching.
Some aquatic birds, particularly seabirds and waterbirds, have evolved adaptations for swimming.

overview.text: Hawaii is an island state of the United States in the Pacific Ocean, about 2,000 miles southwest of the mainland. It is the only U.S. state that is an archipelago and the only one not on the North American mainland. Its islands form most of the Hawaiian archipelago, a volcanic island group that belongs geographically and ethnologically to Polynesia. (p1, p2)

Honolulu, the state capital and largest city, is on Oahu, where about two-thirds of Hawaii’s residents live. Polynesians settled the islands, which later became an independent kingdom before annexation by the United States; Hawaii became the most recent state to join the Union in 1959. (p3, p4)

key_facts.text: The eight main islands, northwest to southeast, are Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Maui, and Hawaiʻi, often called the “Big Island.”
Hawaii is one of the two non-contiguous U.S. states, along with Alaska, and the only state south of the Tropic of Cancer.
Hawaii became a unified kingdom in 1810; its monarchy was overthrown in 1893, and the territory was annexed by the United States in 1898.
Japan attacked Hawaii on December 7, 1941, an event that contributed to the United States entering World War II.

overview.text: Angels are spiritual, heavenly, or supernatural beings that often act as intermediaries between God and humanity. In revelation-based belief systems, they help connect earthly life with the transcendent realm; they may serve as messengers, servants, protectors, or guides. The concept has a smaller role in monistic systems, where no such gap between humanity and the divine exists.

Abrahamic religions describe different angelic hierarchies, and Western traditions may distinguish benevolent from malevolent intermediary beings. Angels are commonly represented in art with human forms, wings, halos, and divine light, although some depictions are frightening or inhuman.

key_facts.text: Gabriel and Michael are examples of named angels; seraphim and archangels are described as particular kinds or ranks in some Abrahamic traditions.
Fallen angels are often believed to be malevolent angels expelled from heaven; some traditions identify the devil or devils with such beings.
Guardian angels are associated with protecting and guiding humans.

overview.text: Nineteen Eighty-Four, also published as 1984, is a dystopian speculative-fiction novel by English writer George Orwell, published in 1949. Its fictional future places Great Britain, renamed Airstrip One, inside Oceania, a totalitarian superstate led by Big Brother. The Party maintains control through government surveillance, propaganda, and harsh regimentation.

The novel matters as political fiction because it explores how authorities can manipulate truth and facts while suppressing individuality and independent thought. Orwell described it as a satire, and its influence on literary and public language is reflected in terms that remain widely recognizable.

key_facts.text: The story is set in a year believed to be 1984, although that date is uncertain; much of the world is in perpetual war.
The Party uses the Thought Police and the Ministry of Truth, which is associated with historical negationism and constant propaganda.
The novel popularized “Orwellian” and terms including Big Brother, doublethink, thoughtcrime, Newspeak, and Thought Police.
It was Orwell’s ninth and final completed book, published by Secker & Warburg on 8 June 1949.
The novel has been adapted across media, including a 1984 film starring John Hurt, Suzanna Hamilton, and Richard Burton.

overview.text: Women's suffrage means women's right to vote in elections. Historically, women often lacked that right even in governments that presented themselves as democratic. During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, organized campaigns by women and male supporters helped change public attitudes and secure laws or constitutional amendments.

In U.S. history, the United States extended voting rights to women in 1920. The movement also had international importance: suffrage expanded across Australasia, Europe, and the Americas, and by the middle of the twentieth century it had become a norm of democratic governance.

key_facts.text: The first national grant of women's suffrage occurred in New Zealand in 1893.

The first wave, from 1893 to 1930, centered on English-speaking countries, Scandinavia, and parts of Europe; a second wave, from 1930 to 1970, spread through much of Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and countries where voting rights came later.
The International Woman Suffrage Alliance was founded in Berlin in 1904 to coordinate efforts for women's voting rights.
Some places first granted limited suffrage—for example, to literate women or property owners—before extending voting rights more broadly.

overview.text: Watergate was a U.S. political scandal centered on President Richard Nixon’s administration. On June 17, 1972, operatives associated with Nixon’s reelection campaign were caught burglarizing and planting listening devices in the Democratic National Committee headquarters at Washington, D.C.’s Watergate complex. Efforts to conceal the administration’s involvement expanded the scandal into obstruction, evidence destruction, and bribery.

Investigations by reporters and the Senate brought increasing attention to the cover-up. A dispute over secret Oval Office recordings led to the Saturday Night Massacre, a Supreme Court order to release the tapes, and a House Judiciary Committee recommendation for impeachment. Facing impeachment, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974; Gerald Ford succeeded him and later pardoned him.

key_facts.text: The Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein reported on Watergate with guidance from the anonymous source known as “Deep Throat.”
Nixon invoked executive privilege—the claimed presidential power to withhold internal communications—to resist releasing the Oval Office tapes.
The “Smoking Gun” tape showed Nixon ordering the CIA to stop the FBI’s investigation of the break-in.
The House Judiciary Committee cited obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress as grounds for recommending impeachment.
The scandal helped popularize the suffix “-gate” as a label for scandals in the United States and elsewhere.

overview.text: Franz Kafka was a German-language Jewish Czech writer from Prague. His fiction combines realism with the fantastique—strange or unreal elements—and often places isolated protagonists in bizarre situations involving incomprehensible bureaucratic powers. This distinctive atmosphere produced the adjective “Kafkaesque,” used for situations resembling those in his writing.

Kafka’s major works include the novella The Metamorphosis and the novels The Trial and The Castle. He also wrote brief fables and aphorisms that could combine comedy with darker themes. His writing later influenced artists, philosophers, filmmakers, and other scholars.

key_facts.text: Kafka was born in Prague on 3 July 1883 and died on 3 June 1924.
He trained as a lawyer and worked in legal and insurance positions, though he regarded writing as his true vocation.
Only a minority of his works appeared during his lifetime; published examples included Contemplation, A Country Doctor, and The Metamorphosis.
After Kafka’s death, his friend and literary executor Max Brod published remaining works despite Kafka’s wish that they be destroyed.
The Metamorphosis was published in 1915; The Trial and The Castle appeared in 1925 and 1926.

overview.text: Of Mice and Men is a 1937 novella by American author John Steinbeck. It follows George Milton and Lennie Small, displaced migrant ranch workers who move through California in search of jobs during the Great Depression. The work centers on the instability and movement experienced by these workers.

The novella’s title connects it to Robert Burns’s poem “To a Mouse,” while its place in school curricula has made it a recurring subject of public debate. It is taught in many schools but has also faced censorship and book bans over vulgarity and language that some consider offensive and racist.

key_facts.text: Steinbeck drew on his teenage experience working alongside migrant farm workers in the 1910s.
The title alludes to Burns’s line meaning that the best-laid plans of mice and men often go wrong.
The book appears on the American Library Association’s list of the Most Challenged Books of the 21st Century.

overview.text: The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems attributed to Homer. Divided into 24 books and written in dactylic hexameter, it is one of the oldest extant works of literature still widely read by modern readers.

Set in the final weeks of the Trojan War, it follows Achilles’ anger after a quarrel with Agamemnon and the events leading to Hector’s death. Its heroic treatment of war connects battlefield action with pride, fate, glory, and wrath, while Olympian gods intervene on behalf of favored warriors and cities.

key_facts.text: The poem likely took shape around the 8th century BC, although its date, authorship, historicity, and oral-versus-written composition remain debated.
Unlike later stories about Troy, the Iliad does not depict Troy’s fall or mention the Greek Trojan Horse.
In ancient Greece, professional reciters called rhapsodes performed it at festivals such as the Panathenaia, and it formed part of standard education.
The poem also moves beyond combat to social and domestic scenes in Troy and the Greek camp.

overview.text: The Trojan War is a legendary conflict in Greek mythology between the Achaeans (Greeks) and the city of Troy. In the traditional story, Paris of Troy took Helen from her husband Menelaus, king of Sparta, leading to the Greek siege. The war became a major source for Greek and Roman literature: Homer’s Iliad presents a central episode, while the Odyssey follows Odysseus’s journey home. Its historicity remains debated, so it is best studied as a mythic tradition with a possible historical core.

key_facts.text: The core of the Iliad covers four days and two nights during the tenth year of a decade-long siege, not the entire war.
Other episodes appeared in an epic-poem cycle that survives only in fragments; the war also inspired Greek tragedy and works by Roman poets such as Virgil and Ovid.
Ancient Greeks placed Troy near the Dardanelles. Excavations at Hisarlık in modern Turkey led most scholars to accept that location as the site of Troy.
The war’s historicity remains an open question; proposed historical interpretations include a fusion of Bronze Age sieges and expeditions or a conflict associated with the burning of Troy VII.

overview.text: Mass is an intrinsic physical quantity of a body. In modern physics, it is generally defined through the strength of a body's gravitational attraction to other bodies, and it is also linked to the body's energy content through E=mc².

Mass also measures inertia: a body's resistance to acceleration, or a change in velocity, when a net force is applied. It is not the same as weight, which is a force affected by both mass and gravity; changing gravity can change weight without changing mass.

key_facts.text: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
An object on the Moon has the same mass as on Earth but weighs less because lunar gravity is weaker.
In the Standard Model, elementary-particle mass is believed to result from coupling with the Higgs boson through the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism.

overview.text: The Apollo program, also called Project Apollo, was NASA’s United States human-spaceflight effort to send people to the Moon. Conceived during Project Mercury and carried out after Project Gemini, it served President John F. Kennedy’s goal of landing humans on the Moon and returning them safely to Earth.

Apollo 11 achieved that goal in July 1969: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the lunar module while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit. Five later missions also landed astronauts, and Apollo 17 ended the program’s lunar landings in December 1972; twelve people walked on the Moon across the six successful landing missions.

key_facts.text: Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to leave low Earth orbit and orbit another celestial body; Apollo 11 was the first crewed lunar landing.

Apollo 1 suffered a fatal cabin fire during a 1967 ground test. Apollo 13’s landing was aborted after an oxygen-tank explosion, but its crew returned safely using the lunar module as a temporary lifeboat.
Apollo missions launched on the Saturn family of rockets. Related Apollo applications included Skylab and the joint U.S.–Soviet Apollo–Soyuz Test Project.
Lunar samples returned by Apollo improved scientific understanding of the Moon’s composition and geological history, while the program also advanced avionics, telecommunications, and computers.

overview.text: John Yossarian is a fictional character and the protagonist of Joseph Heller’s satirical novel Catch-22 (1961). During World War II, he serves as a captain and B-25 Mitchell bombardier in the Army Air Forces, stationed on Pianosa, an island off Italy. His central conflict is the desire to be relieved of combat duties, placing his feelings about military service at odds with continued participation in the war. Yossarian also appears in Heller’s 1994 sequel, Closing Time.

key_facts.text: Yossarian is 28 years old in Catch-22.
He serves in the 256th Squadron of the Army Air Forces.
His military specialty is flying as a bombardier in a North American B-25 Mitchell.
The character draws some elements from Heller’s wartime experience as a bombardier stationed near Italy; his name came from Heller’s fellow bombardier Francis Yohannan.

overview.text: In Eddic Norse mythology, dwarfs are supernatural beings especially associated with craftsmanship and magical treasures. They create weapons, objects, and other valuables for gods, linking their stories with craftsmanship and treasure.

The familiar idea that every dwarf is tiny is not secure in the earliest material: early Old Norse sources describe dwarfs vaguely, while later sagas more often call them short. Some Eddic passages also associate dwarfs with svartálfar, or “black elves,” but whether that term was interchangeable with dark elves—and whether it reflected a broader Norse belief—is uncertain.

key_facts.text: The brothers Brokkr and Sindri craft Mjölnir, Draupnir, and Gullinbursti for the gods.
The Sons of Ívaldi make Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, and Sif’s hair for the gods.
Fjalarr and Galarr kill Kvasir and brew the Mead of Poetry from his blood; drinking it grants poetic skill.
When Alvíss seeks Þórr’s daughter Þrúðr in marriage, Þórr keeps him talking until dawn, when the dwarf turns to stone.
According to the Prose Edda, Norðri, Suðri, Austri, and Vestri hold up the four corners of the sky, made from the skull of Ymir.

overview.text: A Raisin in the Sun is Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 Broadway play about a Black family on Chicago’s South Side trying to improve its financial circumstances after the death of its patriarch brings an insurance payout. As the family considers how to use that money, the drama explores housing discrimination, racism, and assimilation. Its title connects the play to Langston Hughes’s poem “Harlem,” also known as “A Dream Deferred,” making the poem an important recognition association for the work.

key_facts.text: The play debuted on Broadway in 1959.
Its title comes from Langston Hughes’s poem “Harlem,” also called “A Dream Deferred.”
The family lives on Chicago’s South Side.
An insurance payout follows the death of the family’s patriarch and shapes its financial choices.
The New York Drama Critics’ Circle named it the best play of 1959.

overview.text: The Starry Night is an oil-on-canvas painting by Dutch Post-Impressionist Vincent van Gogh, painted in June 1889. It transforms the view from his room at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence into a swirling sky filled with stars, Venus, and the Moon, with enlarged cypress trees in the foreground. Van Gogh added an imaginary village rather than copying the landscape exactly. Described as a touchstone of modern art, the painting is also part of the Museum of Modern Art’s permanent collection in New York City.

key_facts.text: Van Gogh’s letters suggest that he treated the cypress trees mainly as aesthetic elements, not as symbols.
The Moon is not depicted with astronomical accuracy, while Venus was visible in the sky when the scene inspired the painting.
Interpretations of the painting include religious symbolism, Van Gogh’s emotional turmoil, and possible connections to contemporary astronomy.
The Museum of Modern Art acquired The Starry Night in 1941 through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest.

overview.text: Buddhism, also called Buddhadharma, is an Indian religion and philosophy based on teachings attributed to the Buddha, a wandering ascetic and religious teacher. It began as a movement in the eastern Gangetic plain in the 5th century BCE and spread throughout much of Asia, influencing Asian culture and spirituality.

Its central aim is awakening and liberation from dukkha, often translated as suffering or unsatisfactoriness, through nirvana. Buddhism presents a Middle Way between severe asceticism and sensory indulgence, combining meditation with ethical conduct rooted in non-harming. Key teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path.

key_facts.text: Theravada emphasizes attaining nirvana and ending the cycle of death and rebirth.
Mahayana emphasizes the bodhisattva ideal: working for the liberation of all sentient beings.
Scholars generally recognize Theravada and Mahayana as the two major extant branches; Vajrayana may be treated as a separate branch or as a Mahayana tradition.
Zen and Pure Land are among the traditions included within Mahayana; Tibetan Buddhism is a form of Vajrayana.

overview.text: Erwin Schrödinger (1887–1961) was an Austrian theoretical physicist who made foundational contributions to quantum theory. His namesake equation provides a way to calculate a system’s wave function and how it changes over time. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac for contributions to atomic theory (p1).

Schrödinger also coined the term “quantum entanglement” and became widely associated with Schrödinger’s cat, a thought experiment familiar from popular culture. His other writings covered fields including statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, relativity, cosmology, and theoretical biology (p1, p2).

key_facts.text: In What Is Life?, Schrödinger examined genetics from the perspective of physics (p2).
After fleeing Austria during the Nazi takeover, he eventually lived in Dublin, Ireland, until retiring in 1955 (p3).
He wrote about philosophical aspects of science, as well as ethics and religion (p2).

overview.text: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker associated with the Romantic Age and sometimes described as “Pre-Romantic.” His work is symbolically rich and joins poetry with visual art, while imagination and philosophical or mystical ideas form major threads.

Blake’s distinctive outlook makes him difficult to classify. Although he was little recognized during his lifetime, later critics and readers valued his expressiveness and creativity, helping establish him as a significant figure in poetry and visual art.

key_facts.text: Blake lived in London almost all his life, apart from three years in Felpham.
His wife, Catherine Boucher, helped create many of his books as a printmaker and colorist.
Blake was hostile to the Church of England and to nearly all forms of organized religion.
His ideas were influenced by the French and American Revolutions and by the thinker Emanuel Swedenborg; he also maintained an amicable relationship with Thomas Paine.

overview.text: Photosynthesis is a group of biological processes in which plants, algae, and cyanobacteria capture light energy and store it as chemical energy in organic compounds, especially carbohydrates. In oxygen-releasing (oxygenic) photosynthesis, water is split and oxygen is released. The process helps maintain atmospheric oxygen and supplies much of the biological energy that supports complex life.

Light-dependent reactions produce ATP and NADPH, which power later sugar-building reactions. In plants, the Calvin cycle uses these molecules to incorporate atmospheric carbon dioxide into carbohydrates such as glucose. Chlorophyll pigments are held in chloroplasts and reflect green light, helping explain the color of plant leaves.

key_facts.text: In oxygenic photosynthesis, water is split during the light-dependent reactions, producing oxygen gas and helping form ATP and NADPH.
In plants, chlorophyll pigments are held inside chloroplasts; in cyanobacteria, photosynthetic pigments are embedded in the plasma membrane.
The Calvin cycle incorporates carbon dioxide into organic compounds and uses ATP and NADPH to produce carbohydrates.
Some bacteria perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, using substances such as hydrogen sulfide instead of water and releasing sulfur rather than oxygen.

overview.text: Benzene is an organic hydrocarbon with formula C6H6. Six carbon atoms form a planar hexagonal ring, with one hydrogen attached to each carbon. Its continuous pi bonds and compliance with aromaticity and Hückel’s rule classify it as an aromatic hydrocarbon.

Benzene matters both as a basic example of an aromatic hydrocarbon and as an industrial chemical. It occurs naturally in petroleum and is used mainly as a precursor to chemicals with more complex structures; its toxicity limits its use in consumer items.

key_facts.text: Benzene is colorless, highly flammable, and sweet-smelling; it also contributes to gasoline’s aroma.
Examples of chemicals manufactured using benzene as a precursor include ethylbenzene and cumene.
Benzene is a volatile organic compound.
Benzene is classified as a carcinogen.

overview.text: The Trail of Tears was the forced displacement of Native peoples by the United States government as part of Indian removal. Between 1830 and 1850, members of the Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw, and Choctaw nations were forcibly moved from their Southeastern homelands to designated Indian Territory west of the Mississippi River.

Those removed endured exposure, disease, and starvation during the journey; thousands died before reaching their destinations or soon afterward. Scholars classify the Trail of Tears variously as an example of genocide or ethnic cleansing.

key_facts.text: The Cherokee removal in 1838 was the last forced removal east of the Mississippi River.
The removals followed passage of the Indian Removal Act in 1830.
The discovery of gold near Dahlonega, Georgia, in 1828 brought on the Georgia Gold Rush and the Cherokee removal.
The five nations were commonly called the “Five Civilized Tribes”: Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw, and Choctaw.

overview.text: Berlin is Germany’s capital and largest city, built along the Spree River, which flows into the Havel in western Spandau. It is also one of Germany’s states and is surrounded by Brandenburg. First documented in the 13th century, Berlin developed at the crossing of historic trade routes and became a political capital and a scientific, artistic, and philosophical hub.

After World War II, the occupied city was split into West Berlin and East Berlin by the Berlin Wall. East Berlin was the capital of East Germany, while Bonn was the West German capital; after reunification in 1990, Berlin again became the capital of all Germany. The city combines this political history with universities, museums, media, and an extensive public-transport network.

key_facts.text: Berlin served as capital of Brandenburg, Prussia, the German Empire, the Weimar Republic, and Nazi Germany.
Its three UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Museum Island, the Palaces and Parks of Potsdam and Berlin, and the Berlin Modernism Housing Estates.
Landmarks include the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag building, Potsdamer Platz, and the Berlin Wall Memorial.
Forests, parks, gardens, rivers, canals, and lakes make up about one-third of Berlin’s area.

overview.text: Diffusion is the net spreading of particles or other entities from a region of higher concentration toward one of lower concentration. It results from random motion rather than from a directed flow, producing mixing or mass transport. The idea is used across physics, chemistry, and biology, although its central scientific meaning is the spreading of a substance from a more concentrated location.

A concentration gradient is a change in concentration across distance, and it helps describe the conditions associated with diffusion. Diffusion differs from advection, which is transport by bulk motion; convection combines diffusion and bulk flow.

key_facts.text: Diffusion is stochastic: the individual motion of particles is random, while the overall result is a net spread.
A process described by Fick’s laws is called normal, or Fickian, diffusion; otherwise it is called anomalous, or non-Fickian, diffusion.
The word “diffusion” comes from the Latin diffundere, meaning “to spread out.”

overview.text: Candide, or Optimism (Candide, ou l’Optimisme) is a French satirical novella by Voltaire, first published in 1759. Its sheltered young hero is taught by Professor Pangloss that he lives in “the best of all possible worlds.” After this protected life ends, Candide experiences repeated hardships and gradually becomes disillusioned with that optimistic philosophy.

The fast-moving, fantastical story parodies adventure and romance conventions while mocking religion, governments, armies, and philosophical systems. It engages the Enlightenment-era problem of evil through humor and suffering, contrasting Pangloss’s formula with the practical closing principle “we must cultivate our garden.”

key_facts.text: The novella’s events are often based on historical happenings, despite its fantastical storytelling.
Candide was published secretly and was soon banned on grounds of blasphemy and sedition.
English versions have appeared under titles including Candidus: or, All for the Best and Candide: or, The Optimist.
The work has inspired later authors and artists and is frequently taught as part of French literature.

overview.text: Merlin (Welsh: Myrddin) is a mythical Arthurian figure best known as a prophet and magician. The familiar version of the character was shaped by Geoffrey of Monmouth, a 12th-century cleric, who combined earlier Welsh prophetic traditions and presented Merlin as an adviser to Arthur’s father, Uther Pendragon.

Later French poets and prose writers expanded Merlin into a more complex figure. In traditional stories, he uses prophecy, shapeshifting, and other magic, helps bring about Arthur’s birth, and mentors the young king. His eventual fate varies between accounts, including supernatural imprisonment, retirement, or death.

key_facts.text: Geoffrey’s composite name for the character was Merlinus Ambrosius, combining traditions about the Welsh figures Myrddin and Emrys (Ambrosius).
Some traditional biographies portray Merlin as a cambion—a being born to a mortal woman and an incubus—which explains his supernatural abilities within those stories.
Merlin’s commonly attributed powers include prophecy and shapeshifting.
One popular French prose tradition says that Merlin’s student, the Lady of the Lake, bewitched and permanently sealed or killed him after he fell in love with her.

overview.text: Silicon is the chemical element Si, with atomic number 14. It is a hard, brittle, blue-gray crystalline solid in group 14 of the periodic table; it is sometimes considered a metalloid and is a semiconductor. Silicon is widely used in transistors, solar cells, and integrated circuits, making it a key material in electronic devices.

Silicon rarely occurs in pure form in Earth’s crust, instead appearing mainly in silica and silicate minerals. Silicon-containing materials are important in construction, glassmaking, ceramics, and abrasives. Silicon compounds also form the basis of synthetic polymers called silicones.

key_facts.text: Jöns Jakob Berzelius first prepared and characterized silicon in pure form in 1823; its strong affinity for oxygen made this difficult.
Silicon oxides form a family of anions called silicates.
Most animals need only trace amounts of silicon, while diatoms and radiolaria form silica skeletons and many plants deposit silica in their tissues.
The late-20th- and early-21st-century Digital or Information Age has also been called the “Silicon Age” because of silicon’s impact on the modern economy.

overview.text: Antonio Vivaldi was an Italian Baroque composer and virtuoso violinist whose work helped make the solo concerto a widely accepted musical form. His best-known composition is The Four Seasons, a set of violin concertos. He also wrote concertos for many instruments, sacred choral music, and more than fifty operas.

Vivaldi was ordained as a Catholic priest but received permission to stop saying public Masses because of a health problem. Many of his compositions were written for the all-female ensemble at Venice’s Ospedale della Pietà. After a long decline in reputation, his music was revived in the early twentieth century and remains widely performed.

key_facts.text: Vivaldi pioneered developments in orchestration, violin technique, and programmatic music.
He began studying for the priesthood at 15 and was ordained at 25.
His operas were staged in cities including Venice, Mantua, and Vienna.
Many compositions once thought lost have been rediscovered, with some discoveries occurring as recently as 2015.

overview.text: Vishnu is one of Hinduism’s principal deities, also known as Narayana and Hari. In the Trimurti, the triple deity of supreme divinity, he is the Preserver alongside Brahma and Shiva. Vaishnavism, a major Hindu tradition, regards Vishnu as the supreme Lord.

A central Vishnu association is the avatar, or incarnation: when the world is threatened by evil and chaos, Vishnu descends to restore cosmic order and protect dharma. The Dashavatara are his ten primary avatars; Rama and Krishna are especially widely worshipped, with temples in India and beyond.

key_facts.text: The name Vishnu is glossed as “All-Pervasive.”
In a benevolent depiction, Vishnu rests on the serpent Shesha’s coils in the Ocean of Milk, with Lakshmi; Shesha represents time.
In Smarta Hinduism’s Panchayatana puja, Vishnu is one of five equivalent deities.
Vaishnava theology describes Vishnu as having definite form while remaining limitless, transcendent, and unchanging.

overview.text: Salvador Guillermo Allende Gossens was a Chilean socialist politician who served as president from 1970 to 1973. A longtime Socialist Party leader, he won the presidency as the Popular Unity coalition’s candidate and promoted a program he called the “Chilean Path to Socialism,” seeking to pursue major change through democratic institutions.

As president, Allende sought to nationalize major industries, expand education, and improve working-class living standards. On September 11, 1973, the military launched a CIA-supported coup against his elected government. While troops surrounded La Moneda Palace, Allende refused to resign and later died by suicide in his office; the precise circumstances remain disputed.

key_facts.text: Before becoming president, Allende served as a senator, deputy, and cabinet minister during nearly four decades in Chilean politics.
Allende was described as the first Marxist elected president in a liberal democracy in Latin America.
His government faced opposition from right-wing parties controlling Congress and from the judiciary.
After Allende’s death, General Augusto Pinochet prevented a return to civilian rule; the military junta dissolved Congress and suspended Chile’s 1925 Constitution.
The dictatorship persecuted alleged dissidents, with at least 3,095 civilians reported disappeared or killed, before Chile’s transition back to democracy.

overview.text: Thor (Old Norse Þórr) is a prominent god in Germanic paganism and Norse mythology. He is associated with thunder and storms, as well as strength, protection, fertility, and farmers. His defining object is the hammer Mjölnir. Thor mattered both in mythic storytelling and historical religious practice: hammer emblems were worn during the Christianization of Scandinavia, and later records preserve invocations to him.

In Old Norse narratives, Thor is Odin’s son, Sif’s husband, and a goat-chariot-riding figure who repeatedly battles jötnar and monsters. The Poetic Edda especially links him with Jörmungandr: at Ragnarök, Thor kills the Midgard Serpent but soon dies from its venom. A contrasting comic association comes from Þrymskviða, in which he retrieves his stolen hammer by disguising himself as Freyja’s bride.

key_facts.text: Thor’s Germanic name-forms include Old English Thunor and Old High German Donar; English Thursday derives from “Thunor’s day.”
Runic charms and amulets invoke Thor for healing or protection, while hammer images appear on several Scandinavian runestones.
His goat team is named Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr; the myths say Thor can eat and resurrect these goats.
In Hymiskviða, Thor uses an ox’s head as bait, catches Jörmungandr, and strikes the serpent with Mjölnir.
In Þrymskviða, the jötunn Þrymr hides Mjölnir and demands Freyja as his bride; Thor instead goes disguised as the bride and recovers the hammer.

overview.text: Apollo is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology. He has many connected roles, including light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery. He is the son of Zeus and Leto and the twin brother of Artemis.

Apollo’s religious associations include the Delphic Oracle, where people sought prophetic guidance, and ritual purification. He could protect against illness but was also linked with plague. Music is another major association: Apollo presides over song, dance, and poetry, and the lyre is one of his common attributes.

key_facts.text: Apollo was the patron deity of Delphi and was known there as Apollo Pythios.
Apollo was associated with protecting young people and marking their passage into adulthood.
Apollo had pastoral roles as a protector of herds, flocks, and crops, and he was also connected with founding towns and giving laws.
From the 5th century BCE, Apollo was often identified with Helios, the personification of the Sun; this association developed over time rather than being identical in every classical source.

overview.text: Samurai were members of Japan’s professional warrior class in the pre-industrial era.
