They came from warrior families, served as retainers to lords, and trained in swordsmanship, archery, and horsemanship. Their education could also include literature, calligraphy, and Confucian philosophy, reflecting work as bureaucrats under shoguns.

Their social role changed with Japan’s political conditions. Medieval samurai were tied to military service, landholding, lord-vassal relationships, and local authority. During the Tokugawa shogunate’s prolonged peace, samurai became a hereditary status and administrative class, working as officials, police, teachers, or domain administrators. The Meiji Restoration dismantled the institutions and privileges supporting samurai status through measures including domain abolition and conscription.

key_facts.text: In much of Japanese history, samurai were often the only people permitted to possess certain weapons.
Under Tokugawa rule, many samurai received stipends and retained status distinctions, access to office, and the right to bear arms.
After samurai institutions were dismantled, most former warriors became shizoku, while former samurai feudal lords joined the kazoku nobility.
The kazoku and shizoku classes remained legally recognized until 1947.

overview.text: A hurricane is a strong tropical cyclone occurring in the Atlantic Ocean or northeastern Pacific Ocean. It is a rapidly rotating, low-pressure storm with a closed circulation, powerful winds, and spiral thunderstorms that bring heavy rain and squalls. Tropical cyclones develop over relatively warm ocean water, drawing energy from evaporation and the later condensation of rising, cooling moisture.

Hurricanes can cause serious coastal and inland hazards, including strong winds, heavy rain, high waves, storm surge, tornadoes, and widespread flooding. Coastal areas often experience the strongest direct damage, but rainfall and flooding can affect areas far from the shore.

key_facts.text: The same type of storm is called a typhoon in the northwestern Pacific and a tropical cyclone in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.
Tropical cyclones rarely form within about 5° of the equator because their rotation depends on effects related to Earth’s rotation.
Unlike many mid-latitude cyclones, which are powered mainly by horizontal temperature differences, tropical cyclones receive their main energy from ocean moisture and condensation.

overview.text: Shiva, also called Mahadeva and Shankara, is one of the principal deities of Hinduism. He is the Supreme Being in Shaivism, a major Hindu tradition; in Shaivite tradition, he creates, protects, and transforms the universe. He is also known as the Destroyer within the Trimurti, alongside Brahma and Vishnu. This title is only one aspect of his character: Hindu depictions present him in both benevolent and fearsome forms.

Shiva combines contrasting roles: he appears as an ascetic yogi and as a householder with Parvati and their sons, Ganesha and Kartikeya. Common imagery includes the serpent Vasuki, crescent moon, Ganga flowing from his matted hair, a third eye, a trident, and a damaru. He is usually worshiped in the aniconic form of the lingam.

key_facts.text: Nataraja portrays Shiva as the “Lord of Dance.” Its powerful dance, the Tandava, is associated with destruction; the graceful Lasya is attributed to Parvati.
Ardhanarishvara combines Shiva and Parvati in one form, symbolizing the synthesis of masculine and feminine energies of the universe.
Dakshinamurti represents Shiva as a teacher of yoga, music, and wisdom who instructs sages on the shastras.
In the Smarta tradition’s Panchayatana puja, Shiva is one of five equivalent deities.

overview.text: Copper (Cu) is the chemical element with atomic number 29. It is a soft, shapeable metal with a pinkish-orange surface and very high thermal and electrical conductivity. These properties make it useful for carrying heat and electricity, construction, and alloys such as sterling silver, cupronickel, and constantan.

Copper compounds are associated with blue or green minerals and pigments, while exposed copper roofing can develop a green coating called verdigris. Copper also has an essential biological role in aerobic organisms, including processes involved in oxygen metabolism.

key_facts.text: Copper is one of the few metals found naturally in directly usable, unalloyed form; people used it as early as about 8000 BC.
Around 3500 BC, copper became the first metal purposely alloyed with tin, producing bronze.
Copper compounds are used as bacteriostatic agents, fungicides, and wood preservatives.
In living organisms, copper occurs in proteins and enzymes involved in oxygen transport and cellular respiration, including hemocyanin and cytochrome c oxidase.

overview.text: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale is Herman Melville’s 1851 epic novel, narrated by the sailor Ishmael. Its central plot follows Captain Ahab of the whaling ship Pequod as he pursues Moby Dick, a giant white sperm whale, seeking vengeance after an earlier encounter cost him a leg.

The novel combines a sea adventure with detailed depictions of whaling and shipboard life, while exploring class, good and evil, and the existence of God. Though initially commercially unsuccessful, it gained a major literary reputation in the 20th century and became associated with the idea of the “Great American Novel.”

key_facts.text: Melville drew on his own experience as a sailor and on whaling literature; the whale was modeled partly on the famously elusive albino whale Mocha Dick.
The book uses many forms besides straightforward narrative, including songs, poetry, catalogs, soliloquies, and Shakespearean stage directions.
Its famous opening, “Call me Ishmael,” is one of the best-known opening lines in world literature.
The novel first appeared as The Whale in London in October 1851 and as Moby-Dick; or, The Whale in New York the following month.

overview.text: Indonesia is a country in Southeast Asia and Oceania, lying between the Indian and Pacific oceans. It is an archipelagic state of 13,000–17,000 islands, including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and parts of Borneo and New Guinea. Tropical forests and marine ecosystems support its very high biodiversity.

Indonesia’s many islands make sea and air transport important links. Java is especially significant: more than half of the population lives there, and much economic activity is concentrated there. Indonesia participates in regional and global organizations including ASEAN and the United Nations.

key_facts.text: Its official name is the Republic of Indonesia.
Indonesian, a standardized variety of Malay, is the official and national language and serves as a lingua franca.
Indonesia has hundreds of ethnic groups and more than 700 languages; its national motto means “unity in diversity.”
The country consists of 38 provinces, some of which have greater autonomy than others.
The archipelago became connected to regional and international maritime trade networks by the first millennium BCE; later, European powers competed to monopolize trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku.

overview.text: Claude McKay was a Jamaican-American writer and poet who became a central figure in the Harlem Renaissance. Born in Jamaica, he first came to the United States for college and moved to New York City in 1914.

His work included poetry, novels, short stories, autobiography, and essays. “If We Must Die,” a 1919 sonnet responding to post–World War I race riots and lynchings, is a key association. His collection Harlem Shadows was among the Renaissance’s first books, while Home to Harlem made a major contribution to its fiction.

key_facts.text: His full name was Festus Claudius McKay.
His fiction includes the novels Banjo and Banana Bottom, as well as the novella Romance in Marseille.
Harlem: Negro Metropolis is a collection of essays on the social and political history of Harlem and Manhattan, including political, social, and labor organizing.
McKay encountered socialism early, joined the Industrial Workers of the World, and traveled to the Soviet Union in 1922–1923; he later criticized the Party apparatus and its authoritarianism.
After returning to Harlem in 1934, McKay later converted to Catholicism and died in 1948.

overview.text: Egypt, officially the Arab Republic of Egypt, is a transcontinental country spanning northeastern Africa and southwestern Asia through the Sinai Peninsula. It faces the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the Red Sea to the east, while bordering Libya, Sudan, Palestine, and Israel; the Gulf of Aqaba separates it from Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Egypt is considered a regional power in the Middle East and North Africa. Its historical heritage is traced along the Nile Delta, and Cairo is its capital and largest city.

key_facts.text: Alexandria, Egypt’s second-largest city, is an important center for industry and tourism.
Ancient Egypt is described as a cradle of civilization, with early developments in writing, agriculture, urbanization, organized religion, and central government.
Arabic is Egypt’s official language, and Islam is its official religion.
Egypt gained independence in 1922 as a monarchy and became a republic after the 1952 revolution.

overview.text: A mechanical spring is a device made from an elastic but largely rigid material, often formed into a coil. It can return toward its original shape after being compressed, stretched, or twisted, storing energy during that deformation. Although coil springs are common in everyday use, springs have many designs.

For a conventional spring, the opposing force is approximately proportional to the change from its resting position; this approximation becomes less accurate for large deflections. The spring rate, also called stiffness, measures the change in force divided by the change in deflection.

key_facts.text: Spring steel is the most common spring material; phosphor bronze, titanium, and beryllium copper are also used for specialized purposes.
A torsion spring works by twisting and produces torque proportional to its angle of twist.
Extension and compression spring rates use force-per-distance units, while torsion spring rates use torque-per-angle units.
For springs connected in parallel, stiffness adds; for springs in series, compliance—the inverse of stiffness—adds.

overview.text: Zoroastrianism, also called Mazdayasna, is an Iranian religion associated with Zarathushtra (Zoroaster). Its sacred-text tradition is the Avesta, and it centers on Ahura Mazda, described as the supreme deity. Its moral vocabulary contrasts Asha, truth and order, with Druj, falsehood and disorder, making human ethical choice central.

The Gathas present this conflict primarily as ethical and psychological, with Ahura Mazda above the opposing spirits; later Middle Persian writings developed a more symmetrical cosmic opposition involving Angra Mainyu, or Ahriman. Zoroastrianism also has a long Iranian history: it was the official religion of successive polities for roughly a millennium, and communities that migrated to India became the Parsis.

key_facts.text: The Gathas are the oldest and most central part of the Avesta; they belong to the Yasna, the core of Zoroastrian liturgy.
A concise ethical ideal is humata, hukhta, huvarshta: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds.
Fire, called atar, is sacred and symbolizes Ahura Mazda; it is central to ceremonies in fire temples.
The Amesha Spenta are seven divine entities representing aspects of the universe and the highest moral good.

overview.text: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish poet, dramatist, writer, and literary critic associated with the Irish Literary Revival. He helped found the Abbey Theatre with John Millington Synge and Lady Gregory, led it in its early years, and received the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature.

His early interests included Irish legends and the occult, and his first poetry drew on Romantic and Pre-Raphaelite writers. From about 1900, his poetry became more grounded in physical life, more realistic, and more political, while he retained an interest in cyclical theories of life.

key_facts.text: Yeats was born in Sandymount, Ireland, and spent childhood holidays in County Sligo.
His earliest volume of verse was published in 1889.
He served two terms as a Senator of the Irish Free State.
Works listed in the supplied material include The Land of Heart’s Desire, Cathleen ni Houlihan, The Wild Swans at Coole, and The Tower.

overview.text: A string quartet is both a chamber ensemble of two violins, a viola, and a cello and music written for that group. The genre took shape in the mid-18th century, with Austrian composer Joseph Haydn developing the ensemble into a form based on four roughly equal musical partners.

String quartet writing became a major Classical-era genre and continued through Romantic, early-twentieth-century, and later music. Composers such as Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Bartók, and Shostakovich created important examples, while the form continued to develop beyond its Classical origins.

key_facts.text: The Classical-era model usually has four movements: a fast opening movement, a slow movement, a minuet and trio, and a finale often using rondo form.
Writing for four instruments with broadly similar characteristics can constrain and challenge a composer, helping give the genre its prestigious reputation.
Goethe famously compared string quartet music to “four rational people conversing,” highlighting the interaction among the players.
Some quartet ensembles perform together for many years and become recognized as established groups, much like solo instrumentalists or orchestras.

overview.text: Red is at the long-wavelength end of visible light, next to orange and opposite violet. In the RGB light model it is a primary color; in the CMYK printing model it is a secondary color made from magenta and yellow. Its shades include scarlet, vermilion, crimson, pink, and burgundy.

Red has carried cultural meaning across many societies. Ochre-based red appeared in prehistoric art, while Egyptians, Mayans, and Romans used it ceremonially. Because of its association with blood, red has been linked to sacrifice, danger, and courage; it has also represented passion, love, anger, and joy, as well as happiness and good fortune in China, India, and other Asian countries.

key_facts.text: Red pigment from ochre was among the earliest colors used in prehistoric art.
In Renaissance Europe, wealthy people used brilliant red clothing dyed with kermes and cochineal.
Synthetic red dyes emerged in the 19th century and replaced traditional dyes in many uses.
Red became a political symbol of communism and socialism, including in the flags of the Soviet Union, China, and Vietnam.
Modern surveys in Europe and the United States commonly connect red with heat, activity, passion, sexuality, anger, love, and joy.

overview.text: Rail transport moves wheeled vehicles along tracks, usually two parallel steel rails. Diesel or electric locomotives usually provide power. Because rails spread a train’s weight and create low rolling resistance, rail cars can be coupled into long trains carrying heavy passenger and freight loads efficiently. Rail systems require substantial investment and are less flexible than roads.

Modern rail transport began with the steam locomotive in early-nineteenth-century Britain and spread quickly through North America as part of the Industrial Revolution. In U.S. history, railroads reshaped the country, especially the West: the first U.S. transcontinental railroad made cross-country travel much faster and helped make western farming, ranching, and mining profitable.

key_facts.text: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825 as the first passenger railway.
By lowering shipping costs compared with water or wagons, railways helped create national markets with less variation in prices between cities.
The first U.S. transcontinental railroad reduced cross-country travel from months to days and cost about one-tenth as much as stagecoach or wagon travel.
Railway electrification began with tramways and rapid-transit systems in the 1880s; diesel locomotives began replacing steam locomotives in the 1940s.

overview.text: World War II, also called the Second World War, was a global conflict fought from 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945 between the Allied and Axis coalitions. Nearly every country became involved in a conflict marked by total war and enormous civilian suffering; an estimated 60–75 million people died, including victims of massacres, starvation, disease, and the Holocaust.

The war grew from unresolved tensions after World War I, the rise of fascism in Europe, and Japanese militarism. Fighting spread across Europe, North Africa, Asia, and the Pacific before the Allied victory reshaped international politics, helping produce the United Nations, the Cold War rivalry between the United States and Soviet Union, and widespread decolonization.

key_facts.text: Germany’s invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 led Britain and France to declare war; the Soviet Union also invaded Poland later that month.
Japan’s December 1941 attacks, including the attack on Pearl Harbor, brought the United States into the war. Japan’s Pacific advance was halted at Midway in June 1942.
Germany’s June 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union opened the Eastern Front. The defeat of Axis forces at Stalingrad in early 1943 became a major reversal of German expansion.
The Western Allies invaded France at Normandy in 1944. Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945; after atomic bombings and the Soviet invasion of Japanese-occupied Manchuria, Japan surrendered in September.
After the war, China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States became the permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.

overview.text: Shinto, also called Shintoism, is a Japanese religion often described as polytheistic and animistic. Practitioners often regard it as Japan’s indigenous religion, but there is no central authority, so beliefs and practices vary widely. Shinto centers on kami, supernatural entities believed to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent landscape locations. It has no single creator or specific doctrine; local and regional traditions express relationships with kami through shrines, offerings, festivals, and other rituals.

key_facts.text: Public shrines, called jinja, are staffed by kannushi priests, who oversee food and drink offerings to the kami enshrined there. Household and family shrines are also part of Shinto practice.
Purity is emphasized through ritual washing and bathing, especially before worship. Other practices include kagura dances, rites of passage, and kami festivals.

The eighth-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki are the earliest written traditions about kami worship. Historians trace kami veneration to Japan’s Yayoi period, while debating when Shinto became a distinct religion.

Shinto and Buddhism were historically intertwined in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō. Meiji-era leaders formed State Shinto and expelled Buddhist influence from kami worship; after World War II, Shinto was formally separated from the state.

overview.text: Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, founded and became the first emperor of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty in China. In 1271 he proclaimed the dynastic name Great Yuan and ruled Yuan China until his death in 1294.

His reign connected Mongol imperial politics with Chinese dynastic rule. After succeeding Möngke as Khagan in 1260, Kublai defeated his brother Ariq Böke in a civil war that helped divide the Mongol Empire. By 1279, his conquest of the Song dynasty was complete, making him the first non-Han emperor to rule all of China proper.

key_facts.text: Kublai was also known as Emperor Shizu of Yuan and Setsen Khan.
His real power as Khagan was concentrated in the Yuan Empire, while his influence over other Mongol successor states varied.
The Yuan realm included most of present-day China, Mongolia, Korea, southern Siberia, and nearby regions.
As emperor, Kublai ordered invasions of Japan, Vietnam, Burma, and Java.

overview.text: Mary Elizabeth Truss is a British Conservative politician who served as UK prime minister and Conservative Party leader from September to October 2022. She defeated Rishi Sunak in a leadership election to succeed Boris Johnson. On her fiftieth day in office, Truss stepped down amid a government crisis, making her the shortest-serving prime minister in British history. Before becoming prime minister, she represented South West Norfolk in Parliament and held Cabinet posts under David Cameron, Theresa May, and Johnson.

Truss’s government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee during rising living and energy costs. It also announced large-scale tax cuts and borrowing in a mini-budget; the announcement led to financial instability, while the measures were largely reversed. Facing mounting criticism and loss of confidence in her leadership, Truss announced her resignation as Conservative leader on 20 October 2022. Rishi Sunak succeeded her as prime minister on 25 October.

key_facts.text: Truss studied philosophy, politics, and economics at Oxford, where she was president of the Oxford University Liberal Democrats; she joined the Conservative Party in 1996.
As Justice Secretary and Lord Chancellor, she became the first woman to serve as Lord Chancellor.
As foreign secretary, she led negotiations concerning the Northern Ireland Protocol and Britain’s response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
She campaigned for Britain to remain in the European Union but supported Brexit after the 2016 referendum.

overview.text: Robert Lee Frost (1874–1963) was an American poet whose observant portrayals of rural life often draw on early-20th-century New England. He used everyday American speech while turning familiar rural settings toward complex social and philosophical questions. Frost also became a rare public literary figure with an institution-like stature in American culture. His work connects regional settings and ordinary speech with larger questions about people, society, and ideas.

key_facts.text: His full name was Robert Lee Frost; he lived from March 26, 1874, to January 29, 1963.
Frost is the only poet to have received four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry.
He was appointed United States Poet Laureate in 1958, received the Congressional Gold Medal in 1960, and became poet laureate of Vermont in 1961.
In his 1939 essay “The Figure a Poem Makes,” Frost described poetry as a revelation—or series of revelations—for both poet and reader.

overview.text: The Mississippi River is the main river of the largest drainage basin in the United States. Traditionally traced to Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, it runs generally south for about 2,340 miles to its delta on the Gulf of Mexico. Its watershed reaches parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces, although the main stem lies entirely within the United States.

The river has supported Native American communities for thousands of years and became a major transportation and communications route. Its tributaries, especially the Ohio and Missouri, helped channel nineteenth-century U.S. expansion; the river also has a major place in American literature through Mark Twain.

key_facts.text: It is the second-longest river in the United States, after the Missouri, and ranks tenth worldwide by discharge.
Fertile regions formed from the river’s silt deposits supported agriculture, while steamboats carried agricultural and industrial goods during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
During the Civil War, the Union’s final capture of the Mississippi marked a turning point toward Union victory.
Levees, locks, and dams were built partly to keep the lower river from shifting into the Atchafalaya channel and bypassing New Orleans.
Agricultural runoff is identified as the primary contributor to the Gulf of Mexico’s dead zone amid the river’s modern pollution problems.

overview.text: Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern and Deep South regions of the United States. It borders Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana, and Arkansas, while its southern edge reaches the Gulf of Mexico. The Mississippi River or its former course largely forms the western boundary.
Most of Mississippi lies in the east Gulf Coastal Plain, with lowland plains and low hills. The northwestern part is the Mississippi Delta. Jackson is both the state capital and its largest city.

key_facts.text: Mississippi entered the Union as the 20th state on December 10, 1817.
Woodall Mountain, at 807 feet, is Mississippi’s highest point; the Gulf of Mexico is its lowest point.
Agriculture and forestry are major industries. Mississippi is a major producer of farm-raised catfish, sweet potatoes, cotton, and pulpwood.
Mississippi declared secession in 1861 as one of the original Confederate states and rejoined the Union in 1870.

overview.text: Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist whose research helped found quantum chemistry and molecular biology. He made major contributions to the theory of the chemical bond, including orbital hybridisation and the first accurate scale of electronegativities.

Pauling also studied biological molecules using X-ray crystallography, molecular model building, and quantum chemistry. Beyond research, he was a peace activist and later promoted nuclear disarmament. He also advocated megavitamin therapy and dietary supplements, medical ideas that did not gain much acceptance in the mainstream scientific community.

key_facts.text: He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 for scientific work and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for peace activism.
He is one of five people to win more than one Nobel Prize and the only person awarded two unshared Nobel Prizes.
In protein science, he showed the importance of the alpha helix and beta sheet in protein secondary structure.
His discoveries inspired work by James Watson, Francis Crick, Rosalind Franklin, and Maurice Wilkins on the structure of DNA.

overview.text: Bacteria are mostly free-living, usually single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms, typically a few micrometres long. They occur in nearly every habitat, from soil, air, and water to hot springs and Earth’s deep crust. They are major recyclers in nutrient cycles, decomposing dead matter and helping convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms.

Humans carry many bacteria, especially in the gut and on the skin; most are harmless or beneficial, although pathogenic species cause diseases such as tuberculosis, cholera, and tetanus. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, but resistance is a growing problem. Bacteria also contribute to sewage treatment, food fermentation, biotechnology, and metal recovery.

key_facts.text: Bacterial cells generally have circular chromosomes, lack a nucleus, and rarely contain membrane-bound organelles.
Bacteria and Archaea are separate evolutionary domains; older classifications grouped all prokaryotes together.
The scientific study of bacteria is called bacteriology, a branch of microbiology.
Many bacterial species remain uncharacterized, and some cannot be grown in laboratory conditions.

overview.text: “Rip Van Winkle” is a short story by American author Washington Irving, first published in 1819. It follows Rip, a Dutch-American villager in colonial America, who meets mysterious Dutchmen in the Catskill Mountains, drinks their strong liquor, and falls deeply asleep. He wakes twenty years later in a changed world, having missed the American Revolution. The story’s central association is this dramatic gap between an earlier America and the society Rip returns to.

key_facts.text: Irving connected the story’s origin with a conversation about nostalgia involving his American immigrant brother-in-law.
He wrote it while temporarily living in Birmingham, England.
The story appeared in Irving’s collection The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
Although the story is set in New York’s Catskill Mountains, Irving said he had never visited them when he wrote it.

overview.text: Bronze is an alloy made primarily of copper, commonly with tin and sometimes with other metals, nonmetals, or metalloids. Its varied recipes produce materials with different useful properties. Bronze also gives its name to the Bronze Age, the archaeological period when it was the hardest metal in widespread use. In art history, older records sometimes confused bronze with brass, another copper alloy, so museums and scholars increasingly use the broader term “copper alloy” for historic works.

key_facts.text: A common bronze contains about 12–12.5% tin, though its exact composition can vary.
Alloying additions can make bronze harder than copper and can affect strength, ductility, or machinability.
The Bronze Age began at different times in different regions; in western Eurasia it is conventionally placed in the mid-4th millennium BCE, while in China it began in the early 2nd millennium BCE.
The Bronze Age was followed by the Iron Age, but bronze remained widely used afterward.

overview.text: Serotonin, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), is a monoamine neurotransmitter found in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues. It contributes to mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, appetite, and sleep, and it also participates in processes such as vomiting and blood-vessel narrowing. Biochemically, it is an indoleamine synthesized from tryptophan.

Most of the body’s serotonin is made in the gastrointestinal tract by enterochromaffin cells, where it helps regulate intestinal movement; smaller amounts are made in brainstem raphe nuclei and other tissues. Platelets take up serotonin and release it during clotting. SSRIs and SNRIs block its reabsorption in synapses, elevating serotonin levels.

key_facts.text: The abbreviation 5-HT stands for 5-hydroxytryptamine.
Depending on concentration and context, serotonin can constrict or widen blood vessels and affect blood-pressure regulation and hemostasis.
The liver primarily metabolizes serotonin into 5-HIAA, or 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.
Serotonin occurs in many bilateral animals as well as fungi and plants; in plants and insect venom, it serves a defensive, pain-inducing function.

overview.text: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that struck Europe from 1346 to 1353. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, it spread primarily through flea bites, though some forms could spread through infected materials or respiratory droplets. Its enormous death toll made it one of the most fatal pandemics in human history.

The pandemic produced major population, economic, and cultural effects during the late Middle Ages. Its consequences extended well beyond the initial outbreak: Europe’s population recovered slowly, and plague outbreaks continued in different parts of the world for centuries.

key_facts.text: Estimates place the death toll as high as 50 million: about 30%–60% of Europe’s population and roughly one-third of the Middle East’s population.
It was described as Europe’s second great natural disaster of the late Middle Ages, following the Great Famine of 1315–1317.
Europe’s population did not regain its fourteenth-century level until the sixteenth century.
Historians have tentatively classified it as the second plague pandemic; related outbreaks were separated by roughly 500–600 years.
Plague outbreaks recurred around the world until the early nineteenth century.

overview.text: The Zoot Suit Riots were disturbances in wartime Los Angeles involving American servicemen stationed in Southern California and young Latino and Mexican American residents. Servicemen and white Angelenos attacked and stripped zoot-suit wearers; because the outfits used large amounts of fabric, attackers considered them unpatriotic during World War II rationing.

The violence followed the Sleepy Lagoon murder trial and belonged to a broader pattern of race-related unrest in wartime U.S. cities. Mexican American youths were the main targets, but African American and Filipino American young people were also attacked. The defiance of zoot-suit wearers later inspired Chicanos during the Chicano Movement.

key_facts.text: The riots lasted from June 3 through June 8, 1943.
Los Angeles was one of a dozen wartime industrial cities where race-related riots occurred during the summer of 1943; other examples included Detroit, Mobile, Beaumont, and New York City.
Similar racist violence against Latinos occurred in Chicago, San Diego, Oakland, Evansville, Philadelphia, and New York City.

overview.text: Meditation is a practice for training attention and awareness while stepping back from discursive, ruminating thought. Its aims can include mental clarity and emotional calm and stability. Techniques generally use either focused attention or open monitoring of present experience.

Meditation has a major contemplative role in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism; the earliest recorded examples of dhyāna are found in the Upanishads. Related practices also appear in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as forms of remembrance, prayer, or devotion to God.

key_facts.text: Focused meditation may direct attention to the breath or a mantra.
Open-monitoring meditation observes subjective experiences in the present moment and may involve cultivating wisdom.
Meditation is also practiced outside religious settings, including for health-related purposes.
Asian meditative techniques have been adapted for non-spiritual settings such as business and health.

overview.text: The Mahabharata is one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India and is revered in Hinduism. It tells of a dynastic struggle for the throne of Hastinapura between the Kauravas and Pandavas, leading to the Kurukshetra War. The epic also explores philosophical ideas, including dharma, or duty and rightful action.

A principal section is the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer-guide Krishna about dharma. The work is traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Its main body was probably compiled between the third century BCE and third century CE, with its final form likely reached by the early Gupta period.

key_facts.text: The title can be translated as “Great Bharata,” “the story of the great descendants of Bharata,” or “The Great Indian Tale.”
Beyond the war narrative, the epic includes stories such as those of Shakuntala, Savitri and Satyavan, and Damayanti.
Its longest version contains more than 100,000 shlokas, or verses, and totals about 1.8 million words, including prose passages.
Within Indian tradition, the Mahabharata is sometimes called the “fifth Veda.”

overview.text: Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy by removing or expelling an embryo or fetus. The term generally means induced abortion, which involves intentional action; a pregnancy ending without intervention is called spontaneous abortion or miscarriage. People may seek abortion for reasons including birth timing, family size, health concerns, financial or social circumstances, or pregnancy resulting from rape or incest.

Abortion is both a medical practice and a contested ethical, legal, and social issue. Opponents commonly argue that an embryo or fetus has a right to life, while supporters of legality often describe abortion as a reproductive right. Laws vary widely, and public-health discussions emphasize the difference between safe, legal care and unsafe procedures.

key_facts.text: Modern induced abortions use medication or surgery; a common surgical method dilates the cervix and uses suction.
Unsafe abortions are associated with substantial deaths and hospital admissions, particularly in low-income countries; public-health research links accessible safe care with lower maternal mortality.
Some countries permit abortion broadly, while others allow it only in specified circumstances such as rape, incest, fetal defects, poverty, or danger to the pregnant woman’s health.
Abortion rates have been broadly similar in countries with restrictive laws and countries with more permissive laws, partly because restrictive countries tend to have more unintended pregnancies.

overview.text: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic attributed to Homer. It follows Odysseus, king of Ithaca, during his homecoming after the Trojan War. His voyage lasts another ten years and includes many dangers, while his wife Penelope and son Telemachus face suitors who believe Odysseus is dead.

Composed in Homeric Greek around the eighth or seventh century BC, the poem grew from oral traditions and was performed by singers or reciters. Its central concerns include returning home, wandering, hospitality, tests, and omens.

key_facts.text: The poem is divided into 24 books, like the Iliad.
Odysseus is also known by the Latin name Ulysses.
The Greek term nostos means “return” or “homecoming,” a major idea in the epic.
Women and enslaved people receive notable narrative attention, especially in comparison with the Iliad’s focus on soldiers and kings.
The Odyssey has inspired adaptations and reimaginings in many forms of media.

overview.text: Stars are luminous spheroids of plasma held together by their own gravity. The Sun is the nearest star; because other stars are immensely distant, they appear as fixed points of light. During most of their active lives, stars shine through hydrogen fusion into helium in their cores, releasing energy.

Stars form when gaseous nebulae collapse, and their mass largely determines how they evolve and end. After fusion stops, a star may leave a white dwarf, neutron star, or—if massive enough—a black hole. Stars and their remnants also create heavier elements and return enriched material to space.

key_facts.text: Astronomers estimate properties such as a star’s age, mass, chemical composition, distance, and motion from its brightness, spectrum, and changing position in the sky.
Stars can belong to planetary systems, multiple-star systems, star clusters, and galaxies.
Stellar nucleosynthesis produces almost all naturally occurring elements heavier than lithium; stellar mass loss and supernovae help recycle these elements into new stars.

overview.text: Arthur Asher Miller (1915–2005) was an American playwright and essayist associated with 20th-century American theater. His popular plays include All My Sons (1947), Death of a Salesman (1949), The Crucible (1953), and A View from the Bridge (1955).
Miller also wrote screenplays, including The Misfits (1961). His public profile included testimony before the House Un-American Activities Committee and a marriage to Marilyn Monroe.

key_facts.text: Death of a Salesman is considered one of the best American plays of the 20th century.
Miller was often in the public eye during the late 1940s, 1950s, and early 1960s.
He received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
His later honors included the St. Louis Literary Award, Praemium Imperiale, Prince of Asturias Award, Jerusalem Prize, and Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize.

overview.text: The Sun is the star at the center of the Solar System. It is a sphere of extremely hot plasma whose core produces energy through nuclear fusion. That energy reaches space mainly as visible and infrared light, with some ultraviolet, and is the main source of energy for life on Earth.

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago when matter in a molecular cloud collapsed. The central mass became hot and dense enough for fusion, while remaining material formed the disk that became the Solar System. It is classified as a G-type main-sequence star, or G2V.

key_facts.text: The Sun–Earth distance is about eight light-minutes. That distance was historically used to define the astronomical unit; the unit is now fixed at 149,597,870.7 kilometers.
The Sun is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System, containing about 99.86% of the system’s total mass.
The photosphere, the Sun’s surface layer, consists mostly of hydrogen and helium, with smaller amounts of heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon, and iron.
Models suggest that when core hydrogen fusion declines, the Sun will expand into a red giant and later shed its outer layers, leaving a cooling white dwarf.

overview.text: The Metamorphosis is Franz Kafka’s 1915 novella about Gregor Samsa, a salesman who wakes to find himself inexplicably changed into a huge insect or “monstrous vermin.” Gregor and his family struggle to adjust to the transformation, a situation that has prompted varied literary interpretations. Popular adaptations often portray the creature as a cockroach, although the original description is less specific.
At about 70 printed pages, it is the longest story Kafka considered complete and published during his lifetime.

key_facts.text: The original German title is Die Verwandlung; The Transformation is another English translation.
The novella first appeared in October 1915 in the journal Die weißen Blätter, edited by René Schickele.
Its first book edition was published in December 1915 in the series Der jüngste Tag, edited by Kurt Wolff.

overview.text: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Hades is the god of the dead and riches and the king of the underworld. His name also came to mean the underworld itself, making him closely associated with the realm of the dead.

Hades is the eldest son of Cronus and Rhea and a brother of Zeus and Poseidon. After the brothers defeated the Titans, they divided cosmic domains: Hades received the underworld, Zeus the sky, and Poseidon the sea.

key_facts.text: Hades is also associated with wealth, reflected in the title Plouton, meaning “the rich one.”
The Romans and Etruscans connected Hades with figures including Aita, Dis Pater, and Orcus.
Pluto is the Latinized form of Plouton and became a merged Roman-era identity associated with Hades.

overview.text: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, a region of icy and rocky bodies beyond Neptune. Once regarded as the ninth planet, it was reclassified after the International Astronomical Union adopted a new definition of “planet” in 2006. Pluto is much smaller than the inner planets and has minor-planet number 134340.

Clyde W. Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930. Discoveries of additional distant objects, especially the more massive Eris, increased doubts about Pluto’s planetary status. New Horizons was the first spacecraft to visit Pluto and its moons, making a flyby in 2015.

key_facts.text: Pluto’s moderately eccentric, inclined orbit ranges from about 30 to 49 astronomical units from the Sun. A stable orbital resonance prevents it from colliding with Neptune.
Pluto has five known moons: Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra. Pluto and Charon are sometimes considered a binary system because their shared center of mass lies outside both bodies.
Pluto is the largest known trans-Neptunian object by volume by a small margin, but Eris is more massive.

overview.text: Victor Frankenstein is the fictional protagonist of Mary Shelley’s 1818 novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. He is an Italian-born Swiss scientist who studies chemical processes and the decay of living things at university. This work leads him to an insight into creating life, which he uses to bring a creature into existence.

Victor later regrets interfering with nature when his creation endangers him, his family, and his friends while seeking revenge. The novel introduces him while he pursues the creature near the North Pole, where Robert Walton and his crew rescue him.

key_facts.text: Victor is distinct from the creature: the creature is often called Frankenstein’s monster, although popular usage sometimes applies “Frankenstein” to it.
Victor’s scientific background involves chemical processes and the decay of living things; Shelley and people around her were also aware of experiments involving electricity and dead tissue.
Some aspects of Victor may have been inspired by the seventeenth-century alchemist Johann Konrad Dippel; this is presented as a belief, not an established identification.

overview.text: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (UK, also called Britain) is a country in northwestern Europe. It consists of England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. Its territory includes the island of Great Britain and the northeastern part of Ireland; it shares a land border with the Republic of Ireland and is surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean and nearby seas.

The UK is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy. England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland form three jurisdictions; Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own governments and parliaments for devolved matters. England and Scotland united in 1707, Ireland joined in 1801, and the present United Kingdom was created in 1927 after most of Ireland left in 1922.

key_facts.text: London is the UK’s capital and largest city; Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast are the capitals of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
The UK became the first industrialised country and was a leading world power during much of the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Its 19th-century power was associated with industrial capacity, international trade, and London’s role as a major financial centre.
The UK maintains sovereignty over the Crown Dependencies and the British Overseas Territories; these are distinguished from the four parts of the UK itself.

overview.text: Niccolò (or Nicolò) Paganini (1782–1840) was an Italian violinist, guitarist, and composer. Celebrated for technical brilliance and showmanship, he became a leading violin virtuoso of his era and helped shape modern violin technique.

His 24 Caprices for Solo Violin are among his best-known compositions and inspired prominent composers. From 1809 onward, Paganini toured extensively and achieved continental fame during the following two and a half decades.

key_facts.text: As a teenager, Paganini toured northern Italy with his father.
His teachers included Alessandro Rolla, Ferdinando Paer, and Gasparo Ghiretti.
By 1805, Paganini was serving as first violin under Elisa Bonaparte, who then ruled Lucca.
He ended his concert career in 1834 amid declining health and died in Nice in 1840 at age 57.

overview.text: The Four Seasons (Italian: Le quattro stagioni) is a set of four violin concertos by Antonio Vivaldi. Each concerto gives musical expression to one season and uses descriptive scenes such as birds, hunting, storms, frozen landscapes, and winter fires. This makes the collection an early and detailed example of program music: instrumental music with a narrative or illustrative element.

Vivaldi published the concertos in 1725 with accompanying sonnets that explained the intended scenes and helped connect the poetry directly to the music. The works were issued alongside eight other concertos in a collection titled Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione, or The Contest Between Harmony and Invention.

key_facts.text: Each concerto has three movements arranged fast–slow–fast.
The sonnets may have been written by Vivaldi, but their authorship is not certain.
In the second movement of “Spring,” the viola section represents the barking dog while the goatherd sleeps.
The concertos were composed around 1718–1723 and published in Amsterdam in 1725.

overview.text: Fitzwilliam Darcy, usually called Mr. Darcy, is one of the two central characters in Jane Austen’s 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice. He is a romantic interest of Elizabeth Bennet and is portrayed as an aloof romantic hero. Darcy initially offends Elizabeth, but as they grow closer and mend their differences, his character develops.

key_facts.text: Darcy’s first name, Fitzwilliam, is mentioned only twice in the novel.
Characters and the narrator generally call him “Mr. Darcy” or “Darcy.”
His characterization is associated with being brooding, reserved, and magnetic.
Film portrayals of Darcy have included performances by Colin Firth, Matthew Macfadyen, and Laurence Olivier.

overview.text: A magnetic field is a property of space that describes magnetic influence at a particular location. Because its strength and direction can vary from place to place, it is represented as a vector field, assigning a vector to every point. Magnetic fields can deflect moving charges, twist magnets, attract or repel magnets and materials such as iron, and induce currents in conductors.

Magnetic fields are central to the relationship between electricity and magnetism, called electrodynamics. This relationship helps explain phenomena such as light and supports technologies including motors, generators, transformers, electromagnets, and inductors.

key_facts.text: The symbols B and H denote two closely related vector fields that may be called magnetic fields, either separately or together.
The Hall effect uses magnetic forces to provide information about charge carriers in a material.
Earth’s magnetic field creates a magnetosphere that shields the planet and its ozone layer from the solar wind.
Magnetic-field measurements help geologists and geophysicists study Earth’s interior and support mineral exploration.

overview.text: Akhenaten, originally named Amenhotep IV, was the tenth ruler of Egypt’s Eighteenth Dynasty. In the fifth year of his reign, he adopted the name Akhenaten.

His reign brought a major religious shift: he abandoned traditional polytheistic worship and promoted Atenism, centered on the Aten. He built Akhetaten, also called Amarna, as a new capital for that worship. Egyptologists debate whether his policy was fully monotheistic or gave the Aten special status within a different religious system.

key_facts.text: His reign is generally dated to about 1353–1336 or 1351–1334 BCE.
After his death, traditional Egyptian religious practices were gradually restored, notably under his successor Tutankhamun.
Later rulers dismantled his monuments, destroyed statues, and omitted his name from some ruler lists.
Akhenaten was nearly lost to history until Amarna was rediscovered in the late nineteenth century; the identification of a mummy from tomb KV55 as Akhenaten remains questioned.
Modern interest in him is connected with Nefertiti, Tutankhamun, the distinctive art produced under his patronage, and his attempted religious transformation.

overview.text: Paris is the capital and largest city of France, located on the Seine in the Île-de-France region. It is nicknamed the “City of Light,” a reference to its role in the Age of Enlightenment. Paris is also a major transportation hub and an important political and international center.

The city is known for its museums, architecture, and Seine-side historic areas. Its modern form was shaped in part by Haussmann’s nineteenth-century renovation, which added broad boulevards, parks, and public works.

key_facts.text: Paris is divided administratively into 20 arrondissements, or districts, each with its own cultural identity.
The Louvre is a major Paris museum; other notable museums include the Musée d’Orsay and the Musée de l’Orangerie.
The president of France and both houses of the French Parliament sit in Paris.
Paris has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924, and 2024.

overview.text: Guru Nanak (1469–1539), also known as Baba Nanak, was an Indian spiritual teacher, mystic, and poet regarded as the founder of Sikhism and the first of its ten Sikh Gurus.

His teaching centered on Ik Onkar: one God present in every creation and embodying eternal Truth. Nanak connected this belief with equality, fraternal love, goodness, and virtue, giving his message both spiritual and social significance. His poetic hymns became part of Sikh scripture.

key_facts.text: His life dates are traditionally given as 15 April 1469 to 22 September 1539.
Nanak’s writings include 974 poetic hymns, or shabda, in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Important prayers associated with his hymns include Japji Sahib, Asa di Var, and Sidh Gosht.
Sikhs celebrate his birthday in the annual festival Guru Nanak Gurpurab.

overview.text: The Inca Empire, also called Tawantinsuyu (“Realm of the Four Parts”), was a pre-Columbian Andean empire centered at Cusco, its administrative, political, and military capital. It arose in the Peruvian highlands in the early 13th century and, especially from 1438 to 1533, incorporated much of western South America through conquest and peaceful assimilation. Its territory extended across areas now in Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Argentina, Chile, and Colombia, with Quechua as its official language. The empire is notable for organizing a large mountain state through distinctive administration, labor systems, infrastructure, and religious practices. Spanish conquest began in 1532, and the last Inca state was fully conquered by 1572.

key_facts.text: The Qhapaq Ñan was an extensive road network, while Inca builders were known for monumental architecture and highly skilled stonework.
Quipus—bundles of knotted strings—were used for record keeping and communication.
Rather than relying mainly on money or markets, the economy organized exchange through reciprocity and required labor service to the state.
Local worship of sacred huacas continued, while Inca rulers promoted Inti, the sun god; the Sapa Inca was regarded as the “son of the Sun.”

overview.text: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait by Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci and an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance. Its notable artistic qualities include the sitter’s enigmatic expression, a monumental composition, subtle modeling of forms, and atmospheric illusionism.

The sitter has traditionally been identified as the Italian noblewoman Lisa del Giocondo. After Leonardo’s death, King Francis I acquired the painting; it later became property of the French Republic and has normally been displayed at the Louvre in Paris since 1797.

key_facts.text: It is an oil painting on a white poplar panel.
It was believed to have been painted between 1503 and 1506, although Leonardo may have continued working on it as late as 1517.
Vincenzo Peruggia stole the painting in 1911; its recovery in 1914 generated unprecedented publicity and inspired later cultural works.

overview.text: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman, author, and near-continuous dictator of the Roman Republic from 49 to 44 BCE. He gained power through the First Triumvirate with Crassus and Pompey, then expanded Roman control in the Gallic Wars. When his alliance with Pompey collapsed, Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, beginning a civil war that ended with his victory and near-unchallenged power.

As ruler, Caesar enacted reforms including the Julian calendar, changes to the Senate and grain distribution, veteran settlements, and expanded citizenship. Senators led by Brutus and Cassius assassinated him on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, fearing his concentration of power. The ensuing civil wars helped lead to Octavian’s rise and the transformation of the Republic into the Roman Empire.

key_facts.text: In 60 BCE, Caesar, Crassus, and Pompey formed the First Triumvirate, an informal alliance that dominated Roman politics for several years.
The Gallic Wars expanded Roman territory and strengthened Caesar’s political position through military victories and the loyalty of his veteran army.
In early 44 BCE, Caesar was proclaimed dictator in perpetuity.
Caesar’s great-nephew and adopted heir Octavian later became Augustus and the first Roman emperor.
The name Caesar later became an imperial title and contributed to terms such as Kaiser and Tsar.

overview.text: The Tragedy of Julius Caesar, usually shortened to Julius Caesar, is a historical tragedy by William Shakespeare, believed to have been written and first performed in 1599. It dramatizes the conspiracy that leads to the assassination of the Roman dictator Julius Caesar and the civil war that follows in Rome. Shakespeare adapted much of the historical material from Sir Thomas North’s translation of Plutarch’s Parallel Lives.

Although Caesar gives the play its title, it focuses largely on Brutus and his struggle between personal loyalty and public duty. Its central concerns include political persuasion, ambition, and the fragility of republican government when power is contested. The play remains widely studied and frequently performed, with interpretations in varied political contexts.

key_facts.text: Cassius and Brutus lead a group of Roman senators in the conspiracy against Caesar.
Mark Antony and Octavius defeat the conspirators’ forces at the Battle of Philippi.
Critics often regard Brutus, rather than Caesar, as the play’s tragic hero.
The play was among the first works performed at the Globe Theatre and has remained frequently staged.

overview.text: Andy Warhol (born Andrew Warhola Jr.) was an American artist and filmmaker and a leading figure in Pop Art. His work examined the relationship among advertising, consumerism, mass media, and celebrity culture. By embracing mechanical reproduction, Warhol challenged traditional boundaries between high and low culture.

After beginning as a commercial artist in New York, Warhol moved into fine art. His early silkscreen paintings included Campbell’s Soup Can, Marilyn Diptych, and Coca-Cola (3). His Factory studio became a center for avant-garde experimentation, while he also made experimental and underground films.

key_facts.text: The Factory brought together artists and other creative figures, including drag queens, poets, musicians, and wealthy patrons.
Warhol made films such as Empire and Chelsea Girls, expanding his work beyond painting and prints.
He managed the rock band the Velvet Underground, which performed at his multimedia events known as the Exploding Plastic Inevitable.
After surviving an assassination attempt in 1968, Warhol’s Factory developed into a business enterprise.

overview.text: Gladiators were armed combatants who fought in violent public confrontations during the Roman Republic and Roman Empire. They faced other gladiators, wild animals, and condemned criminals. Although some volunteers entered the arena at personal risk, most were enslaved, trained under harsh conditions, and socially marginalized.

Gladiatorial combat became an important part of Roman political and social life after appearing in funeral rites. The games displayed ideals of martial courage and could bring admiration to fighters, while also serving as major entertainment and cultural spectacle.

key_facts.text: The word gladiator comes from the Latin gladius, meaning “sword.”
The origins of gladiatorial combat are debated; evidence places it in funeral rites during the Punic Wars in the 3rd century BCE.
Gladiatorial games lasted for nearly a thousand years, peaking from the 1st century BCE through the 2nd century CE.
Gladiators appeared in both elite and everyday Roman art and on many kinds of objects across the Roman world.

overview.text: Things Fall Apart is Chinua Achebe’s 1958 debut novel, set in Colonial Nigeria. It follows Okonkwo, an influential leader of the fictional Igbo clan of Umuofia, whose pursuit of strength and status is shaped partly by his rejection of his father’s life.

Personal choices and violence bring exile and loss, while Christian conversion and a new colonial government transform Umuofia. Through these clashes, the novel presents Igbo social life and tensions among established customs, Christianity, and colonial authority. It is regarded as a milestone in African literature.

key_facts.text: Ikemefuna is given to Umuofia as part of a peace settlement. After an oracle orders his death, Okonkwo carries it out despite a warning, fearing he will appear weak.
A gun accidentally kills Ezeudu’s son during the elder’s funeral. Under Umuofia’s customs, Okonkwo and his family are exiled to Mbanta for seven years.
Okonkwo’s son Nwoye leaves after repeated conflict with his father and is introduced to Christianity by the Igbo missionary Mr. Kiaga.
After Okonkwo returns, conflict with the colonial government intensifies: a church is destroyed, and Okonkwo and other Umuofia leaders are imprisoned and mistreated.
The title comes from a verse in W. B. Yeats’s 1919 poem “The Second Coming.”

overview.text: Minecraft is a sandbox game from Mojang, publicly released in alpha in 2009 and formally launched for personal computers in November 2011. Its procedurally generated worlds are built from three-dimensional blocks: players gather materials, make tools and items, construct buildings, encounter creatures, and play with others.

The game has no required objective, allowing different approaches. Survival play involves collecting resources and coping with hazards, while Creative mode provides nearly all resources, instant placement and mining, and optional flight for large building projects. Multiplayer, mods, and custom maps further expand how people play.

key_facts.text: A creeper is a Minecraft creature that sneaks toward the player and explodes.
The Nether is a lava-dominated underworld entered through an obsidian portal; the End is a dark realm of floating islands where the Ender Dragon awaits.
Redstone can be used for mechanical devices, electrical circuits, logic gates, and other complex systems.
Minecraft has Java and Bedrock editions. Bedrock is the unified cross-platform version, and the two editions receive updates concurrently while retaining some differences.

overview.text: Swans are large waterfowl in the genus Cygnus and family Anatidae. They belong to the tribe Cygnini within the subfamily Anserinae; their closest relatives include geese and ducks.
Swans are notable for their size: they are the largest waterfowl and are often among the largest flying birds in the areas where they occur. The group includes living and extinct species.

key_facts.text: Six living species and many extinct species of swan are recognized.
Swans usually mate for life, though pairs may separate, especially after nesting failure; a surviving bird may later take another mate.
A swan’s clutch contains three to eight eggs.

overview.text: Aesop is an ancient Greek fabulist and storyteller associated with tales collectively called Aesop’s Fables. Stories credited to him were gathered across centuries and in many languages; many feature anthropomorphic animals, meaning animals presented with human traits.

Aesop’s historical identity is uncertain: no writings by him survive, and even his existence remains unclear. Ancient sources preserve scattered details, while The Aesop Romance offers an episodic account of his life that is probably highly fictional.

key_facts.text: Ancient writers who mention Aesop include Aristotle, Herodotus, and Plutarch.
The Aesop Romance traditionally portrays him as an enslaved person who gains freedom through cleverness and advises kings and city-states; these details belong to a probably fictional life story.
Older spellings of his name include Esop(e) and Isope.

overview.text: “Nessun dorma” (Italian for “Let no one sleep”) is a tenor aria in the final act of Giacomo Puccini’s Turandot, with text by Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni. It is sung by Calaf, the unknown prince, who has fallen for the beautiful but cold Princess Turandot. In the aria, Calaf expresses confidence that he will win her.

Luciano Pavarotti’s performance at the 1990 FIFA World Cup helped popularize the aria beyond the opera world. The Three Tenors later performed it at several World Cup finals, and many crossover artists have recorded it.

key_facts.text: A man seeking to marry Turandot must answer her three riddles; failure results in beheading.
The Three Tenors—Pavarotti, Plácido Domingo, and José Carreras—performed the aria at FIFA World Cup finals in 1994, 1998, and 2002.
The aria has frequently appeared in films and on television.

overview.text: Colorado is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. Its varied landscape includes much of the Southern Rocky Mountains, northeastern parts of the Colorado Plateau, and the western edge of the Great Plains, along with forests, high plains, mesas, canyons, plateaus, rivers, and desert lands. Colorado also shares the Four Corners region with Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah.

The region has been inhabited for at least 13,500 years. The Pike’s Peak Gold Rush brought an influx of settlers in the late 1850s and early 1860s; Colorado became a U.S. territory in 1861 and the 38th state in 1876.

key_facts.text: The eastern edge of the Rocky Mountains served as a major migration route for early peoples spreading throughout the Americas.
Denver is the state capital and largest city; Colorado Springs is the second-most populous city.
Major parts of Colorado’s economy include government and defense, mining, agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing.
Residents are called Coloradans; “Coloradoan” is an older, occasional form.

overview.text: The Colorado River (Spanish: Río Colorado) begins in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains and flows southwest across the Colorado Plateau and through the Grand Canyon. It reaches Lake Mead at the Arizona–Nevada border, then enters Mexico and approaches its delta at the Gulf of California. Its arid watershed covers parts of seven U.S. states and two Mexican states.

The river is a major water source for about 40 million people. Dams, reservoirs, and aqueducts divert nearly all its flow for irrigation and cities, while its steep gradient also supports hydroelectric power. Heavy use has dried the lower 100 miles, so the river has rarely reached the sea since the 1960s.

key_facts.text: “Colorado” comes from Spanish for “colored reddish,” referring to the river’s heavy silt load.
Hoover Dam, completed in 1935, is identified as the largest of the major dams on the river.
An expedition led by John Wesley Powell was the first to run the rapids of the Grand Canyon.
The river’s management is shaped by international and interstate agreements collectively called the “Law of the River.”

overview.text: Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a Central European country stretching from the Baltic Sea to the Sudetes and Carpathian Mountains. It borders Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia. Warsaw is its capital and largest city.

Poland’s history includes the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, partitions by neighboring states in the late eighteenth century, and the restoration of independence in 1918. German and Soviet invasions in September 1939 marked the beginning of World War II. Later, the Solidarity movement contributed to the fall of the Iron Curtain, and Poland re-established itself as a liberal democracy in 1989.

key_facts.text: Other major cities include Kraków, Wrocław, Łódź, Poznań, and Gdańsk.
Poland is composed of sixteen voivodeships.
Poland is a parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature: the Sejm and the Senate.
Poland is a member of NATO and the European Union, including the Schengen Area.

overview.text: Mao Zedong (1893–1976) was a Chinese communist revolutionary, political theorist, and founder of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). A founding member of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921, he helped develop Chinese Communist guerrilla strategy, became the party’s leader during the Long March, and led the PRC from 1949 until his death, mainly as party chairman.

Mao’s rule combined state-building with severe repression. His Great Leap Forward sought to collectivize agriculture and industrialize China but was followed by the Great Chinese Famine; the Cultural Revolution, launched in 1966, brought violent class struggle, destruction of historical artifacts, and a cult of personality. Maoist thought adapted Marxism–Leninism to China and influenced organizations abroad.

key_facts.text: During the Chinese Civil War, the Communist Red Army fought the Nationalist government, which withdrew to Taiwan after its defeat in 1949.
The Hundred Flowers Campaign briefly allowed greater liberalization before political suppression resumed.
Mao’s China intervened in the Korean War and pursued land redistribution and industrialization campaigns.
Under Mao, the PRC became a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and the fifth country to possess nuclear weapons.
Mao died in 1976; Hua Guofeng initially succeeded him, followed by Deng Xiaoping in 1978.

overview.text: Gilbert Newton Lewis (1875–1946) was an American physical chemist whose work helped shape modern theories of chemical bonding. He developed ideas about covalent bonds and electron pairs, and his Lewis dot structures became closely associated with those ideas. Lewis also developed a theory of acids and bases, extending his influence beyond bonding and molecular structure. His research included thermodynamics, photochemistry, and isotope separation. The central recognition cluster is Lewis structures, electron pairs, chemical bonding, and acids and bases.

key_facts.text: In 1916, Lewis proposed a theory of bonding and connected it with information about electrons in the periodic table.
Lewis coined the term “photon” in 1926 for the smallest unit of radiant energy.
After moving to California in 1912, Lewis taught at the University of California, Berkeley and became dean of its college of chemistry.
His later work included purifying a sample of heavy water during research connected with isotope separation.

overview.text: Argentina, officially the Argentine Republic, is a country in the far south of South America. It is the continent’s second-largest country after Brazil and shares the bulk of the Southern Cone with Chile. Its other neighbors include Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, and Uruguay; the South Atlantic Ocean lies to the east and the Drake Passage to the south.

Argentina is a federal country whose capital and largest city is Buenos Aires, an autonomous city separate from the 23 provinces. Its geography also has an international dimension: Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, and part of Antarctica.

key_facts.text: By area, Argentina is the eighth-largest country in the world.
Argentina covers about 2.78 million square kilometers.
Argentina’s provinces and its capital have their own constitutions within the country’s federal system.

overview.text: The kidneys are a pair of reddish-brown, bean-shaped organs in the retroperitoneal space. They receive blood through renal arteries, filter it in structures called glomeruli, and send excreted urine through ureters to the bladder.

Kidney function helps control body-fluid volume, water concentration, acid–base balance, and electrolyte levels. The kidneys also activate vitamin D and produce the hormones erythropoietin and renin, so they have roles beyond waste removal.

key_facts.text: The nephron is the kidney’s structural and functional unit; each adult kidney contains around one million nephrons.
The adjective renal means “relating to the kidneys.”
Dialysis and kidney transplantation are treatments used for kidney failure.
Nephrology focuses on diseases of kidney function, while urology addresses diseases of kidney and urinary-tract anatomy.

overview.text: Sylvia Plath (1932–1963) was an American poet and author credited with advancing confessional poetry. This style draws on personal experience and often uses direct address.
Her works include The Colossus and Other Poems, Ariel, and The Bell Jar. Critic Al Alvarez described Plath and her contemporaries as fusing their inner lives with their artistic output.

key_facts.text: The Bell Jar is a semi-autobiographical novel published in 1963.
Plath studied at Smith College and the University of Cambridge, where she was a Fulbright student at Newnham College.
In 1959, she attended a Boston University creative-writing seminar taught by Robert Lowell alongside Anne Sexton; the participants gravitated toward confessional poetry.
Her Collected Poems appeared in 1981 and earned her the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1982, after her death.
Plath died by suicide in London in 1963 at age 30.

overview.text: Ashoka the Great (c. 304–232 BCE) was the third ruler of the Mauryan dynasty and emperor of Magadha. From Pataliputra, he ruled an empire covering much of the Indian subcontinent, reaching from present-day Afghanistan to Bangladesh. His reign is closely associated with the Edicts of Ashoka and with Buddhism: after the brutal conquest of Kalinga, the edicts emphasized dhamma, or righteous conduct.

The edicts suggest that Ashoka gradually moved toward Buddhism after the Kalinga War. Buddhist legends also credit him with supporting stupas, a Buddhist council, missionaries, and the sangha, or Buddhist monastic community. His legacy appears in India’s State Emblem, adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka, and in the Ashoka Chakra at the center of the national flag.

key_facts.text: Ashoka’s empire had its capital at Pataliputra and extended from present-day Afghanistan in the west to present-day Bangladesh in the east.
The Edicts of Ashoka place the conquest of Kalinga in his eighth regnal year, around 260 BCE, and describe it as a brutal war followed by an emphasis on dhamma.
Buddhist legends credit Ashoka with establishing stupas, supporting the Third Buddhist council, aiding missionaries, and donating to the sangha.
Knowledge of Ashoka as a historical emperor was restored after nineteenth-century scholars deciphered sources written in the Brahmi script.

overview.text: Aboriginal Australians are the diverse Aboriginal peoples of Australia; many prefer to identify with a specific cultural group. Their ancestors reached the Australian continent roughly 50,000–65,000 years ago, during the last glacial period.

Before British settlement in 1788, Aboriginal societies included about 600 nations or tribes and around 250 languages with varied dialects. Their economies included hunting and gathering, fire-stick farming, fish farming, and the construction of semi-permanent shelters. Colonization was followed by population collapse from disease, violence, and competition over resources.

key_facts.text: From the 19th to mid-20th centuries, government policy removed many children of mixed heritage from Aboriginal communities to assimilate them into the majority white culture.
The 1992 Mabo decision recognized that Indigenous native-title rights existed in Australian common law.
Indigenous communities founded rights-advocacy organizations from the 1930s, and Indigenous people won voting rights in federal and state elections from the 1960s.

overview.text: Vincent Willem van Gogh (1853–1890) was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose landscapes, still lifes, portraits, and self-portraits helped lay foundations for modern art. His work is recognizable for bold colors and dramatic, expressive brushwork. Although he created art for just over a decade, much of his work came during the final two years of his life.

His style changed after he moved to Paris in 1886 and encountered avant-garde artists. Brighter color and a mature approach emerged during his 1888 stay in Arles, where he painted series involving olive trees, wheat fields, and sunflowers. His reputation expanded after his death, influencing the Fauves and German Expressionists and making him a widely remembered, though often romanticized, modern artist.

key_facts.text: Van Gogh’s younger brother Theo supported him financially, and the two maintained a long correspondence.
Before becoming a painter, Van Gogh worked as an art dealer and later served as a Protestant missionary in southern Belgium.
His friendship with Paul Gauguin ended after a razor confrontation in which Van Gogh severed part of his left ear.
Van Gogh spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including one at Saint-Rémy, and died in 1890 after shooting himself in the chest.
He was not commercially successful during his lifetime; broad critical and popular recognition grew after his death.

overview.text: Lake Mead is a major reservoir in the southwestern United States, created when Hoover Dam formed an impoundment on the Colorado River. It lies in Nevada and Arizona, about 24 miles east of Las Vegas. Its stored water serves Arizona, California, Nevada, parts of Mexico, nearly 20 million people, and large areas of farmland. Lake Mead is the largest U.S. reservoir by water capacity.

key_facts.text: At maximum capacity, Lake Mead is 112 miles long and reaches 532 feet at its greatest depth.
At maximum capacity, it covers 247 square miles and holds 28.23 million acre-feet of water.
The lake has remained below full capacity since 1983, with drought and increased water demand identified as causes.

overview.text: Charles XII (Karl XII) was king of Sweden from 1697 to 1718, taking power at age fifteen. In 1700, Denmark–Norway, Saxony–Poland–Lithuania, and Russia attacked Swedish territories, beginning the Great Northern War. Charles led Sweden to several early victories despite being heavily outnumbered, including the Battle of Narva.

Charles’s later campaign against Russia ended in defeat at Poltava. After years of exile in the Ottoman Empire, he returned to attack Norway but was killed at the Siege of Fredriksten in 1718. The war’s outcome ended the Swedish Empire and its effectively organized absolute monarchy.

key_facts.text: At Narva, Swedish forces defeated a much larger Russian army. Peter the Great then sought peace, but Charles rejected the offer.
In 1706, Swedish forces under Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld defeated a combined Saxon-Russian army at Fraustadt.
Charles was incapacitated by a wound before Poltava and could not command actively; the defeat was followed by the Swedish surrender at Perevolochna.
Charles was succeeded by his sister Ulrika Eleonora, who later transferred substantial powers to the Riksdag of the Estates.

overview.text: Indira Priyadarshini Gandhi (1917–1984) was an Indian stateswoman and leader of the Indian National Congress. She served as prime minister from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination, making her India’s first and only female prime minister. The daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, she was also the mother of a later prime minister, Rajiv Gandhi.

Gandhi combined centralized executive power with assertive foreign and domestic policies. Her legacy remains contested: supporters cite her leadership and anti-poverty campaign, while critics focus on her authoritarian rule during the Emergency.

key_facts.text: In 1971, India fought Pakistan in support of East Pakistan’s independence, a conflict that resulted in the creation of Bangladesh.
Gandhi’s government initiated India’s first successful nuclear-weapons test in 1974.
During the Emergency of 1975–1977, she ruled by decree and basic civil liberties were suspended; many political opponents, journalists, and dissenters were imprisoned.
In 1984, she ordered Operation Blue Star, military action at the Golden Temple against Sikh separatists. Two Sikh nationalist bodyguards assassinated her on October 31 of that year.
She chaired the Non-Aligned Movement from 1983 to 1984, becoming the first Indian to hold that position.

overview.text: The Western concert flute refers both to the common C concert flute and, more broadly, to its family of transverse, or side-blown, flutes. These instruments are usually made from metal, wood, or a combination of both. They have a large repertory and appear in many ensemble settings, making the flute family a familiar presence in concert music.

key_facts.text: Related family members include the piccolo, alto flute, and bass flute.
Flutes appear in concert, military, and marching bands; orchestras; flute ensembles; and sometimes jazz combos and big bands.
A flute player is called a “flautist” in British English and a “flutist” in American English.
