overview.text: John Locke (1632–1704) was an English philosopher and physician and one of the British empiricists. He argued that people are born without innate ideas: the mind begins as a blank slate, or tabula rasa, and knowledge is formed through experience and sense perception. His work helped shape later thinking about personal identity and the self.

In political philosophy, Locke held that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed. He defended religious toleration and a right to resist a government that had become tyrannous after losing that consent. These ideas influenced liberal theory, American Revolutionaries, and the language of the Declaration of Independence.

key_facts.text: His major works include A Letter Concerning Toleration, Two Treatises of Government, and An Essay Concerning Human Understanding.
Locke treated private property as a natural right, linking it to the labor a person applies to resources in nature.
Beyond his theory of knowledge, Locke was a major contributor to social contract theory, epistemology—the study of knowledge—and political philosophy.
His writings influenced Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Scottish Enlightenment thinkers, and American Revolutionaries.

overview.text: Brazil is the largest country in South America and covers roughly half the continent’s land area. It faces the Atlantic Ocean on the east and borders every other South American country or territory except Chile and Ecuador. Its varied landscapes include tropical and subtropical regions, wetlands, savannas, plateaus, and low mountains.

Brazil contains most of the Amazon basin, including the world’s largest river system and the most extensive virgin tropical forest. Its varied ecosystems support diverse wildlife and natural resources, while environmental degradation such as deforestation is connected to global concerns about climate change and biodiversity loss.

key_facts.text: Brazil has an Atlantic coastline of about 7,491 kilometers.
Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District; Brasília is the capital.
Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas and has the world’s largest Lusophone population.
Brazil ranks first among 17 megadiverse countries.

overview.text: The American Civil War (1861–1865) pitted the Union against the Confederacy, formed by Southern states that seceded to preserve slavery. After Abraham Lincoln’s 1860 election, secession and Confederate seizures of federal property led to the bombardment of Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, beginning the war. The Confederacy eventually comprised eleven states.

The conflict centered on slavery and secession, and Union victory brought the Confederacy’s collapse and slavery’s abolition. Major associations include the Emancipation Proclamation, the Union’s success at Vicksburg, Robert E. Lee’s failed invasion at Gettysburg, the fall of Atlanta, and Lee’s surrender to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House in April 1865. Reconstruction followed as the nation rebuilt and addressed the rights of freed people.

key_facts.text: Issued on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation made abolition a Union war goal and declared enslaved people in rebel states free.
The Union victory at Vicksburg in 1863 split the Confederacy along the Mississippi River.
A Union naval blockade and attacks from several directions helped bring about Atlanta’s fall in 1864 and Sherman’s March to the Sea.
By the end of the war, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery; Reconstruction sought to rebuild the country and grant civil rights to freed people.
Railroads, telegraphs, steamships, ironclad warships, and mass-produced weapons made the conflict an early example of industrial warfare.

overview.text: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance, active as a painter and draughtsman as well as an engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. His notebooks contain drawings and notes on subjects including anatomy, astronomy, botany, cartography, and painting, showing the breadth of his interests.

For arts recognition, associate Leonardo with the Mona Lisa, The Last Supper, and the Vitruvian Man drawing. The Mona Lisa is widely regarded as the world’s most famous painting, The Last Supper as the most reproduced religious painting, and Vitruvian Man as a cultural icon; many of his other works were lost or unfinished.

key_facts.text: Born in or near Vinci in Tuscany, Leonardo was educated in Florence by the painter and sculptor Andrea del Verrocchio.
He worked for Ludovico Sforza in Milan, later returned to Florence and Milan, briefly worked in Rome, and spent his final years in France.
Leonardo had fewer than 25 attributed major works, including numerous unfinished works, while many other works were lost.

overview.text: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547–1616) was a Spanish writer and novelist. He is chiefly associated with Don Quixote, his two-part novel, which is often described as the first modern novel.

Cervantes also wrote fiction, poetry, and drama, including La Galatea, the Exemplary Novels, Journey to Parnassus, and plays. Although much of his life was marked by poverty and obscurity, his influence is reflected in Spanish being called “the language of Cervantes.”

key_facts.text: Don Quixote was published in two parts: Part One in 1605 and Part Two in 1615.
La Galatea, described as his first significant novel, appeared in 1585.
His other works include the 12 Exemplary Novels, the poem Journey to Parnassus, and a collection of plays and interludes.
Cervantes fought at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, where he was badly wounded; he later spent five years in captivity after being captured by Barbary pirates.

overview.text: Ulysses S. Grant, born Hiram Ulysses Grant, was the Union’s commanding general during the Civil War and the 18th president of the United States, serving from 1869 to 1877. After victories in the western theater and at Chattanooga, Abraham Lincoln placed him in command of all Union armies. Grant’s Overland Campaign ended with Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox.

As president, Grant supported Reconstruction and the Fifteenth Amendment, pursued the Ku Klux Klan, and signed the law creating the Department of Justice. His second term was damaged by executive scandals, while his response to the Panic of 1873 failed to stop the ensuing economic depression.

key_facts.text: Grant’s 1863 Vicksburg campaign gave the Union control of the Mississippi River and dealt the Confederacy a major strategic setback.
He was elected president in 1868 as the Republican candidate and won reelection in 1872.
In 1871, Grant created the first Civil Service Commission.
Grant wrote his memoirs while dying of throat cancer; they were published after his death in 1885 and became a major critical and financial success.

overview.text: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) was a German philosopher and a central figure of the Enlightenment. His systematic work addressed knowledge, metaphysics, logic, ethics, aesthetics, political theory, and religion, making him a major presence in modern Western philosophy.

In the Critique of Pure Reason, Kant’s transcendental idealism holds that space and time are forms through which humans structure experience; people know appearances, not things in themselves. In moral philosophy, he made reason the source of morality and said the categorical imperative binds all rational agents. He also connected aesthetics with disinterested judgment and grounded true religion in morality.

key_facts.text: Kant compared his account of experience to the Copernican Revolution: he proposed that experienced objects conform to human spatial, temporal, and conceptual structures, rather than the mind simply conforming to objects.
The Critique of Pure Reason is associated with the dates 1781 and 1787.
Kant hoped perpetual peace could be achieved through an international federation of republican states and international cooperation.
Although Kant held that true religion is grounded in morality, the exact nature of his own religious views is disputed.

overview.text: Diamond is a mineral form of carbon in which the atoms occupy a rigid crystal structure. It is a strong but brittle solid, conducts electricity poorly, and is colorless when pure. Its exceptional hardness and high thermal conductivity make it useful in industrial cutting and polishing tools.

Most natural diamonds formed 1–3.5 billion years ago deep in Earth’s mantle, commonly 150–250 kilometers below the surface, and later reached the surface in volcanic eruptions that deposited them in rocks called kimberlites and lamproites. Diamonds can also be produced synthetically from carbon under high pressure and temperature or from hydrocarbon gases using chemical vapor deposition (CVD).

key_facts.text: Graphite is another solid form of carbon and is the chemically stable form at room temperature and pressure; diamond changes to graphite only at a negligible rate under those conditions.
Trace impurities and defects can create color: boron can produce blue, nitrogen yellow, defects brown, and radiation exposure green.
Diamond has a very high refractive index and relatively high optical dispersion.
Natural and synthetic diamonds are commonly distinguished through optical techniques or thermal-conductivity measurements.

overview.text: Alcohols are organic compounds with at least one hydroxyl (−OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon atom. This structure gives alcohols distinctive chemical behavior: the hydroxyl group attracts water, making alcohols more hydrophilic than many hydrocarbons, and it provides a site where numerous chemical reactions can occur. The class includes familiar simple compounds such as methanol and ethanol as well as more complex substances, including sugar alcohols and cholesterol.

key_facts.text: The defining functional group of an alcohol is hydroxyl, written −OH.
Alcohols can range from simple molecules to complex compounds.
Examples named in the source include methanol, ethanol, sugar alcohols, and cholesterol.

overview.text: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was a Russian novelist, philosopher, short-story writer, essayist, and journalist. His fiction examines human behavior and moral choice amid the political, social, and spiritual tensions of nineteenth-century Russia, often engaging with philosophical and religious questions. His major novels include Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons, The Adolescent, and The Brothers Karamazov.

Dostoevsky is also strongly associated with Notes from Underground, a 1864 novella regarded as an early work of existentialist literature. His writing influenced later writers and philosophers in Russia and beyond, and contributed to the emergence of existentialism and Freudianism.

key_facts.text: His first novel, Poor Folk, brought him into Saint Petersburg’s literary circles in the mid-1840s.
Arrested in 1849 for involvement with the Petrashevsky Circle, he narrowly escaped execution and spent four years in a Siberian hard-labor camp.
His Siberian experience helped inspire The House of the Dead, published from 1860 to 1862.
Later writers and thinkers influenced by his work include Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Anton Chekhov, Albert Camus, and Jean-Paul Sartre.

overview.text: Babylon was an ancient city on the lower Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. It became the political and cultural center of Babylonia and served as a capital under several empires. Its two major Babylonian imperial periods were the Old Babylonian Empire (19th–16th centuries BCE) and the Neo-Babylonian Empire (7th–6th centuries BCE).

The city grew from a small town into a major center under the Amorite king Hammurabi in the 18th century BCE, though it later experienced Assyrian, Kassite, Elamite, Achaemenid, and other imperial rule. Evidence about Babylon comes from excavations, cuneiform texts, biblical and classical accounts, and later summaries; these sources provide an incomplete and sometimes contradictory picture.

key_facts.text: The earliest known reference to Babylon appears on a clay tablet from the reign of Shar-Kali-Sharri, when Babylon was still a small town within the Akkadian Empire.
Babylon became the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which lasted from 626 to 539 BCE.

The Hanging Gardens and the Walls of Babylon were both counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The gardens’ historical existence remains uncertain because no surviving Babylonian text mentions them.
UNESCO recognized Babylon as a World Heritage Site in 2019.

overview.text: Zora Neale Hurston was an American writer, anthropologist, and folklorist whose fiction and research explored Black American life, folklore, and cultural identity. Her four novels include Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Jonah’s Gourd Vine, and Moses, Man of the Mountain; she also wrote Mules and Men (1935), a literary anthology of African American folklore in North Florida.

Born in Alabama and raised in Eatonville, Florida, Hurston later used Eatonville as a setting for many stories. She studied and conducted ethnographic research with Franz Boas and became a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance. Although her novels went largely unrecognized for decades, Alice Walker’s 1975 article helped revive interest in her work.

key_facts.text: Hurston conducted anthropological and ethnographic research while studying with Franz Boas at Barnard College and Columbia University.
Tell My Horse (1938) documents her research on rituals in Jamaica and Haiti.
She also wrote short stories, plays, an autobiography, ethnographies, and essays, and worked as a documentary filmmaker.
Her nonfiction book Barracoon, about Cudjoe Lewis, was published posthumously in 2018.

overview.text: A pharaoh was the monarch of ancient Egypt. Although “pharaoh” became a ruler’s title during the Eighteenth Dynasty, scholars use it for Egypt’s kings from the First Dynasty, beginning around 3150 BCE, through the Roman annexation of Egypt in 30 BCE. Earlier, the word referred more specifically to the king’s administration.

The king combined civil and religious authority. Pharaohs controlled land, made laws, collected taxes, commanded the military, led ceremonies, and selected temple sites. They were also expected to maintain Maat—the Egyptian ideal of cosmic order, balance, and justice.

key_facts.text: Early kings used titles including the Horus name, the Sedge and Bee name, and the Two Ladies (Nebty) name; the Golden Horus and nomen titles appeared later.
The Red Crown represented Lower Egypt and the White Crown represented Upper Egypt. After unification, their combination, the Pschent, became the official crown of the pharaoh.
The earliest confirmed use of “pharaoh” as a contemporary ruler’s title appears in a letter to Akhenaten; an inscription referring to Thutmose III may be earlier.

overview.text: Federico García Lorca (1898–1936) was a Spanish poet, playwright, and theatre director associated with the Generation of ’27, a mostly poetic group that brought European movements such as symbolism, futurism, and surrealism into Spanish literature.

He first gained fame with Gypsy Ballads (1928), a poetry book depicting life in his native Andalusia. His poetry incorporated traditional Andalusian motifs and avant-garde styles; his later plays included Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba.

key_facts.text: His full name was Federico del Sagrado Corazón de Jesús García Lorca.
A 1929–1930 stay in New York City was documented posthumously in Poet in New York, published in 1942.
Lorca was assassinated by Nationalist forces at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War; his remains have never been found, and the motive remains disputed.

overview.text: Italy, officially the Italian Republic, is a country in Southern and Western Europe. It consists of a peninsula extending into the Mediterranean Sea, with the Alps on its northern land border, plus nearly 800 islands.
Rome is the capital. Other major cities include Milan, Naples, Turin, Palermo, Bologna, Florence, Genoa, Bari, and Venice.

key_facts.text: Notable islands include Sicily and Sardinia.
Italy shares land borders with France, Switzerland, Austria, and Slovenia.
The two enclaves associated with Italy are Vatican City and San Marino.

overview.text: Harriet Beecher Stowe’s *Uncle Tom’s Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly* is an American antislavery novel published in two volumes in 1852. It centers on Uncle Tom, an enslaved Black man whose suffering helps portray the horrors of slavery. Stowe also presents Christian love as a force that could overcome slavery.

The novel had a profound effect on U.S. attitudes toward African Americans and slavery and was credited with helping fuel abolitionism in the 1850s. It is also said to have helped lay groundwork for the American Civil War, making it a major work of nineteenth-century protest literature.

key_facts.text: Stowe was an active abolitionist, a teacher at Hartford Female Seminary, and part of the religious Beecher family.
In the United States, the book was described as the nineteenth century’s best-selling novel and second best-selling book, behind the Bible.
The story that Abraham Lincoln called Stowe the woman who “started this great war” is considered likely apocryphal.
The book and its theatrical adaptations helped popularize stereotypes; “Uncle Tom” later became a term for an excessively subservient person.

overview.text: Leo Tolstoy, also called Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, was a Russian writer whose fiction includes War and Peace, Anna Karenina, and Resurrection. War and Peace and Anna Karenina are often cited as pinnacles of realist fiction.

Tolstoy also wrote novellas, plays, essays, and works on philosophical, moral, and religious themes. After a moral crisis in the 1870s, he experienced what he regarded as a spiritual awakening; his interpretation of Jesus’ ethical teachings contributed to his Christian anarchism and pacifism, including ideas about nonviolent resistance.

key_facts.text: His early acclaimed works included the semi-autobiographical trilogy Childhood, Boyhood and Youth and Sevastopol Sketches, based on his Crimean War experiences.
The Death of Ivan Ilyich is one of Tolstoy’s novellas; it was published in 1886.
Tolstoy’s ideas about nonviolent resistance influenced Mahatma Gandhi, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Luther King Jr., and James Bevel.
He received Nobel Prize nominations in Literature from 1902 through 1906 and in Peace in 1901, 1902, and 1909, but never received a Nobel Prize.

overview.text: Der Ring des Nibelungen—often called the Ring cycle or Wagner’s Ring—is a four-part cycle of German-language epic music dramas by Richard Wagner. Its stories draw loosely on Germanic heroic legend, especially Norse legendary sagas and the Nibelungenlied. Wagner conceived it as a Bühnenfestspiel, or “stage festival play,” with three days of performance preceded by a preliminary evening. Its defining framework combines myth-based subject matter with a planned theatrical structure.

key_facts.text: Wagner wrote both the libretto (text) and music over about 26 years, from 1848 to 1874.
The first cycle performance opened the first Bayreuth Festival in 1876; it began with Das Rheingold and ended with Götterdämmerung.
The individual operas can be performed separately, although their dialogue may refer to events in earlier operas.
Wagner’s term Bühnenfestspiel means “stage festival play,” emphasizing the work’s theatrical conception.

overview.text: Denmark is a Nordic country in Northern Europe and the southernmost Scandinavian country. Metropolitan Denmark includes the northern Jutland Peninsula and an archipelago between the North Sea and Baltic Sea. It lies south of Norway, southwest of Sweden, and north of Germany, with which it shares a short land border.

Denmark is the metropole and most populous constituent of the Kingdom of Denmark, which also includes the autonomous Faroe Islands and Greenland in the North Atlantic. Copenhagen, the capital and largest city of the Danish Realm, is situated on Zealand, Amager, and Slotsholmen.

key_facts.text: Most of Denmark is flat, low-elevation, arable land with sandy coasts and a temperate climate.
Zealand is the largest and most populated island in Metropolitan Denmark.
The Faroe Islands gained home rule in 1948; Greenland gained home rule in 1979 and further autonomy in 2009.
North Schleswig became Danish again in 1920.

overview.text: Lungs are the primary respiratory organs in humans and many other animals. In humans, the two lungs sit on either side of the heart and exchange gases: oxygen enters the bloodstream, while carbon dioxide leaves it to be exhaled.

Inhaled air travels through the trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles to microscopic alveoli, where gas exchange occurs. The diaphragm helps drive human breathing, and airflow from the lungs also supports speech.

key_facts.text: The right lung is larger and has three lobes; the left lung has two lobes and shares chest space with the heart.
Each lung is enclosed by a pleural sac whose two layers slide over one another during breathing with little friction.
Lung diseases include pneumonia, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and emphysema; some chronic conditions can be related to smoking or harmful substances.
During fetal development, the lungs form as an outgrowth of the foregut. At birth, air begins passing through them and the ductus arteriosus closes.

overview.text: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882) was an American poet and educator associated with the New England “fireside poets.” His recognizable narrative poems include “Paul Revere’s Ride,” The Song of Hiawatha, and Evangeline. Longfellow’s poems often use musical language to retell mythology or legend, linking his work to storytelling as well as lyric poetry.

Longfellow became highly popular in the United States and successful overseas. His career also connected literature with teaching: he taught at Bowdoin and Harvard before retiring from teaching in 1854 to concentrate on writing.

key_facts.text: He was born in Portland, Maine, graduated from Bowdoin College, and later taught at Bowdoin and Harvard College.
His first major poetry collections were Voices of the Night (1839) and Ballads and Other Poems (1841).
He was the first American to completely translate Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy.
Critics faulted his poetry for imitating European styles and for being too sentimental.

overview.text: Tom Brady (Thomas Edward Patrick Brady Jr.) is a former American professional football quarterback who played 23 NFL seasons. He spent his first 20 seasons with the New England Patriots, helping define the franchise’s successful period from 2001 to 2019, and finished his career with three seasons for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. His career is associated with both franchises and exceptional longevity.

After playing college football at Michigan, Brady became the Patriots’ starting quarterback in his second season and helped them win their first Super Bowl. After joining Tampa Bay in 2020, he won another Super Bowl, becoming the central figure in a career marked by championship appearances, victories, and quarterback records.

key_facts.text: Brady was selected 199th overall, in the sixth round of the 2000 NFL draft.
As the Patriots’ primary starter, he led the team to nine Super Bowl appearances and six titles.
His Tampa Bay victory in Super Bowl LV extended his totals to 10 Super Bowl appearances and seven wins.
He holds major NFL quarterback records for career passing yards, completions, touchdown passes, and quarterback wins, and he won Super Bowl MVP with two different franchises.
Brady is the only quarterback to win a Super Bowl in three separate decades.

overview.text: Snell's law—also called the Snell–Descartes law or law of refraction—describes how light and other waves pass between different media such as air, water, and glass. It relates the angle at which a wave reaches a boundary to the angle at which it travels afterward, making it a central rule for understanding refraction in optics.

For a given pair of media, the law connects the sines of those two angles with the media's refractive indices. This relationship supports both practical calculations of transmitted rays and measurements of optical materials.

key_facts.text: Its standard relationship is sin θ₁ / sin θ₂ = n₂ / n₁ = v₁ / v₂, linking angle sines, refractive indices, and phase velocities.
Optical ray tracing uses the law to calculate transmission or refraction angles; experimental optics uses it to determine a material's refractive index.
Snell's law follows from Fermat's principle of least time, which is connected to the wave propagation of light.
The law also applies to specialized metamaterials, where a negative refractive index can produce backward refraction.

overview.text: Earth’s Moon is its only natural satellite, orbiting at an average distance of about 384,399 kilometers. Its roughly 29.5-day cycle produces the familiar lunar phases. The Moon’s gravity is the main driver of Earth’s tides, while tidal locking synchronizes its rotation with its orbit so that the same near side generally faces Earth.

The Moon’s heavily cratered surface includes bright highlands and dark maria: broad plains of ancient basaltic lava, concentrated mostly on the near side. Its origin remains uncertain, although a leading explanation holds that material was ejected from Earth by an impact with a Mars-sized body about 4.5 billion years ago. The Moon became a central target of space exploration, including the first human lunar landing by Apollo 11 in 1969.

key_facts.text: “Mare” means “sea” in Latin. The maria only look like seas; they are solidified basaltic lava plains formed largely in ancient impact basins.
The Moon’s surface gravity is about one-sixth of Earth’s, and its atmosphere is only an extremely tenuous exosphere—nearly a vacuum.
Mascons are large positive gravitational anomalies associated with some impact basins; dense mare basalt helps produce them, and they can affect spacecraft orbits.

Liquid water cannot persist on the exposed lunar surface. Evidence for polar hydrogen and water-related signatures exists, but some radar interpretations have been disputed; possible water ice in permanently shadowed craters remains important for future exploration.
Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to reach lunar orbit, and Apollo 11 brought humans to the surface on July 20, 1969. By 1972, six Apollo missions had landed twelve people there.

overview.text: U.S. Prohibition was the national policy from 1920 to 1933 that prohibited the production, importation, transportation, and sale of alcoholic beverages. It began through the Eighteenth Amendment and was regulated by the Volstead Act; the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it in 1933. Federal law still permitted some religious use of wine and did not universally outlaw private possession or consumption.

The movement grew from reformers’ concerns about alcoholism, domestic violence, and saloon-based political corruption. Supporters were called “drys,” while opponents were “wets.” People seeking alcohol used loopholes or illegal methods, resulting in black markets and crime syndicates; Prohibition’s long-term effects on drinking and crime remain disputed.

key_facts.text: The Eighteenth Amendment was ratified on January 16, 1919, before Prohibition began nationwide.
The Woman’s Christian Temperance Union helped build the movement, and the Anti-Saloon League coordinated it nationally after 1900.
The Volstead Act defined which alcoholic beverages were prohibited and established federal enforcement rules.
The Twenty-first Amendment is the only U.S. constitutional amendment adopted to repeal another amendment.
During Prohibition, some health measures improved, including rates of liver cirrhosis, alcoholic psychosis, and infant mortality.

overview.text: A train is a connected series of vehicles that travels on railway tracks to carry people or freight. Locomotives commonly pull or push the cars, although some trains are self-propelled. Steel wheels on steel rails create low friction, helping trains move efficiently; railways are built to a particular gauge, the distance between their rails.

Train travel expanded rapidly after steam locomotives appeared, making overland passenger and freight transport faster and cheaper. Diesel and electric power later replaced steam in many systems. Trains remain important for bulk freight, city and commuter travel, and high-speed journeys that can compete with cars and airplanes over shorter distances.

key_facts.text: Rapid-transit and tram systems emerged in the late 1800s to move large numbers of people within cities.
Freight trains commonly carry bulk goods such as coal and grain, while also helping reduce truck traffic on roads.
Specialized railway systems include monorails, funiculars, and rack railways, which are designed for different track layouts or steep slopes.
Maglev trains use magnetic levitation to float above a guideway; experimental versions can exceed the speeds of conventional trains.
Natural gas and hydrogen are among the alternative fuels being used or developed for trains in the 21st century.

overview.text: Henry Ford was an American industrialist who founded Ford Motor Company in 1903. The company’s 1908 Model T helped transform transportation and American industry, while “Fordism” became associated with making automobiles affordable to middle-class Americans. Ford’s effort to lower costs also produced business innovations such as franchised dealerships.

Ford’s legacy combines industrial change with major political and social controversies. He was known for pacifism early in World War I, although his company later supplied weapons. In the 1920s, he promoted antisemitism through his newspaper, The Dearborn Independent, and the book The International Jew.

key_facts.text: Ford left home at 16, moved to Detroit for work, and later repaired and built engines before working with a division of Edison Electric.
He was among the pioneers of the five-day workweek and helped establish a dealership franchise system across North America and major cities on six continents.
Ford promoted the League of Nations but later opposed U.S. entry into World War II and served for a time on the America First Committee.
Ford transferred control of the company to his grandson Henry Ford II in 1945; most of his wealth went to the Ford Foundation after his death.

overview.text: London is the capital and largest city of England and the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in southeastern England and grew from the Roman settlement of Londinium. The City of London remains the city’s ancient core and financial centre, while Westminster has been a center of national government and Parliament for centuries.

London matters as a global center of finance, culture, education, transport, and communications. Its familiar cityscape includes historic sites such as the Tower of London, Westminster Abbey, St Paul’s Cathedral, Tower Bridge, and Trafalgar Square.

key_facts.text: The London Underground is the world’s oldest rapid-transit system.
Major cultural institutions include the British Museum, National Gallery, Natural History Museum, Tate Modern, British Library, and West End theatres.
London hosted the Summer Olympics in 1908, 1948, and 2012, becoming the first city to host the Games three times.
Since 1965, Greater London has largely formed the city’s administrative area, governed by 33 local authorities and the Greater London Authority.

overview.text: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840–1893) was a Russian composer of the Romantic period whose music made a lasting international impression. His output covered concert and theatrical music, including symphonies, an opera, and ballets.

He received formal, Western-oriented training at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory, setting him apart from the nationalist composers known as The Five, with whom his professional relationship was mixed.

key_facts.text: His concert repertoire included the 1812 Overture, First Piano Concerto, Violin Concerto, and Romeo and Juliet Overture-Fantasy.
His ballets include Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, and The Nutcracker.
His repertoire also included the opera Eugene Onegin and several symphonies.
Initially educated for civil service, he graduated from the Saint Petersburg Conservatory in 1865.
Early reactions were divided: some Russian critics found his music insufficiently native, while some Europeans praised it for avoiding mere exoticism.

overview.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD), also called clinical depression, is a mental disorder in the mood-disorder category. It involves at least two weeks of pervasive low mood, low self-esteem, and loss of interest or pleasure in normally enjoyable activities. Its course varies: an episode may last months, or the condition may involve recurrent episodes over a lifetime. MDD can affect personal life, work, education, sleep, eating habits, and general health.

key_facts.text: The term was introduced by U.S. clinicians in the mid-1970s and adopted into the DSM-III in 1980.
Diagnosis uses the person’s experiences, reports from family or friends, and a mental-status examination; no laboratory test confirms MDD.

Proposed contributors include genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. Listed risks include family history, major life changes, childhood trauma, chronic health problems, some medications, lead exposure, and substance-use disorders.
Common treatments include psychotherapy and antidepressant medication. Hospitalization may be necessary when self-neglect or a significant risk of harm to self or others is present.

overview.text: James Joyce (1882–1941) was an Irish novelist, poet, and literary critic associated with modernism. His major works include Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Ulysses, and Finnegans Wake. In Ulysses, episodes from Homer’s Odyssey are paralleled through varied literary styles, especially stream of consciousness.

Joyce’s fictional universe centers on Dublin, and Ulysses uses the city’s streets and alleyways as its setting. His writing is associated with interior monologue, wordplay, close attention to detail, and radical changes to traditional plot and character development; these innovations influenced other writers and artists.

key_facts.text: Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922; publication in the United Kingdom and United States was prohibited for years because of perceived obscenity.
A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was published in 1916 and began appearing serially in The Egoist.
Joyce began Finnegans Wake in 1923, and the novel was published in 1939.
Joyce spent much of his adult life abroad, living at different times in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris while continuing to write about Dublin.

overview.text: George Frideric Handel (1685–1759) was a German-British composer of the Baroque era, associated with opera, oratorio, anthems, concerti grossi, and organ concerti. Born in Halle, he worked in Hamburg and Italy before settling in London, where he spent most of his career and became a naturalised British subject.

His career connected Italian opera with English choral music: after the success of Messiah, he turned away from Italian opera and concentrated on English choral works. Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks remain popular orchestral works, while Zadok the Priest is a coronation anthem performed at every British coronation since 1727.

key_facts.text: Handel’s style drew on the Middle-German polyphonic choral tradition and Italian Baroque composers.
His work helped establish English oratorio and the organ concerto as important musical genres.
He started three commercial opera companies that supplied Italian opera to the English nobility.
His music was admired by Classical-era composers including Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.

overview.text: John Keats’s “Ode to a Nightingale” is one of his 1819 odes. Inspired by a nightingale’s song, the personal poem explores nature, fleeting experience, and human mortality. Its central contrast is between the bird’s song, which seems able to endure, and human life, which cannot escape death.

The poem moves away from simply pursuing pleasure and toward accepting that pleasure cannot last. The speaker imagines losing the physical world and even pictures himself dead while the nightingale continues singing, making the bird a focus for the poem’s meditation on transience.

key_facts.text: Keats reportedly composed the poem in a single day after hearing a nightingale near his Hampstead home; accounts differ about the exact garden where he wrote it.
The poem was first published in Annals of the Fine Arts the July after its composition.
Near the end, the speaker imagines himself dead, with a “sod” over him while the nightingale sings.
The poem is frequently anthologized in English, though some critics have found its structure flawed because it sometimes wanders from its main idea.

overview.text: Lava is magma expelled from Earth or another terrestrial world onto its surface. It may emerge from a volcano or a crack in the crust, on land or underwater, and can be ejected into the atmosphere before falling back. The term usually describes the molten material, but it can also refer to the solid volcanic rock formed when that material cools.

key_facts.text: Lava is usually erupted at temperatures of about 800–1,200 °C.
Most molten lava has a viscosity roughly like ketchup and is about 10,000–100,000 times more viscous than water.
A solid crust quickly forms on lava exposed to air, insulating the liquid beneath and allowing it to flow long distances before solidifying.
Lava flows come from effusive eruptions; explosive eruptions instead produce volcanic ash and other fragments called tephra.

overview.text: Carmen is a four-act opera by Georges Bizet, with a libretto by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy based on Prosper Mérimée’s novella. First performed in Paris in 1875, it uses the opéra comique format—musical numbers separated by spoken dialogue—and is set in southern Spain.

Its plot follows Don José, a soldier whose relationship with Carmen leads him to abandon his sweetheart and military duties. Carmen’s love shifts to the torero Escamillo, and José kills her in a jealous rage. The opera’s notable numbers include the Habanera, Seguidilla, and Toreador Song.

key_facts.text: Bizet died suddenly after the opera’s 33rd performance, before its later international acclaim.
Early reviews were mostly critical, and the opera was not revived in Paris until 1883; productions abroad helped build its reputation.
Its depictions of working-class life, lawlessness, and an onstage murder challenged conventions in French opera.
The music is noted for its melody, harmony, atmosphere, orchestration, and depiction of the characters’ emotions and suffering.

overview.text: The Frogs (Bátrakhoi) is an ancient Greek comedy by Aristophanes, performed at the Lenaia festival in Athens in 405 BC. Its comic journey follows Dionysus, the god of theater, and his slave Xanthias into the underworld: Dionysus wants to revive Euripides, whose death has left him worried about tragedy’s quality and theater’s future. At Pluto’s palace, Dionysus judges a contest between Euripides and Aeschylus.

As a work of Old Comedy, The Frogs combines irreverent humor with satire of Athenian politics, religion, and theater. Its extended debate treats poetry as a civic concern, making the play both an underworld adventure and a substantial work of literary criticism.

key_facts.text: The title comes from the first choral interlude, in which a chorus of frogs sings and vexes Dionysus.
Aeschylus wins the debate, and Dionysus revives him instead of Euripides.
The contest compares the two tragedians’ different approaches to tragedy.
The play received first place at its Lenaia performance.

overview.text: In Greek mythology, Sisyphus (also Sisyphos) is a king and founder of Ephyra, later known as Corinth. He angers Zeus by revealing Zeus’s abduction of Aegina to the river god Asopus. After cheating death and eventually dying of old age, Sisyphus receives an eternal underworld punishment: pushing an immense boulder up a hill. The story’s cultural importance comes from this futile repetition, which has influenced modern language.

key_facts.text: The boulder rolls back whenever it nears the top, preventing Sisyphus from ever completing the task.
The adjective “Sisyphean” describes work that is laborious, futile, and never-ending.
The name is also written Sisyphos.

overview.text: The Satanic Verses is the fourth novel by British-Indian writer Salman Rushdie, first published in September 1988. It draws on the life of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and uses magical realism, combining fantastical elements with contemporary events and people in its construction.

The title points to a group of Quranic verses concerning the three pagan Meccan goddesses Allāt, Al-Uzza, and Manāt; the relevant part of the novel drew on accounts by al-Waqidi and al-Tabari. Perceived blasphemy surrounding the book sparked debates about censorship and religiously motivated violence.

key_facts.text: The novel was a finalist for the 1988 Booker Prize and won the 1988 Whitbread Award for novel of the year.
Critic Timothy Brennan characterized it as an especially ambitious treatment of the immigrant experience in Britain.
Fearing unrest, the Rajiv Gandhi government banned its importation into India.
In 1989, Iran's Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini declared a fatwa against Rushdie, after which the author received UK police protection.
The controversy also affected people connected to the book, including Japanese translator Hitoshi Igarashi, who was stabbed to death in 1991.

overview.text: Albania is a country in the Balkans of Southeast Europe. It has coastlines on both the Adriatic and Ionian Seas, which are parts of the Mediterranean, and Tirana is its capital and largest city.

Its geography combines rugged mountain ranges with fertile coastal lowlands. In broad quiz-bowl recognition, Albania also connects to Skanderbeg’s 15th-century resistance to Ottoman expansion and to the later communist rule of Enver Hoxha.

key_facts.text: Albania borders Montenegro, Kosovo, North Macedonia, and Greece.
Important physical features include the Albanian Alps, the Korab Mountains, and lowland plains along the Adriatic and Ionian coasts.
Other major cities named in the source are Durrës, Vlorë, and Shkodër.
Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg led resistance to Ottoman expansion in the 15th century; his campaigns repelled Ottoman advances for more than two decades.
Albania declared independence in 1912 and later experienced a communist regime under Enver Hoxha.

overview.text: Jordan Haworth Peele is an American actor, comedian, and filmmaker whose career spans sketch comedy and horror-oriented film. He began in improv, joined Mad TV in 2003, and later partnered with Keegan-Michael Key. Together they created and starred in Comedy Central’s Key & Peele (2012–2015), a sketch-comedy series.

Peele then moved toward writing and directing psychological horror with comedic elements. His 2017 directorial debut, Get Out, earned him the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay; he later wrote, directed, and produced Us (2019) and Nope (2022).

key_facts.text: Peele was a Mad TV cast member for five seasons, from 2003 to 2008.
Key & Peele won two Primetime Emmy Awards and a Peabody Award.
Get Out also received Academy Award nominations for Best Picture and Best Director.
Peele founded Monkeypaw Productions, a film and television company, in 2012.
He hosted and produced the 2019–2020 revival of the anthology series The Twilight Zone.

overview.text: Alfred Joseph Hitchcock (1899–1980) was an English filmmaker whose six-decade career included more than 50 feature films. Known as the “Master of Suspense,” he became unusually recognizable through interviews, cameo appearances in most of his films, and hosting and producing the television anthology Alfred Hitchcock Presents (1955–65).

His first successful film, The Lodger, helped shape the thriller genre. By 1939, Hitchcock had earned international recognition. Producer David O. Selznick persuaded him to move to Hollywood, where his filmography included Rebecca, Rear Window, Psycho, Vertigo, and North by Northwest.

key_facts.text: Hitchcock entered the film industry in 1919 as a title-card designer and made his directorial debut with the silent film The Pleasure Garden in 1926.
Rebecca won the Academy Award for Best Picture, but Hitchcock never won Best Director despite five nominations.
He repeatedly collaborated with major stars including Cary Grant, James Stewart, Ingrid Bergman, and Grace Kelly.
In a 2012 worldwide British Film Institute poll of hundreds of critics, Vertigo displaced Citizen Kane as the choice for greatest film ever made.

overview.text: The American Revolutionary War was the armed conflict between Britain and Patriot forces from April 1775 to September 1783, forming the final eight years of the broader American Revolution. Tensions between Britain and the Thirteen Colonies had escalated after 1763, including disputes surrounding the Stamp and Townshend Acts. Fighting began at Lexington and Concord; the Second Continental Congress then organized the Continental Army under George Washington and adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776.

The war was fought across North America, the Caribbean, and the Atlantic Ocean. A Franco-American victory at Yorktown in 1781 helped bring about negotiations, and the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognized the sovereignty and independence of the United States, establishing it as an independent nation.

key_facts.text: After driving British forces from Boston in 1776, the Continental Army faced William Howe’s capture of New York City; Washington then won victories at Trenton and Princeton.
The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 helped persuade France and Spain that an independent United States was possible. France allied with the American revolutionaries in 1778.
At Yorktown, French and American forces besieged Cornwallis while the French navy blocked his escape, leading to his surrender in October 1781.
Signed on September 3, 1783, the Treaty of Paris ended the war and required Great Britain to acknowledge the independence and sovereignty of the United States.

overview.text: A permutation is a rearrangement of every member of a set; formally, it is a bijection from the set to itself, so each element appears exactly once as an output. For n distinct objects, the number of permutations is n!, or n factorial—the product of all positive integers up to n.

Permutations are an important topic in combinatorics and group theory. They also have applications in sorting-algorithm analysis, descriptions of particle states in quantum physics, and representations of RNA sequences in biology.

key_facts.text: The set {1, 2, 3} has six permutations, corresponding to its six possible ordered triples.
An anagram of a word with all different letters is a permutation of those letters.
A k-permutation, or partial permutation, is an ordered arrangement of k distinct elements selected from a set.
All permutations of a set form its symmetric group; the group operation is composition, meaning one rearrangement is performed after another.

overview.text: The violin is a wooden chordophone, or string instrument, and the smallest and highest-pitched regular member of the violin family. Most violins have hollow wooden bodies and four strings, usually tuned in perfect fifths. Players most commonly draw a bow across the strings, though they can also pluck them using a technique called pizzicato.

First created in 16th-century Italy, the violin is prominent in Western classical music as both an ensemble and solo instrument. It is also used in folk music, jazz, and some forms of rock and jazz fusion; electric violins are used in some rock and jazz fusion.

key_facts.text: “Fiddle” is another name for the violin, regardless of the musical style in which it is played.
Violin strings may be made from gut, Perlon or other synthetics, or steel; the instrument’s components are usually made from different woods.
A person who makes or repairs violins is a luthier or violinmaker. A bow maker or repairer is an archetier or bowmaker.
Historical violins by makers such as Stradivari, Guarneri, Amati, and Stainer are highly prized, although claims about their uniquely unmatchable sound are disputed.

overview.text: Oedipus is a mythical king of Thebes and the tragic hero at the center of Sophocles’ Oedipus Rex. In the myth, he unknowingly fulfills a prophecy that he will kill his father and marry his mother, bringing disaster to his family and city. His story explores human fallibility, limited knowledge, and the difficult relationship between individual action and destiny.

Oedipus Rex is followed in narrative sequence by Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone; together, these works are called Sophocles’ three Theban plays. Oedipus’s investigation into the murder of Laius leads to the revelation that he killed his own father and married Jocasta, his mother. The Sphinx episode is another central part of the legend: solving its riddle wins him the throne of Thebes.

key_facts.text: Oedipus was born to Laius and Jocasta but was raised by Polybus and Merope after Laius tried to have him abandoned.
After hearing the prophecy at Delphi, Oedipus fled because he mistakenly believed Polybus and Merope were his biological parents.
When Jocasta recognized the truth, she hanged herself; Oedipus then blinded himself with pins taken from her dress.
Sigmund Freud later used the myth as the namesake and mythic precedent for the Oedipus complex.

overview.text: Carthage was an ancient city on the eastern side of Lake Tunis in present-day Tunisia. It grew from a Phoenician colony into the capital of a Punic empire that controlled large parts of the southwestern Mediterranean. Carthage was also a major trading center and one of the classical world’s wealthy cities.

Rome destroyed the ancient city after a nearly three-year siege in 146 BC, during the Third Punic War. About a century later, Roman Carthage was rebuilt and became a major city in the Roman province of Africa.

key_facts.text: Tradition identifies the founder as Dido, also called Elissa or Alyssa, a legendary woman from Tyre; her historical existence remains uncertain.
The founding myth says Dido obtained as much land as an oxhide could cover by cutting the hide into thin strips and outlining the city’s perimeter.
Carthage continued to have cultural and economic importance during the Byzantine period before Umayyad forces destroyed it in 698.
The ruins are an archaeological site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site; scholars have disagreed over whether ancient Carthage practiced child sacrifice.

overview.text: John Christopher Depp II is an American actor, musician, and filmmaker. He began as a musician, made his film debut in A Nightmare on Elm Street, and rose to prominence as a teen idol on 21 Jump Street. He became associated with eccentric characters and repeated collaborations with director Tim Burton.

Depp gained worldwide stardom by playing Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean films. Other major roles included J. M. Barrie in Finding Neverland and the title character in Sweeney Todd. His public profile also includes two defamation cases following his marriage to Amber Heard, with different rulings in England and the United States.

key_facts.text: Depp received a Golden Globe Award and a Screen Actors Guild Award, along with three Academy Award nominations.
He collaborated with Tim Burton on eight films, including Edward Scissorhands, Ed Wood, Sleepy Hollow, and Sweeney Todd.
He portrayed Gellert Grindelwald in two films from the Wizarding World's Fantastic Beasts series.
Outside acting, Depp founded the film company Infinitum Nihil and formed the rock group Hollywood Vampires with Alice Cooper and Joe Perry.
In the English case, the High Court ruled that Depp engaged in domestic abuse against Heard; in the 2022 U.S. case, a court ruled that Heard had defamed Depp.

overview.text: The Nazi Party, officially the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), was a far-right German political party active from 1920 to 1945. It grew out of post–World War I extremist nationalist, racist, and populist paramilitary culture, opposed communism, and gained support during the Great Depression amid unemployment and falling living standards. Its ideology increasingly emphasized antisemitism and anti-Marxism.

Adolf Hitler, its leader from 1921, became chancellor in 1933 and quickly established a totalitarian regime known as the Third Reich. Nazism imagined a racially defined “people’s community” that excluded groups it labeled undesirable; Nazi persecution culminated in the Holocaust, including the genocide of around six million Jews and millions of other targeted victims.

key_facts.text: The party’s precursor, the German Workers’ Party (DAP), existed from 1919 to 1920.
Early Nazi strategy used socialist rhetoric to attract lower-middle-class support, then deemphasized it while seeking backing from business leaders.
Nazi persecution targeted Jews, Slavs, Romani, people with physical or intellectual disabilities, homosexuals, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and political opponents.
After Germany’s defeat in World War II, the party was declared illegal; Allied denazification and the Nuremberg trials addressed Nazi crimes and leadership.

overview.text: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka was a unanimous 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision concerning racial segregation in public schools. The Court ruled that state laws requiring segregated schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause, even when the facilities provided for different races were equal. This rejected the constitutional basis of the “separate but equal” doctrine from Plessy v. Ferguson and helped open the way for school integration.

The case arose after Topeka, Kansas, required Oliver Brown’s daughter to attend a segregated Black school farther from home instead of the nearby school. The Browns and other families challenged the policy; represented by NAACP chief counsel Thurgood Marshall, they appealed to the Supreme Court. Brown became a major victory of the civil rights movement.

key_facts.text: Brown was heard alongside similar cases from the South and was decided 9–0 in May 1954.
Brown I did not specify how schools should end segregation; Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation “with all deliberate speed.”
Many Southern leaders responded with “massive resistance,” a campaign against desegregation associated with the Little Rock crisis.
In Cooper v. Aaron, the Court reaffirmed Brown and stated that state officials could not nullify its ruling.

overview.text: A Mass is a musical composition that sets the text of the Western Christian Eucharistic liturgy, especially the Catholic Mass. Its usual cycle contains five movements: Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei.
Masses may be abbreviated or expanded with additional liturgical texts. They can be written for unaccompanied choir, instruments, or full orchestra, and are also performed in concert halls.

key_facts.text: The Latin name for a Mass is missa; related names include messa, messe, and Messe.
A missa brevis is an abbreviated Mass, while a missa plena includes some or all of the Mass Proper.
A Requiem is a special type of Mass named for the opening word of its Introit.
Before the Second Vatican Council, Catholic Mass settings generally used Latin; later settings also used approved vernacular translations alongside new Latin settings.

overview.text: The Ku Klux Klan (KKK) is an American Protestant-led white-supremacist hate group and secret society. Historians identify its organized threats, assaults, killings, and intimidation as terrorism used to influence political and social conditions, especially in the post-Civil War South. Across its major iterations, the Klan targeted African Americans and other groups, including Jews, Catholics, and immigrants. [p1]

The first Klan arose during Reconstruction to oppose expanded rights for formerly enslaved people. A second Klan, founded in 1915, spread nationally and promoted nativism, segregation, and “100 percent Americanism”; a smaller third wave emerged amid resistance to the civil rights movement. Klan members sometimes presented themselves as defenders of morality and law, but historians emphasize the movement’s documented violence and coercion. [p2][p4]

key_facts.text: The first Klan was founded by former Confederate soldiers and attacked Black voters, officeholders, and white allies supporting Reconstruction governments. [p2]
Federal Enforcement Acts and prosecutions beginning in 1871 significantly weakened the first Klan. [p2]
The second Klan reached its peak in the 1920s and attracted millions from segments of the native-born white Protestant population. [p2]
Major Christian denominations, including leading Protestant bodies, formally condemned Klan ideology and methods as incompatible with Christian theology. [p3]
Modern scholarship documents the Klan’s use of intimidation, lynching, and political violence as part of systematic racial oppression and domestic terrorism. [p4]

overview.text: Blood is a specialized connective tissue and body fluid in vertebrates. The heart pumps it through blood vessels, where it delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries metabolic waste away.

It consists of plasma with suspended blood cells: red cells, white cells, and—in mammals—platelets. These components support oxygen transport, resistance to infections and parasites, and blood clotting.

key_facts.text: Plasma is mostly water and also contains proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones.
Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which reversibly binds oxygen and helps transport it through the body.
White blood cells, or leukocytes, help the body resist infections and parasites.
Platelets, also called thrombocytes, are important in blood clotting.
In animals with lungs, oxygen-rich arterial blood is bright red, while oxygen-poor venous blood is dark red.

overview.text: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims worldwide observe it through fasting, communal prayer, Quran study, reflection, charity, and strengthening community ties. Ramadan’s annual observance is regarded as one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

The month is associated with the belief that the Quran was revealed to Muhammad; this event is known as Laylat al-Qadr. During fasting hours, Muslims refrain from food and drink as well as behavior considered sinful in Islam.

key_facts.text: Ramadan lasts 29 or 30 days, determined by sightings of the crescent moon.
Suhur is the predawn meal, while iftar is the evening meal that breaks the fast.
Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty, with exceptions including illness, travel, old age, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and menstruation.
Muslims believe that the spiritual rewards of fasting are multiplied during Ramadan.

overview.text: Acts is the fifth book of the New Testament and the second part of the two-volume work Luke–Acts, following the Gospel of Luke. It continues the story after Jesus’ death and resurrection, beginning with his ascension and Pentecost, then tracing the founding of the Christian Church and the spread of its message from Jerusalem across the Mediterranean world. (p1, p3)

The later narrative follows Paul’s mission and ends with his imprisonment in Rome while awaiting trial. Acts also addresses how a movement centered on the Jewish Messiah came to include an overwhelmingly non-Jewish church, presenting Jesus’ followers as a Jewish sect entitled to legal protection. (p3, p4)

key_facts.text: Tradition identifies Luke the Evangelist as the author, but the text does not name its author and critical opinion remains divided. (p2)
Acts is usually dated to approximately 80–90 CE. (p2)
Its early chapters include Pentecost, the shared life of the first believers, and the establishment of the church at Antioch. (p3)
The title Acts of the Apostles comes from the Koine Greek Práxeis Apostólōn and the Latin Actūs Apostolōrum. (p1)

overview.text: The Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) was a Latin Christian expedition called by Pope Innocent III to recapture Jerusalem, with Egypt as its intended first target. A transport contract with Venice and a shortfall in expected crusaders created a payment problem; the army instead attacked Zara (Zadar), a rebellious Adriatic city, which was then brought under Venetian control.

The crusaders next became involved in Byzantine dynastic politics by supporting Alexios Angelos’s effort to restore his father, Isaac II, to the throne. When promised payments failed to materialize, they conquered and plundered Constantinople in April 1204. The conquest fragmented the Byzantine Empire and produced Latin states; Byzantine rule returned when the Nicaean Empire reconquered the city in 1261.

key_facts.text: Venice built a dedicated fleet, but the crusaders arrived in smaller numbers than expected and could not pay the agreed cost. Venetian Doge Enrico Dandolo proposed attacking Zara instead.
Zara was the first Catholic city attacked by a Catholic Crusader army. Pope Innocent III opposed the attack and temporarily excommunicated the army.
Alexios was crowned co-emperor in August 1203, but a popular uprising deposed him in January 1204, preceding the decision to conquer Constantinople.
After Constantinople fell, Byzantine successor states emerged around Nicaea, Trebizond, and Epirus, alongside the Latin Empire of Constantinople.

overview.text: A solvent is a substance that dissolves a solute, producing a solution. Although solvents are commonly liquids, they can also be solids, gases, or supercritical fluids. Water is a central example: it dissolves polar molecules and is the most widely used solvent by living things, keeping cellular ions and proteins in solution.

Solvents connect basic chemistry to everyday products and industry. They are used in paints, inks, dry cleaning, detergents, perfumes, and chemical processes such as synthesis and purification. Their safety varies: some petrochemical solvents are toxic and release volatile organic compounds, while biobased alternatives are intended to be less toxic and biodegradable.

key_facts.text: Acetone is used in nail-polish removers and for dissolving glue; ethanol is used in perfumes.
Tetrachloroethylene is an example of an organic solvent used in dry cleaning.
Toluene and turpentine are used as paint thinners.
Biobased solvents can be made from materials such as starch, sucrose, vegetable oils, and industrial waste products.

overview.text: Italian (Italiano; lingua italiana) is a Romance language in the Indo-European family. Its standardized form is based on literary Florentine Tuscan, and, alongside Sardinian, it is described as one of the Romance languages least differentiated from Latin.

Italian has broad institutional and cultural reach: it is official in several European states and Vatican City, has important roles in European organizations and the Holy See, and has contributed internationally used vocabulary in music, opera, fashion, cuisine, and other fields.

key_facts.text: Italian is official in Italy, San Marino, Vatican City, and Switzerland’s Ticino and part of the Grisons.
It has official minority status in parts of Croatia, Slovenia, Romania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Brazil.
In the Holy See, Italian is the main working language and a lingua franca—a common language—of the Roman Catholic hierarchy.
Italian has seven vowel sounds and distinguishes short from long consonants; doubling a consonant is called gemination.

overview.text: Linear momentum, also called translational momentum, is a vector quantity equal to an object's mass multiplied by its velocity. It has both magnitude and direction. In Newtonian mechanics, the net force on a body equals the rate at which its momentum changes. In an inertial reference frame, the total momentum of a closed system remains constant when no external force acts on it; this conservation reflects translational symmetry of space and time.

key_facts.text: The SI unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second (kg⋅m/s), which is dimensionally equivalent to the newton-second.
Momentum depends on the chosen frame of reference, so its value can differ between observers.
In Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, generalized momentum can differ from kinetic momentum, which is defined as mass times velocity.
In quantum mechanics, momentum is represented by an operator on a wave function and is related to position through the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

overview.text: The Vietnam War was both a Cold War proxy conflict and a civil war fought in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, opposed South Vietnam, backed by the United States and other anti-communist countries. After the 1954 Geneva Conference divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, North Vietnam supported the communist Viet Cong insurgency in the south.

U.S. involvement expanded after the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident, bringing bombing campaigns and large combat deployments. Communist forces used guerrilla tactics, while the 1968 Tet Offensive—though a tactical defeat—helped increase opposition to the war in the United States. Nixon’s Vietnamization shifted combat responsibility to South Vietnam as U.S. forces withdrew; Saigon fell in 1975, and Vietnam reunified in 1976.

key_facts.text: The Ho Chi Minh trail, established through Laos, supplied the Viet Cong; North Vietnam also sent PAVN soldiers south by 1961.
U.S. forces relied on air power, heavy firepower, and rural “search and destroy” operations, while communist forces used concealed bases in the countryside and jungle.
Estimated deaths among Vietnamese soldiers and civilians range from 970,000 to 3 million; 58,220 U.S. service members also died.
The war’s aftermath included the Vietnamese boat people and a broader Indochina refugee crisis, in which millions left the region.

overview.text: In monotheistic belief, God is the supreme deity and ultimate cause of existence: the creator, sustainer, and ruler of the universe. God is often conceived as incorporeal and independent of material creation. Conceptions vary; some theists describe God as omnibenevolent, while deism holds that God is not involved with humanity beyond creation.

Some traditions understand religious life as a relationship with God expressed through worship and prayer, and regard God as the source of moral obligation. God may be described without gender or through gender-specific language; names and titles differ across languages and cultures and may emphasize different attributes.

key_facts.text: Atheism rejects belief in God or any deity; agnosticism treats God’s existence as unknown or unknowable.
Some theists hold that knowledge of God comes through faith.
Theologians and philosophers have developed arguments both for and against God’s existence.
In polytheistic beliefs, a god may be understood as a being believed to create or control some part of the universe or life and is often worshipped.

overview.text: Cancer is a group of diseases in which cells grow uncontrollably. This growth typically produces tumors; malignant tumors can invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body, unlike benign tumors. More than 100 types of cancer affect humans.

Cancer develops through genetic changes in cells, which can result from environmental factors or inherited defects. Suspected cancer may be investigated through symptoms, screening, imaging, and biopsy. Treatment often combines surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted therapy; immunotherapy, which uses the patient’s immune system, is an emerging approach.

key_facts.text: Infections cause approximately 16–18% of cancers worldwide; examples include HPV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Helicobacter pylori.
Approximately 5–10% of cancers are attributed to inherited genetic defects; many genetic changes may be needed before cancer develops.
Cancer risk can be reduced by not smoking, limiting alcohol, maintaining a healthy weight, eating vegetables, fruits, and whole grains, and receiving certain vaccinations.
The chance of survival depends partly on the cancer’s type and how extensively it has spread when treatment begins.

overview.text: Jane Austen (1775–1817) was an English novelist whose six novels examine and comment on the English landed gentry at the end of the eighteenth century. Her plots often explore women’s dependence on marriage for social position and economic security, making class and marriage important subjects in her fiction.

Austen’s writing combines social commentary, realism, wit, and irony. It also represents a transition toward nineteenth-century literary realism and implicitly critiques the eighteenth-century novels of sensibility. Her work gained broad acclaim and readership after her death and has frequently been adapted for film and television.

key_facts.text: Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park, and Emma were published anonymously during Austen’s lifetime, from 1811 to 1815.
Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published after Austen’s death, both in 1817.
Austen began the unfinished novel Sanditon and also left the unfinished The Watsons and the short epistolary novel Lady Susan.
Austen wrote major novels before age 22 but was not published until age 35.

overview.text: The cell membrane, also called the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane, is a semipermeable biological boundary that separates and protects a cell’s interior from the extracellular space. Its lipid bilayer selectively controls the movement of ions and organic molecules into and out of the cell.
Beyond regulating exchanges, the membrane participates in cell adhesion, ion conductivity, and cell signaling. Its proteins also help the cell interact with its surrounding environment.

key_facts.text: The bilayer is made mainly of phospholipids and glycolipids.
Integral proteins span the membrane and can transport substances; peripheral proteins attach to its surface and may act as enzymes.
Sterols, such as cholesterol in animal cells, are interspersed in the membrane and help maintain suitable fluidity across temperatures.
The membrane provides attachment surfaces for the cell wall, the carbohydrate-rich glycocalyx, and the cell’s internal cytoskeleton.

overview.text: In mathematics, slope (or gradient) is a number describing the direction of a line on a plane. It is the ratio of vertical change (rise) to horizontal change (run), commonly written as m; it measures a ratio rather than a direct distance or angle.

A positive slope rises from left to right, while a negative slope falls. Horizontal lines have slope zero, and vertical lines have undefined slope. In calculus, the slope of a curve at a point is defined using its tangent line; nearby secant lines can provide an approximation.

key_facts.text: For two points, slope is calculated as m = Δy/Δx = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
The absolute value of slope measures steepness: a larger absolute value means a steeper line.
A 45° rising line has slope +1; a 45° falling line has slope −1.
The concept is used for physical or diagrammed features such as roads and roofs, as well as in geography and civil engineering.

overview.text: The Glass Menagerie is a memory play by Tennessee Williams that premiered in 1944. Its strong autobiographical elements draw on Williams’s family, with characters based on the author, his mother, and his sister. The play was his first successful work and propelled him from obscurity toward a major career in American drama. Its path from an uncertain Chicago start to Broadway shows how critical support shaped its early reception.

key_facts.text: The play premiered in Chicago on December 26, 1944.
After its shaky beginning, critics Ashton Stevens and Claudia Cassidy helped attract audiences and move the production to Broadway.
It won the New York Drama Critics’ Circle Award in 1945.
Williams developed the play from an earlier short story and a screenplay titled The Gentleman Caller.

overview.text: Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Cask of Amontillado” is a short story set in an unnamed Italian city during Carnival. Montresor seeks fatal revenge against Fortunato, whom he believes has insulted him. The story is presented from the murderer’s perspective, giving readers Montresor’s account of the crime.

Montresor draws Fortunato into the family vaults, which also serve as catacombs, by promising him amontillado wine. The promise is a trap: Montresor entombs Fortunato alive. This act of immurement means sealing a living person inside a tomb or enclosed space.

key_facts.text: The story was first published in the November 1846 issue of Godey’s Lady’s Book.
Fortunato is portrayed as a wine expert, and he has already drunk enough to impair his judgment. Montresor exploits Fortunato’s interest in wine.
Montresor reveals that fifty years have passed since the revenge and that Fortunato’s body remains undisturbed.
Montresor’s motive is unclear. He may be insane, while other clues connect his resentment to his family’s lost status and his blame of Fortunato.

overview.text: Boris Johnson (Alexander Boris de Pfeffel Johnson) was a British politician and writer who led the Conservative Party and served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2019 to 2022. Earlier, he was Mayor of London from 2008 to 2016 and Foreign Secretary from 2016 to 2018. He was also a prominent campaigner for leaving the European Union in the 2016 referendum.

As prime minister, Johnson reopened Brexit negotiations, won the December 2019 general election, and led the UK when it left the EU in January 2020. His government used emergency powers during the COVID-19 pandemic and approved a national vaccination programme. Controversies including Partygate and the Chris Pincher appointment led to his resignation in July 2022; Liz Truss succeeded him.

key_facts.text: Johnson resigned as foreign secretary in 2018, opposing Theresa May’s Brexit approach and the Chequers Agreement.
The UK Supreme Court ruled that Johnson’s 2019 prorogation, or suspension, of Parliament was unlawful.
In April 2022, Johnson received a fixed-penalty notice after lockdown gatherings at 10 Downing Street breached COVID-19 social-distancing laws.
A Commons Privileges Committee investigation later found that Johnson had lied to Parliament on numerous occasions; he resigned as an MP in June 2023.
Johnson remains a divisive figure: supporters praised his Brexit leadership, vaccination programme, and support for Ukraine, while critics accused him of dishonesty, elitism, cronyism, and bigotry.

overview.text: A Good Man Is Hard to Find is a short story by American author Flannery O’Connor and part of the collection A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories. The collection links this title with serial killers and frames its stories around original sin, violence, spiritual change, and morally difficult life-or-death situations. Its Catholic influence gives the collection a strong religious and ethical dimension.

key_facts.text: The collection was first published in 1955 by Harcourt, Brace and Company.
O’Connor characterized the collection as a group of stories concerned with original sin.
Most of the collection’s stories contain jarring violence that prompts characters to undergo spiritual change.
The stories frequently place Catholic moral questions in life-or-death situations.

source.title: A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories

overview.text: Ray Douglas Bradbury (1920–2012) was an American author and screenwriter who wrote across fantasy, science fiction, horror, mystery, and realistic fiction. His career also included television scripts and poetry, so he is broader than a single-genre science-fiction label.

Key literary associations include Fahrenheit 451 and the short-story collections The Martian Chronicles, The Illustrated Man, and The October Country. His range also includes coming-of-age fiction, dark fantasy, a fictionalized memoir, and works adapted for film, television, and comics.

key_facts.text: Fahrenheit 451 was published in 1953.
Dandelion Wine (1957) is a coming-of-age novel, while Something Wicked This Way Comes (1962) is dark fantasy.
Green Shadows, White Whale (1992) is described as a fictionalized memoir.
Bradbury wrote or consulted on screenplays and television scripts, including Moby Dick and It Came from Outer Space.
His poetry appeared in collections such as They Have Not Seen the Stars (2001).

overview.text: Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician active around 300 BC and associated with Alexandria. He worked as a geometer and logician and is chiefly remembered for the Elements, a treatise that established foundations of geometry. The system associated with this work is called Euclidean geometry.

In the Elements, Euclid presented geometry deductively, deriving theorems from a small set of axioms. This framework dominated geometry until the early 19th century. His writings also addressed subjects including perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, and number theory.

key_facts.text: The Elements synthesized theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus, Hippocrates, Thales, and Theaetetus.
Euclid wrote Optics, described as an important early work in optics, as well as Data and Phaenomena.
Very little is known about Euclid’s life; much of the surviving information comes from the later scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria.
Euclid’s authorship of On Divisions of Figures and Catoptrics has been questioned.

overview.text: England is a country within the United Kingdom occupying most of the island of Great Britain. It borders Scotland to the north and Wales to the west, while the North Sea, English Channel, Celtic Sea, and Irish Sea surround its other sides. Its landscape is mainly low hills and plains, with uplands concentrated in the north and west. London is its largest city.

England became a unified state in the 10th century and later joined Scotland in the 1707 creation of Great Britain. It is associated with the origins of the English language, common-law legal systems, association football, and the Industrial Revolution.

key_facts.text: The name England comes from the Angles, a Germanic tribe that settled there in the fifth and sixth centuries.
The Kingdom of England ceased to be a separate sovereign state in 1707, when the Acts of Union formed Great Britain with Scotland.
The University of Oxford was founded in 1096, and the University of Cambridge in 1209; they are described as the two oldest universities in the English-speaking world.
The Industrial Revolution began in 18th-century England and helped transform it into the first industrialized nation.

overview.text: Emily Elizabeth Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet born in Amherst, Massachusetts. After studying at Amherst Academy and briefly attending Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, she returned home to Amherst. Her poetry was largely unpublished and little known during her lifetime, but it later became canonical.
