It served as major north–south waterborne transport infrastructure and remains heavily used by cargo barges south of the Yellow River.

The canal’s importance came from connecting fertile Jiangnan with northern capitals, population centers, and armies on the northern frontiers. Successive dynasties restored and improved it despite floods, wars, rebellions, and periods of decline. The Grand Canal is also a World Heritage Site.

key_facts.text: The oldest sections date to the early 5th century BCE; Emperor Yang of the Sui expanded and completed a major network in 609.
The present Jing–Hang route is divided into six main subsections and passes through Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shandong, Hebei, Tianjin, and Beijing.
After the capital moved to Khanbaliq, now Beijing, under the Yuan dynasty, the canal’s importance increased and continued under later Ming and Qing rule.
In the 10th century, the Song official and engineer Qiao Weiyue invented the pound lock, helping canal shipping handle higher elevations.

overview.text: Qin Shi Huang, also known as Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng, founded the Qin dynasty and became China’s first emperor. In 221 BCE, after conquering the other warring states, he unified China. He introduced the title huangdi, replacing the older title of king; this imperial title remained in use in China and elsewhere for about two millennia.

Working with his minister Li Si, Qin Shi Huang pursued reforms to standardize practices among the former states. His major projects included incorporating earlier state walls into a single Great Wall, building a national road system, and constructing a mausoleum guarded by the life-sized Terracotta Army. Traditional accounts portray him as a tyrant and strict Legalist, but later scholarship has questioned that judgment.

key_facts.text: Before becoming emperor, he ruled as King Zheng of Qin; Ying Zheng and Zhao Zheng are names associated with him.
Qin expansion added the Yue lands of present-day Hunan and Guangdong and conquered the Ordos Plateau from the Xiongnu.
He died in 210 BCE during his fifth tour of eastern China.

overview.text: Buoyancy, also called upthrust, is the upward force a fluid exerts on an object partly or completely immersed in it. Fluid pressure increases with depth, so the greater pressure beneath an immersed object produces a net upward force.

The force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object, a relationship known as Archimedes’ principle. Comparing an object’s average density with that of the surrounding fluid helps explain whether it tends to sink or float.

key_facts.text: An object denser than its surrounding fluid tends to sink; an object less dense than the fluid can be kept afloat by buoyancy.
Buoyancy can drive convection currents in fluid mixtures, including the separation of air and water or oil and water.
The center of buoyancy is the center of gravity of the volume of fluid displaced by an object.
Buoyancy depends on gravity or another source of acceleration; without such an acceleration, buoyancy does not occur.

overview.text: Titration is a laboratory method of quantitative chemical analysis used to determine the concentration of an identified analyte—the substance being analyzed. It works by reacting the analyte solution with a prepared standard solution whose concentration and volume are known. The amount of this reagent that reacts is measured as the titration volume, linking a known standard to the concentration being sought.

key_facts.text: Titration is also called titrimetry or volumetric analysis.
The known-concentration reagent is called the titrant or titrator.
The substance being analyzed is the analyte; it may also be called the titrand.
The volume of titrant that reacts with the analyte is the titration volume.

overview.text: Coulomb's law describes the electrostatic force between two point charges at rest. The force's magnitude is proportional to the product of the charges and decreases with the square of the distance between them: |F| ∝ |q₁q₂|/r². The force acts along the straight line joining the charges. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb first published the law in 1785, helping make electric charge a measurable part of electromagnetism.
Its inverse-square form connects Coulomb's law with Newton's law of universal gravitation, but electric forces can either attract or repel, whereas gravity is always attractive.

key_facts.text: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
In the formula, q₁ and q₂ are the charges, r is their separation, and the proportionality factor is called the Coulomb constant.
Coulomb's law and Gauss's law can be derived from one another; for a single point charge at rest, they express the same physical law in different forms.
The law has been tested over distances ranging from 10⁻¹⁶ meters to 10⁸ meters.

overview.text: Friction is a force that resists relative motion when solid surfaces, fluid layers, or material elements slide or grind against one another. It has several physical contributors, including deformation of tiny surface irregularities, electrical charges, and changes in local structure. The study of friction and related processes is called tribology.

As interacting bodies move, friction transforms some mechanical energy into heat and other forms of dissipated energy. Because the microscopic interactions are complex, friction is often analyzed with empirical methods rather than calculated entirely from first principles.

key_facts.text: Recognized types include dry, fluid, lubricated, skin, and internal friction; this is not a complete list.
Friction from rubbing pieces of wood together can be used to start a fire.
Friction can cause wear, which may reduce performance or damage components.
The retarding frictional force can be expressed as dissipated energy per unit distance: F = E/d.

overview.text: Infrared (IR) is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light—starting just beyond red—but shorter than microwaves. It cannot be seen by the human eye. The band is commonly divided into near infrared, at shorter wavelengths, and thermal infrared, at longer wavelengths; nearly all radiation from objects near room temperature lies in the IR band.

IR is closely linked with heat: Earth receives slightly more than half of the Sun’s energy as infrared, and the balance between absorbed and emitted IR influences climate. Its practical and scientific importance ranges from thermal imaging and remote temperature sensing to spectroscopy and astronomy, where IR instruments can look through dusty space and detect highly red-shifted objects.

key_facts.text: William Herschel identified infrared radiation in 1800 by measuring its effect on a thermometer.
Infrared spectroscopy studies how molecules absorb and transmit IR as their rotational-vibrational motions change.
Thermal-imaging cameras can reveal heat loss in insulation, aid firefighting, and identify overheating electrical components.
Active near-infrared illumination supports night vision while allowing an observer to remain difficult to detect.

overview.text: Mary was a first-century Jewish woman from Nazareth, identified in the Gospels as the mother of Jesus and wife of Joseph. Matthew and Luke present her as a virgin chosen by God to conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit. After Jesus’s birth in Bethlehem, Mary and Joseph raised him in Nazareth; she was also present at his crucifixion and with the apostles after his ascension.

Mary is central to Christian devotion, honored through titles, prayers, feast days, images, churches, and pilgrimages. Several Christian traditions call her Theotokos, or “Mother of God,” while Catholic and some Oriental Orthodox teachings include the Immaculate Conception and her bodily Assumption. Eastern Christians often call this event the Dormition. Mary also has a prominent place in Islam, including a Quran chapter named after her.

key_facts.text: Western Christianity calls Mary’s bodily raising into heaven the Assumption; Eastern Christianity commonly calls it the Dormition. The Bible does not describe the end of her life.
The Church of the East historically used the title Christotokos for Mary, contrasting with the title Theotokos used by many other Christian traditions.
The Immaculate Conception is a distinctive Marian dogma of the Catholic Church and some Oriental Orthodox churches.
Mary has been a recurring subject in Byzantine, medieval, and Renaissance art, as well as in Christian prayers, hymns, and feast days.

overview.text: Slaughterhouse-Five is Kurt Vonnegut’s 1969 semi-autobiographic, science-fiction-infused anti-war novel. It follows Billy Pilgrim from his early life through World War II service and into the postwar years. Billy’s repeated movement through time is tied to a temporal crisis arising from postwar psychological trauma. The novel’s wartime center is Billy’s capture by the German Army and survival of the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war, an experience Vonnegut also endured as an American serviceman.

key_facts.text: Its full title is Slaughterhouse-Five, or, The Children’s Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death.
During World War II, Billy serves as both an American soldier and a chaplain’s assistant.
The novel has been translated into at least 11 other languages.

overview.text: The Matterhorn is a near-symmetric, pyramid-shaped mountain in the Pennine Alps, standing on the watershed and border between Switzerland and Italy. Its summit is 4,478 meters high, placing it among the highest peaks of the Alps and Europe. It overlooks Zermatt in Switzerland and Breuil-Cervinia in Italy, while its four steep faces rise above surrounding glaciers.

The Matterhorn is an enduring emblem of Switzerland and the Alps. It remained unclimbed after most other great Alpine peaks had been attained and became the subject of an international competition for its summit. Since railways were built in the area in the late nineteenth century, it has attracted visitors, climbers, and trekkers, including people who follow a circuit around the mountain.

key_facts.text: Edward Whymper led the first ascent from Zermatt in 1865; during the descent, four of the seven climbers died.
The four faces point roughly toward the cardinal directions: the north, east, and west faces are on the Swiss side, while the south face is in Italy.
Theodul Pass, just east of the mountain, has served as a passage between the valleys and a trade route since Roman times.
The north face was first climbed in 1931, and the west face was completely climbed in 1962; the north face is one of the Alps’ three major north faces, called “The Trilogy.”
Glacial cirque erosion helped create the Matterhorn’s present shape, and the mountain has been part of Switzerland’s Federal Inventory of Natural Monuments since 1983.

overview.text: Queen Victoria (Alexandrina Victoria) ruled the United Kingdom from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her 63-year reign defined the Victorian era, a period of major industrial, political, scientific, and military change accompanied by expansion of the British Empire. In 1876, Parliament granted her the additional title Empress of India.

Victoria married Prince Albert in 1840, and their nine children married into royal and noble families across Europe, earning her the nickname “grandmother of Europe.” After Albert died in 1861, she withdrew from public life during a period of mourning, though her popularity later recovered and her jubilees became public celebrations.

key_facts.text: Victoria became queen at age 18 after the deaths of her father and grandfather and the deaths of her father’s three elder brothers without surviving legitimate children.
She was the daughter of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, and was raised under close supervision by her mother and John Conroy.
Victoria privately tried to influence government policy and ministerial appointments, while publicly becoming associated with strict personal morality.
She was the last British monarch of the House of Hanover and was succeeded by her son Edward VII.

overview.text: Captain Ahab is a fictional character in Herman Melville’s 1851 novel Moby-Dick. As captain of the whaling ship Pequod, he transforms its voyage into a revenge hunt after the white whale Moby Dick bites off his leg. He wears an ivory prosthesis and pressures the crew to support his mission. Ahab’s obsession drives the novel’s tragic climax: when the whale appears, his hatred overwhelms his caution, and Moby Dick drags him to his death as the Pequod sinks. The character presents fanaticism as a destructive force.

key_facts.text: Scholar Andrew Delbanco describes Ahab as a powerful embodiment of fanaticism; another scholar characterizes him as an almost godlike but ungodly figure.
Ahab’s literary background includes Shakespeare, Milton, biblical and classical figures, and Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s lecture on Hamlet.
His ivory prosthesis has been interpreted as a possible reference to the Oedipus myth.
Ahab influenced J. M. Barrie’s Captain Hook, whose obsession centers on a crocodile rather than a whale.

overview.text: Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) was a Mexican painter known for portraits and self-portraits rooted in Mexican popular culture, nature, and artifacts. Her folk-art style mixed realism with fantasy while addressing identity, gender, class, race, and postcolonialism in Mexican society; she also painted about chronic pain. Often linked with surrealism or magical realism, she also belonged to the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, which sought to define Mexican identity. Rediscovered in the late 1970s, she later became a recognized figure in art history and an icon associated with Mexican and Indigenous traditions and feminist interpretations of the female experience.

key_facts.text: A bus accident at age 18 caused lifelong pain and medical problems; during recovery, Kahlo returned to art after considering a career in medicine.
She married fellow Mexican artist Diego Rivera in 1929.
André Breton arranged Kahlo’s first solo exhibition, in New York in 1938; the Louvre later purchased her painting The Frame.
La Casa Azul, Kahlo’s family home in Coyoacán, is now the Frida Kahlo Museum.

overview.text: Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway follows Clarissa Dalloway through a day in post-First World War London. She prepares for a party she will host that evening, while the narrative moves backward and forward in time to build a picture of her life and the interwar social structure. Through an interior perspective and stream-of-consciousness narration—a style that follows the flow of characters’ thoughts—the novel connects multiple stories and examines how time is experienced personally. The party-day frame and shifting consciousness are its central literary features.

key_facts.text: Woolf published Mrs Dalloway on 14 May 1925.
The novel’s working title was The Hours.
It originated from the short stories “Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street” and the unfinished “The Prime Minister.”
In October 2005, it was included on Time magazine’s list of the 100 best English-language novels written since its first issue in 1923.

overview.text: Apartheid was a system of institutionalized racial segregation imposed in South Africa and South West Africa from 1948 to 1994. It gave political, social, and economic dominance to the white minority and classified South Africans into racial groups. Laws separated public life, controlled interracial relationships, and assigned housing and employment by race.

Apartheid became a major focus of domestic resistance and international condemnation. Negotiations between the National Party and the African National Congress led to non-racial elections in April 1994, but inequality and other social effects of the system continued afterward.

key_facts.text: The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified South Africans as Black, White, Coloured, or Indian, with further subcategories.
Between 1960 and 1983, apartheid laws forcibly removed about 3.5 million Black Africans to segregated areas, including designated bantustans.
The system faced United Nations condemnation and international measures including arms embargoes and economic sanctions against South Africa.
From 1987 to 1993, the National Party negotiated with the ANC to end segregation and introduce majority rule.

overview.text: Rosalind Elsie Franklin (1920–1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose research examined the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, coal, graphite, and viruses. Her work at King’s College London on DNA helped facilitate the correct description of its double-helix structure.

Franklin is especially associated with DNA X-ray diffraction images, including Photo 51, and with the work that led to the DNA double-helix model linked to Francis Crick, James Watson, and Maurice Wilkins. Photo 51 was taken by her student Raymond Gosling, while Wilkins showed it to Watson without Franklin’s permission.

key_facts.text: Franklin earned her Cambridge PhD in 1945 after researching coal at the British Coal Utilisation Research Association.
She became an accomplished X-ray crystallographer during postdoctoral research in Paris before joining King’s College London in 1951.
After moving to Birkbeck College in 1953, Franklin led pioneering research on the molecular structures of viruses.
Her DNA contributions were largely unrecognized during her lifetime, although her work on coal and viruses was appreciated while she lived.
Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at age 37 while working on the structure of tobacco mosaic virus.

overview.text: Fallingwater is a house museum in Stewart Township in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands, designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as a weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr. and Liliane Kaufmann. Its defining feature is its placement partly over a waterfall on the Bear Run stream, connecting the residence closely to its natural setting.

The building is recognized for its projecting outdoor terraces, which are cantilevered—supported at one end—and for its use of local stone, reinforced concrete, steel, and plate glass. Fallingwater is a National Historic Landmark and one of eight Wright buildings included in the World Heritage Site The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright.

key_facts.text: The Kaufmanns hired Wright in 1934, began using the house in 1937, and later commissioned a guest wing completed in 1939.
The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has operated Fallingwater as a public attraction since 1963; tours began in July 1964.
Wright designed most of the house’s built-in furniture, while the interiors also contain art, textiles, and Tiffany glass.
Structural problems, including sagging terraces and poor drainage, prompted major renovations in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

overview.text: John F. Kennedy (JFK) was the 35th U.S. president, a Democrat from Massachusetts who served from 1961 until his assassination in 1963. He was the first Catholic president and the youngest person elected to the office, at age 43. Before becoming president, he served in both houses of Congress and won the 1960 election over Republican Richard Nixon.

Kennedy’s presidency centered on Cold War tensions involving the Soviet Union and Cuba. His administration faced the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which nearly resulted in nuclear war. He was assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963, and Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson succeeded him.

key_facts.text: During World War II, Kennedy commanded PT boats in the Pacific. After PT-109 sank, his rescue of fellow sailors earned him the Navy and Marine Corps Medal.
While serving in the Senate, Kennedy published Profiles in Courage, which won a Pulitzer Prize.
After the Berlin Wall was erected in 1961, Kennedy sent a U.S. Army convoy to reassure West Berlin and gave a major speech there in 1963.
Initiatives associated with his administration included the Peace Corps, the Alliance for Progress with Latin America, and continuation of the Apollo Moon program.
The FBI and Warren Commission concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone in Kennedy’s assassination, while conspiracy theories have continued to circulate.

overview.text: The Chinese zodiac is a traditional classification system tied to the Chinese calendar. It organizes years into a repeating twelve-year cycle of animal signs, each assigned reputed attributes. In Chinese folk belief, a person’s sign is associated with personality. Originating in China, the tradition remains popular in parts of East, Central, and Southeast Asia and among immigrant communities from those regions.

Its resemblance to the Western zodiac is limited: both divide time into twelve parts and connect those divisions with personality or life events, but they are different systems. The Chinese zodiac also reflects traditional Chinese philosophy and folkways, placing it within a broader context of cultural beliefs.

key_facts.text: Beliefs associated with the signs can extend beyond personality to careers, compatibility, marriages, and fortunes.
Two conventions identify the beginning of a zodiac year: Chinese New Year or the start of spring.
The tradition remains popular in countries including Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Malaysia, Mongolia, and Singapore.

overview.text: The Soviet Union (USSR), officially the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, was a multinational federal state spanning much of Eurasia from 1922 until its dissolution in 1991. Governed by the Communist Party through Marxism–Leninism and soviet councils, it had a centrally planned economy and its capital was Moscow.

Its roots lay in the 1917 October Revolution and the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War. Under Stalin, it underwent forced industrialization and severe repression before becoming a decisive Allied power after Germany invaded in 1941. After World War II, rivalry with the United States produced the Cold War, while Soviet influence expanded across Eastern Europe.

key_facts.text: Stalin’s policies of forced collectivization and rapid industrialization coincided with a devastating 1930s famine, the expansion of the Gulag labor-camp system, and the Great Purge.
The Soviet Union suffered around 27 million casualties in World War II, the most deaths of any country, and afterward consolidated a sphere of influence in Central and Eastern Europe.
The Cold War divided the major blocs: NATO formed in 1949, the Warsaw Pact in 1955, and their rivalry included proxy wars and the Cuban Missile Crisis.
Beginning in 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev pursued reform through policies called glasnost and perestroika; nationalist movements and political crises preceded the USSR’s dissolution in 1991.
The Soviet Union was a nuclear superpower with the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, a significant space program, and a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council.

overview.text: Cubism was an early-20th-century avant-garde movement that began in Paris. Rather than showing a subject from one fixed viewpoint, Cubist artists analyzed, fragmented, and reassembled it through multiple perspectives and abstracted geometric forms.

Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque pioneered Cubism together, joined by artists including Juan Gris and Fernand Léger. Its influence extended beyond painting: Cubism helped establish collage as a modern art form and influenced later movements such as Futurism, Dada, Constructivism, De Stijl, and Art Deco.

key_facts.text: Cubist works are associated especially with Paris, including Montmartre, Montparnasse, and nearby Puteaux, during the 1910s and 1920s.
Paul Cézanne’s late work was a primary influence on Cubism; exhibitions and commemorative retrospectives of his paintings were held from 1904 to 1907.
French offshoots of Cubism included Orphism, abstract art, and later Purism.
Cubism also sparked innovations in music, ballet, literature, and architecture.

overview.text: In European folklore, a vampire is an undead, human-like being believed to feed on human vital essence, usually blood. Stories describe vampires returning to communities where they once lived and bringing mischief or death. Older accounts may portray them as shrouded, bloated, and ruddy or dark in appearance, unlike the pale, gaunt image common in modern fiction.

Vampire-like beings appear in cultures around the world, but the term became prominent in Western Europe through 18th-century reports linked to Southeastern and Eastern European beliefs. Today, vampires are generally treated as fictional. John Polidori’s 1819 story The Vampyre helped establish the sophisticated modern type, while Bram Stoker’s 1897 Dracula provided a major basis for later vampire fiction and horror.

key_facts.text: Regional names include shtriga in Albania, vrykolakas in Greece, and strigoi in Romania.
During 18th-century vampire panics, some suspected corpses were pierced with stakes.
A theory linking vampire legends to porphyria received publicity in 1982 but was later largely discredited.
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu’s Carmilla was published in 1872, before Dracula.

overview.text: The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyam is Edward FitzGerald’s 1859 English translation of a selection of Persian quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, the “Astronomer-Poet of Persia” (1048–1131). The familiar English work is therefore FitzGerald’s rendering of poems associated with Khayyam, not an English original by FitzGerald.

After an initially poor commercial reception, FitzGerald’s version gained popularity from 1861 and was widely popular in the English-speaking world by the 1880s. Its reception included multiple editions, Omar Khayyam clubs, and later translation efforts in Hindi and other languages.

key_facts.text: Whitley Stokes helped popularize FitzGerald’s version beginning in 1861.
The third edition, printed in 1872, increased interest in the United States.
The Pre-Raphaelites in England greatly admired FitzGerald’s work.
The work appeared in several hundred editions and inspired translation efforts in Hindi and other languages.

overview.text: Aaron Copland (1900–1990) was an American composer whose open, slowly changing harmonies are associated with vast American landscapes and pioneer imagery. In the 1930s and 1940s, he wrote major works in an accessible style often called “populist,” or, in his own term, “vernacular.” These include the ballets Appalachian Spring, Billy the Kid, and Rodeo, along with Fanfare for the Common Man and the Third Symphony. Copland also composed chamber, vocal, operatic, and film music. Later, he incorporated twelve-tone techniques into works such as Connotations and Inscape.

key_facts.text: Copland studied in Paris with Nadia Boulanger for three years, and her broad musical approach influenced his own broad taste.
During the Great Depression, he shifted from modernist orchestral writing toward a more accessible style in the mid-1930s.
During the Depression years, Copland traveled to Europe, Africa, and Mexico and formed an important friendship with Mexican composer Carlos Chávez.
His serial works include Piano Quartet, Piano Fantasy, Connotations, and Inscape; he used tone rows as sources for melodies and harmonies.
From the 1960s onward, Copland increasingly focused on conducting and made recordings of his own music.

overview.text: Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, in the province of North Holland. Founded at the mouth of the Amstel, where a dam helped control flooding, it grew from a 12th-century fishing village into a major world port during the 17th-century Dutch Golden Age. At that time, it became a center of finance, trade, and secular art. Its canals, narrow gabled houses, and cycling culture remain central features of the city.

key_facts.text: Amsterdam’s canal network is a UNESCO World Heritage Site; the canals contribute to its nickname, “Venice of the North.”
Although Amsterdam is the official capital, the national government and foreign embassies are located in The Hague.
Major cultural landmarks include the Rijksmuseum, the Van Gogh Museum, the Anne Frank House, and the Concertgebouw.
The Amsterdam Stock Exchange was founded in 1602 and is considered the world’s oldest modern securities-market stock exchange.
Notable historical residents include Rembrandt, Vincent van Gogh, Baruch Spinoza, and Anne Frank.

overview.text: “The Road Not Taken” is a narrative poem by Robert Frost centered on paths that diverge, both literally and figuratively. Its interpretation is complex and potentially divergent, so the poem is not confined to one straightforward reading.

key_facts.text: The poem first appeared in the August 1915 issue of The Atlantic Monthly.
It was later published as the first poem in Frost’s 1916 collection Mountain Interval.
The 1915 and 1916 versions differ slightly: line 13 changes “marked” to “kept,” and line 18 replaces a comma with a dash.

overview.text: The Divine Comedy (Italian: Divina Commedia) is an Italian narrative poem by Dante Alighieri, divided into Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Its imagined afterlife reflects the medieval worldview of the Latin Church and helped establish Tuscan as the standardized Italian language. It is regarded as a major work of Italian and Western literature.

The poem examines the soul after death and a system of divine justice in which actions receive fitting punishment or reward. Allegorically, Dante’s journey moves from recognizing and rejecting sin, through penitence, toward ascent to God. The work draws on medieval Catholic theology and Thomistic philosophy.

key_facts.text: Virgil, symbolizing human reason, guides Dante through Inferno and most of Purgatorio. Beatrice then guides him from the end of Purgatorio, while Saint Bernard appears in the final cantos of Paradiso.

The poem was originally titled Comedìa, later adjusted to the modern Italian Commedia. The adjective Divina appears in a biographical work by Giovanni Boccaccio from 1351–1355; the first edition titled Divina Comedia was published in 1555.
The three sections portray Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, corresponding to stages in the soul’s movement toward God.

overview.text: Ronald Wilson Reagan (1911–2004) was an actor and Republican politician who served as the 40th U.S. president from 1981 to 1989. Before entering the White House, he was governor of California, and his 1964 “A Time for Choosing” speech helped establish him as a leading conservative figure.

Reagan’s presidency is associated with Reaganomics, which combined tax and government-spending cuts with economic deregulation, and with a tougher Cold War policy. His administration increased military spending before negotiating with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev; Reagan’s foreign policies also contributed to the Cold War’s end. His tenure marked a realignment toward conservative policies in the United States.

key_facts.text: In 1983, Reagan ordered the U.S. invasion of Grenada.
In 1984, Reagan won reelection by defeating former vice president Walter Mondale in a landslide.
Reagan’s administration secretly and illegally sold arms to Iran to fund the Contras.
During Reagan’s first term, his administration had a slow response to the AIDS epidemic.
Negotiations with Mikhail Gorbachev culminated in the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty.

overview.text: Zero represents an empty quantity and serves as the additive identity: adding or subtracting it leaves a number unchanged. Multiplication by zero always gives zero, so division by zero is generally undefined in arithmetic. This role extends across the integers, rational and real numbers, complex numbers, and other algebraic structures. The expression 0^0 can be undefined, depending on convention.

key_facts.text: As a positional digit, 0 shows that a place contributes no power of the base; in 205, the tens place contributes nothing. The same principle works in binary and hexadecimal notation.
Modern positional use of zero derives from Indian mathematics, reached Europe through medieval Islamic mathematicians, and was popularized by Fibonacci. The Maya used zero independently.
English names for 0 include zero, nought, naught, and nil; historical names include cipher, ought, and aught.
When nearby digits distinguish it from the letter O, zero may be pronounced “oh” or “o.” Informal terms include zilch and zip.

overview.text: A train is a connected set of vehicles that runs on railway tracks to carry people or freight. A locomotive commonly pulls or pushes it, but multiple units and railcars can propel themselves. Passenger and cargo cars may be called carriages, wagons, or railroad cars. Most trains use steel wheels on steel rails; their low friction helps make rail transport efficient. A railway’s gauge is the distance between its rails.

Rail travel grew from horse- or cable-drawn wagonways after steam locomotives emerged in the United Kingdom in 1802. Trains then spread worldwide, moving people and goods over land faster and more cheaply. Diesel and electric locomotives later displaced steam. Today, high-speed, commuter, and freight rail remain important parts of transportation.

key_facts.text: High-speed rail, first built in the 1960s, can compete with cars and airplanes for short- to medium-distance travel.
Commuter rail expanded as an alternative to congested highways, while light rail became more prominent in the 21st century.
Freight trains carry bulk goods such as coal and grain and can reduce road congestion caused by trucks.
Specialized trains include monorails, funiculars and rack railways for steep slopes, and maglevs that use magnetic levitation.

overview.text: Impressionism is a 19th-century visual-art movement that emerged among Paris-based artists and became prominent through independent exhibitions. It is associated with visible brushwork, open compositions, ordinary subjects, unusual viewpoints, and careful attention to light as it changes over time. Rather than treating movement as incidental, Impressionist art makes motion part of how human perception and experience are represented.
The movement met harsh opposition from France’s conventional art community. Its focus on changing light, time, and ordinary subject matter helped define its distinctive approach to visual experience.

key_facts.text: Independent exhibitions brought Paris-based Impressionists to prominence during the 1870s and 1880s.
The movement’s name came from Claude Monet’s painting Impression, Sunrise.
Critic Louis Leroy coined “Impressionism” in a satirical 1874 review of the First Impressionist Exhibition in Le Charivari.
Related styles later developed in other media, including Impressionist music and Impressionist literature.

overview.text: Paul Revere was a Boston-born American silversmith, military officer, and industrialist who supported the Patriot cause during the American Revolutionary War. In 1775, he made a midnight ride to alert nearby minutemen that British troops were approaching before the battles of Lexington and Concord. He also helped organize an intelligence and alarm system to watch British movements.

Revere’s ride became a lasting American folk-hero story after Henry Wadsworth Longfellow dramatized it in his 1861 poem “Paul Revere’s Ride.” After the war, Revere returned to silversmithing and expanded into metalworking, including iron, bronze, and copper production.

key_facts.text: Revere joined the Sons of Liberty and became a strong supporter of the Patriot cause.
He later served as an officer in the Massachusetts Militia; his service ended after the Penobscot Expedition, for which he was absolved of blame.
In 1800, Revere became the first American to successfully roll copper into sheets for naval-vessel sheathing.

overview.text: Odin (Old Norse Óðinn) is a widely revered god in Norse mythology and Germanic paganism. Norse sources portray him as head of the Æsir pantheon and associate him with warfare and the dead. He receives slain warriors, the einherjar, at Valhöll in Asgard. In the mythic future of Ragnarök, he leads them and is killed by Fenrir.

Most surviving stories about Odin come from the 13th-century Prose Edda, the Poetic Edda, and related Old Norse writings. These sources include stories about his role in creating the world and giving life to the first humans.

key_facts.text: Odin is described as long-bearded and sometimes as an old man; he has one eye after sacrificing the other for wisdom.
His animal companions include the ravens Huginn and Muninn and the wolves Geri and Freki.
Odin’s family includes Frigg, his wife, and sons Baldr and Thor; Thor’s mother is the earth-goddess Jörð.
The Prose Edda describes Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé creating the world by killing the primordial being Ymir. Odin also gives life to Ask and Embla, the first humans.
Alongside other Germanic gods, Odin has lent his name to Wednesday in many languages.

overview.text: Minnesota is a state in the Upper Midwest. It borders the Canadian provinces of Manitoba and Ontario, the states of Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota, and South Dakota, and—across Lake Superior—Michigan. Minneapolis and Saint Paul form the “Twin Cities,” the state’s main political, economic, and cultural hub.

Minnesota is associated with the nickname “Land of 10,000 Lakes,” as well as a landscape of forests, prairie, and farmland. It became the 32nd U.S. state in 1858; its name comes from the Dakota language, reflecting the region’s important Native history.

key_facts.text: Minnesota’s official motto is L’Étoile du Nord, meaning “The Star of the North”; it is the only U.S. state motto in French.
French explorers and missionaries were the earliest Europeans to enter the region, where they encountered Dakota, Ojibwe, and other Anishinaabe peoples.
Much of present-day Minnesota was once part of French Louisiana, which the United States acquired in 1803.
Minnesota has 11 federally recognized Native American reservations: seven Ojibwe and four Dakota.

overview.text: Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, with Colombia to the north, Peru to the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean to the west. Its territory also includes the Galápagos Islands, located about 1,000 kilometers west of the mainland. Quito is the capital, while Guayaquil is the largest city. Ecuador’s geography is especially associated with the Galápagos’ distinctive plants and animals; the country is recognized as one of the world’s megadiverse countries.

key_facts.text: The Galápagos Islands form part of Ecuador’s Galápagos Province.
Ecuador became independent in 1820 as part of Gran Colombia and emerged as a sovereign state in 1830.
Spanish is the main official language, and recognized native languages include Quechua and Shuar.
Ecuador’s 2008 constitution legally recognized enforceable rights of nature, a world first according to the source.

overview.text: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, an English author, poet, mathematician, photographer, and Anglican deacon. His central literary works are Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and its sequel, Through the Looking-Glass (1871), both important examples of Victorian literature. Carroll is especially associated with wordplay, logic, and fantasy: “Jabberwocky” and The Hunting of the Snark are literary nonsense poems, and some of Wonderland’s unusual logic reflects his published work on mathematical logic.

key_facts.text: Alice Liddell, daughter of Christ Church dean Henry Liddell, is widely identified as the inspiration for Alice, although Carroll denied this.
Carroll spent most of his life at Christ Church, Oxford, as a scholar, teacher, and Anglican deacon.
He created the word-ladder puzzle Doublets, which appeared in Vanity Fair from 1879 to 1881.
A memorial stone to Carroll was unveiled in Poets’ Corner at Westminster Abbey in 1982.

overview.text: Michelangelo’s David is an Italian Renaissance sculpture carved in marble from 1501 to 1504. Standing 5.17 meters tall, it was the first colossal marble statue made in the High Renaissance and the first since classical antiquity.
David was a favored subject in Florentine art, and this statue soon became a symbol of the defense of civil liberties associated with the 1494 constitution of the Republic of Florence.

key_facts.text: It was originally commissioned as one of twelve prophets for the roofline of Florence Cathedral’s east end.
Instead, it was placed in the public square before the Piazza della Signoria, Florence’s civic-government seat, and unveiled on September 8, 1504.
The statue moved to Florence’s Galleria dell’Accademia in 1873; a replica was installed at its original site in 1910.

overview.text: David is described in the Hebrew Bible and Old Testament as a leader of Judah who became the second king of the united Kingdom of Israel. In the biblical narrative, he begins as a shepherd and harpist, gains fame by defeating the Philistine warrior Goliath, and eventually makes Jerusalem the capital of a united Israel.

David is a major figure in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions. Biblical accounts present both his royal achievements and serious wrongdoing, including his treatment of Bathsheba and Uriah. Many psalms are attributed to him, and later traditions connect him with the Hebrew Messiah, Jesus’s ancestry, and the Islamic prophet-king Dawud.

key_facts.text: After Saul and Jonathan die in battle, David is anointed king first by Judah and eventually by all the tribes of Israel.
David brings the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem and wants to build a temple, but the biblical narrative says he is denied because of the bloodshed during his reign.
David’s son Solomon, born to Bathsheba, succeeds him rather than his eldest surviving son, Adonijah.
The biblical narrative portrays David as arranging the death of Bathsheba’s husband, Uriah the Hittite, after committing adultery with her.
The Quran and hadith describe David as both an Israelite king and a prophet of Allah.

overview.text: In ancient Greek religion, Hera is a goddess associated with marriage, women, and family, and she protects women during childbirth. Greek myth places her among the twelve Olympians and presents her as queen on Mount Olympus; she is both sister and wife of Zeus and daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Stories often emphasize her jealous, vengeful responses to people who offend her, especially Zeus’s lovers and children born outside his marriage.

key_facts.text: Hera was the patron goddess of lawful marriage, presiding over weddings and marital unions.
Her Roman counterpart is Juno.
In art, Hera is often shown as a dignified, crowned or veiled married woman; the cow, cuckoo, and peacock are among her sacred animals.
A pomegranate may appear as one of her symbols, representing immortality.

overview.text: Porgy and Bess is an English-language opera by American composer George Gershwin, with a libretto by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin. It developed through a chain of adaptations: DuBose and Dorothy Heyward’s play Porgy was itself based on DuBose Heyward’s 1925 novel.

First performed in Boston in 1935 before moving to Broadway, the opera follows Porgy, a disabled Black street beggar in Charleston, as he tries to rescue Bess from Crown and Sportin’ Life. Its songs include “Summertime,” which became popular and frequently recorded.

key_facts.text: The production featured a cast of classically trained African-American singers, described as a daring artistic choice for its time.
Crown is Bess’s violent, possessive lover, while Sportin’ Life is her drug dealer.
A 1976 Houston Grand Opera production helped renew the opera’s popularity.
The work was later adapted for smaller performances and became a 1959 film.

overview.text: A square number, or perfect square, is an integer made by multiplying an integer by itself: for example, 9 = 3² = 3 × 3. In the real-number system, square numbers are nonnegative, and a nonnegative integer is a square exactly when its square root is an integer. The standard notation is n², read “n squared.”

Square numbers connect arithmetic with geometry: a square with side length n has area n², and n points can be arranged in a square array when n is a square number. This makes them a type of figurate number, alongside other shape-based number patterns.

key_facts.text: The nth nonnegative square is n²; 0² = 0 is the zeroth square number.
A positive integer with no square divisors other than 1 is called square-free.
Squares can be extended to rational numbers: for example, 4/9 = (2/3)².

overview.text: Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) was an Italian Dominican friar, priest, theologian, and philosopher. He became one of the most influential thinkers in Catholic theology and Western philosophy and gave his name to Thomism, a school joining theology and philosophy.

Aquinas combined Christian principles with ideas from Aristotle. His approach treated both natural reason and religious faith as ways of understanding God, helping connect ancient philosophy with medieval Christian thought. His work continued to influence Catholic thought and later discussions of ethics, aesthetics, and mind.

key_facts.text: His Five Ways are arguments intended to demonstrate the existence of God.
The unfinished Summa Theologiae, written from 1265 to 1274, presents a comprehensive guide to Catholic theology.
Aquinas also wrote commentaries on Christian Scripture and Aristotle and composed Eucharistic hymns used in Catholic liturgy.
He was canonized in 1323 by Pope John XXII and is a Doctor of the Church.
Recognizing titles for Aquinas include Doctor Angelicus (Angelic Doctor) and Doctor Communis (Universal Doctor).

overview.text: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is the United States’ principal federal law-enforcement agency and its domestic intelligence and security service. As part of the Department of Justice and the U.S. Intelligence Community, it combines criminal investigations with counterterrorism and counterintelligence work. Its primary focus is domestic, unlike the CIA, which collects intelligence abroad and has no law-enforcement authority. The FBI also coordinates with foreign security services through offices at U.S. embassies and consulates, though it usually does not conduct unilateral operations overseas.

key_facts.text: The FBI began in 1908 as the Bureau of Investigation and adopted its current name in 1935.
It reports to both the attorney general and the director of national intelligence.
Its jurisdiction covers violations of more than 200 categories of federal crimes.
The FBI maintains a Top Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.
Its headquarters is the J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D.C.

overview.text: California is a Western U.S. state on the Pacific Coast, bordered by Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, and Mexico’s Baja California. Its geography includes coastal cities, the Sierra Nevada, northwest forests, the Mojave Desert, and the fertile Central Valley, producing climates from temperate rainforest to alpine snow and interior desert. Sacramento is the capital, while Los Angeles is the most populous city. California’s broad recognition also comes from its historical transformation after the Gold Rush and from major roles in agriculture, technology, and entertainment.

key_facts.text: California became part of Mexico in 1821, was ceded to the United States in 1848 after the Mexican-American War, and entered the Union as the 31st state in 1850 as a free state.
The 1848 Gold Rush brought major social and demographic changes, including the California genocide.
The Central Valley is a major agricultural region; California leads the nation in agricultural output, with dairy, almonds, and grapes among its named products.
Silicon Valley in the San Francisco Bay Area is a center of the global technology industry, while Hollywood remains an important center of U.S. filmmaking.

overview.text: The Catcher in the Rye is J. D. Salinger’s 1951 American coming-of-age novel. It was partly serialized in 1945–1946 before appearing as a novel, and it presents Holden Caulfield’s account of recent events in his life.

The novel is strongly associated with adolescent angst and alienation, as well as criticism of social superficiality. Its themes include innocence, identity, belonging, loss, connection, sex, and depression; Holden has become an icon of teenage rebellion.

key_facts.text: The work was originally intended for adults but is often read by adolescents.
Holden Caulfield serves as the novel’s main character and narrator.
Its publication history began with serial installments in 1945–1946 and culminated in the 1951 novel.
The novel has been translated widely and has appeared on several major lists of notable English-language fiction.

overview.text: A Doll's House (Et dukkehjem) is Henrik Ibsen's three-act play, first staged in Copenhagen in 1879. Set in a Norwegian town around that time, it examines the constrained life of a married woman in a male-dominated society.

The play centers on the limited opportunities for women's self-fulfillment in its social setting. It became a major public controversy that extended beyond the theater into newspapers and wider society, even though Ibsen denied intending to write a feminist play.

key_facts.text: It premiered at Copenhagen's Royal Danish Theatre on December 21, 1879, after being published earlier that month.
The title is also translated as A Doll House; its Danish and Bokmål title is Et dukkehjem.
Its reception produced a “storm of outraged controversy” that reached newspapers and society outside the theater.
UNESCO placed Ibsen's autographed manuscripts of the play on the Memory of the World Register in 2001 for their historical value.

overview.text: Iron (Fe, from Latin ferrum) is chemical element 26, a transition metal in group 8 of the periodic table. By mass, it is the most common element on Earth, forming much of the planet’s inner and outer core, and it is also abundant in Earth’s crust.

Iron ores require very high-temperature furnaces to yield usable metal. The spread of iron tools and weapons helped mark the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age; today, iron alloys such as steel are widely used because they combine useful mechanical properties with low cost.

key_facts.text: Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form rust. Rust flakes away rather than protecting the underlying metal, allowing corrosion to continue.
Iron’s most common oxidation states are iron(II) and iron(III), though its compounds span oxidation states from −2 to +7.
In the human body, most iron is found in hemoglobin and myoglobin, supporting oxygen transport in blood and oxygen storage in muscles.
Iron is also present at the active sites of many redox enzymes involved in cellular respiration and oxidation-reduction reactions.

overview.text: Benjamin Franklin was an American Founding Father whose career connected colonial society to the creation of the United States. A successful Philadelphia printer and newspaper publisher, he wrote Poor Richard’s Almanack under the name Richard Saunders, helped establish civic and educational institutions, and became the first postmaster general.

Franklin was also a diplomat and statesman: his efforts helped secure French aid during the American Revolution, and he later served as president of Pennsylvania. His research on electricity made him an important figure in the history of physics, while his inventions included the lightning rod, bifocals, glass harmonica, and Franklin stove.

key_facts.text: Franklin charted and named the Gulf Stream current.
He was the only person to sign the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris peace with Britain, and the Constitution.
As deputy postmaster-general for the British colonies, appointed in 1753, he helped create the first national communications network.
Franklin owned slaves earlier in life but later argued against slavery, became an active abolitionist, and promoted African American education and integration.
His portrait appears on the U.S. $100 bill.

overview.text: Cleopatra VII Philopator was queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt from 51 to 30 BCE and its last active Hellenistic pharaoh. She descended from Ptolemy I, a Macedonian Greek general who had served with Alexander the Great. After her death, Egypt became a Roman province, ending the Hellenistic period.

Her reign became closely tied to Rome’s civil wars. After a conflict with her brother Ptolemy XIII, Cleopatra became involved with Julius Caesar and later worked with Mark Antony. Octavian defeated their fleet at Actium in 31 BCE and invaded Egypt; Antony died by suicide, and Cleopatra reportedly killed herself, probably by poisoning.

key_facts.text: Cleopatra’s first language was Koine Greek, but she was the only known Ptolemaic ruler to learn Egyptian; she also knew several other languages.
Her father, Ptolemy XII, named her heir. She initially ruled jointly with her brother Ptolemy XIII, whose conflict with her led to civil war.
Her relationship with Julius Caesar produced Caesarion, whom she later named co-ruler as Ptolemy XV.
The Donations of Alexandria assigned territories to the children of Cleopatra and Antony; Octavian presented this arrangement as treason and used it in the conflict with Antony.
Cleopatra became a recurring subject in Roman and later European art, literature, opera, theater, film, and popular culture.

overview.text: Perseus is a legendary Greek hero and demigod in Greek mythology, the son of Zeus and the mortal Danaë. He is identified as the founder of the Perseid dynasty and as a monster-slaying hero from before the days of Heracles. His major myths involve Medusa and Andromeda.

key_facts.text: Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa while carrying out a task for Polydectes.
He saved Andromeda from Cetus, a sea monster.
Perseus is described as both Heracles’s half-brother and his great-grandfather.

overview.text: Electrical resistance measures how strongly an object opposes the flow of electric current. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω). Conductance is the reciprocal idea: it measures how easily current passes. Resistance is defined as voltage divided by current, R = V/I.

Resistance depends on the material, size, and shape of an object, as well as factors such as temperature or strain. Insulators generally have high resistance, while conductors such as metals generally have low resistance; a wire’s resistance increases when it is made longer and thinner.

key_facts.text: Ohm’s law describes materials in which voltage and current are directly proportional; their resistance remains constant under the relevant conditions, and they are called ohmic materials.
Resistance and conductance are reciprocals: G = 1/R, and conductance is measured in siemens (S).
In devices such as diodes, batteries, light bulbs, and transformers, voltage and current may not be directly proportional. The ratio V/I can still be called static or chordal resistance.
Differential resistance describes the local relationship between voltage and current using dV/dI.
Superconductors are identified here as an exception to ordinary resistance: they have zero resistance.

overview.text: Coal is a black or brownish-black sedimentary rock made mostly of carbon. It forms when dead plants first become peat and are then changed by heat and pressure during millions of years of burial. Many large deposits began in ancient tropical wetlands known as coal forests.

Coal is burned mainly as fuel and became especially important during the Industrial Revolution because of the steam engine. Its extraction and combustion harm human health and the environment, including through carbon dioxide emissions that contribute to climate change.

key_facts.text: In 2020, coal supplied about one-quarter of the world’s primary energy and more than one-third of its electricity.
Coal is also used in some iron- and steel-making and other industrial processes.
Coal burning produced more than 15 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2024, over one-quarter of global greenhouse-gas emissions.
China mines almost half of the world’s coal and is its largest consumer and importer; Indonesia and Australia are leading exporters.

overview.text: Franz Joseph Haydn (1732–1809) was an Austrian composer of the Classical period. He played a major role in the development of chamber music, especially the string quartet and piano trio, and became associated with the development of the symphony and sonata form.

After early work as a cathedral chorister and freelance musician, Haydn spent much of his career directing music for the wealthy Esterházy family at Eszterháza in rural Hungary. His isolation there encouraged originality, while publication spread his music widely. His notable symphonic works include the Paris and London symphonies; late works include the oratorios The Creation and The Seasons.

key_facts.text: Haydn mentored Mozart and taught Beethoven; the three are sometimes called the First Viennese School.
Haydn’s elder brother was the composer Michael Haydn.
Haydn died in Vienna in 1809 at age 77, after spending his final years in poor health and unable to compose.

overview.text: Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer, conductor, and pianist whose work expanded the symphony, piano sonata, and string quartet. He helped move Western art music from the Classical style associated with Haydn and Mozart toward the Romantic period. Born in Bonn, he moved to Vienna at 21, studied composition with Joseph Haydn, and established a reputation as a virtuoso pianist.

Beethoven’s career is commonly divided into early, middle, and late periods. He began experiencing hearing loss around 1798. His later period included the Ninth Symphony, Missa solemnis, innovative piano works, and late string quartets, while his music as a whole remains among the most performed in the world.

key_facts.text: His Third Symphony is known as the Eroica; it premiered in 1805 and was unusually large in scale and scope.
The Fifth Symphony premiered in 1808 during Beethoven’s middle period.
The Moonlight Sonata, dedicated to his pupil Julie Guicciardi, is among Beethoven’s most popular works.
The Ninth Symphony premiered in 1824 and was an early major example of a choral symphony.
Beethoven’s other notable works include the opera Fidelio, the Violin Concerto, and the Seventh Symphony.

overview.text: The trumpet is a brass wind instrument. A player produces its sound by vibrating their lips against a mouthpiece, and modern trumpets generally use three valves to change pitch. The most common trumpet is pitched in B-flat.

Trumpets appear in orchestras, concert bands, chamber groups, jazz ensembles, popular music, and school bands. The trumpet family also includes higher and lower instruments, such as the piccolo trumpet and bass trumpet.

key_facts.text: Trumpet-like instruments were used for signaling in battle and hunting before they began serving as musical instruments in the late 14th or early 15th century.
A B-flat trumpet is a transposing instrument: its written notes sound a whole step lower than written.
The piccolo trumpet has the highest register in the brass family, while the bass trumpet sounds an octave below a standard B-flat or C trumpet.
The cornet resembles the trumpet but has a conical bore, while the trumpet has a cylindrical bore.

overview.text: Baghdad is Iraq’s capital and largest city, located on the Tigris River in central Iraq. It is also a major financial, commercial, governmental, and cultural center. [p1, p4]

Founded in 762 by al-Mansur, Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and an intellectual and cultural center during the Islamic Golden Age. Its House of Wisdom was among the city’s important academic institutions. The Mongol Empire largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258, beginning a long period of decline. [p2]

key_facts.text: The site had settlements dating back at least to the Neo-Babylonian period before al-Mansur founded Baghdad. [p2]
During the Abbasid era, Baghdad’s population reached more than one million, making it one of the world’s largest cities at the time. [p2]
Baghdad’s post-1258 decline lasted for centuries and was linked to plagues and changing control by successive empires. [p2]
Historic Baghdad included mosques, churches, mandis, and synagogues, reflecting its long religious diversity. [p4]

overview.text: Don Quixote is Miguel de Cervantes’s Early Modern Spanish novel about Alonso Quijano, a hidalgo from La Mancha who becomes Don Quixote de la Mancha after immersing himself in chivalric romances. He adopts the role of a knight-errant, hoping to restore chivalry and serve his nation. His companion, Sancho Panza, is a farm laborer who becomes his squire.

The novel contrasts Don Quixote’s imagined world of knightly adventures with ordinary reality, while Sancho’s grounded wit contrasts with his master’s elevated rhetoric. Published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, it is considered a foundational work of Western literature and the first modern novel.

key_facts.text: The work was written in Early Modern Spanish.
“Hidalgo” refers here to a member of the lowest nobility; Alonso Quijano is the protagonist’s original name.
The novel’s influence appears in direct references in Alexandre Dumas’s The Three Musketeers and Edmond Rostand’s Cyrano de Bergerac, as well as in the word “quixotic.”

overview.text: Notre-Dame de Paris is a medieval Catholic cathedral and basilica on the Île de la Cité, an island in the Seine. Dedicated to the Virgin Mary, it serves as the cathedral church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Paris and is a major example of French Gothic architecture.

Its architecture is known for rib vaults, flying buttresses, enormous colorful rose windows, and abundant sculptural decoration. The cathedral is also widely recognized as a symbol of Paris and France.

key_facts.text: Construction began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully, and the cathedral was largely completed by 1260.
Victor Hugo’s 1831 novel Notre-Dame de Paris helped inspire a restoration supervised by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc from 1844 to 1864.
A fire in April 2019 caused serious damage and led to extensive repairs; the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
Since 1905, the French government has owned Notre-Dame, while the Roman Catholic Church has exclusive rights of use.

overview.text: The Battle of Actium was a naval engagement fought on 2 September 31 BC in the Ionian Sea near Actium, Greece. Octavian’s fleet, commanded by Marcus Agrippa, faced the combined fleets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra during their long rivalry.

Octavian’s victory allowed him to consolidate power over Rome and its territories. His later titles, Princeps and Augustus, are associated with the transition that historians generally view as the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire.

key_facts.text: Agrippa helped cut Antony’s southward communications with Egypt through the Peloponnese before the battle.
Antony’s fleet tried to break through the straits of Actium, but Octavian’s smaller, more maneuverable ships routed it.
Octavian later defeated the remaining forces at Alexandria on 1 August 30 BC; Antony and Cleopatra then took their own lives.

overview.text: “Ode on a Grecian Urn” is a poem by the English Romantic poet John Keats, written in May 1819. Its speaker addresses an ancient Greek urn and considers the images shown on it, exploring the relationship between material art and ideal or worldly reality.

The poem focuses on two pictured moments: a lover pursuing his beloved and a village sacrifice involving villagers and a priest. It closes by giving the urn a message for future generations—“Beauty is Truth, Truth Beauty”—a line that has prompted sustained critical debate.

key_facts.text: The poem was first published anonymously in Annals of the Fine Arts for 1819.
It is one of Keats’s “Great Odes of 1819,” alongside poems including “Ode to a Nightingale” and “Ode to Psyche.”
The poem consists of five stanzas, each containing ten lines.
After finding existing poetic forms unsatisfactory for his purpose, Keats presented a new development of the ode form in his collection of Great Odes of 1819.
Contemporary critics initially received the poem poorly, but it began to be praised by the mid-19th century.

overview.text: The Tale of Genji (Genji Monogatari) is a classic work of Japanese literature, said to have been written by the noblewoman, poet, and lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu around the peak of the Heian period, in the early 11th century. It has gained global recognition and holds a cultural stature in Japan compared with that of Shakespeare’s works in English.

The work depicts the lives of high Heian courtiers. Its opening section follows the early life and romantic encounters of Hikaru Genji, the emperor’s son who is removed from succession for political reasons and made a commoner with the surname Minamoto. Later sections cover his old age and death before shifting to his grandson Niou and supposed son Kaoru.

key_facts.text: The text is written mostly in hiragana, a phonetic script associated with women’s writing of the period, rather than kanji, the script used for more prestigious literature.
The original manuscript no longer survives; more than 300 later copies exist, with varying reliability.
Its original physical format was concertina-style orihon: sheets pasted together and folded alternately in opposite directions.
Arthur Waley produced an almost complete English translation from 1925 to 1933, omitting chapter 38; later translators produced complete versions.

overview.text: Isoroku Yamamoto was an admiral of the Imperial Japanese Navy and commander-in-chief of its Combined Fleet from 1939 until his death in 1943. He led the fleet during the opening of the Pacific War, a period that included both early Japanese successes and defeats.

His experiences in the United States led him to stress the importance of oil and industrial capacity in modern naval warfare, and he believed Japan had little hope of defeating the United States. Tasked with planning a war strategy, he favored a surprise attack, carried out at Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

key_facts.text: Yamamoto lost two fingers while serving in the Russo-Japanese War at the Battle of Tsushima.
He studied at Harvard University and later served as Japan’s naval attaché in Washington.
As navy vice minister, he opposed Japan’s 1940 alliance with Germany and Italy in the Tripartite Pact.
The Battle of Midway in June 1942 halted Japan’s early naval gains after four Japanese carriers were sunk.
In April 1943, U.S. code breakers intercepted Yamamoto’s flight plans, enabling U.S. Army Air Forces aircraft to shoot down his plane and kill him.

overview.text: A glacier is a persistent body of natural ice that moves under its own weight. It forms where snow accumulation exceeds ablation over many years. As it flows and deforms, a glacier abrades bedrock and debris, helping create landforms such as cirques, moraines, and fjords.

Most glacial ice lies in polar ice sheets, while mountain glaciers occur across much of the world. Glacial ice is Earth’s largest freshwater reservoir, and seasonal meltwater can support plants, animals, and human communities when other water sources are limited. Changes in glacier mass are also sensitive indicators of climate change and contribute to sea-level variation.

key_facts.text: Glaciers originate on land, unlike sea ice and lake ice, although they may flow into bodies of water.
About 99% of Earth’s glacial ice is contained in polar ice sheets, also called continental glaciers.
Dense glacier ice can appear blue because pressure removes air bubbles and the ice absorbs other colors more readily than blue.

overview.text: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish author, poet, and playwright who became a key figure in late-19th-century Aestheticism, a movement emphasizing the value of art. He gained fame in London for his literary range, epigrams, and sharp public wit.

Wilde is associated especially with the Gothic novel The Picture of Dorian Gray and society comedies such as An Ideal Husband and The Importance of Being Earnest. After his 1895 conviction and imprisonment, he wrote De Profundis during imprisonment and The Ballad of Reading Gaol afterward.

key_facts.text: The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890) was Wilde’s only novel; it develops themes of decadence, duplicity, and beauty.
Wilde wrote Salome in French in 1891, but it was not licensed for the English stage because biblical subjects could not be portrayed there.
At Trinity College Dublin and Oxford, Wilde studied the classics and became associated with Aestheticism through tutors including Walter Pater and John Ruskin.
De Profundis, written during Wilde’s last year in prison, is a long letter reflecting on his spiritual journey through his trials.
The Ballad of Reading Gaol (1898), written after Wilde’s release in France and Italy, commemorates the harshness of prison life.

overview.text: Mexico, officially the United Mexican States, is a country in North America and the northernmost country in Latin America. It borders the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the southeast. Its maritime boundaries reach the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Caribbean Sea to the southeast, and the Gulf of Mexico to the east, giving it both continental and maritime geographic associations.

key_facts.text: Mexico covers 1,972,550 square kilometers and is identified as the world’s 13th-largest country by land area.
Mexico City is both the national capital and the country’s largest city.
Mexico is a federation of 32 states, with government organized at federal, state, and municipal levels.

overview.text: DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) is a colorless, almost odorless crystalline organochloride first developed as an insecticide. Its effectiveness led to use during World War II against malaria and typhus and to heavy reliance in WHO anti-malaria campaigns during the 1950s and 1960s. Widespread use later drew scrutiny because of environmental and health concerns, including threats to wildlife.

Rachel Carson’s 1962 book Silent Spring helped focus opposition to agricultural DDT and contributed to the 1972 U.S. ban on agricultural use. International rules later formalized a worldwide agricultural-use ban, while allowing WHO-guided public-health use in malaria-prone countries when effective alternatives are not feasible. DDT therefore remains associated with both disease control and environmental controversy.

key_facts.text: Othmar Zeidler first synthesized DDT in 1874; Paul Hermann Müller discovered its insecticidal action in 1939 and received the 1948 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for that discovery.
DDT was available for public sale in the United States by October 1945 and was promoted for agricultural and household use.
The Stockholm Convention formalized a worldwide ban on agricultural use, in effect since 2004; public-health use within WHO guidelines is exempt.
DDT still has limited use in disease-vector control because it kills mosquitoes and can reduce malaria infections. WHO guidance requires confirming that mosquitoes lack DDT resistance before use.

overview.text: Africa is the world’s second-largest and second-most populous continent. It straddles the equator and prime meridian and is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea, Atlantic Ocean, and Indian Ocean. Madagascar and other archipelagos are also part of the continent.

Africa has a long, varied history and is widely accepted as the origin of modern humans and the great apes. Its societies have included major kingdoms and empires such as ancient Egypt, Mali, Asante, Kongo, and Great Zimbabwe, alongside diverse traditions of oral history, art, music, religion, cuisine, and dress.

key_facts.text: Africa includes 54 fully recognized sovereign states; Algeria is the largest by area, while Nigeria is the largest by population.
The African Union provides a framework for cooperation among African nations and is headquartered in Addis Ababa.
Africa has the greatest number of megafauna species of any continent, but faces desertification, deforestation, water scarcity, pollution, and severe climate vulnerability.
Modern humans are believed to have originated in Africa roughly 350,000–260,000 years ago.
Most present-day African states emerged through decolonization after World War II, generally retaining colonial-era borders.

overview.text: The Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) is a proposed amendment to the U.S. Constitution intended to guarantee equal legal rights regardless of sex. It is not currently part of the Constitution. The amendment became increasingly prominent alongside the U.S. women’s movement of the 1960s and remains associated with debates over how the law should treat men and women.

The ERA’s supporters argued that it would end legal distinctions involving areas such as employment, property, and divorce. Opponents argued that it could remove special protections for women, including workplace protections, and potentially expose women to military conscription.

key_facts.text: Alice Paul and Crystal Eastman wrote the ERA, which was first introduced in Congress in December 1923.
Representative Martha Griffiths reintroduced it in 1971; the House approved it that year and the Senate approved it in 1972, sending it to the states under Article V.
Congress set a 1979 ratification deadline and later extended it to 1982. The ERA remained three states short of the 38 needed for ratification when both deadlines passed.
Early debate included class differences: many middle-class women supported the amendment, while some working-class advocates favored continuing special protections for women workers.

overview.text: Officially the Republic of the Philippines, the Philippines is an archipelagic country in Southeast Asia in the western Pacific Ocean. Its islands are organized into three broad geographical divisions—Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao—and lie among major surrounding seas, giving the country a distinctly maritime regional setting.

Its location near the Pacific Ring of Fire and the equator connects its physical geography with exposure to earthquakes, monsoon rains, and typhoons. The Philippines also has globally significant biodiversity, making both environmental variety and natural hazards important geographic associations.

key_facts.text: The archipelago has about 7,641 islands and covers about 300,000 square kilometers.
The South China Sea borders it to the west, the Philippine Sea to the east, and the Celebes Sea to the south.
Manila is the capital, while Quezon City is the most populous city; both are within Metro Manila.
The Philippines shares maritime borders with Taiwan, Japan, Palau, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, and China.

overview.text: The waltz is a ballroom and folk dance that originated in German-speaking regions of Europe during the 18th century. It is performed in triple meter (3/4 time), typically with dancers in closed position. In late-18th- and early-19th-century publications, the waltz could be grouped under the broad label “German Dance,” along with the ländler and allemande. Its core associations are German-speaking Europe, triple time, and traditional closed-position dancing.

key_facts.text: The name comes from the German word Walzer, meaning “to roll or revolve.”
The waltz belongs to both ballroom and folk-dance traditions.
Older publications sometimes grouped the waltz, ländler, and allemande under the generic term “German Dance.”

overview.text: Oxidation is the electron-losing half of a redox (reduction–oxidation) reaction: a substance is oxidized when it loses electrons or its oxidation state increases. Reduction happens at the same time elsewhere in the reaction, when another substance gains electrons or its oxidation state decreases.

This concept connects oxidation states to familiar chemistry. In rusting, iron’s oxidation state rises as the metal becomes an oxide, while oxygen accepts the released electrons. Redox chemistry underlies cellular respiration, photosynthesis, combustion, metal corrosion, batteries, electrochemical cells, and several industrial processes, making oxidation a recurring idea in biology, energy, and materials.

key_facts.text: Redox reactions can involve electron transfer or atom transfer; electron-transfer reactions are often described using redox couples and electrode potentials.
Industry uses redox chemistry to extract metals from ores by smelting and to electroplate objects.
Redox reactions are used to manufacture chemicals such as nitric acid.
Redox gradients help drive the cycling of elements in soils, sediments, and water.

overview.text: A proton is a positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus of every atom. Along with neutrons, it is a nucleon. The number of protons is an element’s atomic number, making the proton count the key identifier of an element and a determinant of its electron arrangement and chemical characteristics.

Modern particle physics classifies the proton as a composite hadron rather than an elementary particle. Its quarks are held together by the strong-interaction fields associated with quantum chromodynamics; these binding effects account for most of its mass.

key_facts.text: Its common symbol is p, and its electric charge is +1 elementary charge; H+ is another notation used for it.
Each proton contains two up quarks and one down quark. Their charges combine to give the proton its net positive charge.
Ernest Rutherford gave the name “proton” to the hydrogen nucleus in 1920, following earlier work involving nitrogen nuclei.
Free protons are used in proton-therapy accelerators and in particle-physics experiments, including work at the Large Hadron Collider.
A proton is slightly less massive than a neutron and about 1,836 times as massive as an electron.

overview.text: Otto von Bismarck was a German statesman and diplomat who rose through Prussian politics, oversaw German unification, and served as the German Empire’s first chancellor from 1871 to 1890. His Realpolitik—associated with firm governance and power-balancing diplomacy—earned him the nickname “Iron Chancellor.”

Prussia’s wars against Denmark, Austria, and France helped clear the way for a North German Confederation and then a unified empire under Prussian rule. As chancellor, Bismarck used domestic policies as well as diplomacy: he created a welfare state to weaken socialist opponents and fought the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf, a conflict he later ended.

key_facts.text: The Kulturkampf was unsuccessful: Catholics formed the powerful Centre Party, and Bismarck later allied with it against the Socialists.
Bismarck concentrated political power in a strong bureaucracy and the Junker elite, while sidelining the Imperial Reichstag.
He was dismissed by Wilhelm II and then retired to write his memoirs.
Bismarck became a hero to German nationalists, while critics condemned his persecution of Catholics and authoritarian rule.

overview.text: Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863) was a French Romantic artist regarded as a leader of the French Romantic school. His approach contrasted with Neoclassical perfectionism: he emphasized color and movement over clear outlines and carefully modeled forms, while dramatic and romantic subjects became central to his mature work.

Delacroix’s expressive brushwork and study of optical color effects influenced the Impressionists, while his interest in exotic subjects inspired Symbolist artists. He also worked as a muralist and lithographer and illustrated works by Shakespeare, Walter Scott, and Goethe.

key_facts.text: His influences included Rubens, Venetian Renaissance painters, Théodore Géricault, and Lord Byron.
