key_facts.text: The theory developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s; notable contributors included Alexei Starobinsky, Alan Guth, and Andrei Linde.
Many physicists connect inflation with explanations for the universe’s flatness and the absence of observed magnetic monopoles.
The hypothetical field responsible for inflation is called the inflaton, but its detailed particle-physics mechanism remains unknown.

COBE observations from 1992 found nearly scale-invariant temperature-anisotropy spectra predicted by inflationary models; WMAP results are described as strong evidence, although some scientists dissent.

overview.text: Oxygen is the highly reactive nonmetal with symbol O and atomic number 8. At standard conditions, it occurs mainly as dioxygen (O₂), a colorless, odorless gas made of two covalently bonded oxygen atoms. It readily forms oxides with many elements and compounds.

Oxygen is central to life and Earth’s atmosphere: eukaryotic organisms use it in cellular respiration to obtain energy, while photosynthesis continually replenishes atmospheric oxygen. Oxygen also occurs widely in Earth’s crust as part of compounds such as water, silicates, and iron oxides.

key_facts.text: Ozone, O₃, is a less common allotrope of oxygen. In the lower stratosphere, it helps shield the biosphere from harmful ultraviolet radiation; at the surface, it is an air pollutant.
Priestley called oxygen “dephlogisticated air,” while Antoine Lavoisier later recognized it as an element and correctly explained its role in combustion.
Industrial oxygen is used in steelmaking, welding and metal cutting, rocket propellant, oxygen therapy, and life-support systems.

overview.text: Mary Flannery O’Connor was an American novelist, short-story writer, and essayist associated with a sardonic Southern Gothic style. Her writing often uses regional settings, grotesque characters, and violent situations.

Her work frequently reflects her Catholic faith while examining morality, ethics, and grace. O’Connor described her stories as showing grace acting on characters who resist it, though readers may experience them as harsh, hopeless, or brutal.

key_facts.text: She lived from March 25, 1925, to August 3, 1964.
She wrote two novels and 31 short stories, along with reviews and commentaries.

Her stories’ drama is typically underpinned by an unsentimental acceptance or rejection of characters’ limitations or differences, including those related to disability, race, crime, religion, or sanity.
The posthumously compiled Complete Stories won the 1972 U.S. National Book Award for Fiction.

overview.text: The Lernaean Hydra, also called the Hydra of Lerna, is a serpentine lake monster in Greek and Roman mythology. It lived at Lerna in the Argolid and was defeated by Heracles as the second of his Twelve Labours.

The Hydra was especially difficult to defeat because later versions of the myth gave it regenerative heads: cutting one off caused two to grow back. Heracles needed help from his nephew Iolaus, who used fire to burn the necks after the heads were removed.

key_facts.text: Hesiod makes the Hydra a child of Typhon and Echidna.
Its breath and blood were described as poisonous, with even its scent said to be deadly.
Accounts disagree about the exact number of heads the Hydra possessed.
The Greek phrase meaning “cutting off a hydra” referred to a hopeless or endlessly futile task.

overview.text: The Stanford prison experiment, also called the Zimbardo prison experiment, was a controversial psychological study conducted at Stanford University in August 1971. It was designed as a two-week simulation of prison life to examine how situational conditions affected participants’ behavior. Twenty-four selected volunteers were randomly assigned to act as prisoners or guards.

The study became associated with worsening psychological abuse by the guards and ended on its sixth day after psychologist Christina Maslach challenged the conditions. It is important in discussions of research ethics, but its scientific validity and interpretation remain disputed: later researchers had difficulty reproducing it, and critics alleged that the guards were encouraged to behave in ways that supported the planned conclusions.

key_facts.text: Recruiters offered male college students $15 per day to participate in a study of prison life; 24 volunteers were selected after psychological assessments.
The guards received uniforms intended to reduce their individuality and were told to prevent prisoners from escaping.
The simulated prisoners were arrested by real Palo Alto police before the study officially began.
The experiment is often discussed as an unethical study, and the harm associated with such research contributed to stronger university requirements for reviewing experiments involving human subjects.

overview.text: The Attack on Pearl Harbor was Japan’s surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on Oahu, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, while the United States was still neutral in World War II. Japanese commander Isoroku Yamamoto planned it as a preemptive strike meant to keep the Pacific Fleet from interfering with Japan’s planned actions in Southeast Asia. The attack followed months of U.S.–Japanese negotiations involving sanctions, China, and access to resources.

The raid damaged all eight U.S. battleships present and sank four, killing 2,403 Americans. The United States declared war on Japan the next day, and Franklin D. Roosevelt famously called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy.”

key_facts.text: Japanese planners used the names Hawaii Operation, Operation AI, and Operation Z for the attack.
The attack came in two waves involving 353 Japanese aircraft launched from six aircraft carriers.
The three U.S. aircraft carriers assigned to Pearl Harbor were at sea, and the base’s oil-storage and repair facilities were not attacked.
Pearl Harbor was part of a wider offensive that also struck the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
After Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11, the United States declared war on both countries.

overview.text: The bassoon is a woodwind instrument with a distinctive sound and a range centered in the tenor and bass registers. In its modern form, it emerged in the 19th century and became a prominent voice in orchestral, concert-band, and chamber music; it also appears occasionally in pop, rock, and jazz. Its broad range and versatility allow it to take varied musical roles in both large ensembles and smaller chamber groups.

key_facts.text: A modern bassoon is usually made of wood and consists of six pieces.
Sound comes from air making the instrument’s reed vibrate as the player blows while shaping the embouchure—the way the lips are positioned.
The two modern bassoon systems are the Buffet, or French, system and the Heckel, or German, system.
Bassoonists usually play while seated with a seat strap, though a harness allows standing performance.

overview.text: The Beat Generation was a postwar literary subculture whose writers challenged conventional narrative and economic materialism. Its recurring concerns included spiritual searching, interest in American and Eastern religions, candid portrayals of human experience, sexual liberation, and experimentation with psychedelic drugs.

Major Beat works include Allen Ginsberg’s Howl, Jack Kerouac’s On the Road, and William S. Burroughs’ Naked Lunch. Several central figures later gathered in San Francisco, and elements of the movement influenced the 1960s hippie and broader counterculture movements.

key_facts.text: The early core included Herbert Huncke, Allen Ginsberg, William S. Burroughs, Lucien Carr, and Jack Kerouac, who met around Columbia University in 1944.
A 1950s “Beatnik” subculture grew around the movement, though major Beat authors often viewed that subculture critically.
Neal Cassady helped connect the Beat and hippie generations through his role driving Ken Kesey’s bus Furthur; Ginsberg also participated in 1960s hippie culture.

overview.text: An alpha particle is a group of two protons and two neutrons, identical to the nucleus of a helium-4 atom. It is generally produced through alpha decay and is a form of particle radiation. Alpha particles strongly ionize matter but have low penetration at standard radioactive-decay energies, so they travel only short distances through air or tissue.

key_facts.text: The symbol for an alpha particle is α; it can also be written as He²⁺, a helium ion missing two electrons.
Alpha particles have net spin zero and typically carry about 5 MeV of kinetic energy when produced in standard radioactive decay.
At standard decay energies, a few centimeters of air or the skin can stop alpha particles.
Higher-energy helium nuclei, including some cosmic rays, can penetrate much farther than alpha particles from ordinary nuclear decay.

overview.text: The Great Depression was a severe worldwide economic downturn lasting from 1929 to 1939. It began in the United States around the Wall Street crash of 1929 and spread through falling production, international trade, employment, and confidence in financial institutions. Bank and business failures, poverty, and unemployment made it a major social as well as economic crisis.

In the United States, the crisis intensified as spending and manufacturing declined. After defeating Herbert Hoover in 1932, Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced New Deal programs beginning in 1933 to provide relief and create jobs. The Depression’s exact causes remain debated, including the stock-market crash, earlier economic weaknesses, and failures of monetary policy.

key_facts.text: The Depression followed the speculative boom of the Roaring Twenties, when loose lending, widespread debt, and limited bank regulation increased economic vulnerability.
By 1933, U.S. unemployment had reached 25%, and about one-third of farmers had lost their land.
From 1929 to 1932, worldwide GDP fell by an estimated 15%, while international trade fell by more than half and prices declined in a pattern known as deflation.
In Germany, severe unemployment contributed to political extremism and helped the Nazi Party rise to power in 1933.
The outbreak of World War II in 1939 stimulated factory production and employment, ending the Depression according to the supplied account.

overview.text: RYB—red, yellow, and blue—is a subtractive color model for paint and pigment in art and applied design. Traditional color theory treats these as primary colors, and the model influenced artists, designers, and art-school teaching, including Bauhaus-related education. Its practical role is to use a limited set of pigments as a starting point for exploring many mixed colors. RYB concerns paint rather than light, so it differs from RGB and from the more accurate CMY model used for paint, pigment, and ink.

RYB remains used in artistic settings, although it is scientifically obsolete under a definition of complementary colors requiring a neutral or black mixture. It can still be treated as an approximation of the CMY model.

key_facts.text: Mixing RYB primaries produces the secondary colors orange, green, and purple.
The model emerged when access to many pigments was limited by availability and cost, encouraging artists to explore color through mixing.
Art and design instruction often added white and black to the primary pigments, enabling tints, shades, and a broader range of colors.
Traditional color theory associated RYB with Moses Harris, Michel Eugène Chevreul, Johannes Itten, and Josef Albers.

overview.text: I. M. Pei (Ieoh Ming Pei; 1917–2019) was a Chinese-American architect born in Guangzhou. He studied at MIT and Harvard Graduate School of Design, worked for New York real-estate developer William Zeckendorf, and founded an independent design firm in 1955.

Pei designed the John F. Kennedy Library in Massachusetts, Dallas City Hall, and the East Building of the National Gallery of Art. In Paris, he created a controversial glass-and-steel pyramid for the Louvre. His international work also included the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong and museums in Japan, China, Qatar, and Luxembourg.

key_facts.text: Pei’s first major recognition came from the Mesa Laboratory at the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado, designed in 1961 and completed in 1967.
He returned to China in 1975 to design a hotel at Fragrant Hills and later designed the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong.
Pei received the Pritzker Prize in 1983, the AIA Gold Medal in 1979, and the first Praemium Imperiale for Architecture in 1989.
He retired from full-time practice in 1990 and afterward worked mainly as an architectural consultant with his sons’ firm.

overview.text: “The Library of Babel” (Spanish: La biblioteca de Babel) is a short story by Argentine author and librarian Jorge Luis Borges. It imagines a universe formed as a vast library containing all possible 410-page books written in a defined format and character set. The library is therefore the story’s central premise, not merely its setting.
The story first appeared in Spanish in 1941 in El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (The Garden of Forking Paths), a collection later included in Ficciones.

key_facts.text: The Spanish title is “La biblioteca de Babel.”
Jorge Luis Borges lived from 1899 to 1986 and was both an author and a librarian.
Ficciones was published in 1944 and included the collection in which the story first appeared.
Two English translations appeared around 1962: one in Labyrinths and one in a translation of Ficciones.

overview.text: Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China on the southern coast, just south of Shenzhen. Its territory includes Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, and the New Territories.

Its modern identity reflects both colonial history and global commerce. Britain expanded the colony after Qing China ceded Hong Kong Island, and the territory was transferred to China in 1997. Hong Kong remains a major financial centre and commercial port, with separate governing and economic systems from mainland China under “one country, two systems.”

key_facts.text: Hong Kong was occupied by Japan from 1941 to 1945 during World War II.
The Hong Kong dollar is the territory’s currency.
Hong Kong has a highly developed, skyscraper-filled urban environment and severe housing pressure.
Public transport accounts for more than 90 percent of usage in Hong Kong.

overview.text: “The Second Coming” is a poem by Irish poet William Butler Yeats that uses Christian imagery associated with the Apocalypse and the Second Coming to frame an allegorical portrayal of post-war Europe. It is considered a canonical work of modernist poetry. For recognition, connect its title and author with religious imagery, post-war European atmosphere, and modernist literary history.

key_facts.text: Yeats wrote the poem in 1919.
It was first printed in The Dial in November 1920.
The poem appeared in Yeats’s 1921 collection Michael Robartes and the Dancer.
It has been reprinted in collections including The Norton Anthology of Modern Poetry.

overview.text: Ulysses is a modernist novel by Irish writer James Joyce. It follows three Dubliners—including Stephen Dedalus, Leopold Bloom, and Molly Bloom—through a single day in Dublin. The title invokes Homer’s Odyssey, linking Joyce’s characters to figures from that epic.

The novel is notable for its stream-of-consciousness technique, which presents characters’ thoughts and perceptions alongside their speech and actions. Joyce also uses shifting styles, puns, parodies, epiphanies, and literary allusions, helping make Ulysses a classic of modernist literature. Its subjects include sexuality, antisemitism, Catholicism, Irish nationalism, and British rule in Ireland.

key_facts.text: Ulysses was serialized in The Little Review from 1918 to 1920 and published in full in Paris by Sylvia Beach on February 2, 1922.
The novel’s single day is June 16, 1904; readers commemorate it annually as Bloomsday.
Its title is the Latinized form of Odysseus: Leopold Bloom parallels Odysseus, Molly Bloom parallels Penelope, and Stephen Dedalus parallels Telemachus.
Ulysses attracted controversy, including a 1921 obscenity trial in the United States and later disputes over the authoritative text.

overview.text: Odysseus is a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer’s Odyssey. He also plays an important role in the Iliad and related works of the Greek epic cycle. His defining quality is mêtis, or “cunning intelligence”: he is portrayed as brilliant, guileful, and versatile. The Odyssey centers on his nostos, or homecoming, which takes ten eventful years after the decade-long Trojan War.

key_facts.text: Odysseus is also known by the Latin name Ulysses.
His wife is Penelope, and his son is Telemachus.
His parents are Laërtes and Anticlea.
An epithet for him is “Odysseus the Cunning,” reflecting his mêtis, or cunning intelligence.

overview.text: Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky (1882–1971) was a Russian composer and conductor who later held French and American citizenship. A pivotal figure in modernist music, he is centrally associated with three ballets commissioned by Sergei Diaghilev for the Ballets Russes: The Firebird, Petrushka, and The Rite of Spring (1910–1913).

Stravinsky’s career is often divided into Russian, neoclassical, and serial periods. Across these phases, he moved from Russian styles and folklore to classical forms and themes, then to twelve-tone methods. His stylistic versatility influenced later composers and encouraged new approaches to rhythm and musical form.

key_facts.text: While studying law at the University of Saint Petersburg, Stravinsky studied music with Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov until Rimsky-Korsakov’s death in 1908.
The Rite of Spring’s 1913 premiere nearly caused a riot because of its avant-garde nature; the work later affected ideas about rhythmic structure.
In his neoclassical period, Stravinsky used sonata form in Octet and drew on Greek mythology in works including Apollon musagète and Oedipus rex.
In his serial period, he adopted twelve-tone techniques associated with Arnold Schoenberg and the Second Viennese School.
His innovations influenced composers including Aaron Copland, Philip Glass, Béla Bartók, and Pierre Boulez, particularly in rhythm and musical form.

overview.text: Truman Garcia Capote, born Truman Streckfus Persons, was an American novelist, screenwriter, and playwright. He is also regarded as one of the founders of New Journalism. His professional career began with short stories and later included novels, plays, and journalistic work.

His literary work includes Other Voices, Other Rooms (1948), Breakfast at Tiffany’s (1958), and In Cold Blood (1966). The first is a novel; the second is a novella about the fictional New York café-society girl Holly Golightly; and the third is a journalistic work about the murder of a Kansas farm family in their home.

key_facts.text: Capote lived from September 30, 1924, to August 25, 1984.
The success of his 1945 short story “Miriam” attracted Random House publisher Bennett Cerf and led to a contract for Other Voices, Other Rooms.
He spent six years writing In Cold Blood, aided by his lifelong friend Harper Lee, who wrote To Kill a Mockingbird (1960).

overview.text: Nighthawks portrays four people in a downtown diner late at night, viewed through the diner’s large glass window. Light from the diner illuminates a darkened, deserted urban streetscape, creating a central visual contrast between a bright interior and an empty city. The work is associated with Edward Hopper and is described as one of the most recognizable paintings in American art.

key_facts.text: It is a 1942 oil-on-canvas painting.
Nighthawks is classified as part of the American Realism movement.
Within months of its completion, it was sold to the Art Institute of Chicago for $3,000.

overview.text: Quartz is a hard mineral composed of silica, or silicon dioxide (SiO2). Its atoms form a continuous framework of silicon–oxygen tetrahedra, so quartz is classified as a framework silicate and, compositionally, as an oxide mineral.

Quartz matters in earth science because it is abundant and has a distinctive hardness. It also occurs in many varieties, some valued as gemstones, and has long been used in jewelry and hardstone carving.

key_facts.text: Quartz defines 7 on the Mohs hardness scale, a qualitative scratch test for material hardness.
The two forms are α-quartz and high-temperature β-quartz. Their transformation occurs at 573 °C and can cause microfractures because of a significant volume change.
Quartz makes up about 12% by mass of Earth’s lithosphere and is described as the second most common mineral or mineral group there.

overview.text: Giacomo Puccini (1858–1924) was an Italian composer known primarily for opera. His early music grew from traditional late-nineteenth-century Romantic Italian opera, while his later work developed toward verismo, a style associated with realism. He also came from a long family line of composers reaching back to the late Baroque era.

The core works to recognize are La bohème, Tosca, Madama Butterfly, and Turandot. The first three date from 1896, 1900, and 1904; Turandot is dated 1926, was unfinished, and was completed after Puccini’s death by Franco Alfano.

key_facts.text: Puccini belonged to a family of composers whose lineage extended to the late Baroque era.
His work began in traditional late-nineteenth-century Romantic Italian opera before developing toward verismo.
La bohème, Tosca, and Madama Butterfly are dated 1896, 1900, and 1904, respectively.
Turandot was unfinished at Puccini’s death and was completed posthumously by Franco Alfano; it is dated 1926.

overview.text: T cells, or T lymphocytes, are immune-system cells central to adaptive immunity. A T-cell receptor on their surface distinguishes them from other lymphocytes. They arise from stem cells in bone marrow and mature in the thymus, which gives them their name. After leaving the thymus, they continue differentiating into specialized types that shape immune responses.

Two major functional groups are CD8+ cytotoxic, or “killer,” T cells and CD4+ helper T cells. CD8+ cells can directly kill virus-infected and cancer cells, while CD4+ cells activate other immune cells. Regulatory T cells help maintain tolerance, preventing immune attacks against the body’s own cells.

key_facts.text: The CD4 and CD8 labels come from proteins found on the surfaces of these T-cell types.
CD4+ helper T cells include helper 1, helper 2, helper 17, and regulatory subtypes, distinguished by the cytokines they secrete.
Regulatory T cells are also called suppressor T cells; cancer cells can exploit them to reduce immune recognition of tumors.

overview.text: Plant roots are organs of vascular plants that anchor the plant and take in water and nutrients. Most grow below the soil surface, but roots may also be aerial—above ground—or aerating, growing especially above water. By securing the plant and supplying materials needed by its body, roots help plants grow taller and faster.

key_facts.text: Roots are modified plant organs specialized for anchorage and absorption.
Aerial roots grow above ground, while aerating roots grow especially above water.
Root uptake includes both water and nutrients.

overview.text: Gustave Flaubert was a French novelist associated with literary realism and a highly exacting approach to style and aesthetics. His literary profile centers on Madame Bovary, while his Correspondence is another work for which he is known. He is also connected to Guy de Maupassant, who was his protégé. These associations link Flaubert’s fiction, prose style, and literary mentorship.

key_facts.text: He lived from 12 December 1821 to 8 May 1880.
Madame Bovary, published in 1857, was his debut novel.
He has been considered a leading exponent of literary realism in France and abroad.
Flaubert is known for his Correspondence and his scrupulous devotion to style and aesthetics.
Guy de Maupassant was Flaubert’s protégé.

overview.text: Rama, also called Ram, is a major Hindu deity and the seventh avatar of Vishnu. He is the heroic protagonist and central figure of the Ramayana, and is especially important to Vaishnavism.

In Valmiki’s Ramayana, Rama marries Sita, undergoes a 14-year forest exile, and faces her kidnapping by the demon-king Ravana. Many Hindus see his life as illustrating dharma, or dharmic living; his legends have inspired commentaries, literature, and performance arts.

key_facts.text: Rama’s birth, battle victory, and return to Ayodhya are celebrated through Rama Navami, Vijayadashami, and Diwali, respectively.
According to the Ramayana, Rama was born in Ayodhya to Dasaratha and Kausalya.
After his 14-year forest exile, Rama assumed the throne of Kosala.
Jain and Buddhist traditions also recount stories about Rama, though their versions differ from Hindu accounts; Jain texts may call him Pauma or Padma.

overview.text: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 near Waterloo, then in the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and now in Belgium. Napoleon Bonaparte’s French Imperial Army faced two Seventh Coalition armies: a British-led force commanded by Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington, and a Prussian army led by Gebhard von Blücher.

During Napoleon’s Hundred Days return to power, he tried to defeat Wellington and Blücher separately before they could unite. At Waterloo, Wellington’s army resisted repeated French attacks while arriving Prussian forces struck the French flank. The French army was routed, and the defeat ended Napoleon’s return, leading to his abdication four days later and the end of the First French Empire.

key_facts.text: Waterloo was also called the Battle of Mont-Saint-Jean in France and La Belle Alliance in Prussia.
The battle followed Napoleon’s victory over much of the Prussian Army at Ligny and the separate fighting at Quatre Bras on 16 June 1815.
The Anglo-allied army included forces from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Hanover, Brunswick, and Nassau.
Napoleon’s final attack used senior battalions of the Imperial Guard, but the Guard was repulsed as the coalition armies broke the French position.
Coalition forces entered Paris on 7 July 1815 after Napoleon’s defeat.

overview.text: Mozart’s Requiem in D minor, K. 626, is a Requiem Mass begun in Vienna in late 1791. Mozart died on 5 December 1791 before finishing it, making its unfinished state a central part of the work’s identity.

The surviving autograph contains a finished Introit and drafts for the Kyrie, Sequence, and Offertorium. Joseph Eybler and Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed portions of the remainder, while later composers and musicologists created additional versions.

key_facts.text: Count Franz von Walsegg commissioned the Requiem for a February 1792 service commemorating his wife Anna.
Walsegg probably intended to present the Requiem as his own composition, but a public benefit performance for Mozart’s widow, Constanze, disrupted that plan.
Stories about a mysterious messenger and Mozart supposedly writing music for his own funeral are attributed to Constanze’s accounts and are not established facts.
At least 19 alternative completions have been made, including eleven dating from after 2005.

overview.text: Katsushika Hokusai was a Japanese ukiyo-e artist, painter, and printmaker of the Edo period. His woodblock series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji includes the iconic The Great Wave off Kanagawa. Hokusai helped expand ukiyo-e beyond portraits of courtesans and actors into a broader art featuring landscapes, plants, and animals.
Hokusai’s art also became important beyond Japan: his work influenced Vincent van Gogh and Claude Monet during the late-19th-century European interest in Japanese art known as Japonisme.

key_facts.text: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji was connected both to a domestic travel boom in Japan and to Hokusai’s personal interest in Mount Fuji.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa and Fine Wind, Clear Morning were the prints most associated with establishing Hokusai’s fame in Japan and overseas.
Besides woodblock prints, Hokusai worked in painting and book illustration and produced paintings, sketches, prints, and picture-book images.
He began working as a young child and continued developing his style until his death at age 88.

overview.text: In Greek mythology, the Minotaur is a legendary human-bull creature associated with King Minos of Crete. It lived at the center of the Labyrinth, an elaborate maze made at Minos’s command, and the Athenian hero Theseus ultimately killed it. The story’s central recognition chain links Minos, the maze, Ariadne, and Theseus: Ariadne gave Theseus a golden thread that helped him navigate the Labyrinth. In the tradition, Athens was forced to provide young people as sacrificial victims for the Minotaur in retribution for the death of Minos’s son Androgeus.

key_facts.text: The Minotaur is also called Asterion or Asterius.
The Labyrinth was designed by the architect Daedalus and his son Icarus at King Minos’s command.
The Athenian tribute consisted of fourteen young nobles—seven men and seven women—sent every nine years.
The Roman poet Ovid described the creature as partly man and partly bull.

overview.text: Miles Davis (1926–1991) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, composer, and painter. Across a career of nearly five decades, he helped shape several major jazz styles, including bebop, cool jazz, hard bop, modal jazz, avant-garde jazz, and jazz fusion. His influence also reached rock, funk, classical music, and hip-hop.

Davis is closely associated with the Birth of the Cool sessions, the Spanish-influenced orchestral album Sketches of Spain, and Kind of Blue, a highly popular 1959 jazz recording. He also led changing ensembles featuring major musicians such as John Coltrane, while repeatedly moving into new musical territory.

key_facts.text: Davis began playing trumpet in his early teens and made his professional debut with Charlie Parker’s bebop quintet from 1944 to 1948.
The Birth of the Cool sessions helped develop cool jazz, while Davis’s early-1960s work with arranger Gil Evans included Sketches of Spain.
In the 1970s, Davis experimented with rock, funk, African rhythms, and electronic technology; his 1970 album Bitches Brew helped spark renewed commercial interest in jazz fusion.
After a five-year retirement caused by poor health, Davis returned in the 1980s with younger musicians and pop-influenced sounds.

overview.text: Los Angeles, often called L.A. or LA, is a major Southern California city beside the Pacific Ocean. Most of the city lies in the Los Angeles Basin, with parts extending through the Santa Monica Mountains and into the San Fernando Valley. It is the county seat and largest city of Los Angeles County.

The city developed from Tongva lands into a Spanish-founded settlement, then became part of Mexico and later the United States. Oil discoveries and the Los Angeles Aqueduct helped drive its growth. Today, Los Angeles has a diverse economy associated with film and television production, a major container port, and cultural institutions.

key_facts.text: Los Angeles was founded on September 4, 1781, under Spanish governor Felipe de Neve, on the village of Yaanga.
Los Angeles became part of the United States in 1848 through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, following the Mexican-American War.
Oil discoveries in the 1890s brought rapid growth, while the Los Angeles Aqueduct, completed in 1913, supplied water from Eastern California.
Los Angeles hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984 and is scheduled to host them again in 2028.

overview.text: Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, is a landlocked, hilly country in Central Europe. It borders Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia and has a mostly temperate continental and oceanic climate. Prague is its capital and largest city; Brno, Ostrava, Plzeň, and Liberec are other major urban areas. Czechia emerged from the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia: on 31 December 1992, the former federation’s constituent states became the independent Czech Republic and Slovakia.

key_facts.text: Bohemia is a historical name for Czechia.
The Czech lands underwent significant industrialization during the 19th century.
Following World War I and the collapse of Austria-Hungary, most of the Czech lands joined the First Czechoslovak Republic in 1918.
The Velvet Revolution in November 1989 ended communist rule and restored democracy.

overview.text: Netflix is an American subscription video-on-demand service that distributes films and television programs. Its catalog includes both original and acquired screen content, making on-demand streaming its central association.

The streaming service launched in 2007, after Netflix, Inc. had begun a DVD-by-mail movie-rental business nearly a decade earlier. Netflix’s history therefore spans both physical-media rental and internet streaming.

key_facts.text: Its films and television programs cover various genres.
Netflix is available internationally and in multiple languages.
By 2022, Netflix Original productions accounted for half of its U.S. library.
The company expanded into publishing mobile video games through its flagship service.

overview.text: Vaccines are biological preparations that provide active acquired immunity against a particular infectious or malignant disease. They commonly contain weakened or killed microbes, toxins, or surface proteins that resemble part of a disease-causing organism. These agents stimulate the immune system to recognize the threat and respond to it during later encounters. Vaccination is the administration of a vaccine.

Vaccines can be prophylactic, meaning they help prevent or lessen a future infection, or therapeutic, meaning they fight a disease that has already developed. Widespread vaccination was largely responsible for the worldwide eradication of smallpox and helped restrict diseases such as polio, measles, and tetanus across much of the world.

key_facts.text: Edward Jenner described cowpox’s protective effect against smallpox and developed the first vaccine; “vaccine” derives from a term meaning cowpox.
Smallpox was the first disease for which a vaccine was produced. Earlier smallpox-inoculation practices were recorded in China and later spread to Britain.
Some vaccines can produce sterilizing immunity, in which infection itself is prevented.
The science of developing and producing vaccines is called vaccinology.

overview.text: Japan is an East Asian country whose early history moved from Jōmon and Yayoi societies to rule by an imperial court. Buddhism arrived from the Korean kingdom of Baekje, while Chinese influence shaped Japanese writing, government, religion, and art.

From the twelfth century, shōguns and daimyō held political power, with samurai enforcing their rule. Tokugawa unification in 1600 was followed by the forced opening of trade in 1853 and the restoration of imperial power in 1868. Meiji Japan industrialized and built an overseas empire; its defeat in World War II and Allied occupation until 1952 preceded rapid economic growth. Modern Japan is a constitutional monarchy and major industrial power.

key_facts.text: The Taika Reforms of 645 and the Taihō Code helped establish the ritsuryō system, a Chinese-style centralized government.

The Nara period saw compilation of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. After the capital moved to Heian-kyō in 794, the Heian period became associated with distinctly indigenous Japanese culture and The Tale of Genji.

Japan entered World War II as an Axis power after invading China and attacking the United States and European colonial powers. After defeat and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, it surrendered in 1945.
Japan’s constitutional system includes a bicameral legislature called the National Diet, and its constitution renounces the right to declare war.

overview.text: Japan is an island country in East Asia, situated in the Pacific Ocean off the northeastern coast of the Asian mainland. Its archipelago extends about 3,000 kilometers northeast to southwest and contains many islands. Rugged, heavily forested terrain leaves much of the population and agriculture concentrated in coastal lowlands and urban areas.

Japan lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, making earthquakes, tsunamis, and volcanic eruptions important features of its geography. Climate varies substantially across the archipelago: Hokkaido has cold, snowy winters, while the Ryukyu and Nanpō Islands are subtropical; seasonal snowfall and rainfall also differ among coastal regions.

key_facts.text: Japan’s listed main islands are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, and Okinawa; Okinawa is part of the Ryukyu Islands.
Tokyo is Japan’s capital and largest city.
Lake Biwa is Japan’s largest freshwater lake.
Mountains in Chūgoku and Shikoku protect the Seto Inland Sea from seasonal winds, helping give it mild weather throughout the year.

overview.text: The Liberty Bell, formerly called the State House Bell, is a Philadelphia symbol of American independence. Commissioned in 1752 for the Pennsylvania State House—now Independence Hall—it summoned lawmakers and alerted citizens to public meetings and proclamations.

Abolitionist societies adopted the name “Liberty Bell” in the 1830s, after which the bell became associated with the American Revolution. Its distinctive large crack appeared sometime in the first half of the nineteenth century. It is now displayed across from Independence Hall in the Liberty Bell Center at Independence National Historical Park.

key_facts.text: The bell bears the inscription “Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants Thereof.”
It cracked soon after arriving in Philadelphia and was recast twice by local workmen John Pass and John Stow.
The bell was likely among those rung when the Declaration of Independence was read publicly on July 8, 1776, but no contemporary account confirms this.

After World War II, the National Park Service took custody while Philadelphia retained ownership. The bell moved from Independence Hall to a nearby pavilion in 1976 and to the Liberty Bell Center in 2003.

overview.text: Vietnam, officially the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam, lies on the eastern edge of Mainland Southeast Asia. It borders China, Laos, and Cambodia and lies along the Gulf of Thailand and the South China Sea, where some maritime borders are shared or disputed. Hanoi is the capital, while Ho Chi Minh City is the largest city.

key_facts.text: Vietnam covers about 331,000 square kilometres.
Early states developed in the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam during the first millennium BC.
Vietnam’s historical southward expansion reached the Mekong Delta and involved the conquest of Champa.

overview.text: Sri Lanka, officially the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, is an island country in South Asia. It lies in the Indian Ocean, separated from India by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. Colombo is the executive, judicial, and largest city, while nearby Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital.

The island has a recorded history stretching back more than 3,000 years. Formerly called Ceylon, it became independent in 1948 and a republic in 1972. Its position and deep harbors helped make it an important trading center, including during the Anuradhapura period.

key_facts.text: Sri Lanka’s main ethnic groups include the Sinhalese and Tamils, associated primarily with the Sinhala and Tamil languages.
European colonial powers that controlled parts of the island included Portugal, the Netherlands, and Britain.
Sri Lanka’s civil war, fought between the government and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, lasted from 1983 to 2009.
Sri Lanka is a member of regional and international organizations including SAARC, the Commonwealth of Nations, and the Non-Aligned Movement.

overview.text: Florida is a southeastern U.S. state whose main peninsula lies between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. It borders Alabama and Georgia, while the Straits of Florida and The Bahamas lie to the south and southeast. Major population centers include Miami, Jacksonville, Tampa Bay, Orlando, and the capital, Tallahassee.

Florida’s climate ranges from subtropical in the north to tropical in the south. Its distinctive natural geography includes Everglades National Park, the Florida Reef—the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States—and habitats for animals such as manatees, alligators, and the Florida panther. Beach resorts and amusement parks make tourism a major association of the state.

key_facts.text: Florida has the longest coastline among the contiguous U.S. states, measuring about 1,350 miles before counting its many barrier islands.
St. Augustine, founded by Spain in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States.
Florida became the 27th U.S. state on March 3, 1845.
Florida was a principal setting of the Seminole Wars, which lasted from 1816 to 1858.

overview.text: Billie Eilish Pirate Baird O'Connell is an American singer-songwriter known for a distinctive sound and vocal style that often uses layered vocals and harmonies. She first gained public attention with “Ocean Eyes,” written and produced by her brother, Finneas O'Connell.

Her debut album, When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go? (2019), established major recognition through “Bad Guy,” which topped the US Billboard Hot 100. Eilish also writes music for films, including the James Bond song “No Time to Die” and “What Was I Made For?” from Barbie.

key_facts.text: Eilish released the successful debut EP Don't Smile at Me in 2017.
Her second studio album, Happier Than Ever (2021), included “My Future,” “Therefore I Am,” and “Your Power.”
She won Academy Awards for co-writing “No Time to Die” and “What Was I Made For?”
She became the youngest winner of both the Grammy Album of the Year and Record of the Year awards.

overview.text: Comedy is a genre of dramatic works designed to be humorous or amusing, chiefly by inducing laughter. It can appear in books as well as theatre, film, television, radio, and stand-up comedy, so the term covers a range of entertainment media rather than one format.

key_facts.text: Comedy seeks humor or amusement by inducing laughter.
Books and stand-up comedy are both forms or media in which comedy can appear.
Other associated media include theatre, film, television, and radio.

overview.text: T. S. Eliot (Thomas Stearns Eliot) was an American-born poet, essayist, and playwright who became a British subject after moving from St. Louis to England. He was a leading figure in English-language modernist poetry, known for changing poetic language, style, and verse structure.
Eliot also wrote critical essays that reexamined established cultural beliefs and produced plays, connecting his work to literary criticism as well as poetry and theater.

key_facts.text: The 1915 poem The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock first brought Eliot widespread attention.
Major poems include The Waste Land (1922), The Hollow Men (1925), Ash Wednesday (1930), and Four Quartets (1943).
His plays include Murder in the Cathedral (1935) and The Cocktail Party (1949).
Eliot received the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature for his pioneering contribution to poetry.

overview.text: Simón Bolívar (1783–1830) was a Venezuelan military officer and statesman who led independence campaigns against the Spanish Empire in several South American territories. Known as El Libertador (“the Liberator”), he is associated with the independence of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru, and Bolivia.

After returning from exile, Bolívar rebuilt his revolutionary movement and helped defeat Spanish forces across the region. Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, and Panama were united in Gran Colombia, whose presidency Bolívar held. Later political difficulties led to his resignation, and he died of tuberculosis in 1830.

key_facts.text: Born in Caracas to a wealthy criollo family, Bolívar lost both parents as a child and encountered Enlightenment philosophy while living in Spain.
After exile in Jamaica, Bolívar went to Haiti, where revolutionary leader Alexandre Pétion provided support after Bolívar promised to abolish slavery in Spanish America.
Bolivia was named after Bolívar, and Venezuela is associated with the name “Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela.”

overview.text: The Andes, also called the Cordillera de los Andes, are the world’s longest continental mountain range. They form a continuous highland along South America’s western edge and extend through Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, and Venezuela. The range includes multiple mountain groups and high plateaus, especially the Altiplano, and is divided into the Tropical, Dry, and Wet Andes by climate.

The Andes contain major high-elevation cities and some of the planet’s most remarkable peaks. Aconcagua in Argentina is the range’s highest summit, while Ecuador’s Chimborazo is farther from Earth’s center than any other surface location because of the equatorial bulge. The Andes also form part of the American Cordillera, the connected mountain system along the western Americas and Antarctica.

key_facts.text: The Andes are the highest mountain range outside Asia.
Aconcagua rises to about 6,961 meters (22,838 feet).
The Altiplano is the world’s second-highest plateau, after the Tibetan Plateau.
Ojos del Salado, on the Chile–Argentina border, is one of the Andes’ high volcanoes and reaches about 6,893 meters.

overview.text: Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English mathematician and physicist whose work helped establish classical mechanics, the framework for describing motion and forces. His 1687 book *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* formulated laws of motion and universal gravitation, connecting the behavior of objects on Earth with celestial motion and explaining phenomena such as planetary orbits and tides.

Newton shared credit with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz for formulating infinitesimal calculus, though he developed it earlier. In optics, he studied how prisms separate white light into visible colors, built the first reflecting telescope, and collected this work in *Opticks* (1704). Newtonian mechanics was later superseded by relativity, but remains useful for low speeds and weak gravitational fields.

key_facts.text: The *Principia*’s full English title is *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*; it was first published in 1687.
Newton built the first reflecting telescope.
His empirical law of cooling was an early heat-transfer formulation and became a formal basis of convective heat transfer.

overview.text: Beowulf is an anonymous Old English epic rooted in Germanic heroic legend. Set in pagan Scandinavia during the fifth and sixth centuries, it follows Beowulf, a Geatish hero who aids the Danish king Hrothgar when Grendel attacks Heorot, the king’s mead hall. Beowulf defeats Grendel and later Grendel’s mother; after becoming king of the Geats, he fights a dragon and is mortally wounded.

The poem’s mixture of a pagan Scandinavian setting and Christian elements has prompted debate about how and when it was composed and transmitted. Scholars have considered early oral composition, later Christian authorship, and intermediate possibilities.

key_facts.text: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex. The manuscript has no original title; the modern name comes from its protagonist.
The composition date is uncertain, but the surviving manuscript was produced between AD 975 and 1025.
The poem is written mostly in Late West Saxon Old English, with additional dialect forms suggesting a complex transmission across England.
Beowulf has been translated extensively into prose, rhyme, and alliterative verse; modern translators include Seamus Heaney.

overview.text: Swan Lake (Russian: Лебединое озеро) is a ballet composed by Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky in 1875–76. Its scenario, initially in two acts, draws on Russian and German folk tales and centers on Odette, a princess cursed by an evil sorcerer to become a swan. Although the ballet initially failed, it is now described as one of the most popular ballets of all time. Many companies base their performances on the 1895 revival by Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov, whose version included a revision of Tchaikovsky’s score by Riccardo Drigo.

key_facts.text: The first performance was given by the Bolshoi Ballet on 4 March 1877 at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theatre.
Julius Reisinger choreographed the original production.
The Petipa–Ivanov revival was first staged for the Imperial Ballet on 15 January 1895 at St. Petersburg’s Mariinsky Theatre.
Riccardo Drigo revised Tchaikovsky’s score for the 1895 revival.

overview.text: Sweden, formally the Kingdom of Sweden, is a Nordic country on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe, with Stockholm as its capital and largest city. Its historical profile connects Scandinavian state formation with the rise of a major European power.

A unified Swedish state emerged in the late 10th century. Sweden later joined the Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway, then left it in 1523. Its intervention on the Protestant side in the Thirty Years’ War began an expansion that produced the Swedish Empire, a European great power until the early 18th century.

key_facts.text: During its great-power era, Sweden controlled much of the Baltic Sea.
Most Swedish-held territories outside the Scandinavian Peninsula were lost during the 18th and 19th centuries.
Sweden lost its eastern half, present-day Finland, to Imperial Russia in 1809.
In 1814, Sweden forced Norway into a personal union that lasted until 1905.

overview.text: Sweden, formally the Kingdom of Sweden, is a Nordic country on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. It borders Norway and Finland and has a maritime border with Denmark. Because the country stretches from 55°N to 69°N, it has a varied climate.

A unified Swedish state emerged in the late tenth century. Sweden joined Denmark and Norway in the Kalmar Union in 1397 and left it in 1523. Its participation in the Thirty Years’ War began an expansion that produced the Swedish Empire, a major European power until the early eighteenth century with control over much of the Baltic Sea.

key_facts.text: Sweden’s eastern half, present-day Finland, was lost to Imperial Russia in 1809.
Sweden’s last direct war was in 1814, when it forced Norway into a personal union that lasted until 1905.
Sweden is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy; its legislature is the unicameral Riksdag.

overview.text: Diwali (also called Dipavali) is primarily a Hindu festival of lights, with related observances in Jainism and Sikhism. It symbolizes the spiritual victory of dharma over adharma, light over darkness, good over evil, and knowledge over ignorance. Celebrations generally last five or six days and fall around mid-October to mid-November, during the Hindu lunisolar months of Ashvin and Kartika.

Religious associations vary by tradition and region. One Hindu tradition connects Diwali with Rama’s return to Ayodhya with Sita and Lakshmana after defeating Ravana; the festival is also linked with Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, and Ganesha, associated with wisdom and removing obstacles. Jains connect their Diwali with Mahavira’s final liberation, while Sikhs observe Bandi Chhor Divas in connection with Guru Hargobind’s release from Mughal imprisonment.

key_facts.text: Celebrants illuminate homes, temples, and workplaces with diyas (oil lamps), candles, and lanterns; rangoli designs decorate floors.
Hindus in particular observe ritual oil baths at dawn during the festival.
Celebrations include family feasts and mithai, as well as community fairs, parades, music, and dance.
Regional practice differs: Hindus in eastern India and Bangladesh generally worship Kali, while Newar Buddhists worship Lakshmi.
Diwali is also a major cultural event for Hindu, Sikh, and Jain diasporas.

overview.text: Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday commemorating the Maccabean Revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE. Its historical focus is the Maccabees’ recovery of Jerusalem and the Second Temple.

Beginning on 25 Kislev, Hanukkah lasts eight nights and days. Its central ritual uses a nine-branched menorah: eight ceremonial lights plus a shamash, or “attendant,” used to light them. The holiday also has broad cultural significance, especially in the Western world, where its seasonal proximity to Christmas has influenced gift-giving customs among American Jews.

key_facts.text: Hanukkah is the only Jewish holiday that begins in Kislev and concludes in Tevet.
Common customs include playing dreidel, reciting Jewish prayers, listening to Hanukkah music, and eating fried foods such as latkes and sufganiyot.
The holiday was originally instituted as a feast modeled on Sukkot, but it does not carry Sukkot’s corresponding obligations and is relatively minor in strictly religious terms.
Since the 1970s, the Chabad movement has organized public menorah lightings in communities around the world.

overview.text: Cerberus is a multi-headed dog in Greek mythology who guards the gates of the Underworld. His role is to keep the dead from leaving, making him a distinctive guardian figure in stories about the realm of the dead. Cerberus is especially associated with Heracles, who captured him as the final task among his twelve labors.

key_facts.text: Cerberus is also called the hound of Hades.
He is described as the offspring of the monsters Echidna and Typhon.
His usual form has three heads, a serpent tail, and snakes growing from his body.

overview.text: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) was an English novelist and poet who also worked as an architect. He is associated with Victorian realism, and both his novels and poetry show Romantic influence, including that of William Wordsworth. Hardy criticized aspects of Victorian society, especially the declining position of rural people in Britain.

Hardy’s novels frequently center on tragic characters struggling with their passions and social circumstances. Many are set in Wessex, a semi-fictional region rooted in a medieval Anglo-Saxon kingdom and later expanded across parts of southwest and south-central England. Although his novels first made him famous, he wrote poetry throughout his life and regarded himself primarily as a poet.

key_facts.text: His novels include Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Return of the Native (1878), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d’Urbervilles (1891), and Jude the Obscure (1895).
Hardy’s first poetry collection appeared in 1898, despite his writing poetry throughout his life.
Younger Georgian poets regarded Hardy as a mentor; after his death, Ezra Pound, W. H. Auden, and Philip Larkin praised his poems.
Hardy’s Wessex eventually included parts of Dorset, Wiltshire, Somerset, Devon, Hampshire, and Berkshire.

overview.text: Feng shui is a traditional form of geomancy that originated in ancient China. Its name literally means “wind-water.” It connects landscapes, bodies of water, and built spaces with the movement of qi, described as a universal or cosmic current. Its scope includes architectural, geographical, topographical, cosmological, astronomical, and astrological dimensions.

Historically, feng shui helped determine the orientation of buildings, dwellings, and spiritually significant structures such as tombs. In modern Western settings, it has often been narrowed to interior-design advice associated with health and wealth, while Western philosophy of science generally regards it as non-scientific.

key_facts.text: Qi is presented as a cosmic current whose flow through places and structures can be influenced by landscapes and bodies of water.
Feng shui has been applied not only to homes and buildings but also to tombs and other spiritually significant structures.
Its modern global adoption has been complex, with criticism from historical religious opponents, Chinese revolutionaries, and modern skeptics.
Some scientific skeptics classify feng shui more narrowly as a pseudoscience.

overview.text: A pendulum is a weight suspended from a pivot that swings freely. When displaced sideways, gravity provides a restoring force that pulls it toward equilibrium, producing back-and-forth oscillation. Its period—the time for one complete cycle—depends on the pendulum’s length and, somewhat, the width of its swing; the period is measured in seconds.

Regular pendulum motion made it useful for timekeeping and scientific instruments. Pendulums are used in accelerometers and seismometers, and historically served as gravimeters for measuring the acceleration of gravity and as standards of length.

key_facts.text: Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1656.
The Shortt-Synchronome clock achieved accuracy of about one second per year before quartz clocks superseded it as a time standard in the 1930s.
The word “pendulum” comes from the Neo-Latin pendulus, meaning “hanging.”

overview.text: Lemurs are wet-nosed primates in the superfamily Lemuroidea, found naturally only on Madagascar. Most have pointed snouts, large eyes, and long tails, live in trees, and are active at night. Although they resemble monkeys and apes, they evolved independently from them.

Madagascar’s strongly seasonal climate helped produce exceptional lemur diversity. Lemurs also matter to science because their combination of ancestral and other primate traits can provide insight into primate and human evolution.

key_facts.text: Lemuroidea includes eight families, 15 genera, and around 100 living species.
Living lemurs range from the 30-gram mouse lemur to the 9-kilogram indri. More than a dozen larger “giant lemur” species became extinct after humans arrived on Madagascar.
Lemurs often live in groups called troops and communicate especially through scents and vocalizations; female social dominance is also common.
Habitat loss and hunting threaten many lemurs. The ring-tailed lemur is an iconic flagship species for conservation.

overview.text: The 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry, popularly called the Rough Riders, was one of three volunteer regiments raised in 1898 for the Spanish-American War and the only one of the three to see combat. The United States mobilized these forces after the sinking of USS Maine, amid its war against Spain over colonial policies in Cuba.

Although organized as cavalry, the regiment fought in Cuba as light infantry because its horses were not sent there. Leonard Wood commanded it first; after his promotion, Theodore Roosevelt became closely associated with the unit, which was then called Roosevelt’s Rough Riders. The regiment is especially remembered for the Battle of San Juan Hill and the publicity that later made it legendary.

key_facts.text: “Wood’s Weary Walkers” referred to the regiment’s first commander, Leonard Wood, and its unexpected service without horses.
Theodore Roosevelt served as Wood’s second in command after previously serving as Assistant Secretary of the Navy; he later became president.
The regiment attracted a varied group, including Ivy League athletes, singers, Texas Rangers, and Native Americans; recruits had to be skilled horsemen and eager for combat.
The name “Rough Riders” was borrowed from Buffalo Bill’s traveling show, titled Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and Congress of Rough Riders of the World.

overview.text: The Gospel of John is the fourth canonical Gospel in the New Testament. It opens with a brief prologue, then presents Jesus’s ministry through seven signs culminating in the raising of Lazarus. Its later section recounts Jesus’s final week, including the Farewell Discourse and the passion and resurrection narratives.

John is especially associated with presenting Jesus as the Logos, a concept linked with Greek philosophical and Targumic ideas of the divine. It also contains especially explicit identifications of Jesus with the God of Israel in Christian texts. Most scholars date its completion to about AD 90–100, while its historical setting and authorship remain debated.

key_facts.text: The Gospel identifies an unnamed “disciple whom Jesus loved” as its source and perhaps its author.
Scholars generally approach the work as a coherent literary whole by a single author, though questions about its historical context remain contested.
Although distinct from the Synoptic Gospels, John is generally understood to have known and used them, especially Mark.
The Gospel’s seven-sign structure gives its account of Jesus’s ministry a distinctive literary pattern.

overview.text: Kenya is an East African country whose capital and largest city is Nairobi. It borders South Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Tanzania, Uganda, and Lake Victoria, while the Indian Ocean lies to the southeast. Its landscapes range from Mount Kenya’s snow-capped peaks, forests, and fertile regions to arid and semi-arid areas and deserts.

Kenya’s modern political history includes British rule: a protectorate was established in 1895 and the Kenya Colony began in 1920. Conflict with Britain led to the Mau Mau revolution beginning in 1952, followed by independence in 1963. Nairobi is a major commercial hub, while agriculture and tourism are important parts of the economy.

key_facts.text: Mombasa is Kenya’s second-largest and oldest city and a port on Mombasa Island.
Kenya is a presidential representative democratic republic; the president serves as both head of state and head of government.
Agriculture is Kenya’s largest economic sector. Traditional cash crops include tea and coffee, while fresh flowers are a fast-growing export.
Koobi Fora has yielded extensive fossil evidence connected with early human evolution.

overview.text: The Arnolfini Portrait is Jan van Eyck’s 1434 oil painting of a full-length couple in an interior, probably the Italian merchant Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini and his wife. It is associated with Bruges and is held by the National Gallery in London. The work is especially notable for its detailed realism, carefully constructed perspective, and a mirror that extends the apparent picture space. Its objects and actions have prompted extensive interpretation, including the proposal that it represents or records a marriage-related agreement, though the scene’s meaning remains debated.

key_facts.text: It is painted in oil on an oak panel and is signed and dated 1434.
Van Eyck built up thin, translucent layers of paint to create glowing color, subtle shading, and carefully rendered textures.
The mirror and geometric perspective are central to the painting’s complex illusion of an interior space.
Art historian Erwin Panofsky and others interpreted the work as a distinctive form of marriage contract, but this remains an interpretation rather than an established fact.
The painting entered the National Gallery’s collection in 1842.

overview.text: Water is the inorganic compound H₂O. Its polar molecules form strong hydrogen bonds, which help explain many of its physical and chemical properties. Water acts as a solvent and is the fluid in all known living organisms; it is vital to life, although it provides no food energy.

Near Earth’s surface, water naturally occurs as a solid, liquid, and gas. It moves through the water cycle by evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff, connecting oceans, land, ice, and the atmosphere.

key_facts.text: Water covers about 71% of Earth’s surface, and seas and oceans contain most of its total volume.
Clouds contain suspended water droplets or ice; rain, fog, snow, steam, and water vapor are familiar forms of water in the atmosphere or environment.
Water dissolves a wide variety of mineral and organic substances, making it useful in industry, cooking, and washing.
About 70% of the fresh water used by humans goes to agriculture.

overview.text: Hula is a Hawaiian dance form developed by Native Hawaiians in the Hawaiian Islands. It expresses mele, or song, by portraying its words through visual movement. Hand gestures may represent natural scenes such as trees and waves, or feelings such as fondness and yearning.

Its two main categories are hula kahiko and hula ʻauana. Kahiko refers to hula performed before Western encounters and uses chant and traditional instruments; ʻauana developed under Western influence and uses song with instruments such as guitar, ʻukulele, and double bass.

key_facts.text: Hula may be performed seated, called noho, or standing, called luna; some dances use both positions.
Foot and hip movements draw on named steps including kāholo, kaʻo, kāwelu, hela, ʻuwehe, and ʻami.
Hula pahu and hula ʻālaʻapapa are ancient genres, while hapa haole is relatively modern; hula kuʻi and hula ʻōlapa reflect social transformation and Westernization.
Other Polynesian dances, including haka, poi, and ʻoteʻa, come from islands outside Hawaiʻi; hula is unique to the Hawaiian Islands.

overview.text: Chess is a two-player board game played on an 8×8 board. Each side begins with sixteen pieces—one king, queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns—whose movement patterns differ. White moves first, and players alternate turns, capturing opposing pieces while following rules that protect their kings. The main objective is checkmate: placing the opposing king under attack with no legal escape. Games can also end in several kinds of draw.

Chess traces its recorded history to chaturanga in seventh-century India, spreading through Persia and the Arab world before reaching Europe. Its modern rules emerged in Europe in the late fifteenth century, while organized chess arose in the nineteenth century. Chess has also been relevant to computer science: in 1997, Deep Blue defeated reigning world champion Garry Kasparov, and modern engines have influenced chess theory without solving the game.

key_facts.text: Rooks move along ranks or files, bishops diagonally, queens along ranks, files, or diagonals, and knights in an L-shaped jump; the knight alone can leap over intervening pieces.

Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook and places that rook on the square the king crossed. It is allowed only when the king and rook have not moved, the spaces between them are clear, and the king is not in check, does not cross an attacked square, and does not finish on one.

The two distinctive pawn rules are en passant, a one-turn opportunity to capture a pawn that has just advanced two squares past an opposing pawn on an adjacent file, and promotion, which replaces a pawn reaching its last rank with a queen, rook, bishop, or knight.
A stalemate is a draw when the player to move has no legal move but is not in check. Other draws can result from repeated positions or from fifty moves passing without a pawn move or capture.
Competitive games use time controls ranging from classical chess to rapid, blitz, and bullet; a chess clock records each player’s remaining time.

overview.text: A resistor is a passive, two-terminal electronic component whose defining property is electrical resistance. In a circuit, it can reduce current flow, adjust signal levels, divide voltage, or set operating conditions for active components. Resistors are common in circuit networks and electronic equipment.

Some resistors are fixed, while variable resistors let users or circuits adjust settings such as volume or lamp brightness. Variable forms can also sense heat, light, humidity, force, or chemical activity. A resistor’s nominal value is specified along with a manufacturing tolerance.

key_facts.text: High-power resistors dissipate electrical energy as heat and can serve in motor controls, power-distribution systems, or generator test loads.
Resistors can be separate components or built into integrated circuits.
Fixed resistors change only slightly with temperature, time, or operating voltage; variable resistors are designed for adjustment or sensing.
Resistors are manufactured across a very broad range of resistance values, with the nominal value constrained by a stated tolerance.

overview.text: Dante Alighieri, widely known as Dante, was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher of the Middle Ages. His Divine Comedy, first called Comedìa and later given the name Divina, is a major poem of medieval literature.

Dante wrote in the Tuscan vernacular, or everyday language, at a time when Latin dominated scholarly and literary writing. His works helped establish modern standardized Italian, while his depictions of Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven influenced later Western art and literature.

key_facts.text: Dante’s De vulgari eloquentia (On Eloquence in the Vernacular) was an early scholarly defense of writing in everyday language.
Terza rima, an interlocking three-line rhyme scheme, is attributed to Dante.
Dante influenced writers including Geoffrey Chaucer, John Milton, and Alfred Tennyson.
Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio are collectively called the tre corone, or “three crowns,” of Italian literature.

overview.text: The cosmic microwave background (CMB), also called relic radiation, is a faint, nearly uniform glow of microwave radiation filling the observable universe. Sensitive radio telescopes detect it across the sky, where it is not associated with individual stars, galaxies, or other objects.

In Big Bang models, the CMB comes from the time when hot, opaque plasma cooled enough for protons and electrons to form neutral atoms. Radiation then traveled freely, while cosmic expansion reduced its energy. Its small temperature variations provide information about the early universe’s matter and overall curvature.

key_facts.text: Arno Allan Penzias and Robert Woodrow Wilson accidentally discovered the CMB in 1964.
The shell from which the CMB photons were emitted is called the surface of last scattering.
COBE, WMAP, and Planck measured the CMB’s small temperature variations, called anisotropies.
In the CMB power spectrum, the first peak relates to the universe’s overall curvature, while the second and third peaks provide information about normal matter and dark matter densities.

overview.text: Naguib Mahfouz (1911–2006) was an Egyptian writer who helped shape contemporary Egyptian literature. He won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature, whose citation praised his ability to move between clear realism and evocative ambiguity while creating an Egyptian narrative art with broad human reach. His novels are set in Egypt, and the recurring idea of “the lane” serves as a small-scale model of the wider world. His major works include The Cairo Trilogy and Children of Gebelawi; although his fiction is realist, it often explores existential themes.

key_facts.text: Mahfouz is identified as the only Egyptian to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
His career extended from the 1930s to 2004 and included novels, short stories, screenplays, newspaper columns, and plays.
Many of his works were adapted into Egyptian and international films, making him one of the most widely adapted Egyptian authors.
His writing is associated with both realist literature and existential themes.

overview.text: O. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter, an American writer known primarily for short stories. His stories are associated with observational writing, witty narration, and surprise endings. His works include “The Gift of the Magi,” “The Ransom of Red Chief,” “The Caballero’s Way,” and the novel Cabbages and Kings.

His literary legacy includes the O. Henry Award, an annual prize for outstanding short stories. The name also connects a varied career—including work as a pharmacist, drafter, bank employee, and periodical publisher—with a substantial body of short fiction.

key_facts.text: Porter was born in Greensboro, North Carolina, and later settled in Austin, Texas, where he began developing characters for stories while working as a drafter.
After being charged with embezzlement connected to a bank audit, Porter fled to Honduras, later surrendered to U.S. authorities, and served a five-year sentence at Ohio Penitentiary.
While imprisoned, he published 14 stories under various pseudonyms; O. Henry was one of them.
Porter began writing Cabbages and Kings in Honduras and coined the term “banana republic” in that work.

overview.text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948), known worldwide as Mahatma (“great-souled”), was an Indian lawyer and anti-colonial nationalist. After first using nonviolent resistance in a civil-rights campaign in South Africa, he returned to India in 1915 and organized peasants, farmers, and urban workers. His central method, satyagraha, made truth and nonviolence political forces, relying on moral rather than physical power.

As a leader of the Indian National Congress, Gandhi pursued swaraj (self-rule) alongside social reform and religious harmony. His campaigns included the 1930 Salt March against British salt laws and the 1942 Quit India movement. India gained independence in 1947 amid partition and religious violence; Gandhi tried to reduce that violence before a Hindu nationalist assassinated him in Delhi in 1948. His methods later influenced freedom and civil-rights movements worldwide.

key_facts.text: Gandhi led the Indian National Congress from 1921, linking the independence struggle with poverty relief, women’s rights, opposition to untouchability, and religious and ethnic amity.
In the 1930 Salt March, Gandhi and volunteers walked from Ahmedabad to Dandi and made salt to break British salt laws; the campaign was followed by widespread imprisonment.
During Quit India in 1942, Gandhi called for complete non-cooperation and used the phrase karo ya maro (“do or die”); he was imprisoned for two years.
Satyagraha was not simple inaction: it combined civil disobedience and non-cooperation with endurance of suffering, seeking change without using brute force.
October 2, Gandhi’s birthday, is marked in India as Gandhi Jayanti and worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence.

overview.text: Crude oil, also called petroleum, is a naturally occurring yellowish-black liquid found in geological formations and made primarily of hydrocarbons. It is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years from the oxygen-free decay of buried prehistoric organisms, especially plankton and algae. Conventional deposits are recovered by drilling; unconventional sources include oil sands and oil shale.

After extraction, refineries separate crude oil—most easily by distillation—into fuels and chemical feedstocks. Gasoline, diesel, kerosene, and jet fuel are familiar products, while petroleum also supplies materials used in plastics, synthetic rubber, fertilizers, medicines, and more. Its industrial and economic importance is accompanied by greenhouse-gas emissions and pollution from petroleum production and use.

key_facts.text: “Petroleum” can refer either to unprocessed crude oil or to products made by refining it.
Nonfuel petroleum products include bitumen, paraffin wax, lubricants, solvents, and materials used in manufacturing.

Oil spills are direct environmental releases; petroleum use also causes air and water pollution, while burning petroleum fuels releases greenhouse gases that contribute to human-caused climate change.
Proximity to oil deposits, along with access to and pricing of oil, has historically fueled conflicts, diplomatic friction, trade disputes, and other resource conflicts.

overview.text: The Han dynasty was an imperial Chinese dynasty founded by Liu Bang after the Qin. Its rule is divided into Western Han (202 BCE–9 CE) and Eastern Han (25–220 CE), separated by Wang Mang’s brief Xin dynasty. Its influence on later Chinese identity is reflected in the names “Han people,” “Han language,” and “Han characters.”

Han rulers governed through a central court, commanderies, and semi-autonomous kingdoms. From Emperor Wu’s reign, the court officially sponsored Confucianism in education and politics. Campaigns against the Xiongnu secured territory in Inner Asia and helped establish the Silk Road trade route.

key_facts.text: Commanderies were directly controlled by the central government, while semi-autonomous kingdoms gradually lost their independence, especially after the Rebellion of the Seven States.
After the Xiongnu defeated Han forces in 200 BCE, Han rulers initially used marriage alliances and tribute; Emperor Wu shifted to military campaigns beginning in 133 BCE.
Han-era technological advances included papermaking, ship rudders, negative numbers, raised-relief maps, and seismometers that indicated the direction of distant earthquakes.
To finance warfare and frontier settlement, the government nationalized the salt and iron industries in 117 BCE, creating state monopolies later repealed during Eastern Han.
Late court struggles, rebellions such as the Yellow Turban Rebellion, and the rise of warlords weakened imperial authority; Cao Pi ended the dynasty by taking the throne from Emperor Xian in 220 CE.

overview.text: Nitrogen (N) is a nonmetal with atomic number 7 and the lightest member of group 15, the pnictogens. At standard temperature and pressure, it exists mainly as colorless, odorless diatomic N₂ gas, which makes up about 78% of Earth’s atmosphere.

Nitrogen’s strong N≡N triple bond makes atmospheric nitrogen difficult to convert into useful compounds. Even so, nitrogen is essential to living systems because it occurs in proteins, DNA, RNA, and ATP; industrial nitrogen compounds such as ammonia and nitrates are important fertilizers, though excess nitrates can contribute to eutrophication.

key_facts.text: Nitrogen was first isolated by Daniel Rutherford in 1772; the name “azote” is still reflected in some languages and compound names.
Commercial nitrogen is commonly separated from air. It is used as an inert gas in applications such as food packaging and as liquid nitrogen in cryogenic systems.
Important nitrogen-containing compounds include ammonia, nitric acid, organic nitrates, and cyanides.
Nitrogen makes up about 3% of the human body by mass and is the fourth-most abundant element there after oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen.

overview.text: Nelle Harper Lee (1926–2016) was an American novelist whose 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize and became a classic of modern American literature. The novel is Lee's central literary association.

Set in the Deep South of the 1930s and presented through the eyes of two children, To Kill a Mockingbird examines racist attitudes and irrational adult views about race and class. Its plot and characters were loosely based on Lee's observations of family and neighbors in Monroeville, Alabama, along with a childhood event near her hometown.

key_facts.text: Lee assisted her close friend Truman Capote with research for In Cold Blood (1966).
Go Set a Watchman, an earlier draft set at a later date, was published in 2015 as a sequel to To Kill a Mockingbird.
Lee received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2007 for her contribution to literature.

overview.text: Ares is the Greek god of war and courage, one of the Twelve Olympians and a son of Zeus and Hera. He represents both the physical valor needed for battle and war’s brutality and bloodlust. Greek attitudes toward him were ambivalent, and his violent character contrasts with his sister Athena’s association with military strategy and generalship.
