key_facts.text: At age eleven, Schubert became a pupil at the Stadtkonvikt, where he encountered orchestral music by Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.
In March 1828, he gave a critically acclaimed concert devoted to his own works; it was the only such concert of his career.
His instrumental works also include the “Great” Symphony in C major, the “Death and the Maiden” String Quartet, and a String Quintet in C major.
Schubert died at age 31. Typhoid fever was the official cause, while some historians have proposed syphilis.

overview.text: The factorial function assigns a value to each nonnegative integer n and is written n!. It multiplies the positive integers up to n; for positive n, it also obeys n! = n × (n−1)!. In combinatorics, factorials count possible distinct sequences, called permutations, making them useful for counting arrangements.

Factorials also occur in power series for the exponential function and other functions, with applications in algebra, number theory, probability, and computer science. For large values, specialized approximations and extensions help mathematicians study or compute factorials beyond direct multiplication.

key_facts.text: The convention 0! = 1 comes from treating it as an empty product.
Stirling’s approximation estimates large factorials and shows that factorial growth eventually exceeds exponential growth.
The gamma function extends the factorial idea to a continuous function of complex numbers, except at negative integers.

overview.text: Nuclear fusion joins two or more atomic nuclei into a larger nucleus. Changes in nuclear binding energy create a mass difference that can appear as released or absorbed energy. Fusion powers active stellar cores, and fusion nucleosynthesis in the Big Bang and stars creates elements lighter than nickel.

In energy research, fusion generally means thermonuclear fusion, which requires extremely high temperature, density, and confinement time. Tokamaks and stellarators are dominant designs in magnetic-confinement fusion research.

key_facts.text: The light nuclei especially associated with fusion include deuterium, tritium, and helium-3.
Fusion reactions producing nuclei lighter than nickel-62 are generally exothermic. Nuclear fission is the contrasting process and is most energetic for very heavy nuclei, especially actinides.

The extreme conditions for thermonuclear fusion are often summarized as a “triple product” of temperature, density, and confinement time; temperatures are in the kiloelectronvolt, or roughly hundred-million-kelvin, range.
Fusion devices can also be used as neutron sources and for producing superheavy elements.

overview.text: Raphael, born Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino, was an Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance. His art is associated with clarity of form and ease of composition, and it is described as expressing a visual ideal of human grandeur. Alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, he forms the traditional trio of great masters of that period.

In 1508, Raphael moved to Rome at Pope Julius II’s invitation, taking major commissions at the Vatican and beginning work as an architect. The Vatican’s frescoed Raphael Rooms became the largest central project of his career, while The School of Athens, in the Stanza della Segnatura, is identified as his best-known work. He died in 1520 at age 37 after producing a large body of work through an unusually large workshop.

key_facts.text: Raphael probably trained in Pietro Perugino’s workshop and was described as a fully trained master by 1500.
His career moved through three broad settings: Umbria, Florence (1504–1508), and Rome, where he spent his final twelve years working for two popes and their associates.
After his early Roman years, much of Raphael’s work was executed by his workshop from his drawings, with a considerable loss of quality.
Through Johann Joachim Winckelmann’s influence, Raphael’s work became formative for Neoclassical painting; the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood later rejected his techniques.

overview.text: Entropy is a thermodynamic state variable that describes the probabilistic distribution of a system’s accessible microscopic states. It began in classical thermodynamics and later became important in statistical physics, where microscopic arrangements help explain macroscopic behavior.

Entropy is central to the second law of thermodynamics: in an isolated system undergoing spontaneous change, entropy cannot decrease. Such systems tend toward equilibrium, where entropy is highest. In this context, high entropy describes energy as more dispersed or disordered, while low entropy describes it as more concentrated or ordered; some resulting processes are irreversible.

key_facts.text: Ludwig Boltzmann interpreted entropy through the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with a system’s macroscopic condition.
Boltzmann’s work connected microscopic fluctuations with observable macroscopic behavior through a logarithmic law involving the Boltzmann constant.
Rudolf Clausius defined entropy in 1865 in relation to heat and temperature and later coined the term entropy from a Greek word meaning transformation.
The concept is also used in information theory and has applications in chemistry, biology, cosmology, economics, and telecommunications.

overview.text: The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of motion viewed from a rotating reference frame. In physics, the related Coriolis force is treated as a pseudo-force used to analyze that motion. On Earth, rotation makes objects moving over long distances follow curved paths relative to the surface.

The effect matters mainly for large-scale motion: it influences atmospheric winds, ocean currents, and the formation and rotation of cyclones. Its familiar Earth-based pattern is opposite in the two hemispheres, making it a key association in weather and ocean science.

key_facts.text: A mathematical expression for the Coriolis force appeared in an 1835 paper by French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis.
For everyday objects, the effect is usually imperceptible; it becomes noticeable over large distances, long periods, or when very high precision is required.
At Earth’s surface, moving objects deflect to the right of their direction of travel in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
The horizontal deflection is strongest near the poles and decreases to zero at the equator.

overview.text: The Crusades were a papally promoted series of medieval military campaigns, beginning in 1095, initially aimed at recovering and defending the Holy Land from Muslim rulers. They developed into a wider crusading movement, with similar spiritual rewards offered for campaigns against pagans, Christian dissidents, and other enemies of the papacy.

The movement required institutions that connected religion with military and economic organization, including crusade indulgences, military orders, and taxation of clerical income. In the eastern Mediterranean, successive expeditions built, defended, and eventually lost Crusader states; the campaigns also brought major confrontations with Saladin and the Byzantine Empire.

key_facts.text: Pope Urban II proclaimed the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, promising spiritual rewards to participants.

The fall of Edessa prompted the Second Crusade, which failed in 1148. The Third Crusade helped the Crusader states survive after Saladin’s victory at Hattin in 1187, but Jerusalem remained under Muslim control.
The Fourth Crusade, initially directed against Egypt, was diverted to the Byzantine Empire and culminated in the Sack of Constantinople and the establishment of the Latin Empire in 1204.
The Sixth Crusade regained Jerusalem through negotiation in 1229, but the Mamluks captured the Crusaders’ last mainland strongholds in 1291.

overview.text: Sir Edward William Elgar (1857–1934) was an English composer whose music entered British and international classical repertoire. His output includes orchestral works such as the Enigma Variations and Pomp and Circumstance Marches, concertos for violin and cello, two symphonies, choral music, chamber music, and songs.

Although often viewed as a typically English composer, Elgar drew most of his musical influences from continental Europe. Self-taught and feeling like an outsider in musical and social circles, he struggled for recognition until the Enigma Variations became popular in Britain and overseas in 1899.

key_facts.text: The Dream of Gerontius is a choral work based on a Roman Catholic text. It caused some concern in Anglican Britain but became a core repertory work.
Elgar was appointed Master of the King’s Musick in 1924.
A symphony and a violin concerto he wrote in his fifties were highly successful, while his second symphony and cello concerto took years to gain a regular place in British orchestral repertory.
Interest in Elgar’s music revived significantly in the 1960s, helped by new recordings; his works have continued to be performed more often in Britain than elsewhere.

overview.text: Chinua Achebe (born Albert Chinualumogu Achebe) was a Nigerian novelist, poet, and critic who became a central figure in modern African literature. His first novel, Things Fall Apart (1958), brought international attention to his work and occupies a major place in African literary study.

Achebe challenged colonial portrayals of Africa by writing from perspectives shaped by Igbo traditions, Christianity, and the conflict between African and Western values. His works examine culture, colonialism, gender, politics, and history, often using English alongside the storytelling patterns of Igbo oral tradition.

key_facts.text: Things Fall Apart, No Longer at Ease, and Arrow of God form Achebe’s “African Trilogy.”
He studied at the University of Ibadan and became sharply critical of Western literature’s depictions of Africa.
Achebe defended writing in English as a way to reach broad audiences, including readers in colonial nations.
His style combines straightforward narration with Igbo proverbs, folktales, and forms of public speech.
His 1975 lecture criticizing racial perspectives in Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness became influential in postcolonial discourse.

overview.text: In Genesis 1–5, Adam is the name given to the first human. He appears across several religious traditions, including Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Gnosticism, and the Baháʼí Faith, and is associated with humanity’s origins and awareness of God.

Christian interpretation connects Adam’s eating from the tree of knowledge of good and evil in Eden with the arrival of death and sin, humanity’s expulsion, and the need for redemption through Jesus’s crucifixion. In Islam, Adam is described as khalifa on earth; after taking from the Tree of Immortality, he repents, is forgiven, and becomes an example of recognizing wrongdoing and turning back to God.

key_facts.text: Genesis 1–5 presents Adam as the first human and as the first human aware of God.
Christian teaching in this account says Adam’s sinful nature affected all his descendants.
The Islamic title khalifa is explained as “successor” and may mean God’s deputy on earth, the beginning of a new cycle of sentient life, or both.
In the Islamic account, Adam’s forgiveness after repentance provides guidance for people who recognize and turn away from wrongdoing.

overview.text: The human heart is a muscular organ in the chest that pumps blood through blood vessels. Together, the heart and vessels form the circulatory system, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues while carrying metabolic waste toward the lungs. The heart has four chambers—right and left atria and ventricles—and valves keep blood moving in one direction.

Pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial (SA) node create electrical signals that trigger contraction through the atrioventricular (AV) node and the heart’s conduction system. Deoxygenated blood travels through the right side to the lungs; oxygenated blood returns to the left side and leaves through the aorta for circulation around the body.

key_facts.text: The heart is enclosed in the protective pericardium, and its wall has three layers: epicardium, myocardium, and endocardium.
Risk factors for cardiovascular disease include smoking, excess weight, inactivity, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and poorly controlled diabetes.
Heart disease may be evaluated through medical history, a stethoscope examination, an ECG, or an echocardiogram, which uses ultrasound. Heart specialists are called cardiologists.

overview.text: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument of large standing stones on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, about two miles west of Amesbury. An outer ring of upright sarsens topped by horizontal lintels surrounds smaller bluestones; inside are paired uprights joined by lintels. The surviving structure aligns with sunrise at the summer solstice and sunset at the winter solstice.

The monument stands amid one of England’s densest landscapes of Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments, including several hundred burial mounds. Stonehenge is also a British cultural icon: it has been legally protected since 1882, and the site and its surroundings became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

key_facts.text: Construction took place in stages from about 3100 BC to about 1600 BC; the famous circle of large sarsen stones dates to about 2600–2400 BC.
The outer sarsens are joined to their horizontal lintels with mortise-and-tenon joints, a feature described as unique among contemporary monuments.
Stonehenge may have begun as a burial ground: deposits containing human bone date from about 3000 BC and continued for at least another 500 years.
The smaller bluestones were in their current positions by roughly 2400–2200 BC, though they may have reached the site as early as 3000 BC.

overview.text: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791) was a Classical composer and musician born in Salzburg. A child prodigy trained by his father Leopold, he could play keyboard and violin, compose, and perform before European royalty by age five. His early career included a grand tour of Europe and three trips to Italy arranged by his father.

Mozart wrote across major genres of his era, including symphonies, concertos, chamber music, opera, and choral music. After leaving Salzburg employment, he remained in Vienna, where he gained fame and some financial success but no long-term security. His late output includes the Jupiter Symphony, Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the Clarinet Concerto, several operas, and the largely unfinished Requiem.

key_facts.text: Mozart produced more than 800 works, spanning most of the musical genres of his time.
At 17, he became a musician at the Salzburg court; a later job-seeking journey took him through Paris, Mannheim, and Munich.
His Vienna-period works included the “Haydn” Quartets, the Great Mass in C minor, and the opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail.
His final three symphonies culminated in the Jupiter Symphony.
During his Vienna years, Mozart composed more than a dozen piano concertos.

overview.text: The Mayflower was an English square-rigged merchant ship that carried a group of English families—later called the Pilgrims—across the Atlantic in 1620. After a ten-week voyage, its 102 passengers and crew of about 30 anchored near Cape Cod, Massachusetts. The travelers planned to establish Plymouth Colony.

Before disembarking, the passengers wrote and signed the Mayflower Compact, an agreement creating a basic government in which members would contribute to the settlement’s safety and welfare. The ship later became a cultural icon in the history of the United States.

key_facts.text: The Pilgrims had planned to sail with Speedwell, but that ship proved unseaworthy and was left in England; the Mayflower then made the voyage alone.
The Mayflower anchored near the tip of Cape Cod on November 21, 1620 [O.S. November 11].
The colonists faced a harsh first winter, and an outbreak of disease left only half of the original Pilgrims alive.
The following year, survivors celebrated a fall harvest with 90 Wampanoag people; centuries later, this occasion was declared the first American Thanksgiving.

overview.text: John Philip Sousa was an American composer and conductor of the late Romantic era, known chiefly for U.S. military marches. Called “The March King,” he wrote “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Semper Fidelis,” “The Liberty Bell,” “The Thunderer,” and “The Washington Post.”

Sousa’s career was closely tied to military and civilian bands: he directed the U.S. Marine Band and later organized the civilian Sousa Band. He also aided in developing the sousaphone, a marching-tuba design based on the helicon.

key_facts.text: Sousa began his career playing violin and studying music theory and composition under John Esputa and George Felix Benkert.
His father enlisted him as an apprentice in the U.S. Marine Band in 1868; Sousa later returned as its director from 1880 to 1892.
During World War I, Sousa received a lieutenant’s commission to lead the Naval Reserve Band in Illinois.
“The Stars and Stripes Forever” is identified as the national march of the United States, while “Semper Fidelis” is the official march of the U.S. Marine Corps.

overview.text: The Jurassic was the second and middle period of the Mesozoic Era. It lasted from about 201.4 million years ago to the beginning of the Cretaceous, placed at about 143.1 million years ago, and takes its name from the Jura Mountains, where limestone strata from the period were first identified.

The Jurassic began with the Triassic–Jurassic extinction event. As Pangaea rifted, land fauna shifted to one dominated by dinosaurs, and the earliest stem-group birds appeared. The climate was warmer than today, with no ice caps; the formal boundary with the Cretaceous remains undefined.

key_facts.text: Pangaea was breaking apart into the northern landmass Laurasia and the southern landmass Gondwana.
Jurassic seas contained marine reptiles such as ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs, while pterosaurs were the dominant flying vertebrates.
Ferns and gymnosperms, including conifers, dominated Jurassic plant life.
Mammaliaformes continued to diversify, and the first crown-group mammals emerged during the period.

overview.text: The Grapes of Wrath is a 1939 American realist novel by John Steinbeck. Set during the Great Depression, it follows the Joads, poor tenant farmers forced from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, changes in agriculture, and bank foreclosures. They travel to California on the “mother road” with thousands of other “Okies,” migrants seeking work, land, dignity, and a future.

The novel connects one family’s journey with the wider displacement of people during the Dust Bowl era. It won major U.S. literary awards and remains widely taught because of its historical context and enduring literary reputation.

key_facts.text: The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; it was also prominently cited when Steinbeck received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature.
Migrants like the Joads were commonly called “Okies,” even as they traveled from Oklahoma toward California.
A 1940 film adaptation starred Henry Fonda and was directed by John Ford.
The novel is frequently taught in American high school and college literature classes.

overview.text: Asteroids are minor planets: rocky, metallic, or icy bodies without atmospheres that orbit in the inner Solar System or share Jupiter’s orbit. They range from small rubble piles to Ceres, a dwarf planet almost 1,000 kilometers across, and are broadly grouped as C-, M-, or S-types.

The greatest number of asteroids are in the main asteroid belt, a region between Mars and Jupiter. Research has included spacecraft observations and sample returns, while planetary-defense efforts address possible impacts: near-Earth asteroids can have catastrophic consequences if they strike Earth.

key_facts.text: The main asteroid belt lies approximately 2–4 astronomical units from the Sun. Many main-belt asteroids have slightly elliptical, stable orbits lasting about 3–6 years.
The three broad asteroid types are C-type (carbonaceous), M-type (metallic), and S-type (silicaceous).
NASA’s Dawn studied Vesta and Ceres, while Japan’s Hayabusa missions studied and returned samples from Itokawa and Ryugu.
In September 2022, NASA’s DART spacecraft was intentionally crashed into Dimorphos to test planetary-defense technology.
The Chicxulub impact is widely thought to have induced the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction.

overview.text: The Nile is a major north-flowing river in northeastern Africa. The White Nile and Blue Nile meet at Khartoum, after which the river flows through Sudan and Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea near Alexandria, forming a large delta. Its drainage basin spans eleven countries and links wetter upstream regions with largely desert areas downstream.

The river was central to Ancient Egyptian civilization: annual floods deposited fertile silt that supported agriculture, while the Nile enabled transportation, trade, communication, and government. Today, it remains crucial for irrigation and electricity, while dams have altered its flood cycle and become sources of disputes over water, food security, safety, and displacement.

key_facts.text: The White Nile is longer and begins near Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile begins near Lake Tana in Ethiopia and supplies more than twice as much water. They join at Khartoum.
Most Nile water comes from rainfall in Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, while Egypt, Sudan, and South Sudan mainly use the river for irrigation in desert environments.
Nubia, south—or upstream—of the second Nile cataract, was associated with the ancient Kerma culture and the Kushite Empire.
The Aswan High Dam and other dams altered the Nile’s annual flood cycle and restricted downstream silt transport; the Nile Delta has consequently shrunk.

overview.text: Vienna (German: Wien) is Austria’s capital and one of its nine states. It stands on the Danube at the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods, near Slovakia, Hungary, and the Czech Republic.

Vienna developed from the Roman settlement of Vindobona and later became a major Habsburg imperial center. It is widely associated with classical music, historic architecture, and international organizations.

key_facts.text: The Romans established a military settlement called Vindobona at Vienna in the 1st century; it received Roman city rights in 212.
From the 16th century until the Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806, Vienna was generally the seat of its emperors under Habsburg rule.
Vienna’s historic center became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.
Important composers connected with Vienna include Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, Schubert, Brahms, Mahler, and the Strauss family.
The city hosts major international organizations including the United Nations, OPEC, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

overview.text: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it in 1801; it was first announced as a planet, later classified as an asteroid, and eventually recognized as the only confirmed dwarf planet in the asteroid belt. Its minor-planet designation is 1 Ceres, and its orbit lies inside Neptune’s orbit.

NASA’s Dawn spacecraft approached Ceres for an orbital mission in 2015, revealing a surface containing water ice and hydrated minerals. Gravity measurements also suggest a layered interior and a likely internal ocean, while brines may help produce cryovolcanoes such as Ahuna Mons.

key_facts.text: Ceres is the largest known object without a moon.
Its diameter is about one-quarter that of Earth’s Moon, and it is generally too dim to see with the naked eye.
Its surface includes carbonates and clay, along with water and ice.
Ceres has an extremely thin, temporary atmosphere of water vapor released from localized surface sources.

overview.text: The saxophone is a single-reed woodwind instrument with a usually brass, conical body. A reed vibrating against a mouthpiece produces sound; keys open and close holes to alter the tube’s effective length and control pitch.

Saxophones are used in classical, military, marching, jazz, contemporary, rock, and popular music. They can serve as solo or melody instruments or as members of horn sections. Common family members include the soprano, alto, tenor, and baritone saxophones.

key_facts.text: Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax invented the saxophone in the early 1840s and patented it on June 28, 1846.
The modern saxophone family consists entirely of instruments pitched in B-flat or E-flat.
Soprano and tenor saxophones are typically in B-flat; alto and baritone saxophones are typically in E-flat.
Saxophones are almost always treated as transposing instruments, and a player may be called a saxophonist or saxist.

overview.text: Thomas Jefferson was a Founding Father, the primary author of the Declaration of Independence, and the third U.S. president, serving from 1801 to 1809. His political philosophy emphasized republicanism, individual liberty, agrarianism, and limited government, helping shape Jeffersonian democracy. Before becoming president, he served as vice president under John Adams.

Jefferson’s presidency is associated with westward expansion through the Louisiana Purchase, support for the Lewis and Clark Expedition, and efforts to defend American shipping and trade. His legacy also includes the enduring contradiction between his language of liberty and his enslavement of more than 600 people.

key_facts.text: Jefferson and James Madison organized the Democratic-Republican Party to oppose the Federalists during the First Party System.
The Louisiana Purchase, pursued during Jefferson’s presidency, doubled the nation’s geographic size.
The 1807 Embargo Act restricted foreign trade, sought to protect U.S. shipping and industry, and encouraged American manufacturing.
Jefferson served as U.S. minister to France and later as George Washington’s first secretary of state.

overview.text: Nikolai Vasilyevich Gogol (1809–1852) was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, and playwright of Ukrainian origin. His writing often makes familiar situations strange through grotesque and proto-surrealist elements, as in “The Nose,” “The Overcoat,” and “Diary of a Madman.”

Gogol’s early work drew on Ukrainian culture and folklore, while later writing—including The Government Inspector and Dead Souls—satirized political corruption in contemporary Russia. His distinctive methods and works influenced Russian, Ukrainian, and world literature; writers who acknowledged his influence include Dostoevsky, Kafka, Bulgakov, and Nabokov.

key_facts.text: Defamiliarization, a technique associated with Gogol, presents ordinary things in strange ways to encourage new perspectives.
Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka reflects Gogol’s Ukrainian upbringing, culture, and folklore.
Viy and Nevsky Prospekt are additional examples of Gogol’s grotesque writing.
Other recognized works include Taras Bulba, Marriage, and The Carriage.

overview.text: The Mughal Empire was an early modern empire in South Asia, conventionally founded in 1526 when Babur defeated Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat. At its greatest extent, it reached from the Indus Basin and northern Afghanistan through Kashmir and northern India to Assam, Bangladesh, and the Deccan Plateau.

Mughal power combined military conquest with administrative practices and diverse ruling elites, producing more centralized and standardized rule. Agricultural taxes under Akbar formed the basis of imperial wealth. Court patronage, especially under Shah Jahan, supported the arts and architecture; the Taj Mahal is among the empire’s major surviving sites.

key_facts.text: Aurangzeb’s reign saw the empire reach its maximum geographical extent. It later contracted toward Old Delhi and was formally dissolved by the British Raj after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
Taxes were paid in a well-regulated silver currency, helping peasants and artisans participate in larger markets.
Relative peace during much of the seventeenth century contributed to economic expansion, while European Indian Ocean activity and demand for Indian goods generated wealth for the court.
Major surviving Mughal sites include Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun’s Tomb, the Red Fort, Lahore Fort, Shalamar Gardens, and the Taj Mahal.

overview.text: Chicago is Illinois’s most populous city and the most populous city in the Midwestern United States. It stands on Lake Michigan’s western shore and is the seat of Cook County. Incorporated in 1837 near a portage between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River watershed, Chicago grew rapidly during the mid-19th century.

Chicago is an international hub for finance, commerce, industry, education, technology, telecommunications, and transportation. Its culture has contributed to visual arts, literature, theater, comedy, food, dance, and music, including jazz, blues, gospel, hip-hop, and house music.

key_facts.text: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed several square miles and left more than 100,000 people homeless, but the city continued to grow.
Chicago contributed to urban planning and architecture through the Chicago School, the City Beautiful movement, and the development of steel-framed skyscrapers.
The Chicago region is the nation’s railroad hub, and O’Hare International Airport has routinely ranked among the world’s ten busiest airports by passenger traffic.
Major cultural institutions include the Art Institute of Chicago, the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, and the Lyric Opera of Chicago.
Chicago has professional teams in all major professional leagues, including two Major League Baseball teams.

overview.text: Cholesterol is the principal sterol in animals and is found throughout animal tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, as well as in animal fats and oils. Animal cells make it as an essential structural and signaling component of their membranes.

Cholesterol also provides starting material for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. In blood, elevated cholesterol—particularly cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein (LDL)—may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.

key_facts.text: In vertebrates, liver cells typically produce the greatest amounts of cholesterol; brain astrocytes make it and transport it to neurons.
Cholesterol is absent from most bacteria and archaea, although some exceptions exist, including Mycoplasma, which requires it for growth.
François Poulletier de la Salle first identified cholesterol in solid form in gallstones in 1769.
Michel Eugène Chevreul named the compound “cholesterine” in 1815.

overview.text: Henry VIII (1491–1547) was king of England and Ireland from 1509 until his death. The second son of Henry VII and Elizabeth of York, he became heir after his older brother Arthur died and succeeded his father. His early reign was described as that of an attractive, educated, and accomplished king.

Henry’s effort to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon led to a major religious and political break. After Pope Clement VII refused an annulment, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage void in 1533. Henry’s Acts of Supremacy made him Supreme Head of the Church of England, ended his realms’ obedience to the pope, and helped drive the English Reformation, including the dissolution of Catholic monasteries.

key_facts.text: Henry is associated with six marriages, partly because he sought a male heir.
He ordered the executions by beheading of two wives, Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard.
Henry was succeeded by his only surviving son, Edward VI.

overview.text: Franz Liszt (1811–1886) was a Hungarian composer, virtuoso pianist, conductor, and teacher of the Romantic period. His European concert tours in the 1830s and 1840s made him famous for technical brilliance and produced “Lisztomania,” an extraordinary level of public enthusiasm for a virtuoso.

Liszt’s influence extended beyond piano performance. He promoted and arranged works by contemporaries, helped advance the New German School’s programmatic music and harmonic experimentation, and contributed to the symphonic poem and new techniques of thematic transformation. His extensive output influenced contemporaries and anticipated later musical trends.

key_facts.text: Liszt studied with Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri before his major European touring career.
His piano repertoire includes the Hungarian Rhapsodies, Années de pèlerinage, Transcendental Études, “La campanella,” and Piano Sonata in B minor.
He was a prominent representative of the New German School alongside Richard Wagner.
Liszt taught piano performance to hundreds of students and is associated with the masterclass as a method of teaching performance.
Many of his later works experimented with atonality, foreshadowing developments in twentieth-century classical music.

overview.text: The Mediterranean Sea is an intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia, and Africa. It is nearly enclosed by land: North Africa lies south, southern Europe and Anatolia lie north, and the Levant lies east. The Strait of Gibraltar connects it to the Atlantic Ocean; the Bosporus connects it to the Black Sea, and the Suez Canal connects it to the Red Sea.

The Mediterranean served as an important route for ancient merchants, travelers, and migrants, facilitating trade, cultural exchange, colonization, and conquest. The region saw the development of early civilizations including those of Egypt, Greece, and the Fertile Crescent. The Roman Empire maintained nautical hegemony over the sea for centuries.

key_facts.text: Its marginal seas include the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian, and Marmara seas.
Sicily and Sardinia are the Mediterranean’s two largest islands by both area and population.
The sea’s waters are mild in winter and warm in summer; the Mediterranean climate gets most of its precipitation during the cooler months.
Cyprus and Malta are island countries located in the Mediterranean Sea.

overview.text: “The Tyger,” also spelled “The Tiger,” is a poem by William Blake, published in 1794 in Songs of Experience. It examines Christian religious ideas prevalent in late-eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century England.

Its central concern is the intention behind God’s creation of the title creature, especially when considered alongside the contrasting Lamb. The poem therefore focuses on creation, divine purpose, and the difference between these two beings.

key_facts.text: The poem is sometimes titled “The Tiger,” but Blake’s title is “The Tyger.”
It has been the subject of much literary criticism.
It is one of the most anthologized poems in the English literary canon.
The poem has inspired musical settings and other adaptations.

overview.text: Chile, officially the Republic of Chile, is a country in the Southern Cone of southwestern South America. It occupies a narrow strip of land between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. Santiago is both its capital and largest city.

Chile borders Peru, Bolivia, and Argentina, while its southern boundary reaches the Drake Passage. It also administers Pacific islands, including Easter Island, and claims a territory in Antarctica. Spanish is its official and national language.

key_facts.text: Chile is described as the world’s southernmost country and the country closest to Antarctica.
Chile gained its present northern territory after defeating Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879–1883).
Its administered Pacific islands include the Juan Fernández Islands, Isla Salas y Gómez, and the Desventuradas, in addition to Easter Island.
Chile’s Antarctic claim covers about 1,250,000 square kilometers.

overview.text: Brave New World is Aldous Huxley’s dystopian novel, written in 1931 and published in 1932. It is set largely in a futuristic World State, where environmental engineering organizes citizens into an intelligence-based social hierarchy. Reproductive technology, sleep-learning, psychological manipulation, and classical conditioning help create a society that appears utopian. The central challenge comes from John the Savage, an outsider who challenges that engineered order. The novel is often paired with George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four as a companion or inversion counterpart.

key_facts.text: The imagined society combines scientific control of reproduction with sleep-learning and psychological manipulation.
The World State’s hierarchy is produced through environmental engineering and organized around intelligence.
Huxley later reassessed the novel in the essay Brave New World Revisited, published in 1958.
Huxley’s 1962 novel Island is described as a utopian counterpart to Brave New World.
The novel has frequently been banned and challenged since its original publication.

overview.text: Passover, also called Pesach, is a major Jewish holiday commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Its central story is part of the biblical Exodus narrative: Pharaoh enslaves the Israelites, God sends ten plagues, and Pharaoh finally permits them to leave.

According to the Book of Exodus, the holiday’s name refers to the tenth plague: homes whose doorframes were marked with lamb’s blood were spared, or “passed over.” Passover centers on remembering the Israelites’ liberation and the story behind it.

key_facts.text: Pesach begins on 15 Nisan; because the Hebrew day begins at sunset, it begins at sundown on the preceding evening.
The Haggadah is the ritual book used at the Passover Seder; its Magid section recounts the Exodus story.
During the holiday, Jews are forbidden to possess or eat leavened foods, called chametz.
Passover is one of the Three Pilgrimage Festivals.

overview.text: The Michelson–Morley experiment was an 1887 test of the proposed luminiferous aether, a supposed medium thought to carry light waves. American physicists Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley compared the speed of light in perpendicular directions to look for evidence that Earth and their laboratory were moving through this aether.

The experiment found no significant difference between the measured speeds. This negative result provided strong evidence against some aether theories and began a line of research that eventually led to special relativity, which rejects motion relative to an aether.

key_facts.text: The experiment was conducted from April through July 1887 and published in November of that year.
It was performed at the site of what is now Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio.
The experiment was carried out by American physicists Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley.
Later Michelson–Morley-type experiments were repeated with increasing sensitivity and became part of the fundamental experimental tests of special relativity.

overview.text: The Unification Church is an Abrahamic monotheistic new religious movement founded by Sun Myung Moon in Seoul, South Korea, in 1954. It originally used the name Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity and adopted Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (FFWPU) as its official name in 1994.

Its beliefs are set out in Divine Principle. Moon taught that he was the Second Coming of Christ and that his mission included creating an ideal family and a human lineage free from sin. The movement is especially associated with mass wedding ceremonies called Blessings, as well as political and organizational activity beyond religion.

key_facts.text: Members are called Unificationists; “Moonies” is an informal label. Followers honor Moon and his wife, Hak Ja Han, as the “True Parents.”
Related organizations have operated in business, education, politics, and other fields.
The movement has been associated with anti-communism and support for Korean reunification.

Critics have accused the movement of financially exploiting members and have disputed its teachings and social and political influence; “cult” is a critical label rather than a neutral classification.

overview.text: Stranger Things is an American Netflix television series created by the Duffer Brothers. It combines science fiction, horror, mystery, supernatural drama, and coming-of-age storytelling; its first season was released in 2016.

Set in the 1980s in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, the story begins after Eleven, a girl with psychokinetic abilities, opens a wormhole at a secret government research facility. The opening connects Earth to a hostile realm, bringing supernatural danger into an otherwise ordinary community.

key_facts.text: The series draws on 1980s popular culture and was influenced by creators including Steven Spielberg, John Carpenter, David Lynch, Stephen King, and Wes Craven.
The ensemble cast includes Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Finn Wolfhard, Millie Bobby Brown, Gaten Matarazzo, and other major performers.
Its franchise has expanded beyond the television series into a prequel stage play, an animated spin-off, books, comics, and other tie-in media.

overview.text: The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 near present-day Battle, East Sussex. A Norman-French army led by William, Duke of Normandy, faced an English army commanded by King Harold Godwinson. William’s decisive victory began the Norman Conquest of England.

The battle grew out of a succession crisis after childless Edward the Confessor died. Harold had already defeated invasions led by Tostig and Harald Hardrada, but while his forces recovered, William landed in southern England and Harold marched south to meet him. The battle lasted from about morning until dusk; Harold’s death near its end led to the retreat and defeat of most of his army.

key_facts.text: The English army was almost entirely infantry and had few archers; William’s force included infantry, cavalry, and archers.
After early attacks failed to break the English lines, the Normans used feigned retreats—pretending to flee before turning on pursuing troops.
William was crowned king on Christmas Day in 1066, after further marching and skirmishing.
William later founded a monastery at the battlefield; its abbey’s high altar was said to mark the spot where Harold died.

overview.text: Cry, the Beloved Country is a 1948 novel by South African writer Alan Paton. Set in South Africa in the period before apartheid, it follows a Black village priest and a white farmer as they respond to news of a murder.
The novel remains one of the best-known works of South African literature.

key_facts.text: Film adaptations of the novel were made in 1951 and 1995.
A 1949 musical adaptation was titled Lost in the Stars.
Maxwell Anderson wrote the musical’s book, and Kurt Weill composed its music.

overview.text: Mecca (officially Makkah al-Mukarramah) is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia and the capital of Mecca Province. It is considered Islam’s holiest city and the birthplace of Islam and the prophet Muhammad. Mecca is closely associated with the Hajj, a pilgrimage observed in the twelfth month of the Hijri calendar. The city lies in a narrow valley about 70 kilometers inland from Jeddah on the Red Sea.

key_facts.text: The Great Mosque of Mecca, or Masjid al-Haram, houses the Kaaba, which Muslims believe was built by Abraham and Ishmael.
The Kaaba is the qibla—the direction of prayer—for Muslims worldwide.
Muslims believe the Cave of Hira, on Jabal al-Nour just outside Mecca, was where the Quran was first revealed to Muhammad.

overview.text: Theseus is a divine hero of Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur. His myths follow journeys, exploits, and relationships, making him a recurring figure in storytelling. In one major tradition, he is portrayed as a unifying king who brings Attica under Athenian rule, an act called synoikismos, or “dwelling together.”

Theseus is a mythic figure rather than a securely documented historical person: his existence as a real individual has not been proven. Ancient accounts also differ, especially concerning the Minotaur’s death, Theseus’s escape, and his relationship with Ariadne.

key_facts.text: Traditions give Theseus different fathers: Aegeus, king of Athens, or the god Poseidon; his mother is Aethra.
The Minotaur is portrayed as a creature that is half man and half bull.
Theseus was credited with building a palace on the Acropolis. Pausanias also associated him with establishing a cult of Aphrodite on the Acropolis’s southern slope.
Plutarch designed his Life of Theseus to parallel the Life of Romulus, a Roman founding myth, while drawing on several earlier writers.

overview.text: In economics, demand describes the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at different prices during a specified period. It is more than simply wanting something: consumers must also have the ability to pay. Demand is considered across both price and time, making it a way to describe an ongoing pattern of purchases rather than one isolated transaction.

key_facts.text: Demand concerns a good or commodity and is measured by what consumers are willing and able to buy.
Desire without the ability to pay does not count as economic demand.
Demand is expressed over a range of prices, not just one price.
Because it is a flow concept, demand describes purchases per unit of time and can represent a continuing stream of buying.

overview.text: Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is an East African country in the African Great Lakes region. It borders Uganda, Kenya, Mozambique, Malawi, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and has an Indian Ocean coastline. Its modern state formed when Tanganyika and Zanzibar, which became independent separately, united in 1964.

Dodoma is Tanzania’s capital; Dar es Salaam is the former capital and remains the largest city, principal port, and leading commercial center. Tanzania’s physical geography includes Mount Kilimanjaro in the northeast, parts of three African Great Lakes, and the Zanzibar Archipelago offshore. It is also associated with important hominid fossil discoveries.

key_facts.text: Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa’s highest mountain and the world’s highest single free-standing mountain above sea level.
Lake Victoria, Lake Tanganyika, and Lake Malawi are partly within Tanzania; Victoria is Africa’s largest lake, while Tanganyika is the continent’s deepest.
Swahili is Tanzania’s national language; the country has no de jure official language, and more than 100 languages are spoken there.
Many important hominid fossils have been found in Tanzania.

overview.text: Tenochtitlan, also known as Mexico-Tenochtitlan, was a large Mexica city-state built on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico. It served as the capital of the expanding Aztec Empire in the 15th century until Tlaxcaltec and Spanish forces captured it in 1521. Its ruins are located in the historic center of present-day Mexico City, connecting the pre-Columbian Mexica capital with the modern Mexican capital. The city’s island environment was associated with water, boats, and floating gardens.

key_facts.text: The exact founding date is uncertain; 13 March 1325 was selected in 1925 as a commemorative date.
At its peak, Tenochtitlan was the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas.
Tenochtitlan was one of two Mexica polities on the island; the other was Tlatelolco.
After its capture in 1521, Tenochtitlan subsequently became a cabecera of the Viceroyalty of New Spain.

overview.text: The Scream is an image first created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893 and later repeated in different versions. Its agonized face is widely associated with profound existential dread related to the human condition, and the work helped shape the Expressionist movement. It remains one of the most iconic images in art.

In recalling the work’s origin, Munch described sunset light turning the clouds “blood red” and sensed an “infinite scream passing through nature.” Scholars place the viewpoint along a fjord path overlooking Oslo, while proposed explanations for the unusual sky range from a volcanic eruption to a psychological reaction.

key_facts.text: Munch made painted and pastel versions of The Scream and also created a lithograph stone from which several prints survive.
The Norwegian title is Skrik; the German title used when it was first exhibited was Der Schrei der Natur, meaning “The Scream of Nature.”
Both painted versions were stolen from public museums and later recovered.
In 2012, one pastel version achieved the highest nominal price then paid for an artwork at public auction.

overview.text: Native Americans—also called American Indians or Indigenous Americans—are the Indigenous peoples of the United States, particularly the lower 48 states and Alaska. This is a collective term for many communities and tribes, not the name of a single nation. The U.S. Census uses a related category, “American Indians and Alaska Natives,” based on origins plus tribal affiliation or community attachment, so these labels do not always cover exactly the same groups.

U.S. history includes colonization, warfare, disease, enslavement, removal from ancestral lands, discriminatory policies, and forced assimilation directed at Native peoples. It also includes treaties, tribal sovereignty, citizenship, and later self-determination movements. These themes connect the history of expansion with the legal and political status of Native nations.

key_facts.text: The Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 ended federal recognition of independent Native nations, but preserved rights including a significant degree of tribal sovereignty.

The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted U.S. citizenship to Native Americans born in the United States who had not already obtained it; some states continued denying them voting rights for decades.
Many reservations remain independent of state law, with tribal citizens generally subject to tribal courts and federal law there.
Self-determination movements since the 1960s have brought positive changes, although Native Americans continue to face contemporary issues.

source.title: Native Americans in the United States

overview.text: The Amazon rainforest—also called Amazonia or the Amazon jungle—is a moist broadleaf tropical rainforest in the Amazon biome. It covers most of the Amazon Basin, a South American region of about 7 million km²; the forest itself covers about 6 million km² and extends across territory in nine nations, with most of it in Brazil.

The Amazon contains the world’s largest and most biodiverse tract of tropical rainforest and is also home to many Indigenous peoples. Large-scale deforestation is occurring in the forest, creating harmful effects and potentially damaging agriculture severely.

key_facts.text: About 60% of the forest is in Brazil; Peru and Colombia hold the next-largest shares, at 13% and 10%.
More than 30 million people from 350 ethnic groups live in the Amazon, which includes 3,344 formally acknowledged Indigenous territories.
The Amazon represents more than half of the total area of Earth’s remaining rainforests.

overview.text: Orpheus is a Thracian bard, legendary musician, poet, and prophet in Greek mythology. He is especially associated with descending into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice, and with traveling alongside Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece.

His legendary music could charm living things and even stones, making him an archetype of the inspired singer. Greek tradition also connects him with the Orphic mysteries, where he was treated as a founder and prophet. Orpheus has been portrayed or alluded to in poetry, opera, painting, film, and music.

key_facts.text: In the myth, maenads associated with Dionysus kill Orpheus after becoming tired of his mourning for Eurydice.
Works attributed to Orpheus include the Orphic Hymns, Orphic Argonautica, and Lithica; other attributed theogonies are lost.
Shrines believed to contain relics of Orpheus were regarded as oracles.

overview.text: Antarctica is Earth’s southernmost continent, located almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle and containing the geographic South Pole. The Southern Ocean surrounds it, while the Antarctic ice sheet covers most of its land; it is the fifth-largest continent by area.

Antarctica is the coldest, driest, and windiest continent on average, and much of it is a polar desert. Its native animals include penguins and seals, while vegetation is mainly moss and lichen. Research, tourism, and fishing are major human activities in and around Antarctica, which is governed through the Antarctic Treaty System.

key_facts.text: About 70% of the world’s freshwater reserves are frozen in Antarctica; if this ice melted, global sea levels would rise by almost 60 meters.
Antarctica holds Earth’s lowest measured temperature: −89.2 °C (−128.6 °F).
A Norwegian team made the first confirmed landing in 1895, and Roald Amundsen’s expedition first reached the geographic South Pole in 1911.
The Antarctic Treaty System prohibits military activity, mining, nuclear explosions, and nuclear-waste disposal on the continent.

overview.text: Constantine I, known as Constantine the Great, ruled the Roman Empire from AD 306 to 337. After winning the civil wars among the Tetrarchic emperors, he became sole ruler by 324. His reign marked a major shift in Roman history by strengthening Christianity’s public position and reforming imperial government.

Constantine supported the 313 Edict of Milan, which legalized Christian practice, and convened the First Council of Nicaea in 325, associated with the Nicene Creed. He also developed Constantinople from the city of Byzantium as an imperial capital; it remained the empire’s capital for more than a thousand years.

key_facts.text: He was born at Naissus, in the Roman province of Moesia Superior, and was the son of Constantius and Helena.
His reforms separated civil and military authority and introduced the solidus, a gold coin that became an enduring monetary standard.
Although he favored Christianity from 312, Constantine was baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia; scholars have debated the depth and nature of his Christian beliefs.
His political legacy included replacing Diocletian’s Tetrarchy with dynastic succession through his family.

overview.text: Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz (1926–2016) was a Cuban communist revolutionary and politician who led Cuba from 1959 to 2011. He served as prime minister, president, and first secretary of the Communist Party. Guided by Marxist–Leninist and Cuban nationalist ideas, his administration made Cuba a one-party communist state, nationalized industry and business, and introduced socialist reforms.

Castro rose to power by leading guerrillas from the Sierra Maestra against Fulgencio Batista. After taking power, he aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union, contributing to the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis. His government expanded healthcare and education but controlled the press and suppressed dissent. Supporters praised his socialism and resistance to U.S. influence, while critics condemned his authoritarian rule and human-rights record.

key_facts.text: After the failed 1953 attack on the Moncada Barracks and a prison term, Castro helped form the 26th of July Movement in Mexico with Raúl Castro and Che Guevara.
The United States opposed Castro’s government through an economic embargo, counter-revolutionary efforts, and the failed Bay of Pigs Invasion in 1961.
Cuba under Castro sent troops to support allies in the Yom Kippur, Ogaden, and Angolan civil wars and backed revolutionary movements abroad.
Raúl Castro assumed Fidel Castro’s responsibilities in 2006 and became president in 2008; Fidel remained first secretary of the Communist Party until 2011.

overview.text: On January 6, 2021, a mob of Donald Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., while Congress was counting Electoral College votes from the 2020 presidential election. The attackers sought to prevent Congress from formalizing Joe Biden’s victory and keep Trump in power. The attack interrupted the proceedings, but the Capitol was cleared and the count was completed the next morning.

The event became a major crisis in the peaceful transfer of presidential power. It involved assaults on police, violence and property damage inside the Capitol, and later congressional investigations, Trump’s impeachment for incitement of insurrection, and extensive federal criminal cases. The source notes ongoing debate over whether the event should be called a coup; this page uses the neutral term “attack.”

key_facts.text: Before the attack, Trump spoke at a “Save America” rally, repeating false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen and urging supporters to fight.
Among the groups represented in the crowd were the Proud Boys and the Oath Keepers; some participants later faced convictions for seditious conspiracy.
Capitol Police evacuated and secured Congress; rioters briefly occupied the Senate chamber, while police officers and journalists were assaulted.
A week later, the House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection. The Senate vote did not reach the two-thirds majority required for conviction.

overview.text: Walt Whitman (1819–1892) was an American poet, essayist, and journalist often called the father of free verse. His major collection, Leaves of Grass, first published in 1855, was an attempt to reach ordinary people through an American epic. Whitman’s writings incorporated transcendentalism and realism, and Leaves of Grass was controversial at the time for its overt sensuality.

During the Civil War, Whitman worked in Washington hospitals caring for wounded people, and his poetry often addressed loss and healing. After Abraham Lincoln’s assassination, he wrote the poems “O Captain! My Captain!” and “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d,” and later gave lectures about Lincoln.

key_facts.text: Whitman financed the first edition of Leaves of Grass himself and continued expanding and revising the collection until his death.
He left formal schooling at age 11 and later worked as a journalist, teacher, and government clerk.
Whitman was born in Huntington on Long Island and lived in Brooklyn during childhood and much of his career.
Modernist poet Ezra Pound referred to Whitman as “America’s poet.”

overview.text: A central processing unit (CPU), also called a central processor or processor, is a computer’s primary processor. Its electronic circuitry executes program instructions, including arithmetic, logical, control, and input/output operations. It is distinct from main memory, input/output circuitry, and specialized processors such as graphics processing units (GPUs).

A CPU’s control unit directs the basic instruction cycle: fetching instructions from memory, decoding them, and executing them. Its arithmetic–logic unit (ALU) performs calculations and logical operations, while registers supply operands and store results. Modern CPUs also use caches and instruction-level parallelism to improve performance.

key_facts.text: Most modern CPUs are implemented as microprocessors on integrated-circuit chips.
Microprocessor chips with multiple CPUs are called multi-core processors; the individual CPUs are called processor cores.
Processor cores can support CPU-level multithreading.
An integrated circuit containing a CPU may also include memory and peripheral interfaces; such devices can be called microcontrollers or systems on chip (SoCs).

overview.text: The Holocaust, also called the Shoah, was the genocide of European Jews during World War II. From 1941 to 1945, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews across occupied Europe, roughly two-thirds of Europe’s Jewish population. The crime arose from Nazi racist ideology and escalating persecution; Nazi authorities also persecuted and killed millions of non-Jewish civilians and prisoners of war. After the war, survivors emigrated, some perpetrators faced trials, and the Holocaust became commemorated through museums and memorials and central to Western historical consciousness.

key_facts.text: After seizing power in 1933, the Nazis imposed anti-Jewish laws, encouraged violence, and orchestrated Kristallnacht in November 1938. Ghettos were established after Germany invaded Poland in 1939.
Mass shootings across Eastern Europe and poison-gas chambers in extermination camps were principal methods of murder. Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka were among the camps used.
After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators murdered 1.5–2 million Jews; Jewish women and children were soon targeted as well.

By early 1942, the Nazis implemented the “Final Solution.” Some deportees were gassed in extermination camps, while others were sent to forced-labor camps, where many died from starvation, abuse, or exhaustion; some were used as test subjects in experiments.
Although most Holocaust victims were killed in 1942, mass murder continued until the end of World War II in 1945.

overview.text: Andrew Jackson (1767–1845) was the seventh U.S. president, serving from 1829 to 1837. He rose from frontier lawyer and Tennessee militia commander to national prominence as a general; his 1815 victory at New Orleans made him a national hero. His political philosophy, later associated with Jacksonian democracy, shaped his presidency.

Jackson’s legacy remains deeply contested. Supporters praised his appeal to white working Americans and his defense of the Union, while critics emphasize his racist policies toward Native Americans and his wealth derived from the forced labor of enslaved African Americans.

key_facts.text: After Jackson won a plurality but not a majority in the 1824 election, the House chose John Quincy Adams. Supporters’ allegations of a “corrupt bargain” helped form the coalition that became the Democratic Party.
During the Creek War, Jackson won the Battle of Horseshoe Bend and negotiated the Treaty of Fort Jackson, which forced the Creek to cede large areas of present-day Alabama and Georgia.
Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. It displaced tens of thousands of Native Americans from lands east of the Mississippi River and led to thousands of deaths in the Trail of Tears.
In 1832, Jackson vetoed renewal of the Second Bank of the United States, viewing it as an institution controlled by elites; the Bank was later dismantled.
During the Nullification Crisis, Jackson threatened military force after South Carolina challenged a federal tariff. The crisis ended when the tariff was amended.

overview.text: Richard I of England, known as Richard the Lionheart or Richard Cœur de Lion, ruled from 1189 until his death in 1199. He was the son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine; although he was their third son, the deaths of his two older brothers enabled him to inherit the throne. He also ruled major territories in France and held Cyprus.

Richard is strongly associated with the Third Crusade. After Philip II of France left the campaign, Richard led the Christian effort and won several victories against Saladin, but the campaign ended without the recapture of Jerusalem. His reputation as a warrior and chivalric hero lasted for centuries, though historians have debated his relationship to England itself.

key_facts.text: By age 16, Richard commanded an army and suppressed rebellions in Poitou against his father.
His titles included Duke of Normandy, Aquitaine, and Gascony, as well as Count of Poitiers, Anjou, Maine, and Nantes.
Richard was born in England but spent much of his adult life in the Duchy of Aquitaine in southwestern France.
Most of his reign was spent on crusade, in captivity, or defending the French parts of the Angevin Empire; he spent very little time in England.

overview.text: Crime and Punishment is a Russian novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, first published in 1866. It follows Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former law student in Saint Petersburg, as he plans to kill a pawnbroker and then faces the mental and moral consequences of carrying out the deed.

Raskolnikov tries to justify crime through a theory that “extraordinary” people may remove obstacles to higher goals. The novel’s central tension comes from the collapse of that theory under confusion, paranoia, disgust, guilt, and horror, making it a study of moral responsibility and self-deception.

key_facts.text: The novel appeared in twelve monthly installments in The Russian Messenger during 1866 before being issued as a single volume.
It was Dostoevsky’s second full-length novel after his ten years of exile in Siberia.
It is often cited as a major work of world literature and as the first great novel of Dostoevsky’s mature period.

overview.text: Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German priest, theologian, author, hymnwriter, professor, and former Augustinian friar. A central figure in the Protestant Reformation, he rejected parts of Roman Catholic teaching, especially teachings about indulgences and papal authority. His 1517 Ninety-Five Theses opened an international debate over these issues.

Luther taught that justification was received as the free gift of God’s grace through faith rather than earned through human merit. His ideas formed the basis of Lutheranism and challenged the religious authority of the pope and bishops.

key_facts.text: Pope Leo X demanded that Luther renounce his writings in 1520. After Luther refused, he was excommunicated in 1521; later that year, Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms.
Luther taught that the Bible was the only source of divinely revealed knowledge about the Gospel and that all baptized Christians formed a holy priesthood.

His 1534 German Bible translation made scripture more accessible to laypeople, helped shape standard German, and influenced the Tyndale Bible. Separately, his hymns influenced singing in Protestant churches.

Luther’s historical legacy also includes staunchly antisemitic writings that called for expelling Jews and burning synagogues; his works also attacked Anabaptists, Roman Catholics, and nontrinitarian Christians.

overview.text: Gabriel García Márquez (1927–2014), often called Gabo, was a Colombian writer and journalist who became a major Spanish-language author. He began his career in journalism and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.

His novels and short stories are closely associated with magic realism, a style that places magical events in otherwise ordinary, realistic situations. Important works include One Hundred Years of Solitude, Chronicle of a Death Foretold, and Love in the Time of Cholera; some works use the fictional village of Macondo, while solitude is a recurring theme.

key_facts.text: One Hundred Years of Solitude was published in 1967.
No One Writes to the Colonel appeared in 1961.
Macondo was mainly inspired by Aracataca, García Márquez’s birthplace.
He was also affectionately known as Gabito.

overview.text: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was an English poet, writer, and civil servant best known for The Canterbury Tales. His career also included work as a bureaucrat, courtier, diplomat, and member of the English Parliament.

Chaucer’s writing helped legitimize Middle English as a literary language in England, where Anglo-Norman French and Latin were still dominant. His other works include Troilus and Criseyde, Parlement of Foules, and The Book of the Duchess.

key_facts.text: He wrote A Treatise on the Astrolabe, a scientific work composed for his ten-year-old son, Lewis.
His works also include The House of Fame and The Legend of Good Women.
He was the first writer buried in what later became Poets’ Corner in Westminster Abbey.
Chaucer was elected shire knight for Kent.

overview.text: The Communist Manifesto, originally titled Manifesto of the Communist Party, is an 1848 political pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. It presents history as shaped by conflicts between social classes, whose positions depend on their relationship to the means of production. Its analysis focuses especially on capitalism and the struggle between the bourgeoisie, the ruling class, and the proletariat, or wage-earning working class.

Marx and Engels argue that capitalism exploits workers and continually transforms society. They predict that this conflict will produce a proletarian revolution and a classless communist society organized around the shared development of all people. The pamphlet opens with the image of a “spectre” haunting Europe and closes with the famous call, “Workers of the world, unite!”

key_facts.text: The pamphlet was commissioned by the Communist League and published in London during the Revolutions of 1848.
Its historical account moves through primitive communism, antiquity, feudalism, and capitalism, describing a new dominant class emerging at each stage.
The authors connect capitalism’s search for new markets with the worldwide expansion of its economic and social relations.
Proposed transitional measures include a progressive income tax, nationalization of credit and transportation, universal education, and the elimination of child labor.

overview.text: Zen is a Mahayana Buddhist tradition that developed in China during the Tang dynasty, where it was called Chan. It emerged from the meeting of Indian Mahayana philosophies and Chinese Taoist thought, then spread to Vietnam, Korea, and Japan. Its central concerns are meditation, direct insight into one’s own Buddha nature, and expressing that insight in everyday life for the benefit of others. Although some Zen sources favor direct understanding over doctrinal study, Zen schools also practice chanting, ethical precepts, walking meditation, rituals, monasticism, and scripture study.

key_facts.text: Bodhidharma is traditionally credited with bringing Chan to China, but he is described as a semi-legendary Indian or Central Asian monk.
Chan, Seon, Thiền, and Zen are the Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Japanese names associated with related forms of the tradition.
Zen developed into multiple sub-schools and branches rather than remaining a single uniform form.
Zen teachings draw on Buddhist sources including bodhisattva teachings, Yogacara, Madhyamaka, and Tathāgatagarbha texts.
Some Zen sources connect direct understanding with zazen and interaction with a teacher, often called a rōshi in Japanese.

overview.text: Romance of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguo Yanyi) is a Chinese historical novel traditionally attributed to Luo Guanzhong. It follows the decline of the Han dynasty, the Yellow Turban Rebellion, the struggles among Shu, Cao Wei, and Eastern Wu, and the eventual reunification of China under the Western Jin in 280.

The novel blends historical people and events from chronicles and storytelling traditions with fictional scenes, speeches, and supernatural episodes. It gives particular moral and political weight to Liu Bei and Shu Han, making it both a historical drama and a work shaped by literary imagination.

key_facts.text: Its Chinese title is Sānguó Yǎnyì, commonly rendered as Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
Its source traditions include historical records, earlier chronicles, and popular storytelling such as Sanguozhi Pinghua.
It is recognized as one of the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature.
Its influence extends beyond literature into drama, games, and popular accounts of the Three Kingdoms in East and Southeast Asia.

overview.text: The School of Athens (Scuola di Atene) is a fresco by Italian Renaissance artist Raphael. Painted between 1509 and 1511, it was commissioned by Pope Julius II for rooms in the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City, now called the Stanze di Raffaello.

The fresco brings together ancient mathematicians, philosophers, and scientists, with Plato and Aristotle at its center. It uses accurate perspective, a defining characteristic of Renaissance art, and presents themes connected with the revival of ancient Greek philosophy and culture. It is regarded as one of Raphael’s best-known works.

key_facts.text: Figures commonly identified in the fresco include Socrates, Pythagoras, Archimedes, Euclid, Heraclitus, Ibn Rushd (Averroes), and Zarathustra.
Most figures cannot be identified with certainty. The white-robed figure looking toward the viewer is variously identified as Hypatia or Francesco Maria I della Rovere.
Raphael is believed to have represented Leonardo da Vinci as Plato and Michelangelo as Heraclitus; he also included a self-portrait beside Ptolemy.
The fresco’s accurate perspective reflects a defining feature of Renaissance art that Raphael learned from Leonardo.

overview.text: A sonnet is a fixed poetic form traditionally built from fourteen lines and a set rhyme scheme. Originating in 13th-century Sicily, it spread into many European-language traditions. Early sonnets were chiefly associated with romantic love, but writers later used the form for any subject. The sonnet therefore combines a compact, rule-governed shape with a broad range of possible content.

key_facts.text: The name comes from the Italian sonetto, meaning “little song,” ultimately related to a Latin word for sound.
The sonnet was first developed in Sicily before being adopted in many European-language literary traditions.
Later variations sometimes abandon the traditional fourteen-line limit or omit rhyme, especially in modern poetry.

overview.text: Saudi Arabia, officially the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, is a West Asian country occupying most of the Arabian Peninsula. The Red Sea lies to its west; Jordan, Iraq, and Kuwait are to the north; the Arabian Gulf, Bahrain, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates are to the east; Oman is southeast and Yemen south.

Islam emerged in what is now Saudi Arabia in the early seventh century. The country is also a major petroleum state: after oil was discovered there in 1938, the kingdom became a major oil producer and leading exporter.

key_facts.text: Riyadh is the capital and largest city. Jeddah is another major center, while Mecca and Medina are Islam’s two holiest cities.
The modern kingdom was founded in 1932 by King Abdulaziz, who united Hejaz, Najd, and other regions into one state.
Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy under the House of Saud; its official religion is Islam and its official language is Arabic.
Saudi Arabia belongs to the Gulf Cooperation Council, Arab League, OPEC, United Nations, and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

overview.text: The Canterbury Tales is an anthology of 24 short stories by Geoffrey Chaucer, written mostly in verse in Middle English between 1387 and 1400. Its fictional frame presents pilgrims traveling from London to Canterbury to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket while taking part in a storytelling contest.

The work is regarded as Chaucer’s major achievement and had a significant effect on English literature. It may also have helped popularize English vernacular writing at a time when French and Latin were important literary languages.

key_facts.text: Most scholars consider the Tales unfinished when Chaucer died.
The General Prologue introduces roughly 30 pilgrims.
Chaucer’s stated plan called for four stories per pilgrim—two on the journey to Canterbury and two on the return—for about 120 stories in all.

overview.text: Upton Beall Sinclair Jr. (1878–1968) was an American author, muckraker journalist—a writer who investigated and publicized social abuses—and political activist. His writing examined industrialized America from the viewpoints of workers and industrialists, making him a notable literary voice of the Progressive Era.

Sinclair gained particular fame for The Jungle (1906), a novel exposing labor and sanitary conditions in the U.S. meatpacking industry. Public reaction contributed to the passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act a few months later. His other industrial novels include King Coal, Oil!, and The Flivver King.

key_facts.text: Sinclair was an outspoken socialist and ran for office as a Socialist Party congressional nominee and as the Democratic candidate for governor of California.
The Brass Check (1919) was Sinclair’s muckraking exposé of American journalism and publicized the problem of journalistic malpractice.
Sinclair won the 1943 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.
The Flivver King depicts Henry Ford’s rise and later decline into antisemitism as publisher of The Dearborn Independent.

overview.text: The horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal in the family Equidae. Its lineage developed over 45–55 million years from small, multi-toed ancestors such as Eohippus into the modern form. Horses are adapted for running and have strong balance and a fight-or-flight response; they can sleep either standing or lying down.

People began domesticating horses around 4000 BCE in Central Asia, while genetic evidence places the ancestry of modern domestic horses in the western Eurasian steppes. Humans have used horses in riding, agriculture, sport, recreation, police work, therapy, entertainment, and warfare.

key_facts.text: A female horse is a mare, and its young is a foal. Pregnancy lasts about 11 months.
Horse breeds are loosely grouped as hot bloods, cold bloods, and warmbloods according to general temperament and intended use.
A horse living in the wild after domestication is called feral; a true wild horse has never been domesticated.
Most domesticated horses begin training under a saddle or in harness between ages two and four and reach full adult development by about age five.

overview.text: The Ottoman Empire was a transcontinental state centered in modern-day Turkey, emerging from Osman I’s northwestern Anatolian principality around 1299. It expanded through Anatolia and the Balkans, conquered Constantinople in 1453, and made that city its capital. Its position and territories made it a major meeting point between Europe and the Middle East for centuries.

Under Suleiman the Magnificent in the sixteenth century, it became a global power. Its diverse confessional communities received varying autonomy through millets, which managed communal affairs under Islamic law. Later defeats, nationalist movements, and internal reforms reshaped the state: the Tanzimat strengthened its organization, while the Young Turk Revolution restored constitutional monarchy in 1908. After the empire joined the Central Powers in World War I, Allied occupation and partition were followed by Turkish nationalist victory; the sultanate ended in 1922.

key_facts.text: Mehmed II’s conquest of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire.
Conquests under Selim I led Ottoman sultans to adopt the title of caliph.
The Young Turk Revolution of 1908, led by the Committee of Union and Progress, reestablished constitutional monarchy; the group’s 1913 coup established a dictatorship.
The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in World War I, after which the victorious Allies occupied and partitioned it.
The supplied account records that the Ottoman Empire engaged in genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks during the World War I period.

overview.text: Giuseppe Verdi (1813–1901) was an Italian composer best known for opera. He came to dominate the Italian opera scene after Rossini, Bellini, and Donizetti, while also being influenced by French grand opera. His major operatic works include Nabucco, Rigoletto, La traviata, and Aida.

Verdi’s early operas showed sympathy with the Risorgimento, the movement for Italian unification.
