key_facts.text: Its classical Inca construction includes finely crafted dry-stone walls.
Notable features include the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows, and the Intihuatana ritual stone.
Agustín Lizárraga reached the site in the early 20th century; Hiram Bingham III brought it international attention in 1911.
Peru designated Machu Picchu a National Historic Sanctuary in 1981, and UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
Radiocarbon dating places the site’s occupation approximately between 1420 and 1530.

overview.text: “The Tortoise and the Hare” is one of Aesop’s Fables. It belongs to a common folktale pattern about overcoming a stronger opponent and has attracted conflicting interpretations. The story’s central association is an unequal contest in which ingenuity and trickery are set against greater strength.

key_facts.text: The fable is numbered 226 in the Perry Index.
Its central event is a race between unequal partners.
The associated folktale pattern emphasizes ingenuity and trickery rather than doggedness when confronting a stronger opponent.

overview.text: Anansi, also called Ananse, is a figure in Akan religion and folklore who is usually depicted as a spider. He is associated with stories, wisdom, knowledge, wit, mischief, cunning, and trickery. As a trickster, Anansi represents cleverness and rule-breaking within stories shaped by Akan culture and social expectations.

Anansi commonly succeeds by using creativity and wit to outsmart stronger opponents. His tales became part of West African, African-American, and Caribbean folklore after spreading to the Americas through the Atlantic slave trade, making him a major connecting figure across related storytelling traditions.

key_facts.text: “Anansi” or “Ananse” literally translates to “spider.”
A distinctive feature of Anansi is his paradoxical role: his challenges to social order can reinforce the importance of that order in Akan storytelling.
Anansi may appear as either the protagonist or the antagonist of a story.

overview.text: Elizabeth I (1533–1603) was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 until her death, and the last and longest-reigning monarch of the Tudor dynasty. Her 44-year rule gave its name to the Elizabethan era and followed the unstable reigns of her half-siblings.

Elizabeth established an English church that developed into the Church of England and governed through trusted advisers such as William Cecil. She never married, helping create the image of the “Virgin Queen.” Her reign is also associated with flourishing English drama and England’s defeat of the Spanish Armada.

key_facts.text: She was the only surviving child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. After her mother’s execution, Elizabeth was declared illegitimate but was restored to the succession at age ten.
During the reign of her Catholic half-sister Mary I, Elizabeth was imprisoned for nearly a year on suspicion of supporting Protestant rebels.
Elizabeth’s foreign policy maneuvered between France and Spain; by the mid-1580s, England could no longer avoid war with Spain.
In 1570, the pope declared Elizabeth illegitimate; conspiracies against her were countered with help from Francis Walsingham’s secret service.
Elizabeth was succeeded by James VI of Scotland, her first cousin twice removed.

overview.text: A triangle, also called a trigon, is a basic plane polygon with three line-segment sides meeting at three vertices. Its three interior angles add to 180 degrees, and its area is half the product of a chosen base and its height.

Triangles are classified by their side lengths and angles. Relationships between these measurements are a major focus of trigonometry; in right triangles, sine, cosine, and tangent connect angles with side lengths.

key_facts.text: In Euclidean geometry, any three points not all on one straight line determine one triangle in one flat plane.
If one side is chosen as the base, the opposite vertex is the apex; the height is the shortest segment between them.
A geodesic triangle is bounded by three sides that are straight relative to a surface, while a curvilinear triangle has three curved sides.

overview.text: “Daddy” is a poem by American confessional poet Sylvia Plath. It was composed on October 12, 1962, one month after Plath’s separation from Ted Hughes and four months before her death.

The poem uses controversial Holocaust metaphors to explore Plath’s complex relationship with her father, Otto Plath. Its cryptic implications have led to differing academic interpretations. Published posthumously in Ariel in 1965, it became widely anthologized in American literature.

key_facts.text: Otto Plath died shortly after Sylvia Plath’s eighth birthday from undiagnosed diabetes.
“Daddy” appeared in Ariel alongside other late Plath poems, including “Tulips” and “Lady Lazarus.”
The poem’s Holocaust imagery is controversial, and its themes and implications have received different academic readings.

overview.text: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist. He developed historical materialism, a theory of social change centered on class conflict, especially the struggle produced by capitalism. His analysis focused on how capitalism organizes society and generates tensions between social classes.

Marx’s ideas, later called Marxism, became highly influential in socialist thought, political movements, economics, and sociology. His central writings include The Communist Manifesto, written with Friedrich Engels, and Das Kapital, his major critique of political economy.

key_facts.text: Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848 as a program for revolution.
Das Kapital, published from 1867 to 1894, presents Marx’s critique of classical political economy and was written in three volumes.
In Marx’s account of capitalism, the bourgeoisie controls the means of production, while the proletariat works for wages by selling its labor power.

Marx predicted that capitalism’s internal contradictions would encourage working-class consciousness and a struggle for political power, ultimately aiming at a classless, stateless, and moneyless society.
Marxist schools later guided revolutions that established communist states in several countries during the 20th century, while Marx’s economic ideas influenced theories of labor and capital.

overview.text: Austria is a landlocked country in Central Europe, set in the Eastern Alps. It is a federation of nine states, with Vienna serving as both the national capital and one of those states. Its neighbors are Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Italy, Switzerland, and Liechtenstein.

Austria was the heartland of the Habsburg monarchy and a major Central European imperial power; Vienna also served as the Holy Roman Empire’s administrative capital from the 16th century. Austria-Hungary was established in 1867, and the modern Austrian republic emerged after World War I.

key_facts.text: After Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in 1914, Emperor Franz Joseph declared war on Serbia, and the conflict rapidly escalated into World War I.
Austria was annexed into Nazi Germany before World War II, liberated in 1945, and restored its sovereignty after a decade of Allied occupation.
In 1955, Austria declared perpetual neutrality.
Austria is a semi-presidential representative democracy: a popularly elected president is head of state, while a chancellor leads the government.
Austria joined the United Nations in 1955 and the European Union in 1995.

overview.text: Toni Morrison (1931–2019), born Chloe Ardelia Wofford, was an American novelist and editor. Her major fiction includes The Bluest Eye (1970), Song of Solomon (1977), and Beloved (1987). She received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993.

Morrison’s writing is strongly associated with the Black American experience and with the harsh consequences of racism in the United States. Her work combines major literary recognition with sustained attention to those subjects.

key_facts.text: Song of Solomon brought Morrison national attention and won the National Book Critics Circle Award.
Beloved won the Pulitzer Prize in 1988.
In the late 1960s, Morrison became the first Black female fiction editor at Random House in New York City.
She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

overview.text: Franklin Delano Roosevelt (FDR) was the 32nd president of the United States, serving from 1933 until his death in 1945. His first two terms centered on combating the Great Depression, while his third and fourth terms focused on U.S. involvement in World War II. He was the only U.S. president to serve more than two terms.

Roosevelt’s New Deal began during his first 100 days and included relief for unemployed people and farmers, economic-recovery measures, and lasting programs such as Social Security. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, he directed U.S. war mobilization, pursued a Europe First strategy, and worked with Allied leaders toward the United Nations.

key_facts.text: Before becoming president, Roosevelt served as assistant secretary of the Navy and later as governor of New York.
An illness in 1921 permanently paralyzed his legs; with encouragement from Eleanor Roosevelt, he returned to politics and became governor of New York in 1928.
Roosevelt defeated Herbert Hoover in the 1932 election. During his first 100 days, he built the New Deal coalition and realigned American politics into the Fifth Party System.
Some of Roosevelt’s wartime actions have been criticized, including his order for the internment of German, Italian, and Japanese Americans.

overview.text: Venice is a coastal city in northeastern Italy and the capital of the Veneto region. It occupies 126 islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, where canals separate the islands and bridges connect parts of the city. This unusual island-and-water setting is reflected in traditional names such as “City of Canals” and “City of Bridges.”

From 810 to 1797, Venice was the capital of the Republic of Venice, a powerful medieval and Renaissance center of finance, maritime activity, commerce, and art. Its influence extended across the Adriatic and the Italian peninsula, while the Venetian Arsenal supported its naval power. Venice and its lagoon became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

key_facts.text: Napoleon ended Venice’s sovereignty in 1797; the city became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.
The Venetian Arsenal was the base of Venice’s naval power and is considered by several historians to have been history’s first factory.
“La Serenissima” (“The Most Serene”) and “Queen of the Adriatic” are traditional names for Venice.
Venice was the birthplace of Baroque composers Tomaso Albinoni and Antonio Vivaldi.

overview.text: Louisiana is a Deep South and South Central U.S. state bordered by Texas, Arkansas, and Mississippi, with the Gulf of Mexico along its southern coast. Baton Rouge is the capital, while New Orleans is the most populous city. The Mississippi River forms much of the eastern boundary and shapes the state’s lower geography.

Louisiana lies where the Mississippi River system meets the Gulf of Mexico. Sediment carried downstream created large deltas, coastal marshes, and swamps, while the state’s French heritage and multicultural history remain visible in its languages, culture, demographics, and legal system.

key_facts.text: Louisiana is the only U.S. state whose local political divisions are called parishes rather than counties, a term connected to its French heritage.
Northern areas include tallgrass prairie, longleaf pine forests, and wet savannas; more than half of the state is forested.
France claimed Louisiana in 1682; after periods of Spanish and French rule, Napoleon sold the territory to the United States in 1803. Louisiana became the 18th state in 1812.
Its cultural influences include Louisiana French traditions such as Cajun and Creole culture, along with Spanish, Native American, and West African influences.

overview.text: Spin is an intrinsic, quantized form of angular momentum carried by elementary particles and by composite objects such as hadrons, atomic nuclei, and atoms. In quantum mechanics, its possible values occur discretely and are commonly represented by a spin quantum number. Understanding interactions involving spin requires relativistic quantum mechanics or quantum field theory.

Experiments provide evidence for spin: the Stern–Gerlach experiment found that silver atoms could have two discrete angular-momentum values even when they had no orbital angular momentum. Spin is also connected to the Pauli exclusion principle through the spin–statistics theorem.

key_facts.text: Particles of the same kind have the same spin magnitude, although the direction of their spin can change.
Spin may be described mathematically as a vector for photons and as a spinor for electrons.
The spin–statistics theorem links half-integer spin with the Pauli exclusion principle.
Spin uses the same units as ordinary angular momentum, but it is often reported simply as a dimensionless quantum number after division by the reduced Planck constant.

overview.text: Angular momentum is the rotational counterpart of linear momentum. It has both magnitude and direction, and the total angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant. This conservation restricts how a system can move, although it does not determine one unique motion.

For a point particle, angular momentum is represented by the cross product of its position and momentum vectors, so its value depends on the chosen origin. Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum; when no external torque acts, total angular momentum is conserved.

key_facts.text: The angular momentum of a composite system is the sum of the angular momenta of its parts.
Bicycles, motorcycles, flying discs, rifled bullets, and gyroscopes have useful properties linked to conservation of angular momentum.
The change in angular momentum during an interaction is called angular impulse, also known as twirl.
Conservation of angular momentum is also associated with spiral hurricanes and rapidly rotating neutron stars.

overview.text: The cello, also called the violoncello, is a medium-low-pitched bowed string instrument in the violin family. Its four strings are normally tuned in fifths from low C through G, D, and A; the viola’s strings sound an octave higher.

The cello has an extensive solo and concerto repertoire. In chamber music, including string quartets, and in orchestras, it often provides the bass part. In Baroque music, it commonly formed part of the basso continuo alongside chordal instruments such as the harpsichord or organ.

key_facts.text: Cello music is generally written in the bass clef; tenor and treble clefs are used for higher passages.
As a solo instrument, the cello can use a range extending from bass to soprano.
Double basses may reinforce the cello’s part at an octave lower in orchestral string sections.
Cellos appear in varied ensembles, including modern Chinese orchestras and cello rock bands.

overview.text: Formally titled The Year 1812, Solemn Overture, Op. 49, the 1812 Overture is a concert overture in E-flat major by Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Written in 1880, it commemorates Russia’s successful defense against the French invasion of 1812.

This roughly 15-minute work is especially associated with its climax of cannon fire, ringing chimes, and a brass fanfare. It is also commonly performed with fireworks displays on U.S. Independence Day.

key_facts.text: Tchaikovsky wrote the overture in six weeks.
Its first public performance took place in Moscow on August 20, 1882, under a tent near the unfinished Cathedral of Christ the Saviour.
The cathedral near the premiere site also commemorated Russia’s defense in 1812.
The overture became one of Tchaikovsky’s most popular works, alongside his ballet scores for The Nutcracker, The Sleeping Beauty, and Swan Lake.

overview.text: The Taliban is an Afghan religious and political movement that also functions as a militant organization and government, calling its state the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. It emerged in 1994 during the Second Afghan Civil War, drew largely on Pashtun areas of eastern and southern Afghanistan, and captured Kabul in 1996, establishing its first Islamic Emirate.

The U.S. invasion in October 2001 ended the Taliban’s first government. After about two decades of insurgency, a Taliban offensive culminated in the fall of Kabul in August 2021 and the restoration of the Islamic Emirate. Taliban rule has been widely condemned for restricting women’s education and employment and persecuting ethnic and religious minorities.

key_facts.text: Mullah Omar led the movement during its rise; the Northern Alliance opposed the first Islamic Emirate and retained international recognition as a continuation of the previous Afghan state.
During its 1996–2001 rule, the Taliban enforced a strict interpretation of Sharia, banned women from school and most employment, prohibited most music, and destroyed cultural artifacts.

After being overthrown, the Taliban fought an insurgency against the U.S.-backed Islamic Republic of Afghanistan and NATO-led forces; exiled members formed a leadership council in Quetta, Pakistan, in 2002.
The movement rejects democratic participation and considers political parties un-Islamic; its government is centrally organized under a supreme leader with extensive power.

overview.text: Afghanistan is a landlocked country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia. Kabul is its capital and largest city. Much of the country is mountainous, with northern and southwestern plains separated by the Hindu Kush range.

Afghanistan’s modern history has been shaped by prolonged conflict. A 1978 communist revolution established a socialist republic, and infighting was followed by a Soviet invasion in 1979. After the Soviet withdrawal, civil war preceded Taliban control; the Taliban were overthrown in the 2001 U.S. invasion and returned to power after capturing Kabul in 2021.

key_facts.text: Afghanistan borders Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and China.
The modern Afghan state is associated with the Durrani Empire, established in the 18th century under Ahmad Shah Durrani.
Afghanistan became a buffer state in the Great Game, the rivalry between the British and Russian empires.
Afghanistan has deposits of lithium, iron, zinc, and copper and belongs to the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.

overview.text: Osiris was an ancient Egyptian god associated with the dead, the underworld, resurrection, fertility, agriculture, and vegetation. He was traditionally described as the brother and husband of Isis, the brother of Set, and the posthumous father of Horus the Younger.

In the central Osiris myth, Set killed and dismembered him. Isis and Nephthys searched Egypt for the pieces, recovered all but one, and rewrapped his body so that he could return to life. Osiris’s renewed life connected him with hopes for life after death and with recurring natural cycles such as vegetation and the Nile’s flooding.

key_facts.text: Osiris was commonly depicted with a pharaoh’s beard, a distinctive atef crown, and a crook and flail; his legs were partly wrapped like a mummy’s.
His titles included “Lord of Silence” and Khenti-Amentiu, meaning “Foremost of the Westerners.”
After the spread of his cult, Egyptian kings were associated with Osiris after death and hoped to share in his eternal life.
The earliest evidence for Osiris worship dates to the middle of Egypt’s Fifth Dynasty, in the 25th century BCE, although the worship may have begun earlier.

overview.text: Medusa, also called Gorgo or the Gorgon, is a figure in Greek mythology and one of the three Gorgons. She is commonly portrayed as a woman with living snakes for hair; her appearance was said to turn anyone who looked at her to stone. Unlike her sisters Euryale and Stheno, Medusa was mortal.

Her defining mythic connection is to the hero Perseus, who beheaded her. Even after death, her head retained the power to petrify onlookers until Perseus gave it to Athena for her shield. In classical antiquity, Medusa’s head also appeared as a Gorgoneion, an image used to avert evil.

key_facts.text: Medusa and her sisters were usually described as daughters of Phorcys and Ceto.
Accounts differed about where the Gorgons lived: Hesiod and Aeschylus placed them on Sarpedon near Cisthene, while later traditions associated them with Libya.
The name Medusa is glossed from Ancient Greek as “guardian” or “protectress.”

overview.text: Iodine is chemical element I, atomic number 53, and the heaviest stable halogen. Under standard conditions it is a semi-lustrous, nonmetallic solid; heating produces a deep violet liquid and then a violet gas. Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811, and its name refers to an Ancient Greek word meaning “violet.”

Iodine’s central biological association is thyroid health: the body needs it to make thyroid hormones, and deficiency can cause serious intellectual harm. In medicine, iodine-based materials are used for radiographic contrast, while radioactive iodine isotopes can help treat thyroid cancer. Iodine also has industrial uses as a catalyst.

key_facts.text: Iodine occurs in several chemical forms and oxidation states, including iodide, iodate, and periodate ions.
Chile and Japan are identified as the dominant iodine-producing countries.
Iodine appears on the World Health Organization’s List of Essential Medicines.
Industrial iodine catalysis is used in making acetic acid and some polymers.

overview.text: Symphony No. 9 in E minor, “From the New World,” is a symphony by Antonín Dvořák, composed in 1893 while he was director of the National Conservatory of Music of America. It premiered in New York City on December 16, 1893, and is regarded as one of the most popular symphonies.

key_facts.text: It is also known as the “New World Symphony”; its Czech title is “Z nového světa.”
Its catalog designations are Op. 95 and B. 178, and it is in E minor.
Dvořák directed the National Conservatory of Music of America from 1892 to 1895.
Older literature and recordings sometimes call it Symphony No. 5, reflecting its numbering in the first publication.

overview.text: Finnegans Wake is a novel by Irish writer James Joyce. Its base language is English, but Joyce reshapes it by combining and altering words from many languages into a distinctive idiom. Commentators have connected this linguistic mixing with the way memories, people, and places may blend and change in a dreaming or half-awakened state.

The narrative centers on the Earwicker family: father HCE, mother ALP, and their children Shem, Shaun, and Issy. An unclear rumor about HCE leads to ALP’s attempt to clear him, while the sons contest his place; a final monologue belongs to ALP.

key_facts.text: The novel appeared in installments beginning in 1924 under the working title “fragments from Work in Progress”; its final title was revealed upon publication in 1939.
Its early reception was largely negative, and its radical language has given it a reputation for exceptional difficulty.
The ending is cyclical: an unfinished final line completes the fragment with which the book begins.

overview.text: The Book of Revelation, also called the Apocalypse of John, is the final book of the Christian New Testament. Its title comes from a Greek word meaning “revelation” or “unveiling.” The work combines letters, prophecy, and apocalyptic visions: it begins with messages to seven churches in Asia and then presents symbolic visions concerning events before the Second Coming of Jesus Christ.

Revelation has a central place in Christian eschatology. Its striking imagery includes a woman crowned with twelve stars, a seven-headed Dragon, and a seven-headed Beast. Modern biblical scholarship often reads the work as a first-century warning to Christian communities against assimilating into Roman imperial culture, while its symbolism has supported many Christian interpretations.

key_facts.text: Revelation is the only apocalyptic book included in the New Testament canon.
The text identifies its author only as John; the author’s precise identity remains debated.
The book is written in Greek and uses allusions and numerical symbolism derived from the Old Testament.
John is presented as being on Patmos, an island in the Aegean Sea, when he addresses the seven churches.

overview.text: “The Masque of the Red Death” is a Gothic short story by American writer Edgar Allan Poe, first published in 1842. Prince Prospero tries to escape a deadly plague by sheltering with wealthy nobles in an abbey, where they hold a masquerade in seven rooms, each decorated in a different color.

Their celebration is disrupted by a mysterious figure disguised as a victim of the Red Death. After Prospero confronts the stranger, he and the other guests die. The story is often interpreted as an allegory of death’s inevitability, although some critics question relying on an allegorical reading.

key_facts.text: The story originally appeared as “The Mask of the Red Death: A Fantasy.”
It was published in May 1842 in Graham’s Magazine.
The mysterious figure’s costume turns out to contain nothing tangible inside it.
The story has received many interpretations, including debates about the actual nature of the Red Death.
A 1964 film adaptation starred Vincent Price.

source.title: The Masque of the Red Death

overview.text: Germany, officially the Federal Republic of Germany, is a country in Western and Central Europe. It lies between the Baltic Sea and North Sea to the north, with the Alps to the south. It borders Denmark, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium, and the Netherlands. These northern seas, southern mountains, and extensive land borders are central geographic associations for recognizing Germany.

key_facts.text: Germany is organized into 16 constituent states.
Berlin is both the national capital and the country’s most populous city.
Frankfurt is Germany’s main financial centre, while the Ruhr is its largest urban area.
After Germany was divided in 1949 into West Germany and East Germany, reunification took place on 3 October 1990.

overview.text: The German Empire—also called Imperial Germany or the Second Reich—was the German Reich from unification in 1871 until the November Revolution of 1918, when Germany became a republic. It was a federation of 25 states, but Prussia dominated its territory and population; the Prussian king also held the title of German Emperor.

Founded under Wilhelm I, with Berlin as its capital and Otto von Bismarck as chancellor, the empire became a major industrial, scientific, and military power. After Bismarck’s dismissal in 1890, Wilhelm II pursued Weltpolitik, an aggressive and expansionist foreign policy. Germany entered World War I, and military defeat followed by revolution ended the empire.

key_facts.text: Bismarck’s government combined conservative politics with social programs that helped lay foundations for the modern European welfare state.
Germany formed the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, which expanded into the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882.
During the 1880s, Germany entered the colonial competition and acquired territories in Africa, the Pacific, and China.
In World War I, Germany faced stalemate on the Western Front but occupied substantial territory in the east after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
Wilhelm II abdicated during the November 1918 Revolution, leaving a federal republic to govern the defeated empire’s population.

overview.text: In Christian tradition, Satan, also called the Devil, is generally portrayed as a rebel against God and an enticer toward sin or falsehood. Christian accounts often describe him as a fallen angel with temporary power over a fallen world and demons. His background is older and more complex: ha-satan in the Hebrew Bible appears as a heavenly prosecutor subordinate to God, while later traditions develop him into a malevolent opponent.

The Gospels portray Satan tempting Jesus in the desert, while Revelation depicts him as a dragon defeated by Michael and ultimately cast into the Lake of Fire. Christian art commonly gives him horns, cloven hooves, a tail, and a pitchfork, and major literary portrayals include Dante’s Inferno and Milton’s Paradise Lost.

key_facts.text: Genesis does not name Satan specifically, although Christians often identify the serpent in Eden with him.
In Revelation, Satan is bound for one thousand years, briefly released, and then finally defeated.

The familiar horned, cloven-hoofed image is not a biblical description; it developed in Christian art from the ninth century and combines traits associated with figures such as Pan, Poseidon, and Bes.
Satan’s role was relatively minor and often comic in medieval mystery plays, but became more prominent during the early modern period alongside beliefs about witchcraft and demonic possession.

overview.text: Nigeria, officially the Federal Republic of Nigeria, is a West African country between the Sahel and the Gulf of Guinea. It borders Niger, Chad, Cameroon, and Benin. Abuja, in the Federal Capital Territory, is the national capital; Lagos is the largest city.
Nigeria is a highly diverse multinational state. More than 250 ethnic groups speak about 500 languages; Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo are the largest groups, while English is the official language.

key_facts.text: Nigeria is a federation of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.
The population is divided roughly between Muslims and Christians, with indigenous religions also practiced.
Nigeria gained independence on October 1, 1960; a civil war lasted from 1967 to 1970, and stable democracy was established in 1999.
Its modern territorial shape developed after Britain merged the Northern and Southern Nigeria Protectorates in 1914.

overview.text: Ireland is an island in the North Atlantic, in northwestern Europe. The island is divided politically: the sovereign Republic of Ireland occupies about five-sixths of it, while Northern Ireland occupies the remainder and is part of the United Kingdom. The Irish Sea, North Channel, and St George’s Channel separate Ireland from Great Britain.

Ireland’s physical geography combines a low central plain with a surrounding ring of coastal mountains. Its mild, changeable oceanic climate brings frequent rainfall and supports the lush vegetation behind the nickname “Emerald Isle.” Western and southern areas include mountainous, rocky, and karst landscapes, while central limestone regions are comparatively fertile.

key_facts.text: Ireland covers 84,421 km²; the Republic of Ireland occupies about 83% of the island’s area.
Carrauntoohil is a mountain in County Kerry with a height of 1,039 meters.
The River Shannon is the island’s longest river, running about 360.5 kilometers from County Cavan through Limerick.

Ireland, Great Britain, and many nearby smaller islands are collectively known as the British Isles; because the term can be controversial in relation to Ireland, “Britain and Ireland” is sometimes used as a neutral alternative.

overview.text: New Mexico is a landlocked state in the U.S. Southwest and one of the southern Rocky Mountain states. It shares the Four Corners region with Utah, Colorado, and Arizona; it also borders Texas and Oklahoma and shares an international border with Mexico. Santa Fe is the capital, while Albuquerque is the largest city.

The state’s varied landscape ranges from forested mountains to sparse deserts. The Rio Grande and its fertile valley run north to south through the center. New Mexico also has a major federal presence, including White Sands Missile Range and Los Alamos National Laboratory.

key_facts.text: Santa Fe was founded in 1610 and is described as the oldest state capital in the United States.
New Mexico became the 47th U.S. state on January 6, 1912, after spending 64 years as a territory.
The 1680 Pueblo Revolt successfully challenged Spanish colonial rule and is described as the first successful revolution against colonial rule in the Americas.
New Mexico hosted major Manhattan Project facilities during World War II, and the first nuclear test, Trinity, took place there in 1945.
The state contains 19 federally recognized Pueblo communities and part of the Navajo Nation, reflecting its long Indigenous and Spanish colonial history.

overview.text: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), born Sigismund Schlomo Freud, was an Austrian neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysis joined a clinical method for evaluating and treating psychological pathologies through dialogue with a theory of the mind and human agency.

Freud's approach used free association, dream interpretation, and analysis of transference phenomena in clinical settings. His work included theories of the unconscious and repression, as well as a psychic structure composed of the id, ego, and superego. Psychoanalysis remains influential in psychology, psychiatry, psychotherapy, and the humanities.

key_facts.text: Freud treated dreams as wish fulfillments and used them as models for analyzing symptom formation.
He formulated the Oedipus complex after redefining sexuality to include infantile stages.
Freud proposed libido as sexualized psychic energy and described a death drive linked to compulsive repetition, hate, aggression, and neurotic guilt.
Psychoanalysis is less prevalent in diagnostic and clinical practice, and its therapeutic efficacy and scientific status remain subjects of debate.

overview.text: John Keats was an English poet of the second generation of Romantic poets. His work is especially associated with odes, sensuous language, intense emotion, and natural imagery. Important poems include “Ode to a Nightingale,” “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” and the sonnet “On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer.”
Keats’s poetry was received indifferently during his lifetime, but his reputation grew rapidly after his death, eventually placing him in the canon of English literature.

key_facts.text: Keats lived from 1795 to 1821 and died of tuberculosis at age 25.
His poems had been published for fewer than four years when he died.
His medievalist poems include “La Belle Dame sans Merci” and “The Eve of St. Agnes.”
Those medievalist poems strongly influenced the Victorian-era Pre-Raphaelite movement and inspired poets including Algernon Charles Swinburne, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and William Morris.

overview.text: Ozone, also called trioxygen, is an inorganic molecule with the formula O3 and an allotrope of oxygen. It forms when ultraviolet light or electrical discharges act on ordinary oxygen (O2). Ozone exists in low concentrations throughout the atmosphere, with its greatest concentration in the stratospheric ozone layer.

The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet radiation, helping protect Earth’s surface. Ozone’s strong oxidizing ability has useful applications, but it also makes ozone pollution near ground level harmful to animal respiratory tissues and plants.

key_facts.text: Ozone is much less stable than O2 and can break down into ordinary oxygen, especially in the lower atmosphere.
At standard temperature and pressure, ozone is a pale-blue gas with a distinctive pungent odor.
Ozone is a powerful oxidizing agent, which explains both its industrial uses and its ability to damage living tissues at elevated concentrations.

overview.text: The Great Flood is a mythic motif in which one or more deities send a catastrophic flood to destroy civilization, often as divine punishment. The waters may also represent cleansing or purification before humanity is renewed, linking the motif to the primordial cosmic ocean found in some creation myths. Most versions feature a surviving culture hero who embodies humanity’s desire to continue living.

The motif appears in multiple traditions rather than belonging to only one mythology. Its oldest known divinely initiated narrative is associated with Sumerian Mesopotamia; an Akkadian version appears in the Atra-Hasis epic, dated to the 18th century BCE. Related traditions include Genesis, Deucalion in Greek mythology, Hindu manvantara-sandhya, and Indigenous North American cultures.

key_facts.text: Mesopotamian flood traditions include a Sumerian narrative and the Akkadian Atra-Hasis epic.
Atra-Hasis is dated to the 18th century BCE.
Deucalion is the Greek mythological figure associated with a flood tradition.
The biblical Genesis flood narrative is one of the comparable traditions identified with the motif.

overview.text: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish writer, essayist, satirist, and Anglican cleric. His central literary association is Gulliver’s Travels (1726), a satirical prose novel involving the fictional island of Lilliput. He also wrote A Tale of a Tub and A Modest Proposal, whose deadpan, ironic style helped inspire the term “Swiftian.”

Swift wrote across satire, essays, and religious or political commentary, often publishing anonymously or under pseudonyms such as Lemuel Gulliver and Isaac Bickerstaff. His work influenced later writers including John Ruskin and George Orwell, while his connection to St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin gave rise to the name “Dean Swift.”

key_facts.text: Swift lived from 1667 to 1745.
In 1713, he became dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin, leading to the nickname “Dean Swift.”
His satire is described through both Horatian and Juvenalian traditions.
The poem Cadenus and Vanessa (1726) is credited with introducing the popular woman’s name “Vanessa.”
Swift’s later influence includes writers such as John Ruskin and George Orwell.

overview.text: Pablo Neruda (born Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto) was a Chilean poet whose writing ranged from surrealist poems and historical epics to political manifestos, prose autobiography, and passionate love poetry. His 1924 collection Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair is a central literary association. Alongside writing, he held diplomatic posts and served as a senator for Chile’s Communist Party.
His works became popular and influential worldwide, and he is often considered Chile’s national poet.

key_facts.text: Neruda won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature.
He became known as a poet at age 13.
After communism was outlawed in Chile in 1948 and a warrant was issued for his arrest, he escaped through a mountain pass near Maihue Lake into Argentina in 1949.
He advised Chilean socialist president Salvador Allende and served as Chile’s ambassador to France during Allende’s presidency.

overview.text: Genghis Khan, born Temüjin, founded the Mongol Empire and became its first khan. After uniting Mongol tribes, he led campaigns that conquered large parts of China and Central Asia. His rise transformed divided steppe groups into a powerful empire.

In 1206, Temüjin adopted the title “Genghis Khan” and reorganized Mongol society into an integrated meritocracy serving the ruling family. His conquests caused enormous destruction but also enabled extensive commercial and cultural exchange across a vast region.

key_facts.text: In 1219, Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarazmian Empire after his envoys were executed; the campaign toppled the state and devastated Transoxiana and Khorasan.
Jebe and his colleague Subutai led an expedition that reached Georgia and Kievan Rus’.
Genghis Khan died in 1227 while campaigning against rebellious Western Xia. His son and heir Ögedei acceded to the throne in 1229 after a two-year interregnum.
His legacy remains controversial: he is remembered as a ruthless conqueror in Russia and the Arab world, while modern Mongolians recognize him as the founder of their nation.

overview.text: Ivan IV Vasilyevich (1530–1584), known as Ivan the Terrible, ruled Moscow from childhood and became the first tsar and grand prince of all Russia in 1547. His reign marked Russia’s transformation from a medieval state toward an empire, combining administrative reforms and territorial expansion with severe violence and long-term economic costs. Early measures included the Zemsky Sobor assembly, legal and local-government reforms, and the first standing army, the streltsy. He conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, extending Russian control along the Volga.

Later, Ivan sought stronger autocratic control. The oprichniki carried out a violent purge, including the massacre of Novgorod, while the unsuccessful Livonian War weakened Russia’s position in the Baltic. Accounts of Ivan’s character differ, but historians generally believe he killed his eldest son in anger; the succession of his younger son helped lead to the end of the Rurik dynasty and the Time of Troubles.

key_facts.text: The streltsy, established under Ivan, formed Russia’s first standing army.
The oprichniki were Russia’s first political police and carried out a violent purge.
The Livonian War failed to secure Livonia for Russia and ended with the loss of Ingria.
Ivan’s reign included the importation of Russia’s first printing press.
His younger son Feodor inherited the throne; Feodor’s childless death helped end the Rurik dynasty and begin the Time of Troubles.

overview.text: Denver is Colorado’s capital and most populous city. It is an officially consolidated city and county in the South Platte River valley, on the western edge of the High Plains and just east of the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains.

Known as the “Mile High City,” Denver has an official elevation of exactly one mile above sea level. Founded during the Gold Rush, it grew from a prospecting settlement into a commercial and transportation hub for the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain West.

key_facts.text: Denver was founded in 1858 at the meeting point of Cherry Creek and the South Platte River and was named for James W. Denver, then governor of the Kansas Territory.
The Denver metropolitan area functions as an economic and cultural center of the broader Front Range Urban Corridor.
Cultural institutions in Denver include the Denver Performing Arts Complex, Denver Art Museum, and Denver Museum of Nature and Science.

overview.text: Richard Wagner (1813–1883) was a German composer best known for operas, though his mature stage works are often called music dramas. He wrote both the words and music for his stage works. His idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk, or “total work of art,” aimed to unite poetry, music, visual design, and drama in a continuously sung narrative rather than a sequence of separate arias and recitatives.

Wagner’s later music is known for rich orchestration, complex harmony, and leitmotifs—musical phrases connected with characters, places, ideas, or plot elements. His innovations influenced classical music, and Tristan und Isolde is regarded as an important precursor to modernist music.

key_facts.text: His full name was Wilhelm Richard Wagner; he lived from 1813 to 1883.
Der Ring des Nibelungen, often called the Ring, is a four-opera cycle in which Wagner most fully realized his artistic theories.
Wagner had the Bayreuth Festspielhaus built for his artistic vision. It premiered the Ring and Parsifal and remains associated with the annual Bayreuth Festival.
Wagner remains controversial because of his provocative essays, personal conduct, and debated views on religion, politics, and society, including questions about antisemitism in his works.

overview.text: The Persistence of Memory is a 1931 painting by Salvador Dalí and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. Its descriptive alternate titles include “The Melting Clocks,” “The Soft Watches,” and “The Melting Watches.”
The painting has a broad public presence: it is widely recognized, frequently referred to in popular culture, and held by the Museum of Modern Art in New York City.

key_facts.text: Its Catalan title is La persistència de la memòria; its Spanish title is La persistencia de la memoria.
It was first exhibited at the Julien Levy Gallery in 1932.
The painting sold for $250 and was donated by an anonymous donor to MoMA in 1934.

overview.text: Graffiti is writing or drawing on a wall or another surface, usually without permission and in public view. It ranges from simple written “monikers” to elaborate wall paintings. Examples date to ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, and the Roman Empire.

Modern graffiti began in the New York City subway system and Philadelphia in the early 1970s before spreading across the United States and the world. It remains controversial: in most countries, marking or painting property without permission is considered vandalism. Graffiti is distinguished from murals, which are often permitted forms of street art.

key_facts.text: “Graffito” is used as the singular form in graffiti archaeology.
The term includes both simple written marks and elaborate wall paintings.
Modern graffiti is associated with the New York City subway system and Philadelphia.
Murals are often permitted forms of street art and are distinguished from graffiti.

overview.text: Electric charge is a physical property of matter that causes it to experience forces in electromagnetic fields. It can be positive or negative: like charges repel, unlike charges attract, and an object with no net charge is electrically neutral. Charges produce electric fields, while moving charges also produce magnetic fields; their interactions create the electromagnetic, or Lorentz, force.

In ordinary matter, electrons carry negative charge and protons carry positive charge. The total charge of an isolated system remains constant. Charge is quantized, meaning it occurs in integer multiples of the elementary charge, e.

key_facts.text: The elementary charge is about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs; a proton has +e and an electron has −e.
The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C), named after French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb.
Electrical engineering commonly uses the ampere-hour, while chemistry uses the Faraday constant for the charge of one mole of elementary charges.

overview.text: New Jersey is a U.S. state in both the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions, on the Atlantic coast. It borders New York, Pennsylvania, the Delaware River, Delaware Bay, and Delaware.

Its central location in the Northeast megalopolis helped drive rapid growth and suburbanization in the late twentieth century. Since the beginning of the twenty-first century, the state has also had a diversified economy and a major role in Atlantic seaboard logistics and distribution.

key_facts.text: Trenton is the state capital, while Newark is New Jersey’s most populous city.
New Jersey is the fifth-smallest U.S. state by land area but the nation’s most densely populated state.
The state’s name comes from the Channel Island of Jersey, after British control was established during the colonial period.
New Jersey was one of the Thirteen Colonies and hosted pivotal events during the American Revolutionary War, earning the title “Crossroads of the American Revolution.”

overview.text: Homer is the traditional name for an ancient Greek poet credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, two foundational epic poems of Greek literature. His identity and even existence remain debated in the “Homeric Question”; scholars generally regard the two poems as works of separate authors, so the traditional attribution is not a secure biography.

The Iliad centers on a quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles during the Trojan War, while the Odyssey follows Odysseus’s long journey home after Troy’s fall. The poems helped shape ancient Greek ideals of heroism, glory, and honor, and later inspired works of literature, music, art, and film.

key_facts.text: The poems were probably transmitted orally and use Homeric, or Epic, Greek—a literary language with Ionic and Aeolic features and predominantly Eastern Ionic influence.
Their composition is generally placed around the late eighth or early seventh century BC.
Ancient biographies often portrayed Homer as a blind bard from Ionia, but modern scholars regard these accounts as legendary rather than historical.
Plato famously described Homer as the poet who had “educated Greece,” reflecting the epics’ role in ancient Greek culture and education.

overview.text: Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Raven” is a narrative poem with a supernatural atmosphere. A distraught lover mourning Lenore receives a visit from a mysterious raven whose repeated “nevermore” further antagonizes him. The bird perches on a bust of Pallas, while the poem draws on folk, mythological, religious, and classical references.

The poem is noted for its musicality and stylized language, using techniques such as internal rhyme and alliteration. First published in 1845, it helped make Poe popular during his lifetime and was soon reprinted, parodied, and illustrated.

key_facts.text: Poe described composing the poem methodically in his 1846 essay “The Philosophy of Composition.”
Part of the poem’s inspiration came from the talking raven in Charles Dickens’s 1841 novel “Barnaby Rudge.”
Poe based the poem’s complex rhythm and meter on Elizabeth Barrett’s “Lady Geraldine’s Courtship.”

overview.text: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer, poet, editor, and literary critic associated with Romanticism, Gothic fiction, and early American literature. His poetry and short stories are especially linked with mystery and the macabre.

Poe helped make the short story a successful form in the United States and is generally considered a pioneer of detective fiction. He also contributed significantly to science fiction. His 1845 poem “The Raven” achieved instant success, and his work later influenced literature worldwide.

key_facts.text: He was born in Boston in 1809 and died in Baltimore in 1849 at age 40.
After turning toward prose, Poe worked for literary journals and periodicals and became known for his literary criticism.
The cause of his death remains unknown; proposed explanations have included disease, alcoholism, substance abuse, and suicide.
His influence extended beyond literature into fields such as cosmology and cryptography, and his works appeared widely in art, music, motion pictures, and television.
The Mystery Writers of America presents an annual Edgar Award for distinguished work in the mystery genre.

overview.text: The Southern United States—also called the South or Dixie—is one of the U.S. Census Bureau’s four regions. It lies between the Atlantic and the western United States, with the Gulf of Mexico and Mexico to the south. Cultural definitions do not align perfectly with state borders, and the region includes subregions such as the Southeast, South Central, Upper South, and Deep South. The Census Bureau formally places Maryland, Delaware, Washington, D.C., and Virginia in the South, though some of these areas are often associated with the Northeast or Mid-Atlantic.

The South’s historical identity was shaped by slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction, Jim Crow segregation, disenfranchisement, and the Civil Rights era. It also developed distinctive music, food, architecture, and customs amid substantial racial and cultural diversity. Its older collective identity has weakened as many areas have become more culturally mixed, so broad labels can obscure important differences within the region.

key_facts.text: “Southern” is not simply a geographic direction: California is not generally considered part of the South, while Georgia is.
A small rural elite historically dominated much of the region’s politics and economy, while slave labor strongly influenced the Deep South and coastal plain.
The South contains almost all of the Bible Belt, associated with high Protestant church attendance, especially in evangelical churches such as the Southern Baptist Convention.
Studies indicate that Southerners tend to be more conservative than most non-Southerners; liberalism is mostly predominant in urban areas and places with Black majorities.

overview.text: Lake Michigan is one of North America’s five Great Lakes and the only one located entirely within the United States. Its waters are shared by Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan, while the other four Great Lakes are shared by the United States and Canada.

Lake Michigan connects with Lake Huron through the wide, deep Straits of Mackinac; hydrologically, the two bodies are a single lake. Important ports on its shores include Chicago, Gary, Milwaukee, Green Bay, and Muskegon.

key_facts.text: Lake Michigan ranks second among the Great Lakes in volume and depth, and third in surface area.
Green Bay is on the northwest side of the lake; Grand Traverse Bay and Little Traverse Bay are to the northeast.
The name “Michigan” is believed to come from Ojibwe words meaning “great water.”

overview.text: A mathematical proof is a deductive argument showing that assumptions logically guarantee a conclusion. It may use earlier results, but in principle it can be traced back to axioms—basic accepted assumptions—and rules of inference. Unlike checking many examples, a proof must establish a statement for all possible cases, providing logical certainty rather than merely a reasonable expectation from evidence. Proofs combine mathematical symbols with natural language. Most are rigorous but informal; fully symbolic arguments are called formal proofs.

key_facts.text: A statement believed to be true but not yet proved is a conjecture; a frequently used unproved assumption may be called a hypothesis.
Previously established statements, including theorems, can serve as steps within a proof.
Showing that a claim works in many individual cases is not enough to prove it universally.
Fully symbolic proofs without natural language are studied in proof theory; ordinary mathematical writing usually uses rigorous informal logic.

overview.text: A cell wall is a structural layer outside the cell membrane in some organisms. It helps provide support, shape, and protection, can act as a selective barrier, and helps cells withstand osmotic pressure and mechanical stress.
Cell walls occur in most prokaryotes and are common in plants, fungi, and algae, but they are absent from animals. Their chemical composition differs among major groups of organisms.

key_facts.text: In land plants, the primary cell wall contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin; other polymers can also be embedded in or attached to it.
Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, while archaeal cell walls can contain S-layers, pseudopeptidoglycan, or polysaccharides.
Fungal cell walls are made from chitin, a polymer associated with N-acetylglucosamine.
Algal cell walls can contain glycoproteins and polysaccharides such as carrageenan and agar; diatoms have walls made of biogenic silica.

overview.text: Cú Chulainn is an Irish warrior hero and demigod of the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology; related folklore also appears in Scotland and the Isle of Man. Born Sétanta, he gained his better-known name after killing Culann’s guard dog in self-defense and offering to serve in its place until a replacement was raised. His name thus means “Hound of Culann.”

At seventeen, Cú Chulainn defended Ulster alone against the forces of Queen Medb of Connacht in the Táin Bó Cúailnge, or “Cattle Raid of Cooley.” He is also associated with the ríastrad, a terrifying battle frenzy that transforms him into a monstrous, nearly unrecognizable figure.

key_facts.text: His mother was the mortal Deichtine, while he was believed to be an incarnation and son of the god Lugh.
The warrior Scáthach trained him in martial arts and gave him the spear Gáe Bulg.
His wife was Emer; with Aífe, he had a son named Connla, whom Cú Chulainn later killed.
According to the legend, he died in battle after binding himself to a standing stone so that he would die on his feet.

overview.text: The Pullman Strike began as an 1894 strike by Pullman Company factory workers in Chicago after wage reductions during a severe economic depression. When the company refused to recognize the American Railway Union (ARU) or negotiate, the dispute expanded into a national boycott of trains carrying Pullman passenger cars.

Led by Eugene V. Debs and the ARU, the boycott disrupted rail traffic and brought the union into conflict with railroad companies and the federal government. A federal injunction and President Grover Cleveland’s use of the Army helped break the boycott; Debs was imprisoned for violating the court order, and the ARU dissolved.

key_facts.text: Most Pullman factory workers lived in Pullman, a company town designed by George Pullman as a model community.
Workers also objected to company control over town life, high water and gas rates, and the company’s refusal to let them buy homes.
The boycott targeted trains carrying Pullman cars; railroad conductors and porters who worked on those trains did not strike.
At its peak, the boycott involved about 250,000 workers across 27 states, while the AFL and several railroad brotherhoods opposed it.
The conflict became violent: 30 people were killed in Chicago alone, with additional deaths and extensive property damage reported elsewhere.

overview.text: Cosine is a trigonometric function of an angle. For an acute angle in a right triangle, it is the ratio of the length of the side adjacent to that angle to the hypotenuse.

The triangle-based definition extends to arbitrary positive and negative real values through constructions involving a unit circle, and it can also be extended to complex numbers. This places cosine beyond the original acute-angle triangle setting.

key_facts.text: Modern definitions may express sine and cosine as infinite series or as solutions of certain differential equations.

Cosine and sine are used to model periodic phenomena such as sound and light waves, harmonic-oscillator position and velocity, sunlight intensity and day length, and average temperature variation over a year.
Their history can be traced to the jyā and koṭi-jyā functions used in Indian astronomy during the Gupta period.

overview.text: Lead is the chemical element Pb, a name derived from Latin plumbum, with atomic number 82. It is a dense heavy metal that is soft, malleable, relatively unreactive, and has a relatively low melting point. Freshly cut lead looks silvery with a bluish tint but turns dull gray in air.

These properties gave lead a long industrial history: lead alloys could be cast into movable type, while lead’s density, ductility, low melting point, and resistance to oxidation supported uses in plumbing, batteries, solders, weights, paint, leaded gasoline, and radiation shielding. Lead is also a neurotoxin that accumulates in tissue and bone and can damage the nervous system.

key_facts.text: Lead has the highest atomic number of any stable element; three of its isotopes are endpoints of major decay chains of heavier elements.
Lead compounds usually have a +2 oxidation state. Lead and its oxides can react with both acids and bases, a behavior called amphoterism.
Galena is a principal lead ore and often contains silver; Roman interest in silver helped initiate wider lead extraction.
Lead helped the printing press because movable type could be cast relatively easily from lead alloys.
Lead exposure can affect the cardiovascular and renal systems as well as the nervous system, with effects ranging from behavioral problems to brain damage.

overview.text: Journey to the West (Xiyouji) is a Chinese novel published in the sixteenth century during the Ming dynasty and attributed to Wu Cheng’en. It fictionalizes the pilgrimage of the Buddhist monk Xuanzang, who travels to India to obtain Buddhist scriptures, combining the broad outline of his journey with folk tales and invented fantasy.

The traveling group includes Sun Wukong, a monkey who becomes Xuanzang’s first disciple, along with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing. Drawing on Chinese mythology and Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian, and folk-religious traditions, the novel combines comic adventure, satire, and spiritual reflection.

key_facts.text: The story is based on the broad outline of Xuanzang’s reported seventh-century, 19-year pilgrimage to India, but its India is presented as a mythical setting.
Sun Wukong is born from a stone egg on Flower Fruit Mountain and learns Taoist arts, 72 transformations, combat, and secrets of immortality.
Arthur Waley’s 1942 abridged English translation, titled Monkey, helped make the novel widely known in English-speaking countries.
Journey to the West helped inspire xianxia, a literary genre combining martial arts with high fantasy.

overview.text: The Amazon River is a major South American river distinguished above all by the amount of water it carries: it is the world’s largest river by discharge volume. Its length ranking is less settled, since it is described as either the second-longest or longest river system depending on the disputed comparison with the Nile.

Its drainage basin is the world’s largest, covering about 7 million square kilometers, and the river empties into the Atlantic Ocean. Near Manaus, the Rio Negro meets the Solimões; Brazilians call the river the Amazon below this famous Meeting of Waters.

key_facts.text: The Amazon carries about 20% of all river water discharged into the world’s oceans.
A 2014 study identified the headwaters of Peru’s Mantaro River as the basin’s farthest source, replacing the long-held Apurímac designation.
The portion of the Amazon drainage basin within Brazil alone is larger than any other river’s basin.
The Ucayali and Marañón rivers join upstream of Iquitos, Peru, forming what many countries consider the Amazon’s main stem.

overview.text: A rose can mean either a woody perennial flowering plant in the genus Rosa or the flower it produces. Roses belong to the family Rosaceae and are widely cultivated for their showy, often fragrant blossoms. Their flowers vary in size, shape, and color, including white, pink, red, orange, and yellow.

Roses are a diverse garden group whose forms include shrubs and climbing plants. Their broad variation comes partly from the fact that different species hybridize readily, allowing gardeners to develop many cultivated varieties.

key_facts.text: The genus contains more than 300 species and tens of thousands of cultivars.
Most rose species are native to Asia; smaller numbers come from Europe, North America, and northwest Africa.
Many species have sharp prickles on their stems.
Rose plants range from trailing or upright shrubs to climbers reaching about 7 meters.

overview.text: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and also known as Octavian, founded the Roman Empire and became its first emperor, ruling from 27 BCE until his death in 14 CE. His reign established the principate, a system in which the emperor retained power while showing nominal respect for the Senate. It also began the Pax Romana, a period when the Roman world was largely free of armed conflict.

After Julius Caesar’s assassination, Octavian inherited Caesar’s estate and name and joined Mark Antony and Marcus Lepidus in a triumvirate against Caesar’s assassins. After that alliance collapsed, Marcus Agrippa defeated Antony at Actium in 31 BCE. Augustus preserved republican institutions in appearance, but his control of the army gave him autocratic power; the Senate granted him titles including princeps, or “first citizen,” and augustus, meaning “revered.”

key_facts.text: After Antony and Cleopatra died during Octavian’s invasion of Egypt, Egypt became Octavian’s personal property.
Augustus expanded Roman territory but suffered a major setback in Germania; client states and treaties helped secure the empire’s frontiers.
His government reformed taxation and currency, built roads and an official courier system, and established a professional army, the Praetorian Guard, and urban police and firefighting services.
Augustus supported poets such as Virgil. After his death, the Senate deified him, and his stepson and adopted son Tiberius succeeded him.

overview.text: Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire after rising from Persis and defeating the Median Empire. He then absorbed Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, extending Persian control across Anatolia, the Fertile Crescent, and parts of Central Asia. His reign marks the formation of a major Persian imperial state in the ancient Near East.

Cyrus is associated with governance as well as conquest: he developed a central administration for provincial satraps. Jewish tradition remembers him for freeing exiled Jews after Babylon’s conquest and supporting the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. His death is disputed, with one account placing it in battle against the Massagetae and Xenophon claiming that he returned to Pasargadae.

key_facts.text: Other names include Cyrus II of Persia and, in Greek usage, Cyrus the Elder.
His son Cambyses II succeeded him and later led campaigns into Egypt, Nubia, and Cyrenaica.
Pasargadae was associated with Cyrus as both his capital and the location of his tomb.
The Book of Isaiah presents Cyrus as anointed by Yahweh and calls him “messiah,” an unusual designation for a non-Jewish figure.

overview.text: George Gershwin, born Jacob Gershwine, was an American composer and pianist whose work ranged across jazz, popular music, and classical music. His central recognition set includes the jazz standard “I Got Rhythm,” orchestral works such as Rhapsody in Blue and An American in Paris, and the opera Porgy and Bess.

Gershwin wrote Broadway works with his brother Ira and collaborated with Ira and DuBose Heyward on Porgy and Bess. Although that opera initially failed commercially, it later became regarded as an important twentieth-century American opera and cultural classic. His musical Of Thee I Sing was the first musical to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

key_facts.text: Gershwin began as a song plugger before composing Broadway theater works with Ira Gershwin and Buddy DeSylva.
Of Thee I Sing won the 1931 Pulitzer Prize for Drama; Gershwin did not participate in receiving the award as its composer.
After moving to Hollywood, Gershwin composed several film scores, and many of his compositions later became jazz standards or were adapted for film and television.
Gershwin died in 1937 at age 38 from a brain tumor.

overview.text: A piano is a keyboard instrument whose pressed keys activate hammers that strike strings. Modern pianos generally have 88 black and white keys, although the source notes exceptions. The strings’ vibrations pass through a bridge to a soundboard, which amplifies the sound.

The two main forms are the grand piano and the upright piano. Grand pianos generally provide greater sound quality and more precise key control, while uprights are smaller and less expensive. Pianos are widely used in classical, jazz, traditional, and popular music for solo and ensemble performance, accompaniment, composing, songwriting, and rehearsals.

key_facts.text: Felt-coated wooden hammers strike the strings, while dampers stop their vibration when keys are released.
Pedals can lift the dampers, allowing notes to continue after the keys are released and creating sustained, overlapping sound.
Nineteenth-century developments included cast-iron frames, which permitted greater string tension, and aliquot stringing, which improved power, sustain, and tonal richness.
A musician who specializes in playing the piano is called a pianist.

overview.text: Charlotte Brontë (1816–1855) was an English novelist and poet and the elder sister of Emily and Anne Brontë. She is best known for Jane Eyre, which was first published under the pseudonym Currer Bell and became a classic of English literature.

Brontë drew on personal experience in her fiction. The harsh Cowan Bridge school helped provide the model for Lowood School in Jane Eyre, and Constantin Heger, the director of a girls’ boarding school in Brussels, inspired Rochester and The Professor.

key_facts.text: Jane Eyre was published in 1847 and received both praise and controversy.
The Professor was Brontë’s first novel, but publishers rejected it before Jane Eyre was published.
In 1846, Charlotte, Emily, and Anne published poetry using the names Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell.
The sisters’ true identities as the Bell authors were revealed in 1848.

overview.text: Sikhism, also called Sikhi, is an Indian religion and philosophy that originated in the Punjab around the late 15th century. It developed from the teachings of Guru Nanak and nine succeeding gurus. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth guru, ended the line of human gurus by naming the Guru Granth Sahib as his successor; Sikhs regard it as the eternally living 11th guru.

Sikh teachings emphasize devotion to one creator, human equality, meditation and remembrance, honest work, selfless service, and justice. Baptized Sikhs are required to wear the five Ks, including kesh, or uncut hair. After periods of persecution, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 as an order defending freedom of conscience and religion.

key_facts.text: Ik Onkar expresses Sikh belief in one creator; simran means remembering or meditating on God's presence.
Sikh devotional practice may include kirtan, musical expression of meditation, and naam japna, meditation on God's name.
Sikhism rejects the idea that one religious tradition possesses a monopoly on absolute truth and does not actively proselytize, though voluntary converts are accepted.
Khalsa members are associated with the ideal of the sant-sipahi, or “saint-soldier.”
Mughal authorities tortured and executed Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur after they refused to convert to Islam.

overview.text: Communism is a political and economic ideology that aims at a classless society organized around common ownership of the means of production—the resources and institutions used to make goods. In its ideal form, products are distributed according to need; private property, social classes, and eventually money and the state disappear.

Modern communism grew from 19th-century European socialism and became associated with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who offered a new definition in The Communist Manifesto (1848). Its variants differ over how change should occur, ranging from worker self-management and revolutionary spontaneity to party-led state-building. In the 20th century, Communist governments often used one-party rule and state direction of the economy.

key_facts.text: Communist theory divides capitalist society mainly into the proletariat, or working class, and the bourgeoisie, or owning class.
The first government based on Marxism-Leninism came to power in the Soviet Union after the 1917 Russian Revolution; similar governments later appeared in Eastern Europe and parts of Asia.
Communist governments commonly rejected private property and capitalism, controlled economic activity and mass media, and restricted opposition and religious freedom.
The dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 led many governments to end Communist rule, while some retained one-party systems with varying degrees of economic competition.

overview.text: Paradise Lost is John Milton’s epic poem in blank verse, built around the biblical Fall: Satan, a fallen angel, tempts Adam and Eve, who are then expelled from Eden. Its central concerns include free will, obedience, and the moral consequences of disobedience.

Milton presents the poem as an attempt to address divine justice while exploring innocence, guilt, human relationships, and redemption. Satan’s grandeur and ambition have led some readers to interpret him as heroic or sympathetic, while Adam and Eve’s departure from Paradise ends with hope for salvation.

key_facts.text: The 1667 first edition contained ten books; a revised 1674 edition reorganized the poem into twelve books in the manner of Virgil’s Aeneid.
The poem begins in medias res—after Satan and the fallen angels have already been defeated in their rebellion and cast into Hell.
Adam and Eve move from innocence before the Fall to awareness of sin afterward, and their expulsion is linked to a promise of salvation through Christ.
Major philosophical issues include predestination, human agency, and the nature of good and evil.
Satan’s portrayal remains controversial because some readers see him as heroic or sympathetic rather than simply villainous.

overview.text: Gwendolyn Elizabeth Brooks (1917–2000) was an American poet, author, and teacher. Her writing often dealt with the personal celebrations and struggles of ordinary people in her community, making everyday social experience a central association with her work.

Brooks’s career also links Chicago literary life with national recognition. She lived in Chicago all her life and later held both Illinois and U.S. poet-laureate positions; her honors also included a historic place in the American Academy of Arts and Letters.

key_facts.text: Her 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry was awarded for Annie Allen, making her the first African American to receive a Pulitzer Prize.
She served as Poet Laureate of Illinois from 1968 until her death in 2000.
She was U.S. Poet Laureate for the 1985–86 term.
In 1976, she became the first African-American woman inducted into the American Academy of Arts and Letters.

overview.text: Volodymyr Oleksandrovych Zelenskyy (born 1978) is Ukraine’s sixth president, serving since 2019. Before entering politics, he studied law but pursued comedy and entertainment, co-founding Kvartal 95. He played a fictional Ukrainian president in the popular television series Servant of the People; a political party with that name was later founded by Zelenskyy and his associates.

His presidency has unfolded during the Russo-Ukrainian War and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. Zelenskyy stayed in Kyiv as it came under attack, declared martial law and general mobilization, and called on other countries to support Ukraine’s resistance with military aid and sanctions against Russia.

key_facts.text: He was born in Kryvyi Rih into a Russian-speaking Jewish family and earned a law degree there before choosing entertainment.
In the 2019 election, he defeated incumbent Petro Poroshenko; the Servant of the People party also won a snap parliamentary election soon after his inauguration.
Early in his presidency, he sought to implement the Minsk agreements through the Steinmeier formula and pursued dialogue with Vladimir Putin to end the Donbas war.
He presented Ukraine’s Peace Formula in late 2022 and its Victory Plan in late 2024 as part of efforts to end the war.

overview.text: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is designed for infrared astronomy, observing wavelengths longer than visible light. Its sensitive instruments can study objects too old, distant, or faint for Hubble, including early stars and galaxies and the atmospheres of potentially habitable exoplanets.

NASA led Webb’s development with the European Space Agency and Canadian Space Agency. It launched on December 25, 2021, from French Guiana and entered a solar orbit near the Sun–Earth L2 point in January 2022.

key_facts.text: Its primary mirror has 18 hexagonal gold-plated beryllium segments and is 6.5 meters wide.
A five-layer sunshield helps keep the telescope below 50 K, preventing its own heat from interfering with infrared observations.
Webb is named for James E. Webb, who served as NASA administrator from 1961 to 1968.
Its original name was the Next Generation Space Telescope; initial designs began in 1996.

overview.text: An electric battery is a source of electric power made from one or more electrochemical cells. During discharge, electrons move from the negative anode through an external circuit to the positive cathode. A redox reaction changes higher-energy chemical reactants into lower-energy products, delivering the energy difference as electricity.

Primary batteries are single-use devices, such as common alkaline cells. Secondary batteries are rechargeable: an applied current can restore their electrode materials. Lead–acid batteries are associated with automobiles, while lithium-ion batteries power portable electronics and electric cars. Batteries range from tiny watch cells to room-sized backup systems.

key_facts.text: Historically, “battery” meant a device containing multiple cells; today it can also mean a single cell.
The negative terminal is the source of electrons, and the positive terminal is the cathode when the battery supplies power.
Battery applications include hearing aids, wristwatches, flashlights, vehicles, data centers, and telephone exchanges.
Batteries have less energy per unit mass than fuels such as gasoline, though electric motors can convert energy to mechanical work more efficiently than combustion engines.

overview.text: Marcel Duchamp (1887–1968) was a French American artist who played a key role in the development of the avant-garde in the United States and New York City. He spent the last 25 years of his life in New York.

Duchamp is commonly regarded, alongside Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, as one of the artists who helped establish a post-industrial perspective in art history. His work is also considered a progenitor of conceptual art.

key_facts.text: His anti-art work Fountain was a urinal signed “R. Mutt 1917.”
Duchamp was also a chess player and inventor.
In “On the Creative Act,” he presented the artist and spectator as the two poles of artistic creation.
His “art coefficient”—the relationship between intended but unexpressed meaning and unintended expression—influenced later appropriation artists such as Andy Warhol and Richard Prince.

overview.text: In solid geometry, a sphere is the set of points in three-dimensional space that are all the same distance from a central point. The central point is the center, and that fixed distance is the radius. A sphere is analogous to a circle, but in three dimensions.

Spheres are important mathematical models and appear in nature and technology. Soap bubbles become spherical at equilibrium; geography often approximates Earth as a sphere; astronomy uses the celestial sphere. Pressure vessels, curved mirrors, lenses, balls, and ball bearings also make use of spherical shapes.

key_facts.text: The earliest known mentions of spheres occur in the work of ancient Greek mathematicians.
Spheres and nearly spherical shapes occur in both nature and industry.
A sphere rolls smoothly in any direction, helping explain its use in sports balls, toys, and ball bearings.
Most curved mirrors and lenses are based on spherical forms, as are manufactured pressure vessels.

overview.text: Guy de Maupassant was a 19th-century French author celebrated as a master of the short story. Associated with naturalism—a literary school attentive to human lives, destinies, and social forces—he often presents experience in disillusioned or pessimistic terms. His fiction is known for economical style and efficient endings. Many stories examine the futility of the Franco-Prussian War and the lasting effects of conflict on civilians caught in events beyond their control.

key_facts.text: Maupassant lived from 5 August 1850 to 6 July 1893.
He was a protégé of Gustave Flaubert.
His first published story was “Boule de Suif” (“The Dumpling”), published in 1880 and often considered his most famous work.
Besides short stories, he wrote novels, travel books, and verse.

overview.text: Harlem is a neighborhood in Upper Manhattan, New York City. Its history has been shaped by changing populations and economic cycles.
