overview.text: Gold is a chemical element, Au, with atomic number 79. Its yellow color, resistance to corrosion, and ability to be hammered into thin sheets made it valuable for ornaments, coinage, and other objects across many societies. In world history, gold also connected distant trading regions. Caravans crossed the Sahara to exchange West African gold for goods including salt, helping sustain states such as Ghana and Mali. The Mali ruler Mansa Musa carried so much gold on his fourteenth-century pilgrimage that his arrival affected the Cairo market. Later discoveries prompted gold rushes in places including California and Australia. Its physical properties and historical uses explain its lasting importance.

overview.text: Tulip Mania refers to a burst of speculative trading in tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic during 1636 and 1637. Unusual flowers had become fashionable, and some rare bulbs commanded very high prices. Buyers and sellers also made contracts for bulbs that would be delivered later, so trading could continue while the plants were underground. Prices fell sharply in 1637, leaving disputes over those contracts. The episode became famous through later accounts that portrayed an entire society ruined by irrational buying. Modern historians caution that those dramatic stories drew on satire and exaggeration; the available evidence supports a narrower market frenzy, not a collapse of the Dutch economy.

overview.text: Russia, formally the Russian Federation, stretches across eastern Europe and northern Asia, with Moscow as its capital. Its territory includes the broad plains west of the Ural Mountains and the forests and tundra of Siberia. The country has had several forms of government: an empire ruled by tsars, a revolutionary government after 1917, and then the Soviet era. Tsar Nicholas II abdicated during the February Revolution, and Bolsheviks overthrew the provisional government later that year. Russia became a major constituent republic of the Soviet Union after a civil war. When that union dissolved in 1991, the Russian Federation emerged as an independent state and was recognized as its successor.

overview.text: The Battle of Stalingrad was a major Soviet victory over Nazi Germany in 1942–1943. German troops reached the city on the Volga during an offensive aimed partly at southern Soviet resources. Fighting moved through streets, factories, and ruined buildings while Soviet defenders held parts of the riverbank. In November 1942, the Red Army launched Operation Uranus against the German flanks and encircled the Sixth Army. Attempts to supply the trapped force by air failed, and the remaining troops surrendered by early February 1943. The defeat destroyed a large German field army and helped shift momentum on the Eastern Front toward the Soviet Union.

overview.text: Stalingrad was the name used from 1925 to 1961 for the Russian city now called Volgograd. The city lies along the Volga River and was previously named Tsaritsyn. Under the Stalingrad name it grew into an important Soviet industrial center and became the scene of one of World War II’s most destructive battles. German and Soviet forces fought across the city in 1942–1943, leaving much of it in ruins. The government renamed it Volgograd in 1961. Memorials there still recall the wartime defense, including the large Motherland Calls sculpture on Mamayev Kurgan. The name Stalingrad survives especially in accounts of the battle.

It bore the name Stalingrad from 1925 to 1961.

overview.text: Argentina’s Dirty War was the military dictatorship’s campaign of repression against perceived opponents, chiefly from 1976 to 1983. Security forces kidnapped people, held many in secret detention centers, tortured prisoners, and caused thousands to disappear. Victims included political activists as well as people targeted through association or suspicion. Families often received no official account of what had happened. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began publicly demanding answers in 1977, and their white headscarves became a symbol of the search for justice. After civilian rule returned, Argentina formed a commission to investigate disappearances and later pursued prosecutions. A national commission later collected testimony from survivors and relatives of the disappeared.

overview.text: The House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma, was associated with the Abbasid court in Baghdad. Surviving evidence points especially to a royal library and the translation of Persian and other writings into Arabic. Baghdad also supported a much wider scholarly network: translators, physicians, mathematicians, and astronomers worked for caliphs and other patrons. Greek writings reached Arabic readers through several routes, often with the help of Christian scholars working in Syriac. Older accounts sometimes depict one grand academy where all this learning took place, but historians find that picture too simple. The institution matters as part of Baghdad’s lively culture of books and translation, not as the sole source of Abbasid scholarship.

overview.text: Zionism is a modern Jewish national movement that developed in late nineteenth-century Europe and sought a Jewish homeland in the historic Land of Israel, then commonly called Palestine. It arose partly in response to antisemitism and drew on longstanding Jewish ties to that land. Theodor Herzl helped organize political Zionism and convened the first Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897. The British Balfour Declaration of 1917 endorsed a Jewish national home in Palestine; British rule and immigration policies later became contested. The creation of Israel in 1948 fulfilled a central Zionist goal. It followed a United Nations partition proposal amid conflict between Palestinian Arabs and Jews over the land.

overview.text: Hungary is a Central European country whose capital, Budapest, lies on the Danube. Its twentieth-century history included alliance with Nazi Germany, the Holocaust, and Soviet domination after World War II. In 1944 German forces occupied Hungary, and German and Hungarian authorities deported hundreds of thousands of Jews, many to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg and others tried to protect Jews in Budapest. In 1956 a popular uprising challenged Soviet control and the country’s Communist leadership. Soviet troops intervened and crushed it. The revolt became an important symbol of resistance to Soviet rule in Eastern Europe. A later United Nations inquiry described the uprising as a spontaneous movement supported by students, workers, and intellectuals.

overview.text: The Mapuche are Indigenous peoples with a long history in south-central Chile and neighboring parts of Argentina. They resisted Spanish attempts to dominate their homeland during the Arauco War, and later maintained a frontier marked by both conflict and trade. In the nineteenth century, the new Chilean and Argentine states expanded into Mapuche territory through military campaigns. Chile’s occupation and colonization of Araucanía sharply reduced Mapuche control of land and changed community life. Mapuche identity and language, Mapudungun, remain important today, alongside continuing demands connected to land and political recognition. Their history is one of adaptation and persistence as well as resistance to conquest.

overview.text: Jair Bolsonaro is a Brazilian former army captain whose political career moved from Rio de Janeiro city council to the national Chamber of Deputies. He served as a federal deputy through seven legislative terms, beginning in 1991. He resigned his seat when he became Brazil's president on January 1, 2019. His presidency lasted four years, ending January 1, 2023. Bolsonaro ran for reelection in 2022 against former president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Lula won the runoff, according to the official national count. The contrast between Bolsonaro's long congressional career and single presidential term helps place him in Brazil's recent political history.

overview.text: Ahmed Abdallah Mohamed Sambi was president of the island nation of Comoros from 2006 to 2011. A businessman and Muslim religious figure from Anjouan, he won the 2006 election with about 58 percent of the vote. Under a power-sharing arrangement, Anjouan was then entitled to supply the federal president. Although Sunni, Sambi was nicknamed “Ayatollah” by supporters after studying religion in Iran. His election was closely watched because the archipelago had endured repeated coups and island disputes. During his presidency, Comorian and African Union forces ended a separatist crisis on Anjouan in 2008.

overview.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the six-republic Balkan federation that emerged after World War II under communist leadership. Its republics were Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia; Kosovo and Vojvodina were regions within Serbia. Josip Broz Tito led the country for decades. In 1948 his government broke from Soviet control, allowing Yugoslavia to pursue a more independent Cold War position than Eastern Bloc states. During the early 1990s, republics declared independence and the federation disintegrated amid conflict. Serbia and Montenegro formed a separate Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1992, which was not simply a continuation of the six-republic state.

overview.text: Yugoslavia was a name used by several related South Slav states, so its dates depend on which state is meant. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes formed in 1918 and adopted the name Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929. After World War II, a socialist federation of six republics replaced the monarchy. That federation broke apart as four republics declared independence in 1991–92. Serbia and Montenegro then kept the Yugoslavia name for their smaller Federal Republic. The word can therefore mean a monarchy, a six-republic socialist federation, or a later two-republic state. These governments occupied overlapping territory but had different constitutions and political systems.

overview.text: The Ninety-Five Theses were propositions Martin Luther circulated in Wittenberg in 1517 to debate the sale and meaning of indulgences. Luther argued that repentance should shape a Christian's whole life and criticized preaching that made a payment seem able to release a soul from purgatory. He also urged helping poor people rather than spending money on indulgences. The theses were sent to church authorities and quickly circulated in print, helping spark the Protestant Reformation. The familiar image of Luther nailing them to a church door is traditional, but historians dispute whether that episode happened as usually told. The document's original focus was indulgences, not a complete statement of later Protestant doctrine.

Thesis 1 says believers’ whole lives should be lives of repentance.
Thesis 27 rejects the claim that a coin entering a chest releases a soul from purgatory.

The famous church-door nailing story is disputed.

overview.text: A tomb is a place or structure made to hold the remains of a dead person, often also to preserve memory or mark social status. Tombs vary greatly in form: ancient Egyptian rulers were buried in pyramids and later in rock-cut chambers, while Bahrain's Dilmun culture left thousands of burial mounds. Some tombs contain chambers, inscriptions, or objects placed with the dead. Archaeologists study their design and contents to learn about burial customs, craft, and beliefs, and compare grave sizes to understand social differences. A simple grave, a mound, and a monumental pyramid all belong to the broader history of burial, even though their scale and purpose differ.

key_facts.text: Ancient Egyptian royal burial developed from mastaba tombs to pyramids.
Djoser’s Step Pyramid was built as a royal tomb.

overview.text: The Teutonic Order began as a hospital for German-speaking crusaders at Acre during the Third Crusade and became a Catholic military order in 1198. Its knights later campaigned in the Baltic region, especially Prussia, where warfare, conversion efforts, and territorial rule became intertwined. The order built a powerful state with its center at Marienburg, now Malbork in Poland. Its forces and associated Livonian knights fought eastern neighbors; a crusading force was defeated at Lake Peipus in 1242 by Alexander Nevsky's side. The order suffered another major defeat against Polish and Lithuanian forces at Grunwald, or Tannenberg, in 1410. Its history combines religious ideals with conquest and political power.

It received papal sanction as a military order in 1198.

overview.text: Warsaw, Poland's capital on the Vistula River, bears traces of several different twentieth-century struggles. In the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of April–May 1943, Jewish residents resisted Nazi German attempts to deport the ghetto's survivors. A separate Warsaw Uprising began in August 1944, when the Polish Home Army tried to free the city from German occupation. German troops destroyed more than 85 percent of the historic center, which residents rebuilt after the war; its reconstruction is now recognized by UNESCO. In 1955, Warsaw also gave its name to the military alliance commonly called the Warsaw Pact. The two uprisings should be distinguished by their participants, aims, and dates.

The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began April 19, 1943, against German deportations.

overview.text: The Colosseum is the common name for Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre, built under the Flavian emperors in the first century CE. Emperor Titus completed and opened it in 80 CE with an extended series of public spectacles. Gladiators fought there, and animal hunts also entertained crowds. Its elliptical seating surrounded the arena, while underground cages and mechanical lifts helped stage the events. The name “Colosseum” came from a colossal statue that once stood nearby. The archaeological park notes that ancient accounts of the opening celebrations describe aquatic performances. The surviving building offers evidence of both Roman engineering and the importance of public entertainment to imperial rulers.

overview.text: Iraq is a West Asian country whose territory includes much of ancient Mesopotamia, the region associated with the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Baghdad is its capital and a historic city on the Tigris. Modern Iraq emerged from former Ottoman lands and later gained independence after a period of British influence. Under Saddam Hussein, Iraq fought Iran from 1980 to 1988, then invaded Kuwait in August 1990. A United States-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War. Another United States- and British-led invasion began in 2003 and removed Saddam's government. These conflicts are distinct from the far older Mesopotamian civilizations associated with today's Iraqi landscape.

overview.text: Augusto Pinochet was the Chilean army commander who led the September 1973 coup that overthrew President Salvador Allende. He headed the military government that followed and later held the title of president. His dictatorship dissolved Congress, banned political parties, restricted civil liberties, and committed serious human rights violations. It also introduced sweeping market-oriented economic changes. Opposition grew during the 1980s, and voters rejected an extension of his rule in a 1988 plebiscite. Elections followed in 1989, and Pinochet handed over the presidency to Patricio Aylwin in March 1990. He remained army commander for several more years.

overview.text: Ramesses II was a pharaoh of Egypt’s Nineteenth Dynasty who ruled for roughly sixty-six years in the thirteenth century BCE. His name appears on monuments across Egypt, and he commissioned temples on a remarkable scale, including the rock-cut Great Temple at Abu Simbel. His armies fought the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria; neither side gained a decisive victory there. Later, Ramesses concluded a peace treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, preserved in Egyptian and Hittite versions. The battle narratives and building projects helped shape his enduring reputation as one of ancient Egypt’s best-known rulers.

overview.text: The Mongol Empire arose from the conquests of Genghis Khan and his successors during the thirteenth century. It became the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching across much of Eurasia. Expansion continued after Genghis Khan’s death, and the empire reached its greatest extent roughly two generations later. Mongol rulers governed diverse settled populations, often retaining local officials for day-to-day administration. Over time, imperial power was divided among major branches: the Yuan dynasty in China, the Chagatai khanate in Central Asia, the Golden Horde in the western steppe, and the Ilkhanate in Iran. These states remained connected by Mongol dynastic origins.

overview.text: Mikhail Gorbachev led the Soviet Union during its final years and pursued reforms commonly known as perestroika, or restructuring, and glasnost, or openness. His government loosened Soviet control over Eastern European states, helping create conditions for the fall of Communist governments there in 1989. Within the Soviet Union, political changes permitted multiparty elections but also weakened the Communist Party’s hold on power. Hard-line opponents mounted an unsuccessful coup against him in August 1991. As several republics moved toward independence and a new commonwealth formed, the Soviet state unraveled. Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on December 25, 1991.

overview.text: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier of an ancient Greek city-state. The usual equipment included a thrusting spear, a large round shield, and protective pieces such as a helmet, body armor, and shin guards. Hoplites fought in a phalanx: close ranks whose overlapping shields helped protect the men beside one another. This formation made coordinated movement and cohesion especially important. In Athens, the ability to equip oneself for this role was tied to property and civic standing, so hoplite service was also a mark of status. Archers and lighter troops could support the phalanx, rather than every Greek fighter being a hoplite.

overview.text: Richard II became king of England in 1377 at age ten, succeeding his grandfather Edward III. During the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, he personally negotiated a truce with rebels near London. As an adult he supported art and rebuilt Westminster Hall, but his reliance on favored courtiers and confrontations with powerful nobles created lasting opposition. He later punished rivals, including his cousin Henry of Bolingbroke. In 1399 Bolingbroke returned with an army, removed Richard from the throne, and became Henry IV. Richard died in captivity the following year; historical accounts differ on whether he was murdered or starved himself.

overview.text: Richard III was king of England from 1483 to 1485, near the end of the Wars of the Roses. He was the younger brother of Edward IV and became protector after Edward’s death. Later in 1483 he took the crown from his young nephew Edward V. Edward and his brother disappeared from public view after being placed in the Tower of London; their fate remains uncertain, and Richard’s responsibility is debated. Richard faced growing opposition and was killed when Henry Tudor defeated him at the Battle of Bosworth in August 1485. Henry then ruled as Henry VII, succeeding Richard on the English throne.

overview.text: The Third Crusade was a campaign from 1189 to 1192 launched after Saladin, ruler of Egypt and Syria, captured Jerusalem in 1187. Prominent European participants included Richard I of England, Philip II of France, and the Holy Roman emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who died on the journey. Crusader armies captured the port of Acre, while Richard also gained Cyprus. The campaign did not retake Jerusalem, which remained under Muslim control. Its settlement gave European Christian pilgrims access to the city, and Crusader forces held a narrow stretch of Mediterranean coastline. The outcome combined limited territorial gains with failure to achieve the crusade’s central goal.

overview.text: The Russian Civil War grew out of the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 and continued through the early 1920s. The Bolsheviks’ Red Army fought anti-Bolshevik forces commonly called the Whites, who opposed the new Soviet government. Fighting ranged across a vast territory, including campaigns in Siberia, where Admiral Alexander Kolchak became a prominent White leader. The conflict also involved struggles over control of regions beyond Russia’s central heartland. Red victories against major White armies by 1920 helped secure Bolshevik rule, although warfare did not end everywhere at once. Maps of the war commonly cover events through 1922.

Admiral Alexander Kolchak was a White leader in Siberia.

overview.text: The League of Nations was created after World War I as an organization meant to encourage cooperation and collective security among states. Its Covenant formed part of the postwar peace settlement, and members registered treaties with the League. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson strongly advocated a league, but the United States Senate did not approve membership, so the country never joined. The League provided a forum for diplomacy and international work, yet it failed to prevent another world war. The organization ended in 1946, transferring its library, archives, and other assets to the newly established United Nations.

overview.text: The Khmer Rouge was the radical communist movement that ruled Cambodia, then called Democratic Kampuchea, from April 1975 to January 1979. Its leaders, including Pol Pot, tried to remake society through forced agricultural labor and tight political control. After taking Phnom Penh, the movement emptied cities and moved residents into the countryside. Executions, imprisonment, hunger, disease, and harsh work killed an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people; ethnic minorities also faced persecution. Vietnamese forces overthrew the regime in 1979. Decades later, a Cambodian-United Nations tribunal investigated senior leaders and major perpetrators. The term “Khmer Rouge” names the movement and regime, not the Cambodian people as a whole.

overview.text: The Stolen Generations are Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who, as children, were forcibly separated from their families under Australian government removal policies and institutional practices. Many were placed in institutions or non-Indigenous homes, disrupting family ties, language, and culture. Removal occurred across different jurisdictions and periods, so no single date describes every person's experience. Australia's 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry documented the laws and practices behind these removals, recorded personal testimony, and recommended healing and reconciliation measures. In February 2008, Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologized in Parliament to the Stolen Generations. Survivors and descendants continue to describe lasting effects, including grief and intergenerational trauma.

overview.text: The Assyrian Empire grew from northern Mesopotamia and became one of the dominant powers of the ancient Near East in the first millennium BCE. Its rulers moved their capital several times, from the traditional center of Ashur to cities including Nimrud and, under Sennacherib, Nineveh. Palace reliefs at Nineveh depict royal campaigns and ceremonies, revealing how kings presented their power. Ashurbanipal assembled a major collection of cuneiform texts there. Assyrian control at its height reached as far as Egypt. A Babylonian-Median coalition sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; a remnant Assyrian state survived briefly afterward. The empire is remembered through both its military expansion and its preserved art and written records.

overview.text: Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg hereditary lands from 1740 to 1780 after inheriting them from her father, Emperor Charles VI. Other European powers challenged that succession, starting the War of the Austrian Succession. Frederick II of Prussia seized Silesia, which Maria Theresa ultimately had to cede. The shock of war helped spur reforms in administration and the army. Her reign also saw wider modernization of the Habsburg state, although her attitude toward Enlightenment ideas was cautious and she was intolerant of some religious communities. Her son Joseph II later continued reforms, first as her co-ruler and then on his own. Maria Theresa herself was not Holy Roman emperor.

overview.text: Louis XVI was the Bourbon king of France when the French Revolution began. He inherited the throne in 1774 and faced deep financial problems. In May 1789 he summoned the Estates General to Versailles; disputes over representation and power helped turn that assembly into a revolutionary crisis. Popular pressure forced Louis and his wife, Marie Antoinette, to leave Versailles for Paris later that year. The monarchy was abolished in 1792, and Louis was tried by the National Convention. He was executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793. His fall illustrates how the revolution moved from demands for reform of monarchy to the creation of a republic.

overview.text: The European Union is a political and economic partnership whose modern legal form came from the Maastricht Treaty. Six western European countries began earlier cooperation in coal and steel, then created the European Economic Community through the 1957 Treaties of Rome. Maastricht was signed in 1992 and entered into force on November 1, 1993, formally establishing the EU on the foundations of those communities. It expanded cooperation to foreign policy, justice, and home affairs and introduced EU citizenship. A single market supports movement of goods, services, people, and capital. The euro cash changeover began in 2002 for participating countries; EU membership and use of the euro are not identical.

overview.text: The Congo Free State was a central African territory ruled personally by Belgium's King Leopold II from 1885 until Belgium took it over in 1908. It covered much of today's Democratic Republic of the Congo, but it was not initially a colony of the Belgian state. Leopold's administration claimed uncultivated land and granted concessions to companies that extracted ivory and rubber. Those companies imposed forced labor, often under inhumane conditions, and the regime became notorious for violence and other abuses. Reports of mistreatment drew international outrage. Belgium annexed the territory in November 1908, ending the Free State and beginning a different colonial administration. Its name “Free State” concealed coercive rule.

overview.text: The Zulu are a southern African people whose language, isiZulu, belongs to the Nguni group. Their history includes the rise of a powerful kingdom in the early nineteenth century, when Shaka brought many chiefdoms under centralized rule and reorganized military forces. The kingdom survived his death in 1828. Under King Cetshwayo, it resisted British demands to disarm, and Britain invaded Zululand in 1879. The Anglo-Zulu War included the Battle of Isandlwana, where Zulu forces defeated a British column, before British forces won at Ulundi and subsequently divided the kingdom. Zulu communities and language continue today; the people should not be reduced to the history of one king or one war.

overview.text: Leonidas I was a king of Sparta who commanded a Greek coalition at Thermopylae in 480 BCE during the Persian invasion led by Xerxes I. The narrow coastal pass helped the defenders resist a much larger army for several days. The famous 300 Spartan soldiers were only part of the Greek force, which also included troops from other city-states. After Persian forces found a mountain route around the pass, most Greek troops withdrew while Leonidas and a smaller rearguard remained. Leonidas died in the final fighting. The defeat opened the route southward for the Persians, but Greek resistance continued, including later victories at Salamis and Plataea.

overview.text: Chichén Itzá was a major Maya city on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, built near natural sinkholes called cenotes that supplied access to water. Its surviving monuments combine Maya building traditions with influences from central Mexico. El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, rises above the main plaza; the Great Ball Court, Temple of the Warriors, and sacred cenote are other prominent features. The ball court's stone rings and reliefs show that the game had ceremonial as well as athletic meaning. UNESCO recognizes the city as World Heritage for its architecture and regional influence. Its monuments reveal several phases of construction and cultural exchange across the region.

overview.text: The Labour Party is a major political party in the United Kingdom. It emerged from efforts by trade unionists and socialists to give working people representation in Parliament: the Labour Representation Committee formed in 1900, and its elected members adopted the Labour name in 1906. Ramsay MacDonald led the first Labour government in 1924, though it lacked a majority. After the Second World War, Clement Attlee’s Labour government established the National Health Service. The party has alternated in government and opposition with the Conservatives through much of modern British politics. Keir Starmer was elected Labour leader in 2020. Its history links organized labor, parliamentary elections, and debates over public services.

overview.text: Pakistan is a South Asian state that became independent in 1947 as British India was partitioned. Its capital is Islamabad, and its territory meets India, Afghanistan, Iran, and China, with an Arabian Sea coast. At independence, Pakistan had two geographically separated wings, West Pakistan and East Pakistan. Political conflict and war in 1971 led to the eastern wing becoming the independent state of Bangladesh. Pakistan’s present federation includes the provinces of Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as the Islamabad Capital Territory. The events of 1971 show that independence in 1947 did not settle questions of political representation between the country’s two wings.

overview.text: The Thirty Years’ War was a series of connected conflicts fought from 1618 to 1648, centered on the Holy Roman Empire. It began amid a revolt by Protestant estates in Bohemia against Habsburg rule; the 1618 Defenestration of Prague became a symbol of its opening. The imperial and Catholic League victory at White Mountain in 1620 did not end the wider fighting. Other European powers entered, and dynastic and strategic aims joined disputes over religion. Armies and their movements devastated many communities. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended the war and reshaped political arrangements in central Europe. The conflict was neither one continuous battle nor simply a Catholic-versus-Protestant contest.

overview.text: Sargon of Akkad was an early Mesopotamian ruler whose conquests joined previously rival city-states of Sumer under Akkadian rule. The period named for Agade, or Akkad, began around the middle of the third millennium BCE. Sargon took the title of king and campaigned beyond southern Mesopotamia, helping establish a territorial empire that outlasted him. His sons Rimush and Manishtushu succeeded him, while the empire later reached its height under his grandson Naram-Sin. The dynasty’s later campaigns extended its influence toward Anatolia, inner Iran, Arabia, and the Mediterranean. Sargon’s own conquests began a period of rule over multiple regions, though the empire’s greatest reach came after his reign.

overview.text: The guillotine was a mechanical device for executing a condemned person by decapitation with a heavy blade. It became closely identified with the French Revolution after its adoption in 1792 and was used on people from very different social ranks. Joseph-Ignace Guillotin advocated a uniform method of execution, but he did not invent the machine that bears his name; the physician Antoine Louis designed it. Revolutionary figures executed by guillotine included Louis XVI in January 1793. The device was presented by reformers as a more reliable method than a sword or axe, although it remained a tool of capital punishment. France continued using it long after the revolutionary period.

overview.text: Australia is both a sovereign country and the name used for the continental landmass at the center of its territory. It includes the mainland, Tasmania, and many smaller islands, with Canberra as national capital. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on these lands for tens of thousands of years. The modern Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901 when six British colonies federated into one country. The new federal system divided powers between national and state governments, while most First Nations people were excluded from the political process that created it. Australia’s history therefore joins a much older Indigenous past with a newer federal state and its continuing constitutional development.

overview.text: Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom with a long history as a separate kingdom. Its medieval rulers and communities maintained ties across Europe, including the alliance with France remembered as the Auld Alliance. In 1707, legislation passed in Edinburgh and Westminster joined the kingdoms of Scotland and England into Great Britain and created a shared Parliament. Scotland nevertheless retained distinctive legal and educational institutions. A devolved Scottish Parliament began meeting again in 1999 and makes laws in areas assigned to it, while the UK Parliament handles reserved matters. Edinburgh is Scotland’s capital. These different stages explain why Scotland is a country with its own institutions but is not an independent sovereign state today.

overview.text: The Alhambra Decree, also called the Edict of Expulsion, was issued by Ferdinand and Isabella at Granada on 31 March 1492. It ordered Jews living in their kingdoms and lordships to leave by the end of July and forbade their return. The document accused Jews of drawing converted Christians away from Catholic practice, reflecting the rulers’ religious policy rather than an established fact about Jewish communities. Jews faced exile or conversion to Christianity; both choices disrupted long-established families and communities. A contemporary Jewish account describes the losses and uncertainty of departure. The decree concerned Jews who had not converted, and it should be distinguished from later measures directed at Muslims.

overview.text: Shah Jahan ruled the Mughal Empire from 1628 to 1658 and is especially remembered for monumental architecture. After his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, he ordered the Taj Mahal, a marble mausoleum at Agra built by artisans from across the empire and beyond. He also established Shahjahanabad as a new capital at Delhi, with the Red Fort as its palace complex. These buildings combined imperial display with sophisticated garden planning, stonework, and decoration. His reign did not end through a normal succession: his son Aurangzeb forcibly displaced him in 1658. The Taj Mahal’s fame can obscure Shah Jahan’s broader role as a ruler and patron of Mughal urban architecture.

overview.text: Saladin, or Salah al-Din, was a Muslim ruler associated with the Ayyubid dynasty and the struggle against the Crusader states. During the crusade he confronted forces led by England’s Richard I, who won at Acre, Arsuf, and Jaffa; the two sides reached an agreement in 1192. Jerusalem remained under Saladin’s control while European pilgrims were allowed access. His career belongs to the histories of both Egypt and Syria as well as the crusades, and accounts of his conduct should be read in their specific political and religious settings.

overview.text: William Wallace was a Scottish knight and resistance leader during the First War of Scottish Independence. After Edward I of England invaded Scotland, Wallace joined a wider uprising in 1297. He and Andrew Moray led Scottish forces to victory at Stirling Bridge in September of that year. Wallace became a Guardian of Scotland, acting on behalf of the deposed King John Balliol. Edward I defeated his army at Falkirk in July 1298, after which Wallace resigned the guardianship but continued to resist English rule. Captured in 1305, he was taken to London and executed. Records of his early life are sparse, so later legends should be separated from these documented events.

overview.text: Ancient Rome was a civilization that grew from a city on the Italian peninsula into a power spanning much of the Mediterranean world. Its political history included kings, a republic, and rule by emperors. During the republic, aristocratic patricians initially held many privileges, while poorer citizens pressed for representation and land. Expansion through conquest and diplomacy brought wealth but also inequality and civil conflict. After the assassination of Julius Caesar, Octavian emerged dominant and received the title Augustus in 27 BCE. Roman rule continued in western and eastern regions for centuries, while its provinces developed diverse local cultures, cities, and trade networks. Its political institutions and material remains are major sources for studying antiquity.

overview.text: Howard Carter was a British archaeologist whose team uncovered the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. Excavations began in November, and a step found on 4 November led to a sealed entrance. Carter peered into the tomb’s antechamber on 26 November, revealing furnishings and other objects. Lord Carnarvon financed the search; Egyptian workers and a wider group of specialists took part in excavation, documentation, conservation, and removal. The burial chamber was opened in February 1923, and systematic clearance continued for years. Carter’s detailed records now help researchers study the tomb’s objects and the process by which they were recovered.

overview.text: The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was an agreement signed by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union on 23 August 1939. Its public terms promised that the two states would not attack each other. A secret protocol assigned parts of eastern Europe to German or Soviet spheres of influence and planned a division of Poland. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Soviet forces entered from the east on 17 September. The pact gave both governments room for territorial expansion, despite their sharply opposed ideologies. It did not create a lasting peace: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, ending the agreement. The pact’s secret terms are central to understanding Poland’s wartime partition.

overview.text: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon in the eighteenth century BCE whose rule is remembered for both political power and a famous inscribed collection of judgments. The surviving monument, now in the Louvre, is a tall dark stone stela carved around 1750 BCE. Its relief shows the king before Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun god associated with justice. Below are 282 judgments addressing matters such as family, property, trade, and labor. They describe how a ruler presented and applied justice, though the text is not a modern code of law. One provision about injury illustrates the principle of proportionate retaliation often summarized as “an eye for an eye.”

overview.text: The Thermidorian Reaction began with the fall of Maximilien Robespierre and his allies during the French Revolution. On 9 Thermidor Year II in the revolutionary calendar, or 27 July 1794, opponents in the National Convention moved against Robespierre and Saint-Just. They were arrested; Robespierre and other supporters were executed the next day. Their fall ended the dominance of the radical Montagnard leadership and the phase known as the Terror. The reaction was also a longer political turn against institutions and practices associated with that period, not merely a single execution. Opponents of Robespierre combined fear of political purges with rejection of the Terror’s excesses.

overview.text: The Marshall Plan, formally the European Recovery Program, was a United States aid effort to help Europe recover after World War II. Secretary of State George C. American officials also feared that severe economic hardship would strengthen communist movements during the emerging Cold War. The plan brought investment to European industry and became a significant form of U.S. foreign aid. Its name honors Marshall, but the program required congressional approval and cooperation among multiple governments.

overview.text: Hadrian ruled the Roman Empire from 117 to 138 CE after the emperor Trajan. He traveled through the empire and emphasized the defense and organization of existing frontiers. During his visit to Britain in 122, he ordered construction of the wall that bears his name along the northern frontier of the Roman province of Britannia. Soldiers built the fortification; it was not the modern border between England and Scotland. Hadrian’s reign also included the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judaea, fought from 132 to 135 and suppressed by Roman forces. That conflict brought severe harm to Jewish communities. These events show both the reach of Roman administration and the violence that could accompany imperial rule.

overview.text: Nikita Khrushchev emerged as the Soviet Union's leader after Joseph Stalin's death in 1953. At a closed Communist Party meeting in 1956, his “Secret Speech” condemned Stalin's purges and cult of personality, beginning a limited process of de-Stalinization. Khrushchev also promoted “peaceful coexistence” with capitalist countries, although Cold War rivalry continued. In 1962 he agreed with Fidel Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, triggering a confrontation with the United States known as the Cuban Missile Crisis. The missiles were withdrawn after negotiations. His years in power mixed changes inside the Soviet system with grave international tension, including Soviet intervention against the 1956 Hungarian uprising.

overview.text: Mark Antony, or Marcus Antonius, was a Roman general and politician closely allied with Julius Caesar. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Antony joined Caesar's adopted heir Octavian and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, a three-man governing alliance. Their forces defeated Caesar's assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE. Antony then became a leading power in Rome's eastern territories and formed a political and personal partnership with Cleopatra VII of Egypt. Rivalry with Octavian led to civil war. Octavian's forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. Both died the following year, and Egypt came under Roman control.

overview.text: The Qin dynasty created the first centralized Chinese empire in 221 BCE, when its ruler Ying Zheng defeated the last rival Warring States and adopted the title Qin Shi Huang, or First Emperor. His government divided conquered territory into commanderies and standardized writing, currency, weights, and measures. It built roads and joined earlier northern defensive walls, an early stage in the history of the Great Wall. Qin rule also used harsh controls, including the burning of certain classical writings. The famous terracotta army guarded the emperor's tomb complex. Although the dynasty lasted only until 206 BCE, its model of centralized imperial administration influenced the Han dynasty that followed.

overview.text: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, between the Yuan and Qing dynasties. Its early rulers rebuilt imperial authority after the Mongol-led Yuan period. The Yongle emperor moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and developed the palace complex later called the Forbidden City. Ming courts sponsored Zheng He's seven maritime expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean, and East Africa. The era is also known for accomplished porcelain, especially blue-and-white wares that circulated widely. Political and cultural activity continued long after the voyages ended; the dynasty's final crisis in the seventeenth century brought Qing rule to China.

overview.text: Troy was an ancient city in northwestern Anatolia, at the mound of Hisarlık near the Dardanelles in today's Turkey. The site is real, but scholars cannot identify a single excavated destruction with every event in the epic. UNESCO lists the archaeological site as World Heritage.

overview.text: Abolition of slavery is the legal ending of systems that treat people as property. British campaigners including Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp, and William Wilberforce pressed Parliament to end the trade in 1807; legislation passed in 1833 began abolition in much of the British Empire, with final emancipation after an apprenticeship period in 1838. The United States ratified the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. In Brazil, Regent Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law in 1888, ending legal slavery there. Enslaved people's resistance and activism were central to these struggles, and legal freedom did not erase inequality.

overview.text: War is organized armed conflict involving states or other organized groups. International humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions, sets limits on how fighting is conducted. It requires protection for civilians and humane treatment of people who are wounded, captured, or otherwise no longer fighting. overview.text: Tsar was the title associated with Russia’s monarchs from the rise of Muscovy through the Romanov era. overview.text: Cossacks were frontier communities and military groups associated especially with the steppes of today’s Ukraine and Russia. Their history includes warfare against neighboring powers and struggles for autonomy, culminating in a Cossack-led Hetmanate in the seventeenth century. Cossack groups elsewhere followed different paths, so the label describes several related traditions rather than a single uniform people.

overview.text: The Carolingian Renaissance was a revival of learning and the arts supported by Charlemagne and the rulers who followed him in the early medieval Frankish empire. overview.text: The Battle of Agincourt took place in northern France on 25 October 1415 during the Hundred Years’ War. overview.text: Phoenician civilization grew around independent coastal cities of the eastern Mediterranean, including Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, and Arwad. overview.text: The Paris Agreement is an international climate treaty adopted at a United Nations conference in Paris on 12 December 2015. It entered into force in 2016. Each country communicates its own climate plan, called a nationally determined contribution, describing actions on emissions and adaptation. The shared temperature goal guides national action but is not itself a guarantee that warming will stay below either threshold.

overview.text: Thomas More was an English lawyer, humanist writer, and royal official under Henry VIII. His book Utopia, published in 1516, became an influential work of early modern writing. More served as Speaker of the House of Commons in 1523 and became lord chancellor in 1529. He resigned in 1532 as Henry’s break with papal authority advanced. More later refused an oath that affirmed the king’s supremacy over the English church, even though he accepted the new succession. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London, tried for treason, and executed in 1535.

overview.text: Inuit are Indigenous peoples whose Arctic homelands stretch across Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, and Chukotka in Russia. Their communities have distinct local languages and histories while sharing important ties across the circumpolar region. In Canada, the term Inuit Nunangat refers to four Inuit regions and includes land, water, and ice. Hunting and sharing country foods remain important to many families, alongside contemporary work in government, art, and other professions. The Inuit Circumpolar Council, founded in 1977, brings Inuit from the four regions together to advocate for rights, cultural continuity, and protection of the Arctic environment.

key_facts.text: Inuit homelands extend across Alaska, Canada, Greenland, and Chukotka.
Inuit Nunangat is the collective name for four Inuit regions in Canada.

overview.text: New Zealand held two postal referendums in 2015 and 2016 to decide whether to replace its national flag. In the first vote, people ranked alternative designs; the leading choice was a black, white, and blue Silver Fern flag. The second vote, held in March 2016, put that design against the existing flag in a binding choice. The existing flag won with 56.6 percent of valid votes, so no change followed. The process illustrates a two-stage referendum: voters first selected a possible replacement and then decided whether to adopt it. The Electoral Commission recorded both the voting method and official results.

The 2015 vote used rankings to select an alternative design.
The chosen alternative was Silver Fern (Black, White and Blue).
The March 2016 vote was a binding choice between that design and the existing flag.

overview.text: Cleisthenes was an Athenian statesman whose reforms around 508 BCE helped lay the foundations of Athenian democracy. After the fall of the tyrant Hippias, he competed with Isagoras for influence and sought support from Athenian citizens. His reforms reduced the political importance of old family groupings by organizing citizens into local demes and ten new tribes. A council of 500 became a central institution in this system. These changes broadened participation among citizens, but citizenship itself remained limited, especially excluding women. The democracy associated with Cleisthenes developed further under later Athenian leaders, so he is best understood as a founder of its institutions rather than its final form.

The reforms followed the overthrow of the tyrant Hippias.
Citizens were organized into local units called demes.
The new political structure included ten tribes and a Council of 500.
The reforms broadened participation among male citizens, not all residents.

overview.text: The Tet Offensive was a coordinated series of attacks by North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces in South Vietnam beginning during the lunar New Year holiday in late January 1968. Major fighting reached cities including Saigon and Huế, and attackers breached the outer walls of the U.S. Embassy compound in Saigon. U.S. and South Vietnamese forces eventually retook lost ground, inflicting severe losses on the attackers. Yet the scale and surprise of the offensive undermined claims that victory was near and weakened public support for the war in the United States. Its military and political effects therefore pointed in different directions.

North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces attacked targets across South Vietnam.
Saigon and Huế were among the cities struck.

U.S. and South Vietnamese forces retook the lost territory, but U.S. public support for the war weakened.

overview.text: The German Peasants' War was a series of uprisings in the German lands during the Reformation, chiefly in 1524–1525. Rural people challenged labor services, serfdom, and restrictions on access to forests, hunting, and fishing. In 1525, rebels expressed many demands in the Twelve Articles, including the right to choose local pastors. Fighting spread through Swabia, Franconia, Thuringia, and nearby regions, but armies of territorial rulers defeated the poorly equipped rebel bands. Religious reform gave some participants a language for their claims; Martin Luther, however, opposed the armed revolt. The war exposed deep tensions over authority and rural obligations in the Holy Roman Empire.

Peasant demands included hunting, fishing, and forest-use rights.
Some rebels wanted to choose their own local pastor.

overview.text: Charles V was a Habsburg ruler whose titles joined several realms without making them one unified state. He became king of Spain as Charles I in 1516 and Holy Roman Emperor in 1519, ruling as emperor until 1556. His reign coincided with the Protestant Reformation and repeated conflict with France over Italy. Ottoman attacks also threatened Habsburg lands in central Europe. At Augsburg in 1530, Protestant princes presented a statement of belief that Charles rejected. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 offered a temporary settlement within the empire by allowing its rulers to determine their territories' religion. His reign shows how dynastic power stretched across regions yet faced divided loyalties.

He was Holy Roman Emperor from 1519 to 1556.
His reign included wars with Francis I of France over Italian territories.
Ottoman campaigns threatened Austria and Hungary during his reign.

overview.text: Pyramids are monumental structures with sloping or stepped sides, built by different societies for different purposes. At Teotihuacan, in what is now Mexico, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon stand along the Avenue of the Dead within a major ceremonial city. At Chichen Itza on the Yucatán Peninsula, El Castillo, or the Temple of Kukulcan, belongs to a different Mesoamerican tradition. Ancient Egyptians built pyramids within royal funerary complexes; at Giza, the largest was made for Khufu. Similar overall shapes therefore do not imply a shared builder, date, or use. Archaeologists interpret each monument through its own cultural and historical setting.

overview.text: Ancient Egyptian pyramids were monuments of royal burial and remembrance, especially associated with the Old Kingdom. Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara was Egypt's first pyramid: its tiers were formed by stacking six mastaba-like levels. Later builders developed smooth-sided forms, and Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza became the largest Egyptian pyramid. The other two principal Giza pyramids were built for Khafre and Menkaure. A pyramid was only one part of a funerary complex, which could also include temples, a causeway, and smaller tombs. These structures expressed beliefs about kingship and the afterlife as well as the Egyptian state's ability to organize large building projects.

Its stepped form consists of six stacked mastaba levels.
Imhotep may have been responsible for the Step Pyramid's design.

overview.text: Pompeii was a Roman town near Mount Vesuvius in southern Italy. The volcano's eruption in 79 CE buried it and nearby Herculaneum, ending life in both communities but preserving much of their physical fabric. Excavations beginning in the eighteenth century uncovered streets, houses, shops, paintings, and other traces of urban life. Researchers can study both elite decoration and ordinary expression: graffiti in Pompeii's theatre corridor, for example, records writing and drawing in a public space. The nearby villas of Torre Annunziata add evidence of wealthy Roman households. Because so many different kinds of remains survive together, the site is unusually informative about a Roman town at one moment in time.

Archaeological excavation of the buried sites began in the eighteenth century.
Pompeii was a commercial Roman town.

overview.text: The oprichnina was a separate domain and system of rule created by Tsar Ivan IV in 1565. Within it, he controlled land, administration, finances, and armed forces more directly than in the rest of his realm. Ivan used the arrangement to strengthen his personal authority and punish people he suspected of treason, including members of the political and religious elite. This arrangement distinguished the tsar’s own institutions from the administration of remaining lands. Violent repression accompanied the effort to subdue boyar and religious elites. The oprichnina ended in 1572.

key_facts.text: The oprichnina lasted from 1565 to 1572.
The zemshchina was the portion outside Ivan IV's personal domain.
The special domain supplied an armed force serving the tsar.

overview.text: The oprichniki were the armed servitors attached to Ivan IV's oprichnina in sixteenth-century Russia. Selected for loyalty to the tsar, they enforced his separate rule through seizures, intimidation, and violence against people he regarded as enemies. The corps grew beyond its initial thousand members and included men from different backgrounds. Oprichniki participated in the 1570 attack on Novgorod. Some descriptions associate them with black clothing and the symbols of a dog's head and broom, meant to suggest guarding the tsar and sweeping away treason. They predate modern political police, although historians sometimes compare their repressive role with later security forces. Their organization belonged to the policy that ended in 1572.

Their force began with about one thousand men and later expanded.
They participated in the violent attack on Novgorod in 1570.
Accounts describe black dress and dog-head and broom symbols.
They were an early special security force, not a modern police institution.

overview.text: Germany is a modern Central European country whose official name is the Federal Republic of Germany. Its capital is Berlin, and its federal system consists of sixteen states, or Länder. The Basic Law establishes a parliamentary system: voters elect a parliament, while state governments participate in national legislation through the Bundesrat. Today's state includes territory formerly divided between the Federal Republic in the west and the German Democratic Republic in the east; reunification took effect in 1990. Individual states retain responsibilities for schools and culture, reflecting the country's decentralized political structure.

Berlin is Germany's capital.
Germany consists of sixteen federal states.
The Bundestag elects the federal chancellor.

overview.text: East Germany, formally the German Democratic Republic or GDR, existed from 1949 to 1990 in the Soviet occupation zone created after World War II. The Socialist Unity Party dominated its government and built a socialist dictatorship. Its Ministry for State Security, known as the Stasi, monitored and repressed perceived opponents. From 1961, the Berlin Wall split East and West Berlin and became a visible sign of German division. Public protests and a peaceful revolution in 1989 weakened the ruling party; the Wall opened on 9 November that year. On 3 October 1990, the GDR joined the Federal Republic, ending its separate existence.

overview.text: West Germany was the common name for the Federal Republic of Germany during the Cold War division from 1949 to 1990. Founded under the Basic Law, it developed a parliamentary democracy whose Bundestag elected the chancellor. Under Konrad Adenauer, the republic aligned with Western institutions and experienced rapid economic growth often called the Wirtschaftswunder. West Berlin was linked to it politically, but had a special legal status and did not vote directly in Bundestag elections. Chancellor Willy Brandt later pursued Ostpolitik to improve relations with Eastern European states and the GDR. In 1990, eastern states joined the Federal Republic; the republic continued as united Germany rather than disappearing.

overview.text: The Battle of France was Germany’s rapid defeat of France and its allies in May and June 1940. German forces attacked the Low Countries on 10 May, drawing British and French armies into Belgium, while the main armored thrust crossed the Ardennes farther south. The breakthrough reached the coast and trapped Allied troops in the north; many escaped by sea from Dunkirk. German troops entered Paris on 14 June, and France signed an armistice on 22 June. Germany occupied much of France, while a French government based at Vichy cooperated with it. The campaign dramatically changed World War II by removing Britain’s principal continental ally.

The main German attack passed through the Ardennes.
More than 300,000 French and British troops escaped via Dunkirk.
Paris fell on 14 June; France signed an armistice on 22 June.

overview.text: The 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests began after the city’s government proposed an extradition bill that could have sent suspects to mainland China. Huge marches in 2019 pressed for the bill’s withdrawal, but the movement broadened into demands for an independent inquiry into police conduct, release of arrested protesters, and democratic elections. The government withdrew the bill, yet protests and arguments over civil liberties continued. Police and demonstrators clashed during parts of the movement, alongside many peaceful marches. In June 2020, China imposed a national security law on Hong Kong, changing the political setting in which activists operated. The movement became a major contest over Hong Kong’s autonomy and freedoms.

overview.text: Jesuit reductions were mission settlements established among Indigenous peoples in colonial South America, especially among the Guaraní. Jesuit priests sought to spread Catholic Christianity while Guaraní residents lived, worked, and maintained parts of their language and culture within the settlements. The reductions had churches, houses, workshops, ranches, and cultivated land; cattle raising and yerba mate contributed to their economies. Local councils involved Guaraní leaders, although priests retained considerable authority over daily life. The settlements formed part of the Spanish colonial world rather than an independent state. Spain expelled the Jesuits from its territories in 1767, and the mission system changed after their departure. Ruins in Argentina and Brazil are protected as World Heritage sites.

overview.text: Mozambique is a country in southern Africa that became independent from Portugal in 1975 after negotiations involving FRELIMO. Independence did not bring lasting peace. The FRELIMO-led government fought the armed RENAMO movement in a long civil war that brought severe hardship to the country. Leaders of the government and RENAMO signed a General Peace Agreement in Rome on 4 October 1992. A United Nations mission then helped monitor the ceasefire, demobilization, and elections. The country’s history therefore includes both a struggle against colonial rule and a difficult transition from civil war to multiparty politics.

overview.text: The Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE was a decisive Theban victory over a Spartan-led army in ancient Greece. Theban commander Epaminondas concentrated his hoplites in an unusually deep formation on the left, opposite the Spartan king Cleombrotus. Contemporary writer Xenophon describes the Theban line as at least fifty shields deep and the Spartan line as no more than twelve. Theban cavalry helped disrupt the Spartan advance, and Cleombrotus died during the fighting. The defeat shattered Sparta’s reputation for battlefield dominance and opened a period of greater Theban power. Historians debate some details of the battle, but its importance as a turning point is clear.

Epaminondas commanded the victorious Theban forces.
Theban hoplites massed at least fifty shields deep, according to Xenophon.

Leuctra weakened Sparta’s dominance in Greece.

overview.text: The Medici were a Florentine family of merchants and bankers whose wealth gave them great political influence during the Renaissance. In the fifteenth century they dominated Florence without holding a formal hereditary title; later members ruled as dukes and grand dukes. Their support for artists and scholars helped make Florence a center of Renaissance art and humanist learning. Lorenzo de’ Medici was among the family’s best-known patrons, while Cosimo I commissioned the Uffizi building as a center of government in the sixteenth century. The family’s story joins finance, politics, and cultural patronage: works created or collected under Medici rule remain central to Florence’s museums.

overview.text: World War I changed soldiers’ head protection as artillery fragments caused many head injuries. Early-war headwear included the German spiked Pickelhaube, which offered too little protection for trench warfare. France introduced the steel Adrian helmet in 1915, Britain adopted the shallow-brimmed Brodie helmet that September, and Germany introduced its steel Stahlhelm in 1916. Their shapes differed: the Brodie’s broad brim helped shield against falling debris, while the German design covered more of the head and neck. Steel helmets reduced some shrapnel injuries, although the Brodie design left the neck and lower head exposed. The designs became recognizable symbols of the armies that wore them.

Britain adopted the Brodie design in September 1915.
The Brodie’s broad brim protected against falling fragments.
The German M16 Stahlhelm entered service in 1916.

overview.text: The Darien scheme was a Scottish attempt to establish a trading colony on the Isthmus of Panama in the late 1690s. Backed by the Company of Scotland, its first expedition sailed in 1698 and founded a settlement called New Edinburgh. The colonists hoped the location would open trade between the Atlantic and Pacific worlds, but inadequate supplies, disease, difficult farming, and Spanish opposition undermined the venture. Two expeditions failed, costing many lives and much of the money invested by Scots. The financial disaster became one factor in the negotiations that led to the 1707 union with England; it was not the only cause of that political decision.

overview.text: Charles X was king of France from 1824 until the July Revolution of 1830 removed him. A younger brother of Louis XVI and Louis XVIII, he returned from exile after the French Revolution and succeeded Louis XVIII. He favored a stronger traditional monarchy and was crowned at Reims in 1825. In July 1830 he issued ordinances restricting press freedom, dissolving the elected chamber, and changing election rules. The measures helped spark three days of revolt in Paris, known as the Three Glorious Days. Charles abdicated and went into exile; Louis-Philippe then became king. His fall showed how sharply the restored monarchy could clash with demands for constitutional limits.

overview.text: Byzantine Iconoclasm was a series of disputes over religious images in the Byzantine Empire during the eighth and ninth centuries. Opponents of icons feared that honoring images could become idolatry; defenders distinguished respect shown to an image from worship owed to God. Imperial and church leaders took different sides over time. A council called by Constantine V supported iconoclasm in 754, while the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 approved the veneration of icons. Iconoclast policy returned in the early ninth century before the use of icons was restored in 843. The controversy shaped Byzantine worship and art, although scholars caution that policy and practice varied across the empire.

overview.text: Deng Xiaoping was China’s most powerful leader during the 1989 Tiananmen protests, although he did not hold the presidency. After emerging as the central figure in the late 1970s, he promoted economic reforms and greater contact with the outside world. In spring 1989, students and other citizens gathered in Beijing to demand political change. Senior Communist Party figures disagreed over how to respond. Declassified accounts identify Deng and other party elders as decisive supporters of martial law and the military action that ended the demonstrations in early June. Troops killed protesters and bystanders, prompting international condemnation and a sharp disruption in China’s relations with the United States.

overview.text: Jacob Zuma is a South African politician who served as president from 2009 until his resignation in 2018. He had previously taken part in the anti-apartheid movement, held senior positions in the African National Congress, and served as the country’s deputy president. After he left office, a judicial commission investigating allegations of state capture ordered him to testify. Zuma failed to comply with a Constitutional Court order to appear and provide evidence. In 2021, the court found him in contempt and imposed a fifteen-month prison sentence. His imprisonment concerned disobedience of a court order, not a finding that the commission’s corruption allegations had been proved.

overview.text: Koxinga, also called Zheng Chenggong, was a seventeenth-century military leader loyal to the fallen Ming dynasty. During the Ming-Qing transition, he crossed to Taiwan with his forces. In 1661 his forces attacked Dutch East India Company positions near present-day Tainan, including Fort Zeelandia. The Dutch surrendered in 1662, ending their colonial rule in southwestern Taiwan. Koxinga established a Ming-loyalist government there, commonly called the Kingdom of Tungning. His descendants continued to rule until Qing forces defeated the Zheng regime in 1683, making his campaign a turning point in Taiwan’s political history.

overview.text: The Kingdom of Greece was the monarchical form of the modern Greek state that emerged after the war for independence from the Ottoman Empire. Otto became its first king in 1832 and initially ruled as an absolute monarch. An uprising in 1843 compelled a constitution, creating a constitutional monarchy. Otto was removed in 1862; George I then became king under a new constitutional arrangement that emphasized popular sovereignty. The monarchy was interrupted by a republic in the interwar period and later returned. After the military dictatorship ended, a referendum in December 1974 rejected restoration of the crown, and Greece adopted a republican constitutional order.

overview.text: Sutton Hoo is an early medieval burial ground in Suffolk, England, celebrated for an Anglo-Saxon ship burial. In 1939, excavators found the outline of a buried ship and a chamber containing weapons, metalwork, and an elaborate helmet. The objects point to a powerful person with links extending beyond East Anglia, but the individual’s identity remains unknown; King Rædwald is a leading suggestion. Coins help date the burial to around 625 CE. Acidic soil destroyed most organic remains, while chemical evidence showed that a body had once lain in the chamber. The discovery greatly expanded knowledge of wealth, craftsmanship, and long-distance connections in early Anglo-Saxon England.

overview.text: The Russian Empire was the state ruled by Russia’s emperors from Peter the Great’s adoption of the imperial title in 1721 until the monarchy collapsed in 1917. Its territory stretched across northern Eurasia and included many peoples and languages. Peter’s victory over Sweden gave Russia a Baltic foothold, and Saint Petersburg became the imperial capital. During the nineteenth century, the state expanded in the Caucasus and Central Asia, while Alexander II emancipated the serfs in 1861. The last emperor, Nicholas II, abdicated during the February Revolution in March 1917. A provisional government took power before the Bolsheviks seized power later that year.

overview.text: Jan Hus was a Czech preacher and reformer active in Prague in the early fifteenth century. At Bethlehem Chapel he preached in Czech and called for changes in church conduct, including criticism of clerical wealth and abuses. He wrote religious works in both Czech and Latin and became entangled in disputes over church authority and teachings associated with John Wycliffe. After church authorities excommunicated him, Hus traveled to the Council of Constance to defend his views. The council condemned him, and he was burned at the stake in 1415. His death helped energize the Hussite reform movement in Bohemia.

overview.text: A phalanx was a close-packed infantry formation used by ancient Greek armies. The best-known Greek version consisted of hoplites, heavily equipped foot soldiers who carried long spears and large shields. They advanced in ranks so that neighboring shields overlapped, giving the front line collective protection. Its effectiveness depended on discipline and on keeping the formation intact; a broken line exposed soldiers to attack. Greek city-states relied on this style of fighting for centuries. Philip II of Macedon later adapted the formation with a smaller shield and a much longer spear called the sarissa, creating a different Macedonian phalanx used by his successors.

key_facts.text: A Greek hoplite was an armored foot soldier with a spear and shield.
Hoplite phalanxes advanced with overlapping shields.
Some phalanxes were eight or more ranks deep.
Keeping ranks together was essential to the formation’s protection.
Philip II of Macedon introduced a longer spear called the sarissa into his version.

overview.text: The Stasi was the common name for East Germany’s Ministry for State Security, founded in 1950. It served the ruling Socialist Unity Party as a secret police force and foreign intelligence agency. Its officers watched suspected opponents, intercepted communications, carried out interrogations, and operated detention centers. A large network of unofficial collaborators supplied information from workplaces, schools, and personal relationships. In the 1970s, the ministry increasingly used covert intimidation and reputation attacks alongside surveillance. Despite this reach, it did not eliminate public opposition. After East Germany’s peaceful revolution, surviving Stasi files became an important record of how the dictatorship monitored citizens.

key_facts.text: The Ministry for State Security was founded in East Germany in 1950.
Stasi was a common name for the ministry.
It functioned as domestic secret police and a foreign intelligence agency.

overview.text: The Babylonian Captivity refers to the forced exile of people from the kingdom of Judah to Babylonia in the sixth century BCE. After Nebuchadnezzar II captured Jerusalem in 597 BCE, King Jehoiachin and members of the royal court were taken away. A later revolt brought another Babylonian siege, the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, and further deportations. Judean communities continued to live and work in Babylonia, as surviving cuneiform records attest. When the Persian ruler Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, exiles were allowed to return. Biblical accounts describe the return and rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, while Babylonian records independently attest the earlier conquest.

key_facts.text: Nebuchadnezzar II captured Jerusalem and removed its king in 597 BCE.
King Jehoiachin and elite Judeans were deported to Babylonia.
A second siege destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 586 BCE.
Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE.

overview.text: The Katipunan was a secret Filipino organization founded in 1892 to seek freedom from Spanish colonial rule. Andrés Bonifacio was among its founders and became a central revolutionary leader. Members organized clandestinely while the society spread through Manila and beyond; women also joined and helped safeguard its papers. In August 1896, the society moved from secret resistance into open revolt. The episode remembered as the Cry of Pugadlawin includes the symbolic tearing of Spanish tax certificates, or cedulas. Katipunan fighters then fought colonial forces in the Philippine Revolution. The Cry's precise details remain contested, but it marks a decisive turn toward armed resistance.

Andrés Bonifacio was one of its founders.

overview.text: Alexander of Battenberg was chosen in 1879 as prince of Bulgaria, then an autonomous principality under nominal Ottoman suzerainty. A German-born relative of Russia's emperor Alexander II, he initially seemed well placed to balance powerful neighbors. His rule became entangled in disputes over Bulgaria's constitution, Russian influence, and territorial union. In 1885 he accepted the union of the principality with Eastern Rumelia, a separately administered Ottoman province. Bulgaria then defeated a Serbian invasion. A coup by officers opposed to his rule forced Alexander to abdicate in 1886. Bulgaria did not declare full independence from Ottoman suzerainty until 1908, after his reign.

The principality remained under nominal Ottoman suzerainty during his reign.

overview.text: Sri Lanka's economic crisis in 2022 combined a shortage of foreign currency with heavy debt, surging prices, and difficulty importing essentials. Fuel and power shortages disrupted daily life, while food and medicine became harder to obtain. The government suspended external debt payments in April as reserves dwindled. Global rises in food and energy prices added to the strain, but the crisis also reflected longstanding weaknesses in public finances and external accounts. Large protests demanded political change amid the shortages. President Gotabaya Rajapaksa left the country and resigned in July 2022. The effects fell especially hard on lower-income households, making economic recovery and social protection closely linked concerns.

overview.text: The Great Bath is a large brick-lined tank at Mohenjo-daro, a city of the Indus civilization in what is now Pakistan. Built within a substantial architectural complex, it measures roughly 12 by 7 meters and is about 2.4 meters deep. Steps descend into the basin at both ends, and builders used water-resistant materials to help retain water. A nearby well may have supplied it. The city's planned streets, drainage, and other public structures place the Bath in a wider tradition of sophisticated urban water management. Its exact purpose is unknown. Archaeologists often suggest that people used it for communal or ritual bathing, but there is no surviving text that establishes a single definitive use.

The tank measures about 12 by 7 meters and 2.4 meters deep.

overview.text: Dom Pedro II was Brazil's second and last emperor. He inherited the throne in 1831 as a child after Pedro I abdicated, so regents governed until he was declared of age in 1840; his coronation followed in 1841. His long reign included cultural and scientific patronage and the costly War of the Triple Alliance against Paraguay. Brazil also remained a slaveholding society for most of his rule. In 1888 his daughter Princess Isabel, acting as regent, signed the Golden Law abolishing slavery. A military coup ended the monarchy in November 1889, sending Pedro into exile; he died in 1891. His reign therefore spans warfare and profound conflict over slavery and political power.

He was declared of age in 1840 and crowned in 1841.

overview.text: The Gallic Wars were Julius Caesar's campaigns against various peoples of Gaul, beginning in 58 BCE. Gaul was a broad ancient region, not a single unified nation, and its communities made different alliances and choices. Caesar's armies fought groups including the Helvetii, while his published account presented the campaigns from his own point of view. In 52 BCE, Vercingetorix led a major coalition that defeated Roman forces at Gergovia but was later besieged at Alesia. Caesar built extensive siege lines to resist both the defenders and a relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered after Alesia, though fighting did not end immediately. The conquest brought Gaul under Roman domination at immense human cost.

Gallic communities were not one unified state.
Vercingetorix's forces defeated Caesar at Gergovia.
The siege of Alesia occurred in 52 BCE.
