overview.text: An inverse is a mathematical partner that reverses an operation or transformation: applying an operation and then its inverse returns the starting value. For functions, if f(a)=b, then f⁻¹(b)=a; composing the two in either order gives the identity, where defined. A function has an inverse function only when it is one-to-one, meaning different inputs have different outputs; restricting its domain can sometimes make this possible. For a square matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹=A⁻¹A=I, with I the identity matrix. A matrix inverse exists exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Function notation f⁻¹ means “inverse function,” not 1/f.

key_facts.text: For an invertible function, input-output pairs switch: if f(a)=b, then f⁻¹(b)=a. The compositions f⁻¹∘f and f∘f⁻¹ return the original input where defined.
A function must be one-to-one to have an inverse function; on a graph, this is tested with the horizontal line test.
The full function f(x)=x² is not one-to-one, but restricting its domain to x≥0 gives it the inverse f⁻¹(x)=√x.
A matrix inverse is defined for a square matrix A by the two checks AA⁻¹=I and A⁻¹A=I; I has ones on its main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero; if the determinant is zero, it has no inverse.
For a nonzero number a, its multiplicative inverse is its reciprocal, 1/a; zero has no multiplicative inverse.

overview.text: In geometry, a vertex (plural: vertices) is a point where sides or edges meet—the corner of a polygon or a solid. In graph theory, the same word names a dot representing an object; edges represent connections between objects, so a vertex can stand for, for example, an airport in a flight network. Unlike a polygon corner, a graph vertex need not be joined to any edge, and its location or the shape of the drawn edges does not determine the network: what matters is which vertices connect. Graph vertices are also called nodes. Thus, “vertex” links familiar geometric corners with a general way to describe structures and relationships.

key_facts.text: The plural of vertex is vertices.
A polygon’s corners and a solid’s corners are examples of geometric vertices.
In a graph, vertices represent objects and edges represent their connections.
A graph vertex can have degree zero: it may have no edges connected to it.
In graph theory, the arrangement or shape of the drawn edges can change without changing which vertices are connected.

overview.text: Pythagoras of Samos was a Greek thinker of the sixth century BCE, remembered as a philosopher and as the founder of a disciplined community. His early reputation centered more on beliefs about the soul and religious practice than on mathematics. The right-triangle rule now called the Pythagorean theorem became linked to his name, but there is no reliable evidence that he proved it; Babylonians knew the underlying rule earlier. Later accounts also associate Pythagoras with musical intervals described by whole-number ratios, although the evidence for his personal discoveries is uncertain. His significance lies partly in the Pythagorean tradition, whose members connected number, music, and ideas about how the world is ordered.

key_facts.text: He grew up on Samos; accounts place his life around 570–490 BCE, though details of his biography are uncertain.
Pythagoras founded a way of life marked by discipline and religious beliefs, and attracted devoted followers.
The theorem bearing his name relates the squares on a right triangle’s sides; the attribution is later, and evidence that Pythagoras proved it is lacking.
Babylonians knew the underlying right-triangle rule before Pythagoras, though that does not establish that they stated or proved the theorem in the later Greek form.
Later tradition linked Pythagoras to whole-number ratios in musical intervals, but the evidence does not securely show that he personally discovered them.

overview.text: An ellipse is a closed curve and a conic section: it can be formed where a plane cuts a cone, and it can also be defined by its foci. For every point on the curve, the distances to two fixed foci add to the same constant. Its major axis is the longest diameter; the shorter, perpendicular diameter is the minor axis, and the foci lie on the major axis. Eccentricity describes how stretched an ellipse is: zero gives a circle, while values closer to one give more elongated ellipses. Ellipses matter in astronomy because Kepler’s first law describes planetary orbits as ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.

key_facts.text: The foci are fixed points, and the sum of the distances from any point on the ellipse to both foci stays constant.
The major and minor axes cross at the ellipse’s center; the foci lie on the major axis.
Eccentricity measures the ellipse’s shape: it is 0 for a circle and less than 1 for an ellipse.
An ellipse is a conic section, a shape formed by intersecting a plane with a cone.
Kepler’s first law describes planets as orbiting the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.

overview.text: Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), also known as Johann Carl Friedrich Gauss, was a German mathematician, astronomer, and physicist whose research ranged from number theory and geometry to astronomy, geodesy, and magnetism. He studied and later worked in Göttingen, where he directed the observatory and pursued research across mathematics and the physical sciences. In 1801, he published *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*, a major work largely devoted to number theory, and used least-squares methods to predict the orbit of Ceres. One remarkable early result showed that a regular 17-sided polygon can be constructed using ruler and compass. With physicist Wilhelm Weber, Gauss investigated Earth’s magnetism and helped develop an early electromagnetic telegraph.

key_facts.text: Gauss lived from 1777 to 1855 and worked as a mathematician, astronomer, and physicist.
His 1801 book *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* was largely devoted to number theory.
He showed that a regular 17-sided polygon can be constructed with ruler and compass—a notable result in classical geometry.
Gauss used least-squares methods to predict the orbit of Ceres, an asteroid first observed in 1801.
Gauss and Wilhelm Weber studied Earth’s magnetism; Gauss also collaborated with Weber on an early electromagnetic telegraph.

overview.text: The arithmetic mean—often called the mean or, in everyday usage, the average—is a measure of a data set’s center, or central tendency. To calculate it, add every value and divide the total by the number of values; each value contributes to the result. The sample mean is commonly written x̄, while the mean of an entire population is written μ. The mean gives a single summary of a data set, but it may not describe a typical value well: unusually high or low values can pull it away from where most observations lie. When outliers are present, the median may better represent the center.

key_facts.text: Formula: arithmetic mean = sum of all data values ÷ number of values.
The sample mean is denoted x̄ (“x-bar”); the population mean is denoted μ.
If values repeat, you can multiply each distinct value by how often it occurs, add those products, and divide by the total number of values.
The mean is a measure of center, alongside other measures such as the median and mode.
Outliers can strongly affect the mean; the median is less sensitive to them and may be a better summary when extreme values are present.

overview.text: A determinant is a single number assigned to a square matrix; for a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), it is ad − bc. It summarizes how the matrix’s linear transformation changes space: in two dimensions, its absolute value gives the area scale factor, and in any dimension its absolute value gives the volume scale factor. The sign records orientation. A zero determinant means the transformation collapses space and the matrix is not invertible; a nonzero determinant means it is invertible. This makes determinants useful for analyzing square systems of linear equations: when the coefficient matrix has a nonzero determinant, Cramer’s rule can find the system’s unique solution.

key_facts.text: For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc. It can be written det(A) or with vertical bars around the matrix.
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero; a zero determinant signals that it has no inverse.
In two dimensions, the absolute value of a determinant is the factor by which a matrix transformation scales area; in higher dimensions it gives the volume scale factor.
The determinant’s sign can distinguish orientation: for example, swapping two coordinates reflects the plane and gives determinant −1.
Cramer’s rule uses determinants to solve a square system of linear equations when its coefficient matrix has a nonzero determinant.

overview.text: René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French mathematician, natural philosopher, and philosopher whose ideas influenced both mathematics and philosophy. In La Géométrie (1637), he developed ways to connect algebraic equations with geometric curves and solve geometric problems using algebra. The later right-angled coordinate system called Cartesian honors his work, though Descartes’s own approach was not simply the modern coordinate plane. In philosophy, he used systematic doubt to seek secure knowledge, starting from the certainty that he was thinking. He also argued that mind and body are distinct, a view that helped shape the enduring mind–body problem.

key_facts.text: Descartes lived from 1596 to 1650.
La Géométrie appeared in 1637 as part of the Discourse on the Method and presented influential methods joining algebra and geometry.
The term “Cartesian coordinates” honors Descartes, but the right-angled coordinate system developed later; his own coordinate lines did not have to be perpendicular.
His “I think, therefore I am” argument identifies the thinking self as a starting point for certainty in his philosophical inquiry.
Descartes argued that mind and body are distinct; the difficulties of explaining how they interact became a lasting philosophical problem.

overview.text: Logical OR, also called disjunction or inclusive OR, combines two propositions into a Boolean statement, commonly written p ∨ q. It is true when p is true, q is true, or both are true; it is false only when both inputs are false. That gives OR three true outcomes in its four-row truth table and distinguishes it from exclusive OR, which is false when both inputs are true. OR is a basic connective for building and evaluating compound statements, including conditions in computer programs. Programming notation depends on the language: in Java, || is conditional OR, so a true left operand makes the result true without evaluating the right operand.

key_facts.text: For two inputs, the truth table is true for true/true, true/false, and false/true; it is false for false/false.
In logic, OR is inclusive: the result stays true when both inputs are true.
The symbol ∨ is standard in propositional logic; the symbol ⊕ is commonly used for exclusive OR.
OR differs from AND: OR needs at least one true input, while AND requires both inputs to be true.
In Java, || skips evaluating its right-hand operand when the left-hand operand is true; this is Java-specific behavior, not a universal notation rule.

overview.text: Fermat’s Last Theorem is a statement in number theory: for any integer exponent n greater than 2, no positive integers x, y, and z make x^n + y^n = z^n. It concerns integer solutions to a Diophantine equation and is strikingly easy to state, yet resisted proof for centuries. In the 1630s, Pierre de Fermat wrote the claim in a book’s margin; no general proof from him survives, so whether he truly had one is uncertain. Andrew Wiles proved the theorem in the 1990s, drawing on links between elliptic curves and modular forms. The long effort to solve it also advanced number theory.

key_facts.text: The theorem rules out positive-integer solutions for every integer exponent greater than 2; it does not make the same claim for exponent 2.
Fermat’s famous claim appeared in a margin beside a discussion in Diophantus’s Arithmetica. The margin note survives, but no general proof by Fermat does.
Wiles proved the theorem in 1994; the proof was formally published in 1995. Richard Taylor collaborated with Wiles on part of the work.
Wiles and Taylor-Wiles proved a result about semistable elliptic curves and modularity, which in turn proved Fermat’s Last Theorem.
The centuries of attempts to prove the theorem contributed to major developments in number theory.

overview.text: In propositional logic, an implication “if p, then q” has a contrapositive: “if not q, then not p.” It reverses the order of the two parts and negates both. Unlike the converse (“if q, then p”), it has exactly the same truth value as the original for every assignment of truth values, so they are true or false together. This equivalence makes contraposition a useful proof strategy: to establish an implication, prove its contrapositive instead. For example, “if an integer’s square is even, then the integer is even” is equivalent to “if the integer is odd, then its square is odd.” Carefully negating both parts matters; merely reversing them gives the converse, which is not generally equivalent.

key_facts.text: For “if p, then q,” form the contrapositive by reversing the parts and negating each: “if not q, then not p.”
An implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent: they share the same truth value in every case.
The converse, “if q, then p,” only switches the parts; it is not generally equivalent to the original implication.
A proof by contrapositive proves the reversed-and-negated implication directly, then uses its equivalence to conclude the original implication.
For integers, “if the square is even, then the integer is even” has the equivalent contrapositive “if the integer is odd, then its square is odd.”

overview.text: Area measures how much two-dimensional space a flat region covers, and it is expressed in square units such as square centimeters, not linear units such as centimeters. It distinguishes the size of a region from the length of its boundary, making it useful for estimating flooring or paint. For familiar shapes, formulas use dimensions: a rectangle’s area is length times width, and a triangle’s is half its base times its height. For curved regions, calculus can approximate area by adding thin rectangles and taking a limit. A definite integral gives signed area (above the x-axis minus below it); total area counts both portions positively. In two dimensions, integrating 1 over a region gives its area.

key_facts.text: Area is measured in square units; perimeter measures the boundary in linear units.
A rectangle’s area is length × width; a triangle’s area is ½ × base × height.
For curved regions, sums of rectangle areas can approach the exact area as the rectangles become narrower and their number increases.
A definite integral gives signed area: area above the x-axis minus area below it. To get total area, count both portions positively.
A double integral of the constant function 1 over a plane region gives that region’s area.

overview.text: Exponentiation, also called raising to a power, is an arithmetic operation written with a base and a smaller, raised exponent: in 3⁴, 3 is the base and 4 the exponent. For a positive whole-number exponent, it means multiplying the base by itself that many times, so 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. This compact notation records repeated multiplication. It also extends beyond that basic case: for a nonzero base, a zero exponent gives 1, while a negative exponent represents a reciprocal. Exponents matter when reading expressions, too: in standard order of operations, powers are evaluated before multiplication and addition.

key_facts.text: In aⁿ, a is the base and n is the exponent; the exponent is written above and to the right of the base.
For a positive whole-number exponent, 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, which equals 8.
For a nonzero base a, a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: aⁿ × aᵐ = aⁿ⁺ᵐ.
In standard order of operations, exponents are evaluated before multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction.

overview.text: In graphing, an asymptote is a straight-line guide that a curve gets arbitrarily close to in a specified limit; it describes behavior near a particular input or far out at either end. A vertical asymptote is x = a, where function values grow without bound as x nears a from at least one side. A horizontal asymptote y = b describes outputs tending to b as x tends toward positive or negative infinity. An oblique (slant) asymptote is a diagonal line whose distance from the curve tends to zero at an end. These lines help reveal a graph’s shape, but “approaches” does not mean “never meets”: graphs can cross horizontal or slant asymptotes, so asymptotes describe limiting behavior, not barriers.

key_facts.text: A vertical asymptote has the form x = a; the function’s values tend to positive or negative infinity as x approaches a from at least one side.
A horizontal asymptote has the form y = b; it describes the function’s end behavior as x tends to positive infinity, negative infinity, or both.
An oblique, or slant, asymptote is a nonhorizontal line that the graph approaches as x tends toward positive or negative infinity.
Graphs of rational functions may cross horizontal or slant asymptotes; an asymptote is not necessarily a line the graph never meets.
For rational functions, a shared factor in the numerator and denominator can create a hole rather than a vertical asymptote; simplify before identifying vertical asymptotes.

overview.text: Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665) was a French lawyer and government official who pursued mathematics alongside his career. He became especially known for number theory, the study of whole numbers and their properties, and also contributed to early calculus. Two theorems bear his name: Fermat’s Little Theorem describes a pattern in the remainders produced by powers of numbers modulo a prime, while Fermat’s Last Theorem says that positive integers cannot satisfy xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ when n is greater than 2. Fermat left the latter claim as a margin note; it was proved centuries later by Andrew Wiles. Historians cannot be certain Fermat himself had a correct proof.

key_facts.text: Fermat was born in Beaumont-de-Lomagne, France, and died in Castres. His birth year is usually given as 1601, though the biographical record notes some uncertainty about the exact birth date.
He studied law and served as a government official in Toulouse; mathematics was a major pursuit beyond his legal work.
Fermat’s Little Theorem: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1) leaves remainder 1 when divided by p.
Fermat’s Last Theorem states that no positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for n greater than 2.
Fermat’s son published the margin note after Fermat’s death. Andrew Wiles’s proof was accepted after a problem in his initial proof was repaired; whether Fermat had a valid proof remains uncertain.

overview.text: Six is a positive integer with notable roles in number theory and geometry. In number theory, it is the smallest perfect number: its positive divisors other than itself—1, 2, and 3—sum to 6. “Perfect” here has a precise arithmetic meaning, not a judgment about the number. In geometry, six is the side count of a hexagon, whose interior angles total 720°; in a regular hexagon, each of the six equal interior angles measures 120°. These examples show how six can describe both a special divisor pattern and a familiar polygon.

key_facts.text: A positive integer is perfect when its proper divisors—positive divisors other than itself—sum to the number.
Six is the smallest perfect number: its proper divisors are 1, 2, and 3, and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
A hexagon has six sides, and its interior angles total 720°.
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°; three such angles meet at a point in a regular-hexagon tessellation.

overview.text: A geometric line (usually just called a line in elementary Euclidean geometry) is an ideal straight, one-dimensional object with no thickness or endpoints: it continues without limit in both directions. It differs from a segment, which has two endpoints, and a ray, which has one. Lines are useful for describing geometric figures and connecting geometry to algebra: in coordinate geometry, a line can be represented by the points satisfying a linear equation. For a nonvertical line, slope-intercept form, y = mx + b, gives its slope, m, and y-intercept, (0, b). Euclid’s phrase “breadthless length” is associated with lines, but his definition alone did not specify only straight, infinite lines.

key_facts.text: A geometric line is straight, one-dimensional, has no thickness, and extends infinitely in both directions.
A line segment has two endpoints; a ray has one endpoint and continues indefinitely in one direction.
Two points on a line can be used to name it; a line is often drawn with arrowheads at both ends to show that it continues.
For a nonvertical line in slope-intercept form, y = mx + b, m is the slope and (0, b) is the y-intercept.
Euclid described a line as “breadthless length,” but his discussion distinguishes straight lines from lines generally and allows that lines may have ends.

overview.text: Topology is a branch of mathematics that studies spaces and the features they retain under continuous change. A useful picture is to imagine stretching or twisting a shape without tearing it, though topology also has a formal language for spaces and continuity beyond physical shapes. It focuses on properties such as connectivity rather than measurements like exact length or angles. For example, a circle and an ellipse are topologically equivalent. Topology is significant because its ideas help mathematicians compare many kinds of spaces, including surfaces and knots, and its concepts of continuity are used across mathematics.

key_facts.text: In the intuitive “rubber-sheet” view, stretching and twisting are allowed, but tearing is not; this is a guide to the subject, not its full formal definition.
A circle and an ellipse are topologically equivalent, as are a sphere and an ellipsoid: their exact dimensions and outlines differ, but their topological properties match.
Topological invariants include features such as connectivity and dimension—properties used to distinguish spaces even when measurements like distance are set aside.
Topology also studies how one object sits inside another; knot theory grew from questions about such relationships.
Topology includes areas such as general, geometric, algebraic, and differential topology, and its concepts of continuity are used throughout mathematics.

overview.text: Pascal’s triangle is a triangular arrangement of binomial coefficients: start with 1 at the top, place 1s along both edges, and make each interior number the sum of the two numbers diagonally above it. Numbering the top as row 0, row n gives the coefficients in the expansion of (a+b)^n; those coefficients also count ways to choose k items from n. The triangle matters because one simple addition rule connects algebra and counting. Though named for Blaise Pascal, similar arrays were studied earlier in several regions. Chinese mathematician Jia Xian’s work is known through Yang Hui’s surviving 1261 explanation; Jia Xian’s own book is lost.

key_facts.text: The first rows are 1; 1, 1; 1, 2, 1; and 1, 3, 3, 1. Each new row has 1s at the edges, and each interior entry adds the two above it.
In row n, the entry in position k (starting at position 0) is the coefficient of a^k b^(n−k) in (a+b)^n, and counts the ways to choose k of n items.
Entries mirror across the center of each row: the number of ways to choose k items from n equals the number of ways to leave out k items.
The entries in row n add to 2^n, the total number of subsets of a set with n members.
The name varies across mathematical traditions: MathWorld notes the Yang Hui triangle in China, Khayyam triangle in Persia, and Tartaglia’s triangle in Italy.
MacTutor reports that Jia Xian used the triangle in work on binomial expansions and root extraction; his own book is lost, and details come through Yang Hui’s 1261 text.

overview.text: Differentiation is the calculus process of finding a derivative, which describes how a function’s output changes as its input changes. At a particular input, the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change and, on a graph, the slope of the tangent line there. It is defined as the limit of slopes between nearby points—the difference quotient—when that limit exists; writing f′(x) describes the derivative as a new function of x. Derivatives turn changing quantities into useful rates: for example, differentiating a position function gives instantaneous velocity. A function must be continuous to be differentiable at a point, but continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability.

key_facts.text: The derivative at x = a is defined by the limit f′(a) = limₕ→₀ [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, if the limit exists; the fraction is called the difference quotient.
Geometrically, f′(a) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph at (a, f(a)).
The derivative function is commonly written f′(x); other notations include dy/dx and df/dx.
A derivative’s units are output units divided by input units; for a position function measured over time, the derivative represents instantaneous velocity.
Differentiability implies continuity, but not the reverse: |x| is continuous at zero yet has no derivative there.

overview.text: A right angle measures exactly 90°, or one quarter of a full turn. Its two sides meet at a common vertex; when they lie along intersecting straight lines, those lines are perpendicular. Right angles help describe square-corner relationships and classify shapes: acute angles are smaller than 90°, while obtuse angles are greater than 90° but less than 180°. In geometry diagrams, a small square at the vertex marks an exact right angle, even if the drawing does not look perfectly square. The symbol ⟂ is used to show that lines are perpendicular.

key_facts.text: A right angle is exactly 90°; a quarter-turn is 90°.
Two lines that intersect at a 90° angle are perpendicular; the symbol ⟂ denotes perpendicularity.
A small square drawn at an angle’s vertex indicates that it measures exactly 90°.
An angle smaller than 90° is acute; an angle greater than 90° but less than 180° is obtuse.
The right-angle marker is a diagram convention: it specifies an exact measure rather than relying on how the drawing looks.

overview.text: In a two-dimensional Cartesian (rectangular) coordinate plane, the origin is the point where the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis meet; its coordinates are written (0,0). Each zero means there is no displacement from the origin along that axis. The origin is the common reference point for locating others: an ordered pair (x,y) gives the horizontal displacement first and the vertical displacement second, with signs indicating direction. Because it lies on both axes, the origin is not in any of the four quadrants. It serves as the starting point for plotting locations and describing graphs in the plane.

key_facts.text: The origin is the intersection of the x- and y-axes, and its ordered pair is (0,0).
In an ordered pair (x,y), x comes first and represents horizontal displacement; y comes second and represents vertical displacement.
A point with x-coordinate 0 lies on the y-axis; a point with y-coordinate 0 lies on the x-axis. The origin lies on both.
The two axes divide the plane into four quadrants, so the origin, which lies on the axes, is not inside a quadrant.
The origin is a reference point: other points are located by their horizontal and vertical displacements from it.

overview.text: The Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem asked whether a person could walk through 18th-century Königsberg, crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. The city straddled the Pregel River and included two islands, creating four separate land regions. Leonhard Euler showed that no such walk was possible. His key idea was to ignore distances and represent each land region as a vertex and each bridge as an edge. In this graph, all four vertices have an odd number of edges; a walk using every edge once can have at most two odd-degree vertices, so the Königsberg arrangement fails that rule. Euler’s solution is a landmark in the beginnings of graph theory.

key_facts.text: Königsberg, now called Kaliningrad, was divided by the Pregel River and included two islands.
Euler answered the bridge question negatively; the problem is considered a foundational landmark in graph theory.
To make a graph, represent each land region as a vertex and each bridge as an edge.
A route using every edge exactly once can have at most two odd-degree vertices; Königsberg’s graph has more than two.
The walk need not return to its starting point; the challenge is to cross each bridge once, wherever the walk begins or ends.

overview.text: Addition, also called adding or summation, is the operation that combines two or more quantities into a sum; the quantities are addends (or summands), and repeated addition can be written with capital sigma notation. For ordinary numbers, changing the order or grouping of addends does not change the sum, and adding zero leaves a number unchanged. The same idea extends beyond numbers, but the objects must follow rules for their type: vector addition combines directed movements into a resultant, drawable by placing arrows tip-to-tail, while matrix addition adds matching entries and requires matrices of identical dimensions. These extensions make addition useful for describing combined quantities, displacements, and data arrays.

key_facts.text: The result of addition is a sum; the quantities being added are called addends or summands.
For real numbers, addition is commutative (a + b = b + a) and associative ((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)).
Zero is the additive identity for real numbers: adding zero leaves a number unchanged.
To draw a vector sum, place the second vector’s starting point at the first vector’s arrowhead; the resultant runs from the first vector’s start to the second’s end.
Matrix addition pairs corresponding entries, so the matrices must have the same dimensions; the resulting matrix keeps those dimensions.
Repeated addition can be represented using capital sigma notation, with limits indicating the terms included in the sum.

overview.text: SOUR is Olivia Rodrigo’s debut studio album, released May 21, 2021. Its 11 tracks include “drivers license,” “deja vu,” “good 4 u,” and “happier.” Following the breakout success of “drivers license,” the album earned Rodrigo the 2022 Grammy for Best Pop Vocal Album. The record stands out for moving between intimate heartbreak ballads and louder, guitar-driven pop-punk: “drivers license” is a swelling breakup ballad, while opener “brutal” turns adolescent frustration into crunchy guitars. Its lyrics also explore jealousy and self-doubt, and the closer “hope ur ok” turns outward toward people facing hardship, giving the collection a more compassionate finish.

overview.text: Spirited Away (Japanese title: Sen to Chihiro no Kamikakushi) is a 2001 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki for Studio Ghibli. Ten-year-old Chihiro enters a spirit world with her parents; after they are transformed into pigs, she takes a job in a bathhouse for spirits and tries to save them. The bathhouse, filled with unusual beings including a dragon and a witch, gives the film its distinctive setting. Chihiro’s efforts to adapt and act courageously make it a coming-of-age story. The film won the Academy Award for Animated Feature at the 2003 ceremony, a major international recognition for the work.

overview.text: A comic book is a visual storytelling publication in which framed pictures, called panels, work together with words to convey a narrative. Readers interpret artwork and language at once: panel size and arrangement can shape a story’s pace and tone, while dialogue often appears in speech balloons and narration or thoughts may appear in captions. Creators can also use thought balloons and written sound effects. This combination makes comics a distinctive art-and-literature form, able to tell stories through both what characters say and what the pictures show.

key_facts.text: A panel is one framed image; its size and placement can affect the story’s pace and tone.
Speech balloons show dialogue, thought balloons show unspoken thoughts, and captions often carry a narrator’s words.
Written sound effects, such as “WHAM,” can represent sounds within a comic.
Artists can layer speech balloons to show characters talking over one another.
A 1992 example in the Smithsonian collection is a pair of original Brotherman No. 5 comic-book pages that join into one large scene, with speech balloons above people in a crowd.

overview.text: T’Challa is Marvel Comics’ Black Panther: king of the fictional African nation of Wakanda and its protector, who also serves as an Avenger. Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, he first appeared in Fantastic Four #52 in 1966. His role combines royal leadership with superhero action: he defends his people in a panther suit made with Wakanda’s vibranium, a fictional metal that absorbs vibrations and kinetic energy. Wakanda’s advanced technology and T’Challa’s scientific brilliance distinguish him from many heroes. His debut was culturally significant in an era when Black characters were often relegated to secondary roles in comics; in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Chadwick Boseman portrayed him.

In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Chadwick Boseman portrayed T’Challa; his Black Panther costume is part of the National Museum of African American History and Culture’s collection.

overview.text: Black Panther (2018) is a Marvel superhero film directed by Ryan Coogler, with Chadwick Boseman as T’Challa, the hero known as Black Panther. Carter blended African-inspired traditions with futuristic forms, helping create Wakanda’s distinctive visual world. The American Film Institute selected it among 2018’s culturally and artistically significant films.

overview.text: Lil Nas X (Montero Lamar Hill) is an American rapper, singer and songwriter from Georgia who became widely known in 2019 with “Old Town Road.” Blending country signifiers with hip-hop production, the song spread through online promotion and short-form video culture, then reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100; its remix with Billy Ray Cyrus helped extend its run. Its removal from Billboard’s Hot Country chart sparked debate over genre boundaries and how country music is categorized. Hill followed the hit with the EP 7, featuring “Panini,” and the 2021 album Montero. His public coming out as gay during the song’s chart run and his later work helped make LGBTQ representation part of his cultural significance.

overview.text: YouTube is an online video-sharing platform where people upload videos for others to watch and share, with social features such as comments and related-video links. Founded by Jawed Karim, Chad Hurley, and Steve Chen, the site was registered in February 2005; its first upload, “Me at the zoo,” appeared on April 23, 2005. Google acquired the company in 2006. YouTube’s significance lies in making video publishing and viewing easy for a broad public, helping shift the web toward user-created multimedia and social interaction. The Victoria and Albert Museum identifies those early design choices as influential patterns for later social platforms.

overview.text: Monty Python and the Holy Grail is a British comedy released in 1975, written and performed by the Monty Python troupe and co-directed by Terry Jones and Terry Gilliam. It turns Arthurian legend into a deliberately unruly quest: King Arthur gathers knights to seek the Grail, but they face absurd trials, challenges to royal authority, and comic reversals of chivalric heroism. Its muddy, handmade medieval look contrasts with the characters’ solemn behavior, while budget-saving coconut clops stand in for horses. The film carried the group’s sketch-show absurdism into feature-length storytelling and became an enduringly popular comedy, later inspiring the musical Spamalot.

key_facts.text: The film premiered in 1975; it was shot in April and May 1974.
Terry Jones and Terry Gilliam co-directed; Graham Chapman plays King Arthur.
The story parodies Arthurian legend, following Arthur and his knights on a quest for the Holy Grail.
Because the production could not afford horses, performers mimed riding while assistants clapped coconut halves together.

overview.text: Super Smash Bros. is Nintendo’s crossover fighting-game series, first released in 1999 for Nintendo 64. Its central idea is an all-star clash: familiar video-game characters, including Nintendo stars such as Mario, Link, Kirby, and Pikachu, meet on themed arenas instead of remaining in their separate game worlds. Unlike fighting games that rely on a conventional health bar, Smash tracks damage as a percentage; as damage rises, a fighter can be launched farther by an attack. Players try to knock opponents beyond the stage while staying in the fight themselves, using character-specific moves, items, and arena features. This combination of recognizable characters, unusual knockout rules, and battles across varied stages distinguishes the series.

overview.text: The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool and became a defining act of 1960s popular music. Their best-known lineup—John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr—took shape by 1962. The group became a British sensation in 1963 and helped lead the British Invasion of the United States the following year. Their sound combined rock-and-roll energy with close pop harmonies, while their songwriting and experimentation helped expand what rock music could sound like. They drew on American performers and incorporated styles including ballads, hard rock, and traditional Indian music. The Beatles stopped touring in 1966 and broke up in 1970.

key_facts.text: The band began with three teenage musicians in Liverpool in the late 1950s; Ringo Starr joined after earlier lineup changes, and the Beatles had emerged by 1962.
The group became a national sensation in the United Kingdom in 1963, with a run of number-one singles.
Their first appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show was on February 9, 1964, bringing them to a large U.S. audience.
Their musical roots included American performers such as Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, and Fats Domino; later recordings also drew on styles such as traditional Indian music and hard rock.
The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame highlights their original songwriting, pop harmonies, rock energy, and willingness to experiment as distinctive parts of their sound.

overview.text: Facebook is a social-networking service where people connect through profiles, posts, groups, and other shared content. Mark Zuckerberg launched it as “thefacebook” on February 4, 2004, as a directory for Harvard students; its early focus on finding classmates and adding friends helped it spread beyond campus, and the company changed its name to Facebook that June. Today, Facebook is a Meta service with features such as Groups and Marketplace. Its history shows how a campus network grew into a much broader online platform, as well as how social media raised questions about personal data: the FTC filed a complaint alleging Cambridge Analytica used deceptive tactics to collect Facebook users’ information for voter profiling and targeting.

overview.text: Alien is a 1979 science-fiction horror film directed by Ridley Scott and written by Dan O’Bannon. Its story follows the crew of the commercial spaceship Nostromo, who investigate a mysterious signal and encounter alien life. When a creature gets aboard, the crew must try to survive in the isolated ship. Sigourney Weaver plays officer Ellen Ripley. The film stands out for its claustrophobic spaceship setting, its largely unseen threat, and the unsettling creature designs of artist H.R. Giger. The British Film Institute calls it Scott’s breakthrough sci-fi horror, and the American Film Institute records that it won the 1979 Academy Award for visual effects.

key_facts.text: The film was released on May 25, 1979; Ridley Scott directed it, and Dan O’Bannon wrote it.

overview.text: The Walt Disney Company is an American entertainment and media company whose beginnings trace to brothers Walt and Roy Disney’s 1923 cartoon studio. On October 16 that year, Walt signed a distribution contract for the Alice Comedies, which featured a real-life girl adventuring in a cartoon world; the venture eventually became the company known today. Disney’s early fame grew around Mickey Mouse, whose 1928 cartoon Steamboat Willie used synchronized sound and helped establish the character as a lasting company symbol. Today the business extends beyond animation and films: its operations include entertainment media and streaming, ESPN, and experiences such as theme parks, resorts, cruises, vacations, and consumer products, linking stories with places and merchandise.

key_facts.text: The company’s beginnings are dated to October 16, 1923, when Walt Disney signed a contract to distribute the Alice Comedies; Walt and Roy Disney formed the studio together.
The Alice Comedies featured a real-life girl having adventures in a cartoon world.
Steamboat Willie, released in 1928, brought Mickey Mouse to prominence with synchronized sound; the story of Mickey’s creation has multiple versions, so its exact origin is uncertain.

overview.text: Journalism is the practice of gathering, checking, explaining, and sharing information about events and issues through news media. Journalists report and interpret information, using verification and context to help audiences judge what is happening. The work can take different forms and uses skills such as reporting, writing, ethical decision-making, and multimedia storytelling. Journalism matters to public life: UNESCO describes it as a source of fact-based information and an independent watchdog. Credible reporting depends on accuracy and fairness, but also on accountability and care: journalists are encouraged to correct errors, identify sources clearly, separate news from advertising, and weigh the public’s need for information against possible harm.

key_facts.text: Journalism training includes reporting, writing, ethics, and multimedia storytelling.

overview.text: The 1972 film The Godfather is Francis Ford Coppola’s crime drama, adapted from Mario Puzo’s novel. It follows New York crime boss Don Vito Corleone and his son Michael (Al Pacino), whose gradual rise to family leadership tests loyalty and power. Marlon Brando plays Vito. A distinctive sequence intercuts Michael’s participation in his sister’s baby’s baptism with killings of rival leaders, contrasting religious vows with violent business. The film helped shape the American gangster movie and remains culturally important: the Academy named it Best Picture for films released in 1972, and the Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 1990.

key_facts.text: Francis Ford Coppola directed the film and co-wrote its screenplay with Mario Puzo; Marlon Brando and Al Pacino star as Vito and Michael Corleone.

overview.text: Avatar: The Last Airbender is Nickelodeon’s animated fantasy-adventure series, which aired from 2005 to 2008. It is set in a war-torn world divided among the Water, Earth, Air, and Fire nations, where some people can “bend” their nation’s element. The young hero, Aang, is the Avatar—the one person able to master all four—and must help restore balance as the Fire Nation threatens the other nations. This elemental system and the Avatar’s balancing role define the series’ central conflict: Aang’s journey is about more than gaining powers; it is also a struggle to bring peace to a divided world. The original animated series is distinct from the later live-action adaptation with the same title.

overview.text: Parks and Recreation, often called Parks and Rec, is an American sitcom set in Pawnee, a fictional town in Indiana. It centers on Leslie Knope (Amy Poehler), a driven employee in the town’s parks department, and her coworkers as they try to improve their community while navigating bureaucracy and local politics. Co-created by Greg Daniels and Michael Schur, the NBC series began in 2009 and ran for seven seasons. Its documentary-style filming and fourth-wall breaks give the workplace comedy an observational feel, while its small-town government setting makes public service the source of much of its humor. The series balances political satire with hope: Schur described its guiding idea as people working hard to make the world a little better.

overview.text: League of Legends (LoL) is a free-to-play multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) game from Riot Games, whose debut title launched in 2009. In its signature 5-versus-5 mode, players choose champions with distinct roles, cooperate across lanes, and aim to destroy the opposing team’s Nexus. Its mix of team play and a broad cast of champions helps distinguish it among online games. Its importance also reaches competitive gaming: Riot identifies League as the game that began its portfolio and connects it to a World Championship, while independent reporting records League’s inclusion among esports medal events at the 2023 Asian Games.

overview.text: Kanye West, legally known as Ye, is an American rapper, record producer, and fashion designer who grew up in Chicago. He first built a reputation producing music for other artists, then broke through as a rapper with The College Dropout (2004). His early production style often used sped-up soul samples, while later albums explored markedly different sounds, including the expansive My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy, gospel-influenced Jesus Is King, and Donda, named for his late mother. West’s career also extends into fashion: his Yeezy label brought his music persona into clothing and footwear. overview.text: John Lennon (1940–1980) was an English singer-songwriter and musician from Liverpool who became famous as a member of the Beatles, where his songwriting partnership with Paul McCartney helped shape the group’s music. After the Beatles ended, Lennon pursued a solo career, releasing songs including “Imagine” and “Give Peace a Chance.” He also made anti-war activism part of his public work: with artist Yoko Ono, he staged 1969 “Bed-Ins for Peace” and promoted the message “War Is Over! If you want it.” Lennon’s songs combined personal, direct expression with public protest, making him a distinctive figure in popular music. On December 8, 1980, he was shot and killed outside his Manhattan apartment building by Mark David Chapman.

overview.text: Alfred Hitchcock’s 1960 black-and-white film Psycho adapts Robert Bloch’s novel into a suspense story that begins with secretary Marion Crane fleeing after stealing money and checking into the isolated Bates Motel. Norman Bates, the shy proprietor, lives with his unseen mother in a looming house above it. The famous shower murder abruptly shifts the story away from Marion, while sharply edited images and Bernard Herrmann’s piercing string score make suspense central to the experience. Psycho became a landmark of mainstream horror and is especially remembered for Hitchcock’s manipulation of audience expectations: viewers are encouraged to change whom they identify with as the mystery unfolds.

Psycho is based on Robert Bloch’s 1959 novel; Joseph Stefano wrote the screenplay.
The shower murder comes roughly 45 minutes into the film, an early and startling departure from the story’s initial focus on Marion.
Bernard Herrmann’s memorable score uses strings, including the piercing musical cue associated with the shower scene.
Hitchcock sought to protect the plot surprises by discouraging press screenings and having theaters prevent late arrivals from entering after the film began.

overview.text: Marilyn Monroe, born Norma Jeane Mortenson and later baptized Norma Jeane Baker, was an American actress who became one of Hollywood’s most recognizable stars. In The Seven Year Itch, her role as “The Girl” became closely linked to the famous subway-grate scene and its billowing white dress. Although studios often promoted her as a blonde bombshell, Monroe also pursued more dramatic roles and greater creative control, including by forming her own production company. Her image and performances remain part of popular culture.

overview.text: The Washington Post is an American newspaper founded by Stilson Hutchins in Washington, D.C.; its first issue appeared December 6, 1877. Its own founding principles emphasize telling the truth and reporting important affairs in America and around the world. The paper is especially associated with investigative journalism: it published excerpts from the Pentagon Papers in 1971, then covered the Watergate break-in and evidence linking Nixon campaign officials to secret political activity. The Watergate investigation earned The Post the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. These episodes distinguish the paper for sustained reporting on government and public affairs, and illustrate the press’s role in examining the conduct of people in power.

key_facts.text: The Post began publishing on December 6, 1877, as a four-page paper founded by Stilson Hutchins.

The Post’s staff began covering Watergate in 1972; the newspaper received the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for its Watergate investigation.

overview.text: Released in 1915, D. W. Griffith’s epic film The Birth of a Nation follows two white families through the Civil War and Reconstruction, adapting Thomas Dixon Jr.’s novel The Clansman. It presents Reconstruction from a Confederate-sympathetic viewpoint, relies on degrading racist stereotypes of Black people, and portrays the Ku Klux Klan as heroic. Those portrayals are racist distortions, not reliable history. The film’s scale and filmmaking helped establish feature films as a major form of popular entertainment, while its popularity also helped the revived Klan attract supporters. The NAACP protested and campaigned against its screenings, making the film significant both in cinema history and as an example of media shaping public memory.

key_facts.text: Griffith premiered the film in Los Angeles in February 1915; it was based on Thomas Dixon Jr.’s novel The Clansman.
Its plot links two white families to a Confederate-leaning account of the Civil War and Reconstruction.
The film vilifies Black people through racist stereotypes and glorifies the Ku Klux Klan; the NAACP organized protests and sought to stop screenings.
Its filmmaking and popularity helped elevate feature films, but the revived Klan also used the movie’s success as a recruiting tool.

overview.text: Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia launched on January 15, 2001, initially as an English-language project. Unlike reference works written by a fixed editorial staff, it is built through open collaboration: volunteers can create and revise articles, and the Wikimedia Foundation says it does not make editorial decisions about their contents. Wikipedia’s significance lies in making reference material freely accessible while inviting people to help develop it. Openness is paired with community-made rules: English Wikipedia’s policies call for articles to represent significant views fairly and rely on published, reliable sources so claims can be checked. These standards guide the project, but edits can be mistaken or disruptive, so readers should follow citations and assess information carefully.

key_facts.text: Wikipedia launched on January 15, 2001; it began as an English-language project and expanded to other languages.
Its articles are created and curated by volunteers, who discuss and debate what to include.
English Wikipedia’s neutral-point-of-view policy asks editors to represent significant views fairly and proportionately, without editorial bias.
Its verifiability policy says article claims should be checkable against reliable, published sources; certain claims and quotations require inline citations.
The Wikimedia Foundation hosts and protects Wikipedia, but volunteers—not the Foundation—make editorial decisions about its content.

overview.text: “Hijab” has more than one related meaning. In common English usage, it usually names a headscarf worn by some Muslim women that covers the hair and neck while leaving the face visible; more broadly, it can refer to modest dress or ideas of privacy and modesty. It is not the same garment as a niqab, which covers the lower face, or a burqa, which covers the face and body, though names and styles vary across communities. In the Qur’an, the Arabic word hijab most often denotes a screen or partition rather than a headscarf. For some wearers it expresses faith or identity; interpretations, personal practices, and rules about covering differ, and whether it is required is debated.

key_facts.text: In common usage in Europe and North America, hijab often means a headscarf covering the hair and neck while leaving the face visible.
A niqab covers the lower face; a burqa covers the face and body. These are distinct garments, though terminology and styles can vary.
The Quranic Arabic Corpus lists seven occurrences of hijab as a noun and glosses it in context as a screen, partition, barrier, or veil—not as a specific headscarf.
Hijab styles and interpretations differ across communities; some people wear it as an expression of faith, identity, or belonging.
Muslim communities disagree about whether a headscarf is religiously required, and rules about women’s covering vary by place.

overview.text: The Last Supper is the New Testament’s account of Jesus’s final meal with his disciples before his arrest and crucifixion. In Mark’s Gospel, set during Passover preparations, Jesus tells the gathered disciples that one of them will betray him, then shares bread and a cup, interpreting them in relation to his body and blood. Christians have connected this meal with the Lord’s Supper, also called Communion or the Eucharist. Gospel accounts emphasize different details: John describes Jesus washing the disciples’ feet, and the accounts differ over the meal’s timing in relation to Passover. The Last Supper is therefore both a central Christian story and a scene with distinct Gospel tellings.

overview.text: Arjuna is a heroic Pandava prince in the Hindu epic Mahabharata, portrayed as a disciplined warrior and identified in the tradition as the third of five brothers and a son of the god Indra. His defining moment comes at Kurukshetra, where he hesitates to fight relatives, friends, and teachers on the opposing side. Krishna, serving as his charioteer, answers Arjuna’s moral crisis with teachings that form the Bhagavad Gita, a pivotal part of the larger epic. Arjuna is therefore both a central combatant in the war and the listener through whom this influential Hindu religious and philosophical dialogue unfolds. Art often depicts him with bow and arrow beside Krishna.

overview.text: Eurydice is the wife of Orpheus, the legendary musician and poet, in a famous Greco-Roman myth. In Ovid’s telling, she dies from a snakebite while walking with nymphs. Orpheus travels to the Underworld, where his music persuades its rulers to let her follow him back, on one condition: he must not look behind him before they reach the upper world. Just before they emerge, he turns to check on her, and she vanishes back into the Underworld. Eurydice is central to the story’s memorable tension between Orpheus’s hope of recovering her and the rule he cannot break.([classics.mit.edu](https://classics.mit.edu/Ovid/metam.10.tenth.html))

overview.text: Chiron (also spelled Cheiron or Kheiron) is a centaur in Greek mythology, distinguished from many of his kind by his wisdom and skill in healing. Ancient stories make him a teacher and caretaker of heroes: Homer connects him with Achilles’ knowledge of medicine, while Greek poems describe him raising Jason. These stories made Chiron a memorable mentor figure, linking heroic strength with learning and care. Myths commonly name the Titan Cronus and the nymph Philyra as his parents, though details vary across ancient accounts. In art, Chiron appears in scenes with Achilles; an ancient ring gem in the Walters Art Museum shows him teaching the young hero to play the lyre.

key_facts.text: Chiron is a centaur—a part-human, part-horse being—and is remembered as unusually wise and civilized.

In the Iliad, Chiron is associated with teaching Achilles healing knowledge; other ancient Greek poems say he raised or taught Jason.

overview.text: Saint Patrick was a fifth-century Christian bishop who worked as a missionary in Ireland and became its patron saint. The strongest evidence about him comes from two writings attributed to Patrick, especially the Confessio, in which he describes his religious convictions and Irish mission; his precise dates and career details remain uncertain. Later tradition presents him as the sole figure behind Ireland’s conversion, but Christianity was already present there and Patrick did not claim to be the island’s only missionary. His significance lies both in Irish Christian history and in his later role as a central symbol of Irish identity. The familiar claim that he used a shamrock to explain the Trinity is a later tradition, not securely attested from his lifetime.

key_facts.text: Two writings attributed to Patrick survive: the Confessio and a letter concerning the soldiers of Coroticus.
Christian communities existed in Ireland before Patrick’s mission; a separate bishop, Palladius, was sent to Ireland in 431.
The image of Patrick as the island’s single apostle was shaped in later accounts, including a seventh-century Life of Patrick.
The National Museum of Ireland describes the shamrock-and-Trinity story as a relatively late belief, rather than a securely established event from Patrick’s time.
A bell reputed to have belonged to Patrick became an important relic; its ornate shrine was made around AD 1100 and linked the saint with Armagh.

overview.text: Mythological petrification is the supernatural transformation of a living being into stone, often caused by a dangerous gaze or imposed by a god. In Greek stories, Medusa’s gaze could turn people to stone, and her severed head retained that power: Perseus used it against enemies, including King Polydektes, before giving it to Athena. Another tale uses petrification to end an impossible chase: Laelaps, a hound fated to catch its quarry, pursued the Teumessian Fox, fated never to be caught, until Zeus turned both to stone. Ancient tellings differ in details, so these episodes are best understood as distinct mythic examples, not one fixed account.

key_facts.text: Medusa was the mortal Gorgon; the Met describes her petrifying gaze and Perseus’s use of her head as a weapon after her death.
In the Met’s account, King Polydektes of Seriphos tricks Perseus into promising Medusa’s head; Perseus avoids her gaze by looking at its reflection in a bronze shield.
In Apollodorus’s account, the Teumessian Fox could not be caught, while Laelaps was destined to catch whatever it pursued; Zeus turns both to stone when the hound chases the fox.
Pausanias gives a related version in which Dionysus sends the fox to harm the Thebans and both animals become stone as the hound is about to catch it.
Petrification can mark a monster’s threat, serve as a weapon through Medusa’s head, or resolve the fox-and-hound story’s conflict between opposing fates.

overview.text: Mahayana, Sanskrit for “Great Vehicle,” is a broad Buddhist tradition whose beginnings became visible within Indian Buddhism in the early centuries CE. Its distinguishing ideal is the bodhisattva path: practitioners aspire to Buddhahood while cultivating wisdom and compassion to help all beings become free from suffering. Mahayana recognizes a range of scriptures and practices rather than one single routine. As it spread across Asia, it developed into varied forms, including East Asian traditions such as Zen and Pure Land. Its name expresses an aspiration that its proponents understood as a broader vehicle for awakening; it should not be read as a neutral ranking of other Buddhists.

key_facts.text: “Mahayana” means “Great Vehicle”; the vehicle image evokes Buddhist teachings as a way across suffering.

overview.text: Mahavira, also known as Vardhamana, was an ancient Indian religious teacher revered in Jainism as the 24th and final Tirthankara—a guide who shows a path across rebirth. After renouncing household life, Mahavira lived as a wandering ascetic and taught nonviolence, self-discipline, and a path to liberation. His lasting importance lies in shaping Jain teachings and organizing its community, although accounts of his life differ and his precise dates remain uncertain.

The Catholic Church interprets New Testament passages as assigning Peter distinctive leadership among the apostles, regards the pope as his successor, and traditionally counts Peter as the first pope. Christian tradition links Peter’s final ministry and martyrdom to Rome. Historians continue to examine his role in the earliest church and whether, and in what capacity, he went to Rome.

overview.text: Tibetan Buddhism is a diverse Buddhist tradition rooted in Tibet and shaped by sustained exchange with Indian Buddhism. Buddhism reached Tibet by the seventh century, and Indian Buddhist texts were translated into Tibetan. Its teachings draw on Mahayana philosophy and the bodhisattva ideal, alongside Vajrayana ritual and esoteric meditation. The four major traditions—Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, and Gelug—are best understood as lineages of teachers and students, not completely separate religions; they share important teachings and scriptures. Teacher-guided practice, monastic learning, and art used to support meditation are among its distinguishing features. The tradition has had a lasting religious and cultural influence in Tibet and across the Himalayan region.

key_facts.text: Buddhism was introduced to Tibet by the seventh century, became the state religion by the end of the eighth century, and experienced a revival beginning in the late tenth century.

overview.text: In Norse myth, Asgard (Old Norse Ásgarðr) is the fortress of the Æsir, a group of gods, set near the center of the mythic world. Midgard, the human world, lies outside it, and the rainbow bridge Bifrost links the two; Yggdrasil, the world tree, connects the regions of the cosmos. Asgard contains halls associated with particular gods, including Odin’s Valhalla, so Valhalla is a hall within Asgard, not another name for the whole realm. In Snorri Sturluson’s Prose Edda, a giant offers to build a protective citadel, and Loki disrupts the work. These are mythic accounts preserved in medieval texts, not evidence of a historical place; Snorri wrote after Iceland’s conversion to Christianity, so details may reflect later shaping.

overview.text: Apocalypse, as an eschatological idea, concerns the anticipated end or transformation of the world or of its present order. Eschatology also includes beliefs about individual destinies, but this topic focuses on cosmic endings. Traditions differ: an ending may involve judgment and the defeat of evil, yet also renewal or a new age, rather than simple annihilation. The word “apocalypse” originally meant an unveiling or revelation; it is also used for visionary writings about divine realities and events at the end of time. For example, Christian Revelation uses vivid symbolic visions, while Zoroastrian teaching describes frashokereti, a final renovation of creation. These are religious teachings, not verified predictions.

overview.text: Oedipus is a legendary king of Thebes and the central figure of Sophocles’ tragedy Oedipus the King, also called Oedipus Tyrannus or Oedipus Rex. The play is often regarded as a model Greek tragedy. In a well-known version of the myth, an oracle predicts Oedipus will kill his father and marry his mother. Raised by foster parents, he leaves them to escape the prophecy but unknowingly kills his birth father, Laius, on the road. He saves Thebes by solving the Sphinx’s riddle, becomes king, and marries Jocasta, his mother. Later, investigating Laius’s murder, he discovers his identity; in Apollodorus’s account, Oedipus blinds himself. Ancient tellings vary in some details.

overview.text: Kali, also called Kalika, is a Hindu goddess whose fierce form expresses the power of Devi, the Great Goddess. In the Devi Mahatmya, a sacred Hindu text, she emerges from Devi’s forehead during battle and helps defeat demons. In the story of Raktabija, every drop of the demon’s blood that reaches the ground creates another demon, so Kali drinks his blood to stop them multiplying. Her dark complexion, extended tongue, skull garland, and weapons make her recognizable in many images. Though associated with destruction, Kali is also worshipped as a protector and compassionate mother, especially in Bengal; her fierce power can be understood as directed against threats.

Common images show Kali with dark or blue-black skin, an extended tongue, a garland of severed heads, and multiple arms carrying weapons.
Kali is commonly associated with Parvati and Shiva; many images show her standing on Shiva, while devotees also honor her as a protective mother.
Kali is especially prominent in Bengal, where Kali Puja is a major Hindu festival dedicated to her.

overview.text: Dalai Lama is a title for a continuing reincarnation lineage of teachers in the Geluk (often called “Yellow Hat”) school of Tibetan Buddhism. Its name combines Mongolian *dalai* (“ocean”) with Tibetan *lama* (“teacher”). In the sixteenth century, Mongol leader Altan Khan gave the title to Sonam Gyatso; it was later applied to two earlier teachers in the line, making Sonam the third Dalai Lama. Tibetan Buddhists traditionally regard the Dalai Lamas as manifestations of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion—a religious belief. From the fifth Dalai Lama onward, the lineage also governed Tibet; in 2011, Tenzin Gyatso transferred political authority to elected leadership. Recognized as the fourteenth at age two, he has lived in exile in India since 1959.

overview.text: Aphrodite is a major goddess of ancient Greek religion, associated especially with love, beauty, desire, fertility, and the renewal of life. Her origin differs across ancient accounts: Hesiod’s Theogony says she arose from sea foam after Kronos cast Ouranos’s severed genitals into the sea, while Homer presents her as the daughter of Zeus and Dione. In Hesiod’s story she first reaches Cythera and then Cyprus, which explains traditional names such as Cytherea and Cypris. Widely worshipped across the Greek world, Aphrodite also had roles linked to seafaring. Roman worship identified her with Venus, and images of her rising from the sea became a lasting artistic theme.

overview.text: In the Christian Gospel story told in Luke 1:26–38, the Annunciation is the moment the angel Gabriel visits Mary in Nazareth and tells her that, through the Holy Spirit, she will conceive and bear Jesus, called the Son of God. Christians understand this event as the beginning of the Incarnation—the belief that God’s Son took human life—and celebrate it as a major feast. overview.text: Lent is a Christian liturgical season of preparation for Easter, the celebration of Jesus Christ’s resurrection. In the Roman Catholic calendar, Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and ends on the evening of Holy Thursday, with Sundays left out of the forty-day count. Orthodox Christians call the season Great Lent and emphasize preparation for the Resurrection through renewed devotion and care for others. Customs and fasting rules differ among churches and individuals, so Lent is not one identical regimen practiced by every Christian.

overview.text: Ra (also called Re) was a major ancient Egyptian sun god, connected with creation, kingship and renewal. Egyptians pictured the sun’s daily course as a voyage: Ra crossed the sky in a solar boat and entered the underworld at night, with the journey’s return marking the sun’s rebirth. In Egyptian religious accounts, the serpent Apep (also called Apophis) threatened the boat and the sunrise; gods aboard defended Ra. This story made Ra’s voyage more than a description of the sky: it expressed the continuing contest between order and chaos. Ra is often shown as a falcon-headed man wearing a sun disk, though Egyptian beliefs and portrayals changed over time.

overview.text: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, is a Tibetan Buddhist monk and spiritual leader. overview.text: Nowruz (also called Noruz or Persian/Iranian New Year) is a spring festival and new-year observance held at the vernal equinox, traditionally linked with Iranian culture and celebrated in varied forms across many communities. Its name means “new day.” Records connect it to Zoroastrian religious and secular traditions, but its beginnings are not fully certain: the name is absent from surviving Avestan texts, and later stories credit mythical king Jamshid with founding it. The festival matters as a celebration of seasonal renewal and family and community ties. Iranian celebrations may include spring cleaning, visits, and a haft-sin table of symbolic items; in the Bahá’í Faith, Naw-Rúz is a holy day marking the end of the 19-day fast. It is not exclusively a religious holiday; traditions vary by place and faith.

overview.text: Demeter is an ancient Greek goddess of the harvest and agricultural abundance, central to a society dependent on farming. Her daughter is Persephone, and their story offers a mythic explanation for the seasonal rhythm of plant growth: when Hades takes Persephone to the underworld, Demeter grieves and crops fail; when her daughter returns, growth resumes. This is a religious narrative, not a historical account of how seasons work. Demeter was also worshipped with Persephone at Eleusis in the Eleusinian Mysteries, initiation rites whose secret details remain poorly known. In ancient art, she is associated with grain and a scepter, and is sometimes shown with Triptolemos, linked to teaching grain cultivation.

overview.text: The Ramayana is a major Sanskrit epic of Hindu tradition, traditionally attributed to the poet Valmiki. Estimates of its composition vary, and it has circulated in many retellings. Its central story follows Prince Rama, exiled for fourteen years with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. When Ravana, ruler of Lanka, abducts Sita, Rama—with help from Hanuman and other allies—wages war, defeats Ravana, and returns to Ayodhya. The narrative raises questions about righteousness, duty, kingship, and divinity. Revered in Hindu cultures and a lasting source for Indian art, the epic has versions in many languages, with differences in emphasis and sometimes plot.

key_facts.text: The Sanskrit Ramayana is traditionally credited to Valmiki; scholars’ estimates of its composition differ.
In the central story, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana go into a fourteen-year forest exile after Rama is denied the throne.
Ravana’s abduction of Sita leads Rama, aided by Hanuman and other allies, to fight Ravana in Lanka.
The epic is influential in Indian literature and culture, and its story has inspired Indian artists for centuries.
There is no single version: retellings in different languages can vary in emphasis and plot.

overview.text: The Kaaba (also spelled Ka‘bah) is a cuboid sanctuary at the center of the Masjid al-Haram, the Grand Mosque in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Muslims regard it as Islam’s holiest site and face its direction—the qibla—during prayer. Islamic belief identifies it as the House built by Abraham (Ibrahim) for God; this is a religious tradition, not a claim independently established here as archaeological history. During the Hajj, pilgrims circle it seven times in a rite called tawaf. Its striking black embroidered covering, the kiswah, distinguishes it visually, while the Black Stone set in one corner marks the start and end of circumambulation. The Kaaba is both a sacred destination and a shared directional focus for Muslims worldwide.

key_facts.text: The Kaaba stands at the center of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca.
Muslims face toward the Kaaba, the qibla, when they pray.
Pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times during tawaf.
Muslims believe the Kaaba is the House Abraham built for God; the building is covered by a cloth called the kiswah.
The Black Stone is set in a corner of the Kaaba and marks the beginning and end of tawaf.

overview.text: The Four Horsemen are symbolic riders in the Christian Book of Revelation, chapter 6: as the Lamb opens the first four seals of a scroll, each rider appears on a differently colored horse. A common reading associates them with conquest, war, famine, and death: the white rider carries a bow and crown, the red rider a sword, the black rider scales, and the pale-green rider is explicitly named Death, followed by Hades. These images convey disasters within Revelation’s visions of judgment and the end times, and have become enduring subjects of religious art. Interpretations differ about the first rider; some identify him with Christ, while a common reading sees conquest.

key_facts.text: The riders appear as the Lamb opens the first four of the scroll’s seven seals.
Revelation explicitly names the fourth rider Death; Hades follows him.
The first rider’s identity is debated: interpretations include conquest and Christ.
The black horse’s scales and costly grain symbolize famine and food shortage.
Albrecht Dürer depicted the riders in a woodcut made around 1497–98, helping establish their place in Western art.

overview.text: Tandava (also written tāṇḍava) is a form of dance described in the ancient Sanskrit performing-arts treatise Natyashastra and especially associated with Shiva; its mood need not be only fierce, since it may be joyous, violent, sorrowful, or destructive. The iconic image of Shiva as Nataraja (“Lord of Dance”) gives the dance cosmic meaning: in Hindu interpretation, it embodies the recurring processes of creation, preservation, and destruction. In the familiar South Indian bronze image, Shiva dances inside a ring of flame, holding a drum and fire; one foot presses down a dwarf representing ignorance, while the raised foot and hand gestures signify protection and refuge. The Nataraja image’s famous form developed under Chola rule.

key_facts.text: The Natyashastra describes tandava; the dance can express different moods, not only destruction.
Nataraja imagery combines Shiva’s cosmic roles in one figure and evokes cyclical time.
In the familiar icon, the hand drum signifies creation and the flame signifies destruction.
The dwarf under Shiva’s foot represents ignorance; the raised foot and pointing hand suggest refuge for devotees.
The Smithsonian connects Nataraja’s dance of bliss with Chidambaram and describes the dance’s importance in Chola-era culture.

overview.text: The chupacabra (“goat-sucker”) is a legendary creature blamed in stories for attacking goats and other livestock and draining their blood. Reports first drew wide attention in Puerto Rico in the mid-1990s, and the tale spread through Mexico and the U.S. Southwest. Its appearance is not fixed: early Puerto Rican accounts described a small, upright, gray, spiny being, while later reports often portray a doglike animal on four legs. Wildlife specialists explain many modern “chupacabra” sightings as coyotes or other animals severely affected by mange, which can cause hair loss and crusted skin; blood-drinking remains part of the legend, not an established fact. The creature is a modern legend, not a verified species.

key_facts.text: The Spanish name means “goat-sucker”; stories blame the creature for attacks on goats and other livestock.
Reports first became prominent in Puerto Rico in the mid-1990s, then spread to places including Mexico and the U.S. Southwest.
Early Puerto Rican accounts described an upright, gray, spiny creature; later versions often depict a four-legged, canine-like animal.

Texas A&M wildlife specialists say many animals identified as chupacabras resemble coyotes or, less often, raccoons with severe mange; this is an explanation for many sightings, not proof about every report.
A University of Texas Rio Grande Valley archive catalogs chupacabra folktales collected by anthropology students in 1997–1999 as contemporary legends.

overview.text: Merfolk—mermaids and mermen—are fictional folklore beings usually imagined with a human upper body and a fish tail. Traditions give them varied appearances, origins, and personalities, so they are not one fixed character type. They matter as figures people have used to imagine the mysterious sea, appearing in stories and European map art as wondrous or threatening beings. They are distinct from Homer’s Greek Sirens: Homer does not describe their appearance, and Greek art showed them with human heads and bird bodies; later representations shifted until they resembled mermaids. A reported mermaid sighting by Columbus in 1492 is understood as a manatee encounter, not evidence of merfolk.

key_facts.text: The Smithsonian describes mermaid traditions as varied in appearance, origin, and personality.
The Smithsonian identifies Oannes, a Babylonian god, as the earliest recorded half-human, half-fish figure in its account.
Homer’s Odyssey does not describe the Sirens’ looks; Greek art depicted them with human heads and bird bodies, while later portrayals made them resemble mermaids.
The Smithsonian reports Columbus’s 1492 mermaid sighting as an encounter with a manatee, rather than a real mermaid.
A 1550 map by Pierre Desceliers depicts a siren admiring herself among ships, showing how such sea beings appeared in map art.

overview.text: The Bahá’í Faith is a monotheistic religion founded in nineteenth-century Iran by Bahá’u’lláh (1817–1892), emerging from the Bábí movement. Bahá’ís believe that one God has guided humanity through successive messengers, and that the world’s major religions share a spiritual source; the unity of religions and of humankind is central to the Faith. Its teachings connect religious unity with the goal of a more united humanity. A distinctive daily devotional practice is Obligatory Prayer: Bahá’u’lláh revealed three forms, and believers recite one each day, following its directions.

key_facts.text: The Faith began in nineteenth-century Iran and grew out of the Bábí movement.
Bahá’u’lláh (1817–1892) is regarded by Bahá’ís as the Faith’s founder and a messenger of God.
Bahá’í teachings emphasize the oneness of God, the unity of humanity, and the progressive revelation of religious truth.
Bahá’u’lláh revealed three Obligatory Prayers; Bahá’ís choose one to recite each day, according to its directions.
The three prayers differ in timing: the short prayer is said between noon and sunset, the medium prayer in the morning, at noon, and in the evening, and the long prayer once in 24 hours.
