overview.text: Daoism (also spelled Taoism) is a diverse Chinese tradition with philosophical teachings and organized religious forms, not just a single doctrine. Its name comes from dao, usually translated as “the Way,” which foundational texts describe as the natural course or pattern of existence. The Daodejing (also called the Laozi) and the Zhuangzi are central texts traditionally linked to Laozi and Zhuangzi, though Laozi’s identity and the texts’ formation remain uncertain. A notable idea is wu wei, often translated “nonaction,” but better understood as acting without forceful striving and in accord with circumstances. Daoist thought also describes yin and yang as complementary, changing forces; religious Daoism includes temples, rituals, deities, and priests.

key_facts.text: Dao is commonly translated as “the Way”; Daoist texts use it to describe a natural path or order.
The Daodejing is traditionally attributed to Laozi, but the historical identity of Laozi and the text’s formation are uncertain.
Wu wei, often glossed as “nonaction,” does not simply mean doing nothing; it suggests acting without forceful striving, in harmony with the natural flow.
Religious Daoism developed forms involving deities, rituals, temples, and a priesthood.
Yin and yang are presented as complementary, changing forces whose dynamic balance brings cosmic harmony.

overview.text: Muhammad (c. 570–632) was an Arabian religious and community leader whose preaching in Mecca in the early seventh century became the beginning of Islam. Muslims believe God revealed the Qur’an to him through the angel Gabriel; in Islamic belief, he is the final prophet in a line that includes Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. His message called people to worship one God. In 622, he and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina in the hijra, where he helped establish a Muslim community; the migration marks the start of the Islamic calendar. Muslims also look to his reported words and actions, preserved in hadith and sunnah, as guidance alongside the Qur’an. Historical details in later biographies are not all equally certain.

key_facts.text: The broad traditional chronology places Muhammad’s birth in Mecca around 570 and his death in Medina in 632.
Muslims believe the Qur’an consists of revelations given to Muhammad by God through the angel Gabriel.
The hijra, Muhammad and his followers’ migration from Mecca to Medina in 622, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.
The Qur’an is Islam’s sacred text, but it is not a continuous narrative biography of Muhammad.
Hadith reports preserve accounts of Muhammad’s words and actions; his sunnah, or example, is important in Muslim religious life.

overview.text: Pele, also called Pelehonuamea, is a Hawaiian goddess associated with volcanoes and fire. In Hawaiian moʻolelo (traditional stories), she is linked to lava’s power to both destroy existing land and create new volcanic landscapes; one account says she traveled from Kahiki and came to reside at Halemaʻumaʻu crater on Kīlauea. These are cultural narratives, not a single fixed biography: versions of the stories differ, and Hawaiian genealogies give different accounts of her parentage. Pele matters not only as a figure in stories but as a revered presence in Hawaiian cultural life; some people in Puna and Kaʻū regard her as an ʻaumakua, a family or deified ancestor. Her names and volcanic associations distinguish her.

key_facts.text: Pelehonuamea is another name for Pele; the University of Hawaiʻi source also records epithets translated as “earth-eating woman” and “woman of the pit.”
Hawaiian tradition associates Pele’s home with Halemaʻumaʻu crater at Kīlauea on Hawaiʻi Island.
A traditional account describes Pele traveling from Kahiki to the Hawaiian Islands; accounts of her journey differ.
Chants and stories connect Pele with both the creation of new land and the destruction of existing land.
Pele is revered by many Hawaiians; the National Park Service notes that some people in Puna and Kaʻū regard her as an ʻaumakua, or family or deified ancestor.

overview.text: In Genesis, Hagar is an Egyptian enslaved woman in the household of Sarai (later Sarah) and Abram (later Abraham). Sarah gives her to Abram, and Hagar bears Ishmael. After conflict, Hagar flees into the wilderness while pregnant, where an angel promises her many descendants; later, after Isaac is born, Sarah has Hagar and Ishmael sent away. When their water runs out, God hears Ishmael, shows Hagar a well, and promises to make Ishmael a nation. Hagar is distinctive because Genesis gives her a direct divine encounter, lets her name God as the one who sees her, and promises a future for her son beyond Abraham’s household. These episodes belong to Genesis’s sacred narrative; they are not independently verified biography.

key_facts.text: Genesis identifies Hagar as an Egyptian enslaved woman belonging to Sarai; Sarai gives her to Abram, and she becomes Ishmael’s mother.
Genesis recounts two wilderness episodes: Hagar first flees while pregnant, then is sent away with Ishmael after Isaac’s birth.
In the second episode, the water runs out, but God hears Ishmael, shows Hagar a well, and promises that Ishmael will become a nation.
In the first episode, Hagar calls God the one who sees her; the name Ishmael is explained in Genesis in connection with God hearing her affliction.
A later Jewish midrash portrays Hagar as Pharaoh’s daughter; Genesis itself identifies her as Egyptian but does not give that royal family story.

overview.text: Paul Bunyan is a fictional giant lumberjack and folk hero whose stories grew from logging-camp lore in the Great Lakes region. In the tales, his enormous strength and size turn ordinary logging into impossible adventures, often alongside Babe the Blue Ox; the pair are credited with shaping landmarks such as the Mississippi River and Grand Canyon. The stories began circulating among loggers in the mid-1800s, but print and advertising helped make Bunyan widely known in the early 20th century. His familiar image—a bearded lumberjack with an ax—became a symbol of Minnesota’s Northwoods. The legend is also a selective story of logging: it leaves out Native histories and the environmental costs of timber harvesting.

key_facts.text: Paul Bunyan is a legendary character, not a documented historical lumberjack.
The stories began as logger camp tales in the mid-1800s; a first published account appeared in 1904.
A 1914 promotional pamphlet for the Red River Lumber Company helped popularize Bunyan; James Stevens published a collection in 1925.
Babe the Blue Ox is Bunyan’s famous companion, and folklore credits the pair with creating natural landmarks.
The University of Minnesota Libraries’ Paul Bunyan collection includes books, pamphlets, manuscripts, photographs, and materials related to illustrator William B. Laughead.

overview.text: Leviathan is a formidable sea monster named in several poetic passages of the Hebrew Bible. In Job, God describes it as an unmatched, untamable creature, making its power a way to show how much creation exceeds human control. Other poems use Leviathan differently: Psalm 74 portrays God defeating it, Isaiah looks ahead to its destruction, while Psalm 104 presents it as part of God’s living world. Scholars have proposed links to the ancient Near Eastern sea monster Lotan, but the biblical descriptions do not settle whether Leviathan represents a mythic creature, a real animal, or poetic imagery. In later Jewish texts, it becomes part of end-times traditions with Behemoth.

key_facts.text: The Hebrew Bible names Leviathan in Job 3 and 41, Psalms 74 and 104, and Isaiah 27.
Job’s description emphasizes that people cannot capture or master Leviathan; God’s speech culminates by calling it unrivaled.
Its role varies by passage: Psalm 74 depicts God crushing it, Isaiah 27 foretells its destruction, and Psalm 104 includes it among God’s creatures.
The exact identity is uncertain: one reference source reads Leviathan in Job as a crocodile, while scholarship also treats it as a mythic sea monster.
In 1 Enoch and other later Jewish writings, Leviathan appears with Behemoth in end-times traditions, including accounts of a banquet for the righteous.

overview.text: In Greek mythology, the aegis is a divine emblem of protection and battle, most strongly linked in epic with Zeus, though Athena famously bears it too. In Homer’s Iliad, Athena throws it over her shoulders before fighting; it has fringes and terrifying figures, including the Gorgon’s head, and is called a portent of Zeus. Later Greek art often shows the gorgoneion—the image of Medusa’s face—on Athena’s chest as part of her aegis; artists also placed it on shields. Thus, the aegis is not simply an ordinary hand-held shield: its form varies between literary description and visual tradition. In the Perseus myth, he gives Medusa’s severed head to Athena, who uses it as a protective emblem.

key_facts.text: Homer’s Iliad describes Athena throwing the aegis over her shoulders, with fringes, frightening figures, and the Gorgon’s head.
The Met notes that Medusa’s head appears on Zeus’ aegis in the Iliad, while later art commonly places it on Athena’s aegis.
The gorgoneion is the image of Medusa’s head; in the Perseus myth, he gives it to Athena, who places it on her aegis.
The aegis and Athena’s shield are not always the same object: sources and artworks associate Medusa’s image with both.
Medusa’s image could serve as a protective symbol, using a fearsome face to deter danger.

overview.text: Divination is a family of practices for seeking answers about the unknown or future by interpreting signs or consulting an oracle. Its forms vary widely: people may read dreams, omens, natural events, or patterns made with objects such as bones, shells, tea leaves, or cards; some traditions instead involve visions or communication with spirits. A diviner may interpret signs using culturally learned meanings, and a reading can offer diagnosis or guidance as well as prediction. Across societies, divination has served as a way of making sense of uncertainty and, in some settings, as a trusted aid in decision-making or a source of social influence. Beliefs about what produces a reading differ among traditions.

key_facts.text: Divination can be diagnostic—offering guidance or advice—or predictive; the anthropological source also describes forms understood as intervening in a person’s well-being or destiny.
Methods include interpreting dreams, omens, natural events, and objects; examples in the sources include bones, shells, tea leaves, cards, astrology, and communication through mediums.
Some methods depend on a practitioner’s trained interpretation, while others are described as inspirational, such as visions or dreams; many traditions combine both.
Divination can be socially significant: one anthropological account describes it as a trusted way of knowing and making decisions, and as a possible source of social or political influence.

The Encyclopaedia Iranica account documents varied Persian examples, including reading flames, animal behavior, chance events, and randomly opened poetry; these are specific historical and cultural examples, not universal rules.

overview.text: Original sin is a Christian teaching about humanity’s condition after Adam and Eve’s first disobedience in Genesis—not simply the individual wrongs people choose to commit. In Catholic teaching, their act deprived human nature of original holiness; their descendants are born with a wounded nature, subject to suffering and death and inclined to sin, though not personally guilty of Adam’s act or wholly corrupted. The doctrine matters because it explains humanity’s shared need for salvation through Christ. Christian traditions do not describe this inheritance identically: the Orthodox Church in America emphasizes inherited consequences, especially death, while distinguishing them from Adam and Eve’s personal guilt.

key_facts.text: The Catholic Catechism calls original sin a condition people inherit, not a personal act they themselves commit.
Catholic teaching says this condition wounds human nature and inclines people to sin, but does not totally corrupt them or make Adam’s personal fault their own.
The Catechism connects the doctrine to humanity’s need for salvation through Christ.
The Orthodox Church in America describes humanity as inheriting consequences of Adam and Eve’s first sin, especially death, but not their personal guilt.
The Catholic Catechism says the teaching was articulated more precisely in the fifth century, especially through Augustine’s reflections against Pelagianism.

overview.text: The Avesta is the sacred-text collection of Zoroastrianism, not a single work composed at one time. It preserves religious teachings and ritual compositions in Avestan, an ancient Iranian language, and is important both to Zoroastrian worship and as a source for ancient Iranian religion and language. Its surviving contents include the Yasna liturgy, within which the Gathas—seventeen poetic hymns arranged in five groups—form its oldest layer; tradition attributes them to Zoroaster (Zarathushtra). Scholars distinguish these Old Avestan texts from younger compositions, though exact dates remain uncertain. Priests transmitted the texts orally for many centuries before they were written down, probably during the Sasanian period.

key_facts.text: The Gathas are seventeen songs in Old Avestan, grouped into five poetic sections, and are at the core of the Yasna liturgy.
The Yasna is a collection of 72 chapters used in a Zoroastrian ritual offering ceremony.
Other surviving materials include the Yashts, hymns of praise addressed to deities such as Mithra and Anahita.
The Videvdat contains regulations concerning pollution through contact with Evil.
Only part of the ancient Avesta has survived; the complete extent of what was once collected cannot be established with certainty.

overview.text: Māui is a celebrated trickster hero or demigod in Polynesian traditions, but stories differ among island communities rather than forming one uniform account. In Māori tradition, tales credit him with stealing fire, slowing the sun and seeking immortality; one central narrative tells how he used his grandmother’s jawbone as a hook to fish up Te Ika-a-Māui, the North Island, while the South Island is remembered as his canoe. Hawaiian stories tell of Māui snaring the sun at Haleakalā to lengthen daylight. These narratives do more than describe extraordinary feats: Māori traditions connect descent from Māui with tribal relationships to land, while Hawaiian accounts relate stories to local places and natural phenomena.

key_facts.text: In a Māori account recorded from Ngāti Porou tohunga Mohi Ruatapu, Māui uses his grandmother Muri-ranga-whenua’s jawbone as a fishhook; the North Island is the fish he hauls up.
Māori traditions name the North Island Te Ika-a-Māui (Māui’s fish) and the South Island Te Waka-a-Māui (Māui’s canoe); relationships to Māui also figure in tribal traditions of land tenure.
In the Hawaiian story shared by Haleakalā National Park, Māui snares the sun to slow its journey, giving Hina more time to dry kapa, or bark cloth.

A Hawaiian account discussed by cultural advisor Sam Gon describes Māui’s fishhook as an attempt to draw separated islands together, not fish them up; that account attributes island birth to Papa and Wakea.
Māui’s theft of fire from Mahuika is among the legendary feats associated with him in Māori tradition; Te Ara also notes stories of his pursuit of immortality.

overview.text: Helen of Troy—also called Helen of Sparta—is a legendary figure in Greek myth, wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. In Homer’s Iliad, she lives in Troy with Paris, whom she left with or was taken by, depending on the telling; in Book 3, she reproaches him and remembers Menelaus. Her departure is the mythic spark for the Greek expedition against Troy, and her famed beauty made her a lasting symbol in art and literature. Yet ancient versions differ: an alternative tradition says Helen stayed in Egypt while a phantom went to Troy. The celebrated “face that launched a thousand ships” is a later line by Christopher Marlowe, not Homer.

key_facts.text: Homer’s Iliad, Book 3, depicts Helen criticizing Paris after his duel with Menelaus and recalling her former husband.
Traditions differ about whether Helen went willingly with Paris or was abducted.
Some traditions say Helen was Zeus’s daughter; versions differ about whether her mother was Leda or Nemesis.
An alternative tradition places Helen in Egypt while a phantom of her is taken to Troy; scholars note that Homer’s Odyssey leaves the question open to interpretation.
Helen was worshipped as a divine figure at some Greek sites, including Sparta, Rhodes, and Attica.
Christopher Marlowe, not Homer, wrote the later famous line about the face that launched a thousand ships.

overview.text: The Weighing of the Heart was an ancient Egyptian funerary judgment, believed to take place in the afterlife in the Hall of the Two Truths. In scenes from the Book of the Dead, the deceased’s heart—understood as the center of thought and moral character—is weighed against Ma’at, the principle of truth and order, often shown as a feather. Anubis oversees the scales, while Osiris presides over the judgment and Thoth records the result. Egyptians believed a favorable balance meant acceptance into the afterlife; a failed judgment meant the heart was devoured by Ammit and the deceased suffered final death. Heart-scarab amulets could carry a spell asking the heart not to testify against its owner.

key_facts.text: The Met describes the judgment scene in the Hall of the Two Truths, with a panel of 42 judges and Osiris presiding.
The heart represented thought and emotion; the Met also describes it as connected to memory and moral values.
Anubis oversees the weighing, and Thoth records the judgment in the Museo Egizio’s account.
A heart scarab was placed on the mummy’s chest; its Book of the Dead Spell 30B could ask the heart not to speak against its owner.
The Louvre’s Ptolemaic funerary papyrus record identifies Book of the Dead vignettes, including the weighing of the heart and Chapter 125.

overview.text: Sekhmet (also spelled Sakhmet) is an ancient Egyptian goddess whose name means “the powerful one.” Often represented as a lion-headed woman, she was associated with war, violent storms, and pestilence. Yet the same dangerous power could protect and heal when she was appeased, making her a deity of both destruction and recovery. The Metropolitan Museum of Art notes that ancient Egyptian physicians belonged to her priesthood, showing how healing was linked to her cult. Royal devotion is also reflected in the many statues of her made for Amenhotep III’s mortuary temple. A surviving statue in Turin’s Museo Egizio came from the Temple of Mut at Karnak and dates to his reign.

key_facts.text: Her name means “the powerful one,” and she is represented as a lion-headed figure.
She was associated with war, violent storms, and pestilence.
The Met describes her as a healing goddess whose destructive powers could protect when she was appeased.
The Met reports that physicians belonged to her priesthood and that hundreds of her statues stood in Amenhotep III’s mortuary temple.
A statue in Turin’s Museo Egizio dates to Amenhotep III’s reign and came from the Temple of Mut at Karnak.

overview.text: Joseph (Yosef), as portrayed in Genesis, is a son of Jacob (also called Israel) and Rachel, and a central figure in the book’s closing family narrative (Genesis 37–50). His father’s special favor and Joseph’s dreams fuel his brothers’ jealousy; they sell him into slavery in Egypt. There he interprets Pharaoh’s dreams as predicting years of abundant harvest followed by famine, and Pharaoh puts him in charge of preparing food supplies. When famine brings his brothers to Egypt, Joseph eventually reveals who he is and reunites the family. The narrative’s arc—from betrayal to reconciliation—also explains Israel’s migration from Canaan to Egypt in the biblical tradition.

key_facts.text: Genesis identifies Joseph as a son of Jacob and Rachel; Rachel also bore Benjamin. The narrative associates Joseph’s sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with his Egyptian years.
Joseph’s early dreams feature his brothers’ sheaves bowing to his and the sun, moon, and stars bowing to him; the dreams intensify family conflict.
In Genesis, Pharaoh’s dreams foretell seven years of plenty followed by famine; Joseph interprets them and is placed in charge of Egypt’s food preparations.
Famine brings Joseph’s brothers to Egypt for food. Joseph recognizes them, later reveals his identity, and brings the family back together.
Genesis’s note says the Hebrew description of Joseph’s tunic is unclear; the familiar “coat of many colors” comes from a traditional translation.

overview.text: Rastafari is a Jamaican-born religious, spiritual, and cultural movement that emerged in the 1930s amid African-diasporic and anticolonial thought. Its name comes from Ras Tafari, the title and pre-coronation name of Ethiopian ruler Haile Selassie I, crowned in 1930; early Rastafari interpreted his coronation through biblical prophecy, and many regard Selassie as divine or messianic, though beliefs vary. The movement centers African identity and liberation: Ethiopia or Africa may be understood as “Zion,” while “Babylon” names oppressive colonial or Western systems. Ital foodways, dreadlocks, Bible reinterpretation, communal reasoning, and drumming are familiar expressions, but no single practice defines all Rastafari. Reggae helped spread its ideas internationally, yet Rastafari is more than a music style.

key_facts.text: Rastafari took shape in Jamaica around Haile Selassie’s 1930 coronation; “Rastafari” comes from his pre-coronation name, Ras Tafari.
Many Rastafari regard Selassie as divine or messianic, but interpretations of his role differ among followers and groups.
In Rastafari thought, Africa—especially Ethiopia—can symbolize “Zion,” while “Babylon” represents the wider society from which adherents seek spiritual or cultural separation.
Ital foodways, dreadlocks, biblical interpretation, and drumming are associated with Rastafari, but practices and beliefs are not uniform across the movement.
Reggae helped carry Rastafari ideas beyond Jamaica, but the movement has religious, spiritual, cultural, and political dimensions beyond music.

overview.text: First Corinthians is a New Testament letter addressed by Paul to the Christian community in Corinth, a port city where he had helped establish a church. It responds to disputes and questions, urging unity and offering guidance on relationships, worship, food associated with idols, and communal life. Chapters 12–14 discuss spiritual gifts and orderly worship, while chapter 13 presents love as more important than gifts and concludes that faith, hope, and love endure. Chapter 15 focuses on resurrection. Despite its title, it was not the first letter Paul says he sent to Corinth. Its mix of practical advice and theological argument offers a window into an early Christian community.

key_facts.text: The letter addresses a community Paul knew and had taught in Corinth.
Its topics include church divisions, relationships, food offered to idols, worship, and resurrection.
Chapters 12–14 discuss spiritual gifts and their use in worship gatherings.
Chapter 13 describes love as patient and kind and ranks it above spiritual gifts; its closing verse names faith, hope, and love.
The letter refers to an earlier letter Paul had sent to Corinth, so “First” does not mean it was his first letter to that community.

overview.text: Ahura Mazdā (also written Ahuramazda; later Middle Persian Ohrmazd) is the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism, the ancient Iranian religion associated with the prophet Zarathushtra (Zoroaster). In the Gāthās, Zoroaster presents him as uncreated, wise, benevolent, and good: creator and upholder of aša, the principle of truth, right order, and justice. Ahura Mazdā is distinguished from Angra Mainyu, the Hostile Spirit, and from lesser divine beings; the early theology does not simply cast him as an all-powerful source of both good and evil. His importance is also visible in Achaemenid royal inscriptions: Darius calls him creator and credits him with supporting kingship. Scholars caution that the early Persian kings’ exact relationship to Zoroaster’s teachings remains debated.

key_facts.text: The name appears in several historical forms, including Old Persian Ahuramazda and Middle Persian Ohrmazd or Hormizd; scholars differ on whether Mazdā means “wisdom” or “wise.”
In the Gāthās, Ahura Mazdā is described as uncreated, wise, benevolent, and good, and as creator and upholder of aša.
Aša is associated with truth and right order; Ahura Mazdā’s role as its upholder connects him with justice and right conduct.
Zoroaster’s Gathic theology describes Angra Mainyu as Ahura Mazdā’s hostile adversary, while later Zoroastrian tradition develops the account of creation further.

Darius’s inscriptions praise Ahura Mazdā as creator and credit him with granting or supporting the king’s rule; scholars caution that this alone does not settle whether the early Achaemenids followed Zoroaster’s teachings.

overview.text: Bellerophon, also called Bellerophontes, is a hero of Greek myth associated with Corinth. In Homer’s Iliad, he is the son of Glaucus and grandson of Sisyphus; sent to Lycia by King Proetus, he survives ordeals that include killing the fire-breathing Chimera and defeating the Amazons. Later accounts make his winged-horse companion Pegasus central to the story. Traditions differ about his parentage and Pegasus’s role: Homer does not mention the horse in the Chimera episode. The familiar tale of Bellerophon falling while trying to reach the gods is also later; Homer instead says the gods came to hate him and that he wandered alone.

key_facts.text: In the Iliad, Bellerophon’s story is recounted as part of the family history of Glaucus, a warrior at Troy.
Homer describes the Chimera as a composite beast with a lion’s front, a serpent’s rear, a goat in the middle, and fiery breath.
Homer says Bellerophon fought the Solymi and Amazons as well as the Chimera, and survived an ambush arranged after those victories.
Later versions link Bellerophon’s victory over the Chimera to Pegasus, the winged horse; the Metropolitan Museum describes the hero capturing Pegasus at a spring.
The familiar account of Bellerophon’s fall after attempting to ascend to heaven on Pegasus is not Homer’s version; Homer says only that the gods came to hate him and that he wandered alone.

overview.text: Canopic jars were vessels used in ancient Egyptian burial rites to hold the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines removed during mummification. Egyptians believed these organs should be preserved for the dead person's afterlife; some burials instead used a divided chest. Often arranged as a set of four, jars linked each organ to one of the Four Sons of Horus, who were believed to protect it. From the New Kingdom onward, lids commonly identified these guardians by head: human, baboon, jackal, or falcon. The jars therefore joined practical storage with religious protection, and surviving examples vary in material, decoration, and form.

key_facts.text: The four organs were associated with different guardians: Hapy protected the lungs, Imseti the liver, Duamutef the stomach, and Qebehsenuef the intestines.
Lids could show the guardians’ heads: baboon for Hapy, human for Imseti, jackal for Duamutef, and falcon for Qebehsenuef.
Jar designs changed over time: some earlier lids were simple disks or human-headed; animal-headed lids appeared in early New Kingdom examples and became common later in that period.
Not every burial used individual jars: organs could also be placed in a chest divided into four compartments.
Some jars had hieroglyphic inscriptions naming the deceased and invoking protection for the contents.

overview.text: Christian baptism is a water rite practiced across nearly all Christian churches, commonly using immersion or pouring, with spoken words naming the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It marks entry into Christian life and community and is associated with cleansing from sin, new life, and participation in the church; churches differ over whether baptism conveys divine grace or chiefly publicly expresses faith. Some churches baptize infants, while others baptize people only after they can profess their own faith. Water may be applied by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling, though not every form is used in every church. Thus baptism is widely shared, but its meaning, timing, and form are not uniform.

key_facts.text: A common form uses water and words invoking the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, though practices and wording can vary.

The Catholic Catechism describes baptism as freeing people from sin and incorporating them into Christ and the Church; this is a Catholic teaching, not a universal description of every denomination’s beliefs.
Water may be applied by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling; the United Methodist Church recognizes all three methods.
Churches differ on whether to baptize infants or only people who can profess their faith, reflecting different understandings of faith and baptism.
The scholarly overview says early Christians baptized mostly adults, though children were also baptized early; infant baptism became established from the early Middle Ages onward.

overview.text: Hindu marriage, or vivaha, is both a religious rite and a social celebration that joins a couple and connects families. The ceremony is not identical everywhere: regional, family, and community traditions shape its sequence and customs. A common setting is a mandap, a pavilion erected for the rite. Ceremonies may include garlanding, joining hands, and rites around a ceremonial fire. Saptapadi means “seven steps”; couples undertake this rite and, in some ceremonies, also circle the fire while making commitments. In Hindu accounts, Agni—the sacred fire understood as a deity—witnesses the couple’s promises. The vows and blessings express hopes for a shared household and life.

key_facts.text: Marriage is described as a samskara—a significant Hindu life-cycle rite—and wedding gatherings also bring relatives and families together.
A mandap is a pavilion erected for the wedding ceremony; a Houston exhibition describes it as the ceremonial setting for Hindu rites.

In a documented Durban Hindu wedding sequence, the couple circles a fire and makes seven promises in saptapadi, or “seven steps”; the article presents Agni as the deity represented by the fire and witness to the promises.
The University of Houston exhibition describes an anterpat screen being lowered before the couple exchange garlands, and a mangalsutra (wedding necklace) as another ceremony element.
Ritual details differ by region and family. One Hindu wedding guide distinguishes three fire circumambulations from the separate seven-step rite, illustrating why accounts of the sequence may vary.

overview.text: Samson is a figure in the biblical Book of Judges, whose story spans chapters 13–16 and is set during Philistine oppression of Israel. The narrative presents him as a judge chosen before birth and dedicated to God as a Nazirite; his uncut hair marks that vow, while his extraordinary strength is also attributed to God’s spirit. Among his feats, he defeats Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone. Delilah discovers his secret, and after his hair is cut, the Philistines capture and blind him. In the story’s final scene, Samson prays for strength, pulls down the pillars of a temple honoring Dagon, and dies with the Philistines inside. These events are those narrated in Judges, not independently established biographical facts.

key_facts.text: Judges says Samson was dedicated to God as a Nazirite before birth, and that no razor was to touch his head.
The narrative links Samson’s uncut hair to his vow; after Delilah has it cut, his strength leaves him and the Philistines capture and blind him.
In Judges, Samson uses a donkey’s jawbone to kill a thousand Philistines; the text also says he judged Israel for twenty years.
At the end of the account, Samson prays for strength and brings down the pillars of a temple where Philistines are gathered to honor Dagon.

overview.text: Norse stories feature powerful serpent- and dragon-like beings, though medieval terms and modern labels do not always distinguish them the same way. Their surviving accounts come through poems and medieval Icelandic writings that preserved older traditions, so they are evidence for a changing literary record rather than a direct transcript of Viking Age belief. The best-known figures play different roles: Fáfnir becomes a dragon while greedily guarding stolen treasure; Jörmungandr, the Midgard Serpent, coils around the human world and is destined to fight Thor at Ragnarök; and Níðhöggr gnaws at a root of Yggdrasil, the world tree. Together, they connect heroic treasure tales with threats to the cosmic order.

key_facts.text: The Swedish History Museum describes the Poetic Edda as poems probably composed in western Norway and Iceland during the Viking Age; Snorri Sturluson’s Edda was written in the 13th century.
Fáfnir’s story links dragon form to greed and treasure; the hero Sigurd kills him.
Jörmungandr is also called the Midgard Serpent; the account describes him encircling Midgard and fighting Thor at Ragnarök, where they kill one another.
Níðhöggr gnaws at a root of the world tree and is also associated in Norse accounts with death and the dead.
The categories overlap: the academic chapter notes that Old Norse ormr commonly means “serpent,” while these traditions also include dragon-like serpent monsters.

overview.text: Ishmael (Arabic Isma'il; Hebrew Yishmael) is a figure shared by biblical and Islamic traditions. In Genesis, he is Abraham’s son by Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian servant; after Hagar and Ishmael are sent into the wilderness, the story says God protects them, and Ishmael grows up as an archer. Genesis also presents him as the father of twelve tribal rulers and promises he will become a great nation. The Qur’an honors Isma'il as a messenger and prophet and describes him with Abraham raising the foundations of the House. Islamic genealogical tradition connects Muhammad’s community to Abraham through Ishmael—a religious lineage, not a settled historical conclusion.

key_facts.text: The Bible Gateway encyclopedia identifies Ishmael as Abraham and Hagar’s son; it explains his name as meaning “God hears” or similar.
In Genesis, Hagar and Ishmael are sent into the wilderness; the biblical account says God hears and protects them.
The Qur’an describes Ishmael as a messenger and prophet, and praises him as true to his promise.
The Qur’an describes Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the House together.
Genesis lists twelve sons of Ishmael and describes his descendants as tribal groups; Islamic tradition also links Muhammad’s community genealogically to Abraham through Ishmael.

overview.text: The Vedas are a body of ancient Sanskrit sacred literature central to Hindu traditions, not a single book: the name refers to four collections, the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda. Traditionally revered as śruti (“heard” revelation), they were transmitted chiefly through spoken recitation, with exact pronunciation and musical accents important to preservation. Their contents distinguish them: the Rigveda gathers hymns, the Samaveda sets many Rigvedic verses to melody, the Yajurveda supplies formulas for sacrificial rites, and the Atharvaveda includes prayers and incantations addressing protection and everyday concerns. Alongside their religious role, the texts preserve early poetry and ideas that help scholars study Hinduism and ancient South Asian intellectual life.

key_facts.text: In Hindu tradition, Veda is associated with Sanskrit vid, “to know”; the texts are also called śruti, or “what is heard.”
The Rigveda is described as the oldest of the four Vedas and is organized into ten books, or mandalas.
The Samaveda draws many verses from the Rigveda and arranges them for melodic chanting in ritual settings.
The Yajurveda is chiefly associated with liturgical formulas and sacrificial rites; the Vedic Heritage Portal describes it as principally in prose.
Vedic recitation uses careful pronunciation and tonal accents; these techniques help preserve the words through oral transmission.

overview.text: In many Aboriginal Australian traditions, the Rainbow Serpent is an ancestral being linked to the Dreaming, but communities have distinct names and stories rather than one universal account. Its journeys are associated with making landforms and sacred places, and its tracks may connect sites along rivers, creeks, lagoons and billabongs. The figure is significant not only as a creator: stories also describe its power to protect country and life, and warn that it can be dangerous if disrespected. In western Arnhem Land, Kuninjku artists depict Ngalyod in ceremonial contexts, sometimes with features of several animals. Barkandji artist Badger Bates describes Ngatyi as creator and protector of the Darling River and as connected with rain and rainbows.

key_facts.text: Dreaming stories vary across Aboriginal communities; “Rainbow Serpent” is a broad label, not the name of one identical story everywhere.
The Australian Museum describes Rainbow Serpent tracks as associated with waterways and with shaping landscapes; it also notes the being may protect or harm.
In western Arnhem Land, Ngalyod is a name for the Rainbow Serpent. National Museum material describes it creating sacred sites and appearing in art with features of different animals.
Barkandji artist Badger Bates describes Ngatyi as a creator and protector connected with the Darling River; he says it brings rain and makes rainbows.
In the National Museum’s account of Yirawala’s paintings, Ngalyod’s feather headdress indicates a connection with ceremony.

overview.text: Huitzilopochtli was a major deity of the Mexica and their patron god. Museum sources describe him as a god of war associated with the sun, but he should not simply be equated with Tonatiuh, the sun deity. His importance was reflected in Tenochtitlan’s Templo Mayor: its southern shrine was dedicated to Huitzilopochtli, opposite Tlaloc’s northern shrine. In art, Huitzilopochtli was often represented as a hummingbird or an eagle. His Nahuatl name is commonly connected with “hummingbird” and “left,” though specialists note that its translation is debated.

key_facts.text: The Mexica patron god, Huitzilopochtli was associated with war and the sun.
The Templo Mayor’s southern shrine honored Huitzilopochtli; Tlaloc’s shrine stood to the north.
Getty’s iconography record notes that artists often represented him as a hummingbird or an eagle.
His name’s translation is disputed; proposed renderings connect “hummingbird” with “left” or the left-hand side.
INAH distinguishes Huitzilopochtli, who was associated with the sun, from Tonatiuh, the sun itself.

overview.text: In Greek mythology, Ariadne is the Cretan princess, daughter of King Minos and Pasiphae, whose aid is crucial to the story of Theseus and the Labyrinth. In a familiar version, she gives Theseus a ball of thread so he can retrace his path after entering the maze and killing the Minotaur. Theseus leaves her on Naxos, where Dionysus finds and marries her; one account says the marriage makes her immortal. The ending differs across ancient tellings: Homer’s Odyssey instead places her on the island of Dia, where Artemis kills her, with Dionysus mentioned as witness. Ariadne is especially distinguished by the thread that makes escape from the Labyrinth possible and by her changing fate in stories connecting her to Dionysus.

key_facts.text: Ariadne is identified as the daughter of Minos, king of Crete, and Pasiphae.
She gives Theseus a ball of thread to help him find his way out of the Labyrinth.
In the familiar Labyrinth story, Theseus uses her help to escape after slaying the Minotaur.
One account has Theseus abandon her on Naxos, where Dionysus finds and marries her, making her immortal.
Homer’s Odyssey gives a different fate: Ariadne is killed by Artemis on Dia, with Dionysus named as witness.

overview.text: “Great Awakenings” is a historical label for major waves of evangelical Protestant revival in British North America and the early United States; the First and Second were movements, not single organized events. The First, beginning in the 1730s, spread through the colonies as preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield urged heartfelt religious conversion, provoking disputes between revival supporters and critics. Beginning in the 1790s and continuing unevenly into the 19th century, the Second included emotional revivals and outdoor camp meetings, especially in the expanding West. Its religious energy also helped shape Black church institutions and some reform activity. Dates, locations, and effects varied, so historians’ labels describe overlapping regional revivals rather than exact boundaries.

key_facts.text: The First Great Awakening began among Presbyterians in Pennsylvania and New Jersey in the 1730s, then spread to other Protestant communities and regions.
Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield were prominent First Awakening preachers; emotional sermons and itinerant preaching helped make revivalism distinctive.
The Second Great Awakening comprised revivals that began in the 1790s and differed by place; Kentucky’s camp meetings brought families together for several days of outdoor worship.

Black converts participated in the revivals, while racial segregation and unequal treatment helped prompt Black Methodists to form independent churches, including the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

Revival-era ideas and networks were associated with reform activity, including antislavery work and early women’s-rights organizing; this connection did not mean that all revivalists supported those causes.

overview.text: Kami (the Japanese term for Shinto’s sacred beings or presences) are central to Shinto, Japan’s native religious tradition. Often translated as “deities” or “spirits,” kami are not limited to human-like gods: the category can include mythic beings and ancestors, people, animals, plants, mountains, waters, and awe-inspiring natural forces. Kami are honored at shrines, and prayers and festivals connect worshippers and communities with them. In the Kojiki’s traditional creation narratives, Izanagi and Izanami are creator kami; one account tells that Amaterasu, the sun goddess, appeared when Izanagi purified himself. These are religious stories, not claims established as historical events.

key_facts.text: Kami can refer to named deities as well as sacred or extraordinary presences; the term does not describe just one kind of being.
Kami may be associated with natural features and phenomena—including mountains, water, plants, animals, wind, and thunder—as well as people and ancestors.
Shrines, prayers, and festivals are important ways kami feature in Shinto worship and community life.
In the Kojiki creation story summarized by the Shimane Museum, Izanagi and Izanami create many deities, and Amaterasu appears after Izanagi purifies himself.
Kami are not always portrayed as purely benevolent: Shinto explanations describe them as capable of bringing blessings or harm.

overview.text: Arachne is a mortal weaver from Lydia in the story told by the Roman poet Ovid in *Metamorphoses*. Renowned for her extraordinary skill, she challenges Athena to a weaving contest. In Ovid’s version, Athena weaves scenes of divine power, while Arachne’s tapestry depicts gods’ transformations and their amorous encounters with mortals. Athena destroys Arachne’s work and, after Arachne tries to hang herself, transforms her into a spider. The story links Arachne’s weaving to the web-spinning associated with spiders, making her a memorable figure in a tale of artistic skill and divine authority.

key_facts.text: Ovid places Arachne in Lydia and describes her as a gifted weaver whose reputation comes from her art.
Arachne challenges the goddess Athena to compete at the loom.
In Ovid’s account, Arachne’s tapestry shows gods’ amorous adventures; Athena’s shows divine power and warnings against challenging the gods.
After Athena destroys her work, Arachne tries to hang herself; Athena changes her into a spider.
The transformation connects Arachne’s weaving with a spider’s web-making.

overview.text: Iblis is a central adversarial figure in the Qur’an’s account of Adam’s creation. In the Qur’anic telling, God commands the angels to prostrate before Adam; Iblis refuses and is described as arrogant. The Qur’an also explicitly calls him one of the jinn, though the episode’s grouping of him with the angels has prompted differing interpretations. Iblis is often associated with Shaytan, a name or title linked to his role in tempting people; the Qur’an’s accounts present that role as subordinate to God, not as a rival power equal to God. His story highlights disobedience and arrogance, and differs in details from later religious retellings.

key_facts.text: The Qur’an recounts Iblis’s refusal to prostrate before Adam and describes him as arrogant.
Qur’an 18:50 identifies Iblis as one of the jinn; the St Andrews article notes that his appearance in the angel-prostration episode has also led to interpretations connecting him with angels.
The Qur’an associates Iblis’s rebellion with his later opposition to humanity, while the St Andrews article explains that the precise nature of this role varies across Qur’anic passages.
Iblis is a proper name in the Qur’an; Shaytan is often used for the adversarial tempter, and the terms are commonly treated as interchangeable in later Islamic literature.
In the Qur’anic narrative discussed by the St Andrews article, Iblis’s refusal is followed by the account of Adam and his wife being tempted in the Garden.

overview.text: The Yazidis (also called Yezidis or Êzîdîs) are an ethno-religious community, many of whom speak Kurdish, whose faith is distinct from the region’s majority Sunni Kurdish tradition. Yazidism’s sacred teachings have largely been transmitted orally, and its religious landscape is closely tied to northern Iraq, especially Lalish, a major holy place. Yazidis revere Melek Tawûs, the Peacock Angel, among seven Holy Beings; they do not regard him as an evil devil, despite an enduring outsider accusation stemming from confusion with devil figures in other faiths. The community has faced persecution across history; in 2014, ISIL attacked Yazidis in Sinjar, and a UN investigative team later found reasonable grounds that genocide and other international crimes were committed.

key_facts.text: Yazidism is a distinct religion; many Yazidis speak Kurdish, though religious identity and Kurdish ethnicity are not identical.
Melek Tawûs, or the Peacock Angel, is chief among seven Holy Beings in Yazidi belief; Yazidis regard him as divine, not as an evil principle.
Sacred hymns called qewls are central to Yazidi tradition and have been passed down orally.
Lalish in northern Iraq is a principal sacred place and pilgrimage destination for Yazidis.
A UN investigative team reported in September 2024 that it had reasonable grounds to believe ISIL committed genocide and other international crimes against the Yazidi community.

overview.text: Benedict of Nursia (also called Norcia) was an Italian Christian monk born around 480. After a period as a hermit near Subiaco, he established a monastery at Monte Cassino around 529. He is remembered not as the originator of monasticism, but as a major shaper of Western Christian communal monastic life. His Rule, a guide for monks with a prologue and 73 chapters, organized life in a monastery, including shared prayer, work, reading, and community responsibilities. Benedictine communities later spread widely in Europe, helping make his practical guide one of the most influential foundations for Western monastic practice.

key_facts.text: Benedict was born around 480 in Norcia, a town in central Italy.
The Abbey of Monte Cassino dates its foundation by Benedict to about 529, after he came from Subiaco.
The Rule’s 73 chapters address practical community life as well as spiritual commitments; its topics include work, prayer, obedience, and silence.
The Rule calls for monks to divide time between manual labor and reading, alongside their communal religious life.
The ancient account of Benedict’s life was written by Gregory the Great; the available chronology is limited, so exact dates for many events are uncertain.

overview.text: Jehovah’s Witnesses are a Christian religious movement that grew from Bible-study groups associated with Charles Taze Russell in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in the 1870s. The group adopted its present name in 1931. Witnesses describe the Bible as the basis of their beliefs and teach that Jesus is God’s Son, not Almighty God, rejecting the Trinity. Their distinctive practices include preaching from house to house, political neutrality, and refusing military service and blood transfusions for religious reasons. The movement is also significant in U.S. history: legal challenges by Witnesses helped shape First Amendment protections for religious practice, public speech, and door-to-door evangelism.

key_facts.text: The group took the name Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1931; before then, members were known as Bible Students.
Witnesses teach that Jesus is God’s Son but not Almighty God, and therefore reject the Trinity.
House-to-house preaching and sharing religious literature are characteristic forms of Witness evangelism.
Witnesses say their religious beliefs lead them to avoid warfare and blood transfusions.
Court cases brought by Witnesses helped define U.S. protections for religious freedom and public evangelism.

overview.text: The Sun, also called Sol, is the star at the center of our solar system. Its gravity keeps planets and other bodies in orbit, and its energy is essential to life on Earth. Across cultures, the Sun has also been represented or personified in mythology. In a Japanese Shinto myth, the sun goddess Amaterasu hides in a cave, bringing darkness until she is lured out. A Chinese story recorded by the Hong Kong Space Museum tells of ten suns appearing together and scorching Earth, until the archer Hou Yi shoots down nine. These are distinct cultural stories, not scientific explanations of how the Sun works.

key_facts.text: Sol is the Latin word for Sun and is the root of “solar.”
The Sun is made of plasma and has no solid surface; the visible layer is called the photosphere.
Nuclear fusion in the Sun’s core powers its heat and light.
In the Japanese myth described by The Met, Amaterasu’s return from a cave restores light and life to the world.
In one Chinese legend, Hou Yi shoots down nine of ten suns after they appear together and scorch Earth.

overview.text: The Chinese dragon (long) is a mythological creature often understood differently from the treasure-guarding monster of European stories. In Chinese art, it is presented as benevolent and linked to life-sustaining rain, often pictured among clouds with a precious pearl. The dragon appears in two distinct traditions: as one of the twelve animals in the calendrical zodiac, and as the Azure or Green Dragon of the East, one of four celestial guardians paired with the Vermilion Bird, White Tiger, and Black Tortoise. Together, these roles connect the dragon to rain, the cardinal directions, and Chinese cosmology and art.

key_facts.text: The Met describes the Chinese dragon as benevolent and associates it with life-sustaining rain, clouds, and a pearl.
In the four-creature tradition, the Azure Dragon is the guardian of the East; the other guardians represent the South, West, and North.
The dragon is fifth in the conventional sequence of the twelve Chinese zodiac animals.
The Met says the zodiac sequence was established by the Eastern Han dynasty and was later paired with ten calendrical elements to form a 60-part cycle.
A seventh-century Chinese bronze mirror in The Met depicts the four directional creatures, including the green dragon of the East.

references.title: Mirror with symbols of the four cardinal directions

overview.text: Ganesha is a Hindu deity widely revered as the son of Shiva and Parvati. Instantly recognizable by his elephant head and human body, he is worshipped as the remover of obstacles and lord of new beginnings; devotees invoke him before starting undertakings. One widely told story says Parvati made him to guard her door; after Shiva cut off his head in a confrontation, he restored Ganesha with an elephant’s head. Art often shows him with several arms, a broken tusk, and sweets, though stories and depictions vary. His continuing importance is reflected in regular worship and the Ganesha Chaturthi festival.

key_facts.text: Ganesha is identified by his elephant head and human body and is revered as a remover of obstacles and deity of new beginnings.
Devotees invoke Ganesha before beginning new undertakings; he is also associated with guarding doorways.
Accounts of how Ganesha got his elephant head differ. One commonly told story says Parvati created him to guard her door, and Shiva later restored him with an elephant’s head.
Sculptures may show Ganesha with multiple arms, a broken tusk, and sweets; the objects he holds can vary.
Ganesha Chaturthi is an annual festival honoring Ganesha; the Smithsonian describes celebrations that include processions and carrying images to the coast.

overview.text: The Rosary is both a string of Catholic prayer beads and the devotional prayer counted on them. A customary set has a crucifix and beads arranged into five groups, or “decades,” of ten; each decade combines an Our Father, ten Hail Marys, and meditation on a Mystery from Jesus’ life. The standard cycle includes Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious, and Luminous Mysteries; Pope John Paul II proposed the Luminous set in 2002. Repeated prayers are intended to support contemplation, making the Rosary a distinctly Marian devotion that is also centered on Christ, and it may be prayed alone or with others. Its form developed gradually; tradition links it with Saint Dominic, but his role is historically disputed.

key_facts.text: The customary five-decade pattern starts at a crucifix and includes introductory prayers before the five decades.
In each decade, the Our Father is followed by ten Hail Marys while the person praying meditates on a Mystery; a Glory Be follows.
The four sets of Mysteries focus on events in Christ’s life; the Luminous Mysteries highlight parts of his public ministry.
The Vatican describes the Rosary as meditation on Christ with Mary, and the USCCB notes it can be prayed privately or with a group.
The Rosary’s structure developed over time. A tradition associates Saint Dominic with it, but scholars have disputed his role because early accounts of his life do not mention the Rosary.

overview.text: Zeus is the leading god in ancient Greek religion and myth, associated with the sky, weather, thunder, and lightning. In Hesiod’s Theogony, he is the youngest child of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. The poem tells how Rhea hid the infant Zeus in Crete and gave Cronus a wrapped stone instead; later, Zeus freed his swallowed siblings and took power. These are mythic accounts, not verifiable historical events. Zeus’s thunderbolt became a defining attribute: an ancient Greek bronze figure at the Metropolitan Museum of Art may represent Zeus, but could instead be his brother Poseidon—the missing object once held in the figure’s hand would distinguish them.

key_facts.text: Zeus was regarded as the chief deity of the Greek pantheon and a god of sky and weather.
In Hesiod’s account, Zeus is the youngest child of Cronus and Rhea; Rhea conceals him in Crete and gives Cronus a wrapped stone to swallow.
The Theogony says Zeus’s freed relatives gave him thunder and the thunderbolt, which he uses as a sign of his rule.
Zeus is often associated with the thunderbolt, but it can be difficult to identify him in ancient art: the Met’s bronze statuette could show Zeus or Poseidon, depending on what it originally held.

overview.text: Eurystheus is a king in Greek myth, best known for setting Heracles (Herakles) the tasks remembered as the Twelve Labors. In one account, Hera delays Heracles’ birth so his cousin Eurystheus is born first and gains the throne. After Heracles kills his family in a divinely caused madness, Apollo’s oracle directs him to serve Eurystheus and perform labors as atonement, according to some literary versions. Eurystheus is therefore the authority behind the hero’s defining adventures, not their performer: he assigns tasks such as defeating the Nemean Lion and Hydra, then demands two additional feats before accepting the full twelve. Euripides’ later tragedy also portrays him as a threat to Heracles’ children.

key_facts.text: The Met’s account identifies Eurystheus as king of Mycenae and says Hera’s interference with Heracles’ birth allowed Eurystheus to inherit the throne.

In the account summarized by the Met, Apollo’s instruction to serve Eurystheus follows Heracles’ killing of his family during a madness sent by Hera; the museum notes that this sequence appears in some literary accounts.
Eurystheus assigns the Nemean Lion and Lernaean Hydra among the labors; after ten, he rejects two tasks and requires two more, producing the familiar total of twelve.
In Euripides’ Heracleidae, the children of Heracles say that Eurystheus sought to kill them after their father’s death and pursued them as they fled.
The name appears in different transliterations: the Met essay uses “Eurystheos,” while the English translation of Euripides’ play uses “Eurystheus.”

overview.text: Poseidon was a major Greek god whose power centered on the sea, but ancient stories and worship also connected him with earthquakes and horses. The National Archaeological Museum describes him as ruler of waters and a force behind floods and earthquakes; the University of Reading’s Ure Museum notes that horses had a place in his worship. Artists commonly identified him with a trident, and sailors prayed and made offerings for safe voyages. In a famous Athenian myth, Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident to produce salt water while competing with Athena to protect the city. The Acropolis Museum explains that the Parthenon’s west pediment depicted the contest, in which Athena’s olive tree won.

key_facts.text: The trident was one of Poseidon’s identifying symbols; the National Archaeological Museum also lists the dolphin, horse, and bull among his symbols.
Ancient Greeks connected Poseidon with earthquakes and floods as well as the sea.
Poseidon was also associated with horses, and horse-related practices formed part of his worship.
In the Athenian contest myth, Poseidon offered salty water and Athena offered an olive tree; the judges chose Athena’s gift.
The Acropolis Museum dates the Parthenon west-pediment sculpture of Poseidon to 437–432 BCE and describes the figure as raising a hand that would have held a trident.

overview.text: John Henry is the legendary African American “steel-driving man” of a ballad about railroad tunnel construction. Steel drivers hammered hand-held drills into rock while a partner, called a shaker, turned the drill and cleared dust; the holes were then packed with explosives. In the best-known tale, Henry races a steam drill at West Virginia’s Big Bend (or Great Bend) Tunnel, wins, and dies from the effort. The identity of any historical John Henry and the exact events remain uncertain. The legend became a symbol of Black railroad workers and their dangerous labor, and of human skill confronting machinery; songs and stories continue to retell it.

key_facts.text: A steel driver hammered a hand-held drill into rock; a shaker turned it between blows and cleared rock dust. The holes could then be filled with powder to break up the rock.
The ballad places the legendary contest at Big Bend (Great Bend) Tunnel near Talcott, West Virginia, but the historical person and events are uncertain.
In the familiar version, Henry outworks a steam drill, then dies from exhaustion; this is a ballad legend, not a confirmed account of his death.
The National Park Service describes John Henry as a symbol of the African American workers who helped build and maintain West Virginia’s railroads, often under dangerous conditions.
“John Henry” is part of the African American ballad tradition and has been recorded in multiple musical versions.

overview.text: Andromeda is an Ethiopian princess in Greek mythology, daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia. In one ancient account, Cassiopeia’s boast that she surpassed the sea nymphs angered them; Poseidon sent a flood and sea monster, and Andromeda was chained to a rock as the demanded victim. Perseus, returning from defeating Medusa, found her and promised to kill the monster in exchange for her hand in marriage. He freed her after slaying it. The story is distinctive for joining her rescue to Perseus’s adventures and for its striking image of a bound princess facing a sea monster—a scene repeatedly represented in art.

key_facts.text: Apollodorus names Andromeda’s parents as Cepheus, king of Ethiopia, and Cassiopeia.
In Apollodorus’s version, Andromeda is chained to a rock after an oracle requires her to be exposed to the monster; Cassiopeia’s boast provoked the crisis.
Perseus promises to kill the monster if Cepheus gives him Andromeda in marriage; he then kills it and frees her.
Andromeda had previously been betrothed to Phineus, who plotted against Perseus after the rescue.
The Met describes the chained princess and sea monster as a popular artistic subject, including in its 1694 marble sculpture by Domenico Guidi.

overview.text: Reincarnation, also called rebirth or transmigration, is the religious idea that life continues through successive births after death, sometimes in different forms. In several South Asian traditions, karma—the moral consequences of actions—is connected with the conditions of a future birth. Rebirth matters because traditions including Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism often regard the cycle not merely as repeated existence but as something from which spiritual liberation is sought. These traditions share broad themes, but do not teach one identical account: Hindu traditions vary internally, and Jain teaching particularly emphasizes individual souls, karmic consequences, and ahimsa, or nonviolence. The term “reincarnation” is therefore a useful umbrella, not a complete description of every tradition’s beliefs.

key_facts.text: Hindu traditions connect karma with rebirth, but their texts and schools explain these ideas in varied ways.
In these Hindu accounts, the moral quality of actions can shape a person’s future circumstances, including in a later birth.
Jain teaching links karma and rebirth with ahimsa, or nonviolence: harming living things is said to cause bad karma.
Jains believe souls are found in humans, animals, and plants, and also in some nonliving things such as air and water.
Buddhist and Jain traditions share ideas about karma and rebirth, and the goal of escaping rebirth; their stories about past lives also convey and explore those teachings.

references.title: Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories

overview.text: A Tower of Silence, or dakhma (also spelled dokhma), is a Zoroastrian funerary structure where the dead were exposed rather than placed in ordinary ground burials. Chilpik, in present-day Uzbekistan, is a surviving example: a roofless, circular adobe tower on a high hill, with a flat surface where bodies were exposed. The practice reflects concern that a corpse could defile sacred elements; birds and other animals consumed the remains. Exposure of the dead is ancient, but the history of towers is more specific: Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that towers of silence are not attested in Iran until the Islamic period. Dakhmas are therefore both places of ritual and distinctive forms of funerary architecture.

key_facts.text: Dakhma is the Zoroastrian term for an enclosure or structure used for exposing the dead.
Chilpik, a surviving example in Uzbekistan, is a circular adobe tower built on a high hill beside the Amu Darya River.
The exposure practice was connected with protecting sacred elements, including earth, water, and fire, from corpse pollution.
Exposure of the dead is attested in accounts from the fifth and fourth centuries BCE; towers of silence, however, are not attested in Iran until the Islamic period.
In Sasanian times, bones of exposed people were often placed in stone or ceramic ossuaries.

overview.text: Genesis is the opening book of both the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and the first of the Torah or Pentateuch’s five books. Its Hebrew title, Bereshit (“In the beginning”), and Greek-derived English title point to its concern with origins. The book moves from accounts of creation, human beginnings, the Flood, and Babel (chapters 1–11) to stories of Israel’s ancestors—Abraham and Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph (12–50). These narratives explain beginnings and frame Israel’s ancestral identity; they are religious and literary traditions, not straightforward modern history. Scholars debate how and when the traditions were composed, so the patriarchs’ historicity remains uncertain.

key_facts.text: Genesis is called Bereshit in Hebrew, after its opening word; the English title derives from Greek and means “beginning.”
A common outline divides the book into primeval narratives (chapters 1–11) and ancestral narratives (chapters 12–50).
The opening section includes creation, the Flood, and the Tower of Babel; the later stories follow Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph.
Genesis’s final chapters tell the Joseph story and end with Jacob’s family in Egypt.
Scholars debate the book’s composition and the historical setting of its ancestral stories; the USCCB introduction notes no direct extra-biblical evidence confirms or disproves those stories.

overview.text: Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, begins on the first day of Tishrei, the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, and is traditionally observed for two days. Its name means “head of the year.” The holiday opens a period of reflection and repentance that leads through the Ten Days of Repentance to Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. A defining practice is hearing the shofar, a ram’s horn, sounded in synagogue in distinct blasts; Jewish tradition connects the horn with the ram in the biblical story of the binding of Isaac. Families may also share apples dipped in honey as a wish for a sweet year, though this food custom is not commanded in the Bible or Talmud.

key_facts.text: Rosh Hashanah is observed on Tishrei 1 and 2; the holiday begins at sundown before Tishrei 1.
The Torah calls the day Yom Teruah, or “Day of Blasting the Shofar”; the holiday begins the Ten Days of Repentance, which culminate in Yom Kippur.
The shofar’s blasts are named tekiah, shevarim, and teruah. Jewish tradition links the ram’s horn to the ram in the binding of Isaac story.
Apples dipped in honey express a hope for a sweet year. The custom is not prescribed in the Bible or Talmud, and practices can vary.
Jewish tradition describes Rosh Hashanah as a time of judgment and remembrance; these are religious teachings, not historical claims about a literal heavenly court.

overview.text: In Irish and Greek mythology, cattle are often central to conflict and transformation, not just background livestock. In Ireland’s Ulster Cycle, the Táin Bó Cúailnge (“Cattle Raid of Cooley”) begins when Queen Medb seeks the Brown Bull, Donn Cúailnge; Cú Chulainn becomes Ulster’s key defender, and the two rival bulls eventually fight. Greek myths give cattle other roles: Heracles must capture Geryon’s herd, Zeus takes bull form to carry Europa to Crete, and Io becomes a cow or heifer in versions of her story. These are legendary narratives, not zoological descriptions, and details vary among tellings.

key_facts.text: The Táin Bó Cúailnge is a cattle raid led by Medb’s forces to seize Donn Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley; Cú Chulainn defends Ulster.
At the tale’s end, Donn Cúailnge fights Findbennach, the White-Horned Bull of Connacht, and dies from his injuries.
The cattle of Geryon are the subject of one of Heracles’ labors. The herd is guarded by three-bodied Geryon, the two-headed dog Orthros, and the herdsman Eurytion.
In the Met’s account of Europa’s myth, Zeus takes the form of a bull, carries the Phoenician princess to Crete, and becomes the father of Minos.
Io’s transformation varies by telling: Hera or Zeus changes her into a cow, and Hera sends a gadfly to torment her as she wanders.

overview.text: Behemoth is a mighty land creature in the Book of Job, where God describes it while challenging Job to recognize the limits of human power. It eats grass like an ox, has great strength, and rests among reeds beside a river; its tail is compared to a cedar. The text’s identity is uncertain: some scholars see a hippopotamus behind parts of the description, while the USCCB notes also interpret Behemoth as a chaos monster symbolizing forces only God can control. Later Jewish writings developed Behemoth as a monster paired with the sea-dwelling Leviathan, including in traditions about a future banquet for the righteous. This later tradition is distinct from Job’s description.

key_facts.text: In Job 40, God describes Behemoth as a creature God made, which eats grass like an ox.
Job’s description places Behemoth among reeds and trees by a river and emphasizes its strength.
The creature’s identity is debated: some scholars connect it with the hippopotamus, while the biblical description also has mythical elements.
In later Jewish traditions, Behemoth is paired with Leviathan; some writings describe them as land and sea monsters associated with a future banquet for the righteous.

overview.text: Lakshmi, also called Shri, is a Hindu goddess associated with wealth, prosperity, good fortune, beauty, and fertility. She is widely recognized as Vishnu’s consort, and images often show her with a lotus, which is linked in Hindu art to life-giving waters and abundance. Her appearance varies: an early Kushana-period sculpture from Mathura shows Sri Lakshmi standing among lotus flowers and a full vase, emphasizing fertility and plenty, while another museum example shows her on a lotus pedestal holding a lotus bud. These images reflect Lakshmi’s significance as a figure of prosperity and flourishing life.

key_facts.text: Shri is another name for Lakshmi.
She is associated with wealth, good fortune, beauty, prosperity, and fertility.
Lakshmi is commonly described as the consort of Vishnu.
The lotus is a key identifying feature; the Asian Art Museum connects it with life-giving waters and abundance.
A National Museum of India sculpture from early second-century Mathura depicts Sri Lakshmi standing among lotuses and a full vase; its description connects the imagery with fertility and plenty.
A sixteenth-century bronze from Kerala depicts Lakshmi standing on a lotus pedestal and carrying a lotus bud.

overview.text: An imam is a Muslim leader, but the title has different meanings across traditions. In congregational worship, an imam leads ritual prayer; more broadly, it can describe a community leader recognized for religious learning. In Shi‘i Islam, “Imam” also names a distinct succession of leaders from Muhammad’s family, believed to have inherited religious and community leadership after his death. Twelver Shi‘a Muslims hold that there are twelve such Imams, beginning with Ali, and regard their leadership as divinely appointed. These meanings are connected by the idea of guidance, but an imam leading a mosque prayer is not automatically one of the Twelve Imams.

key_facts.text: “Imam” means “leader”; it commonly refers to the person leading daily ritual prayer.
The title can also describe a community leader whose role draws on religious learning.
In Shi‘i belief, an Imam is a divinely appointed successor to Muhammad from his family.
Twelver Shi‘a Muslims believe in twelve Imams, beginning with Ali.
The textbook describes Shi‘i Imams as non-prophets whose role includes protecting Muhammad’s teachings and interpreting scripture.

overview.text: The Christian cross is a principal symbol of Christianity, referring to the cross on which Christians believe Jesus was crucified. In Christian teaching and art, it recalls his death and is associated with sacrifice, salvation, and hope of life beyond death. A plain cross has no figure; a crucifix is a cross bearing an image of Jesus. The symbol’s forms and meanings developed over time: the Museum Schnütgen notes that figureless crosses came to signify victory in the Constantinian era, while images of the Crucifixion appeared later. Crosses also became widespread in devotional and everyday objects, including necklaces and armor.

key_facts.text: The Met describes the cross as a central image in Christian art, associated with Christ’s sacrifice, spiritual salvation, and the Christian Church.
A crucifix is a cross with a depiction of the crucified Jesus; a figureless cross has no such image.
The Museum Schnütgen says images of the Crucifixion date from the 5th century, while the oldest surviving crucifixes date from the 10th century.
A Met pendant cross dated to the 5th–7th century was designed to be worn around the neck; the museum connects the cross with triumph over death and hope of eternal life.
A Met breastplate from Augsburg, dated 1580, depicts Christ on the cross and a soldier praying, showing the symbol used in devotional art beyond churches.

overview.text: The Loch Ness Monster, often called Nessie, is a legendary, unverified creature said to inhabit Loch Ness in the Scottish Highlands. Modern depictions often show a large animal with a long neck rising above the water, and the story became a famous subject of reports, photographs and searches. An older tale in Adomnán’s Life of St Columba recounts an aquatic monster in the River Ness that the saint drives away through prayer; it is a religious narrative, not evidence of a surviving lake species. Nessie’s worldwide fame grew in the 1930s, and the celebrated 1934 “surgeon’s photograph” was later exposed as a staged hoax, helping make the creature an emblem of modern cryptid lore.

key_facts.text: Nessie is a popular name for the purported creature associated with Loch Ness in Scotland.
The modern image of Nessie often features a long neck, sometimes compared to a plesiosaur; this is a description in the legend, not proof of such an animal.
Adomnán’s Life of St Columba tells a religious story of an aquatic monster in the River Ness and Columba driving it away; the tale is not a verified sighting of Nessie.
The modern monster legend gathered attention in the 1930s, when reports described a long-necked creature.
The famous 1934 photograph was a hoax involving a toy submarine disguised with putty; the Science Museum Group notes that the waves helped reveal the trick.

overview.text: The Society of Jesus, commonly called the Jesuits (SJ), is a Catholic religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola and his companions; Pope Paul III formally recognized it in 1540. Unlike older orders centered on monastery life, Jesuits developed as an outward-facing group whose members could be sent where their work was needed. They became known for schools and universities, missionary activity across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas, and scholarship in theology and other fields. In sixteenth-century Europe, Jesuit teachers and theologians helped strengthen Catholic institutions and respond to Protestant challenges, making the order an influential participant in the Catholic Reformation, often called the Counter-Reformation.

key_facts.text: Ignatius and companions formed their group while studying in Paris in the 1530s; Pope Paul III officially founded the Society in 1540.
Jesuits were distinctive among religious orders for making formal education a major ministry; they also undertook missions across several continents.
At Ingolstadt, Jesuit professors helped educate Catholic theologians, contributing to the Society’s role in the Counter-Reformation.
Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Society in 1773; Pope Pius VII restored it in 1814.

overview.text: The normal force is the push that one object’s surface exerts on another object touching it. “Normal” means perpendicular: the force points at a right angle to the contact surface, rather than along it. It helps keep solid objects from passing through one another. A table, for example, pushes upward on a book; on a ramp, the normal force points away from the ramp, not straight up. Its size is not automatically equal to an object’s weight: on a stationary ramp, it balances the part of the weight pressing into the ramp. Friction, by contrast, acts parallel to the contact surface.

key_facts.text: It is a contact force: it acts between objects that touch and pushes away from their shared surface.
The normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface; friction acts parallel to it.
On an incline with no acceleration perpendicular to the slope, its magnitude balances the perpendicular component of the object’s weight—not the whole weight.
The symbol N can represent the normal-force magnitude; it should not be confused with N as the unit symbol for newtons.
In the introductory friction model, kinetic friction is calculated as the coefficient of kinetic friction multiplied by the normal-force magnitude.

overview.text: HeLa is a human cancer cell line grown from a cervical tumor biopsy taken from Henrietta Lacks, a 31-year-old patient treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore in 1951. The name comes from the first two letters of her first and last names. Unlike earlier human cell samples that quickly died in the laboratory, HeLa cells kept growing and dividing, making them an unusually durable, shareable tool for research. Scientists have used them to investigate cancer, infectious diseases, and other questions about human health; research with the cells contributed to major medical advances, including vaccines. Their use began without Lacks’s knowledge or consent, and the story has become significant in discussions of research ethics and family privacy.

key_facts.text: HeLa takes its name from the first two letters of Henrietta Lacks’s first and last names.
The cells came from a cervical tumor biopsy taken while Lacks was receiving treatment in 1951.
HeLa cells could continue growing and dividing in laboratory conditions, unlike earlier samples that quickly died.
Researchers have used HeLa in fields including cancer biology and infectious-disease research.
The cells were used in research without Lacks’s knowledge or consent; later, NIH and the Lacks family agreed on controlled access to HeLa genome data.
