overview.text: JavaScript (often called JS) is a dynamically typed programming language widely used to make web pages interactive. Its core language is standardized as ECMAScript, while browser features such as the Document Object Model (DOM)—which scripts can use to respond to clicks or change page content—come from the browser environment, not the core language itself. Unlike statically typed languages, JavaScript does not require variables to have one fixed data type. It also runs beyond browsers: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime used to build network applications and web servers. This lets developers use JavaScript for both browser interactions and server applications.

key_facts.text: JavaScript is also known as JS; its standardized language specification is called ECMAScript.
It is dynamically typed: a variable can be assigned values of different types without declaring one fixed type for it.
In a browser, JavaScript can use browser-provided objects to respond to user events and interact with a page’s DOM.
Node.js is a runtime for JavaScript that can be used to build network applications and web servers.
JavaScript and Java are different programming languages; the similar names do not mean they are the same language.

overview.text: Meiosis is a specialized nuclear division in eukaryotes that reduces chromosome sets from two (diploid) to one (haploid), producing cells needed for sexual reproduction. In animals, those cells develop into egg or sperm gametes, which can fuse at fertilization to restore diploidy. After one round of DNA copying, meiosis has two divisions: homologous chromosome pairs separate in meiosis I, then sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, usually yielding four haploid cells. During prophase I, paired chromosomes exchange DNA, and their random orientation also reshuffles inherited combinations. These processes make meiotic products genetically different and distinguish meiosis from mitosis, which preserves chromosome-set number in its daughter nuclei.

key_facts.text: Meiosis begins after one round of DNA replication; its first division separates homologous chromosome pairs and reduces the number of chromosome sets.
In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair, and non-sister chromatids can exchange chromosome segments—a process called crossing over.
The random alignment of homologous pairs in meiosis I is called independent assortment and contributes to genetic variation.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids; the process typically ends with four haploid cells, though their fate differs among organisms.
Crossing over exchanges DNA between paired homologous chromosomes and creates new combinations of alleles in egg or sperm cells.

overview.text: Thomas Alva Edison (1847–1931) was an American inventor and businessman whose work helped turn new technologies into industries. At his Menlo Park laboratory, he developed the phonograph, which could both record and replay sound, and pursued electric lighting—not by originating the idea of electric light, but by making an incandescent lamp and a practical lighting-and-power system. He later built a large research operation in West Orange. Edison’s motion-picture work also depended on collaborators, especially William K. L. Dickson: their Kinetograph camera and Kinetoscope viewer helped launch early movies, produced at the Black Maria studio. His legacy is best understood as invention combined with development, manufacturing, and commercialization.

key_facts.text: Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, in 1847, and died in West Orange, New Jersey, in 1931.
His 1877 phonograph used a stylus and tinfoil to record sound and could play the recording back.
Electric lighting was not a new idea; Edison’s notable achievement was developing a practical incandescent lamp and the system needed to supply light and power.
Edison’s motion-picture work included the Kinetograph camera and Kinetoscope viewer; associate William K. L. Dickson played a key role in developing the equipment.
The Black Maria, a studio at Edison’s West Orange complex, produced short films featuring popular variety acts.

overview.text: A tree is a long-lived woody plant, usually recognized by an upright stem or trunk that supports a crown of branches and foliage. The boundary between trees and shrubs is not scientifically sharp: many trees have one trunk, but some have several stems. Roots anchor the plant and take up water and minerals, while leaves—or needles in many evergreens—use sunlight to make food. The trunk’s tissues help support the crown and move water upward and sugars from leaves to other parts. Trees include broadleaf kinds that commonly shed leaves seasonally and conifers that often bear seeds in cones, so their forms and foliage vary widely.

key_facts.text: There is no single scientific cutoff that perfectly separates trees from shrubs; height, trunk size, and crown shape are useful practical clues, not universal rules.
A tree’s main parts are its crown, trunk, and roots. The crown includes branches and leaves; roots anchor the tree and absorb water and minerals.
Trunk tissues conduct water and minerals from roots toward leaves and transport sugars made in leaves to other parts of the tree.
Deciduous trees commonly shed leaves in autumn; most conifers bear seeds in cones, and many retain needle-like leaves through winter.
Many woody stems add growth rings as they grow thicker. Ring width can reflect growing conditions, although it is not a simple measure of age or conditions everywhere.

overview.text: A mass extinction is a geologically brief interval in which biodiversity collapses: a commonly used threshold is the loss of roughly three-quarters of species worldwide in less than about 2.8 million years. Unlike ordinary background extinctions, these crises affect many groups across Earth, and scientists recognize five major episodes within roughly the past 500 million years. They are identified chiefly from changes in the fossil record; their timing, scale and causes vary. The Permian–Triassic “Great Dying” was the most severe, while the Cretaceous–Paleogene event about 66 million years ago eliminated non-avian dinosaurs and many other organisms. Environmental upheaval—including climate shifts, volcanism or asteroid impact—can drive such losses; not every event has a fully settled explanation.

key_facts.text: A commonly used definition is the loss of about 75% of species worldwide within less than 2.8 million years.
The fossil record preserves evidence of past extinctions, including abrupt changes in which organisms appear in different layers.

The Permian–Triassic event, called the “Great Dying,” was Earth’s largest mass extinction; most marine species disappeared. Smithsonian evidence points to global warming and atmospheric changes linked to enormous Siberian eruptions.
The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction about 66 million years ago wiped out non-avian dinosaurs and many other species; evidence supports an asteroid impact near what is now Mexico as a major cause.
Mass extinctions have different causes; examples include rapid climate change, shifting sea levels, major volcanic activity and asteroid impact.

overview.text: A longitudinal wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium while the medium’s particles oscillate parallel to the wave’s direction of travel. The particles move back and forth around their usual positions; the traveling pattern, rather than the particles themselves, carries energy onward. This motion creates alternating compressions, where particles are crowded together and pressure is higher, and rarefactions, where particles are farther apart and pressure is lower. Longitudinal waves are also called compression waves. Familiar examples include sound traveling through air and seismic P waves traveling through Earth. Their defining feature—particle motion along the direction of travel—distinguishes them from transverse waves.

key_facts.text: “Compression wave” is another name for a longitudinal wave.
In a sound wave, compressions are higher-pressure regions and rarefactions are lower-pressure regions.
The wave pattern travels onward even though the medium’s particles oscillate around their equilibrium positions rather than traveling with the pattern.
Sound waves in air and most fluids are longitudinal; sound in solids can have both longitudinal and transverse forms.
Earthquake P waves are longitudinal: they compress and expand the ground in the direction the wave travels.

overview.text: The Hall effect is the appearance of a voltage across the sides of a material carrying electric current when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to that current. The magnetic force deflects moving charge carriers sideways; their buildup on one side creates a transverse voltage called the Hall voltage. In a suitable measurement setup, its polarity can help identify whether electrons or positively charged holes dominate conduction, and its size can help determine carrier concentration. Hall sensors use the effect to detect magnetic fields. Edwin Hall observed it in 1879 in experiments with current-carrying gold foil at Johns Hopkins; semiconductor technology later helped make the effect useful in practical sensors.

key_facts.text: The Hall voltage runs across the material, perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.
In appropriately arranged semiconductor measurements, Hall-voltage polarity can indicate whether electrons or holes are the main charge carriers.
Measuring Hall voltage alongside known current and magnetic field can help determine semiconductor charge-carrier density.
Hall sensors use the effect to measure magnetic fields; the same principle underlies sensors used in many settings.
Edwin Hall observed the effect in 1879 using a current-carrying strip of gold foil at Johns Hopkins University.

overview.text: A base is best understood by what it does in a reaction: in Brønsted–Lowry chemistry, it accepts a proton (H⁺) from an acid. That definition is broader than treating every base as a substance containing hydroxide; for example, ammonia accepts a proton from water and forms ammonium, while water becomes hydroxide. In water at 25 °C, a basic solution has pH above 7 and more hydroxide than hydronium ions; neutral water is pH 7 at that temperature. Bases matter because they can reduce acidity through neutralization. Bases also differ in strength: strong bases form hydroxide extensively in water, while weak bases react only partly. A compound’s base behavior depends on the reaction and solvent.

key_facts.text: A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton; after accepting it, the base becomes its conjugate acid.
Ammonia is a base even though it contains no hydroxide: in water, it accepts a proton and forms ammonium and hydroxide ions.
At 25 °C, aqueous solutions with pH above 7 are basic; the pH boundary depends on temperature, so pH 7 is not a universal definition of a base.
In water, strong bases produce hydroxide extensively, while weak bases react only partly; strength describes reaction extent, not simply how concentrated a solution is.
Adding a base to an acidic solution can lower its acidity and move it toward neutral; this process is called neutralization.

overview.text: A rate constant (usually k) is the proportionality factor in a chemical rate law, such as rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, linking reactant concentrations to reaction speed. Its value and the exponents are determined experimentally; at a given temperature, k is independent of reactant concentration, though its value can vary with temperature. The units of k depend on the overall reaction order, so it is not a universal speed number. In radioactive decay, the analogous first-order constant is commonly written λ: the decay rate equals λN, and λ = ln 2/t₁/₂. This relationship connects the decay constant directly to an isotope’s half-life.

key_facts.text: In chemical kinetics, k appears in a rate law that relates reaction rate to reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers.
The powers in a rate law describe reaction order; they are determined by experiment and are not reliably inferred from the coefficients in the balanced equation.
For a particular reaction at a given temperature, k does not depend on reactant concentration; its value can change with temperature.
The units of k depend on the overall reaction order: for example, a first-order rate constant has units of inverse time, while a second-order one has units of concentration⁻¹ time⁻¹.
Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics: its decay constant λ relates decay rate to the number of nuclei N, and λ = ln 2/t₁/₂.

overview.text: An alloy is a material made by combining two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal; it is not limited to mixtures of two metals, since steel includes carbon, a nonmetal. In many alloys, atoms either replace some atoms in a metal’s crystal arrangement (a substitutional alloy) or smaller atoms fit into spaces between them (an interstitial alloy). These arrangements, along with the proportions of ingredients, can give an alloy properties different from those of its ingredients. Alloying helps tailor materials for particular uses: bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc), and steel (iron with carbon and often other elements) are familiar examples used in tools, instruments, and structures.

key_facts.text: An alloy contains at least two elements, including at least one metal; the other element can be a nonmetal, as carbon is in steel.
In substitutional alloys, some atoms take the place of metal atoms in the crystal structure; in interstitial alloys, smaller atoms fit between them.
Bronze is made from copper and tin; compared with copper, it is harder and easier to cast.
Brass is made from copper and zinc and is used in musical instruments; its malleability and acoustic properties are useful for this purpose.
Steel is primarily iron with carbon and may include elements such as chromium, manganese, or nickel; different steel alloys are used for strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance.

overview.text: Temperature inversion is an atmospheric layer in which air temperature rises with altitude instead of following the troposphere’s usual decrease. In the lower atmosphere this stable arrangement resists vertical mixing: cooler air can remain beneath warmer air, limiting convection and the upward spread of smoke and other pollutants. Such pollutants may build up near the ground and reduce visibility, although an inversion is a temperature pattern, not pollution itself. Near-surface inversions can form as ground cools on clear, light-wind nights; sinking air and fronts can produce other types. The stratosphere also has a temperature inversion because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

key_facts.text: In the troposphere, temperature usually decreases with altitude because the ground warms the air above it.
An inversion layer is stable and generally limits vertical cloud growth; in the lower atmosphere, it can also trap pollutants and reduce visibility.
Common lower-atmosphere causes include surface cooling, sinking air associated with high pressure, and fronts between air masses.
Surface radiation inversions often form on clear, light-wind nights and are strongest near sunrise.
In the stratosphere, ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation, warming the air with increasing altitude.

overview.text: Boron (B) is element 5, in group 13 of the periodic table, and is commonly classified as a metalloid—the lightest element in that category on the table. Metalloids have properties between those of metals and nonmetals, and boron is a poor electrical conductor at room temperature. Pure boron can appear as a dark powder or as silvery crystals. Its importance comes largely from its compounds: boron oxide helps make tough, heat-resistant borosilicate glass, while boron-10 absorbs neutrons and is used in nuclear-reactor controls and neutron detectors. Boron compounds also occur naturally in minerals such as borax.

key_facts.text: Boron’s symbol is B, its atomic number is 5, and it belongs to group 13.

Los Alamos National Laboratory classifies boron as a metalloid and notes that metalloids can sometimes behave as semiconductors; it also cautions that metalloid boundaries can vary between periodic tables.
Elemental boron may occur as a brown or dark powder and as silvery crystals.
Boric oxide is used to make borosilicate glass, which the Royal Society of Chemistry describes as tough and heat resistant.
Boron-10 absorbs neutrons and is used in nuclear-reactor control and neutron-detection instruments.

overview.text: Darwin’s finches are a group of closely related birds from the Galápagos archipelago and nearby Cocos Island, whose descendants diversified from a common ancestor into forms with notably different beaks and feeding habits. A 2024 evolutionary review counts 18 species—17 in the Galápagos and one on Cocos—and describes this diversification as adaptive radiation. Ground finches tend to have broad, deep beaks suited to seeds, while cactus finches have longer, pointed bills and warbler finches slender, pointed ones; these differences track food use. The birds became important to evolutionary biology because their inherited variation and changing survival across conditions show natural selection at work. Darwin collected finches on the Beagle voyage, but John Gould’s later classification helped him recognize their relatedness.

key_facts.text: A 2024 review counts 18 species in the group: 17 on the Galápagos Islands and one on Cocos Island.
Beak shapes vary with feeding habits: ground finches tend to have broad, deep beaks, while cactus finches have longer, pointed beaks and warbler finches slender, pointed beaks.
During a severe drought studied by Peter and Rosemary Grant, finches with larger beaks were better able to crack the hard seeds available and were more likely to survive.
When food conditions later changed, smaller-beaked finches could have the advantage; natural selection’s effects depend on the environment.
Darwin collected finches during the Beagle voyage, but ornithologist John Gould’s later identification of them as a related group helped draw Darwin’s attention to their significance.

overview.text: Neutrons are subatomic particles found with protons in atomic nuclei; ordinary hydrogen-1 is the exception, with a nucleus containing one proton and no neutron. A neutron has no net electric charge and is slightly more massive than a proton. Its three valence quarks are one up and two down, bound by the strong interaction; their charges add to zero. Neutron number distinguishes isotopes of the same element, which keep the same proton count but can have different properties: carbon-12 is stable, whereas carbon-14 is radioactive. Neutrons are also useful in research: neutron scattering helps scientists investigate the properties of materials.

key_facts.text: Neutrons have no net electric charge and are slightly more massive than protons.
A neutron’s three valence quarks are one up quark and two down quarks; their charges combine to make the neutron electrically neutral.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-12 is stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive, illustrating how differing neutron counts can accompany different isotope properties.
Neutron scattering helps researchers investigate material properties, including the shapes and sizes of crystals and molecules.

overview.text: Radiometric dating is a family of methods for estimating the numeric ages of rocks, minerals, and some once-living materials. Radioactive isotopes—atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons—decay at predictable rates, turning into daughter isotopes. By measuring the proportions of parent and daughter isotopes and applying the isotope’s half-life, scientists estimate when the material or a geologic event formed. Different isotope pairs suit different materials and timescales: potassium-argon can date volcanic rocks, while carbon-14 is used for relatively recent organic remains, not rocks themselves. These dates help reconstruct Earth’s history, but the result depends on the material and geological context; sedimentary rocks can be especially difficult to date directly.

key_facts.text: An isotope’s half-life is the time required for half of a sample’s radioactive parent atoms to decay.
Geologists commonly use uranium-lead and potassium-argon dating; different isotope pairs are useful across different timescales.
Carbon-14 dating estimates the age of suitable organic material; it does not directly date rocks.
A date from igneous rock minerals generally records when they crystallized; a date from metamorphic minerals may record mineral formation or later cooling.
Sedimentary rocks can be harder to date because their grains may have formed before the sediment was deposited; dated ash layers can help constrain their age.

overview.text: Coral reefs are complex marine ecosystems built chiefly by reef-building stony corals. A coral is often a colony of tiny animals called polyps; each secretes a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton, and generations of growth add to the reef’s foundation. Many reef-building corals also partner with microscopic algae that provide food through photosynthesis. The reef’s three-dimensional structure offers habitat, food, and shelter for a wide range of marine life, while reefs also benefit people by supporting food resources and helping protect shorelines. Reef forms include fringing reefs along coasts, barrier reefs farther offshore, and atolls—rings of coral surrounding a lagoon.

key_facts.text: Corals are animals; most corals form colonies of polyps, though some are solitary.
Stony corals secrete calcium-carbonate skeletons that build the reef foundation; dead skeletons continue to add structure and habitat.
Many reef-building corals exchange resources with photosynthetic algae living in their tissues; the algae supply food that helps corals grow.
An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef surrounding a lagoon; barrier reefs also lie offshore, separated from land by a lagoon.
Bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel symbiotic algae and turn white; a bleached coral is not necessarily dead, though it is under stress.

overview.text: LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) is a U.S. National Science Foundation-supported research facility, not a telescope that collects light. Its two widely separated detectors—at Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana—each use an L-shaped pair of 4-kilometer vacuum arms. Laser beams travel along the arms and recombine; a passing gravitational wave slightly changes the arm lengths and the resulting light pattern. Comparing signals at both sites helps researchers distinguish cosmic events from local disturbances. In September 2015, LIGO made the first direct detection of gravitational waves, from two merging black holes, confirming a new way to study the universe; the achievement was recognized by the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

key_facts.text: LIGO’s name stands for Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory.
Each LIGO detector has two 4-kilometer arms arranged in an L.
The detectors split and recombine laser light; changes in the light pattern reveal tiny changes caused by passing gravitational waves.
The two U.S. sites are in Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana; comparing their data helps check whether a signal is astrophysical rather than local noise.
LIGO’s first direct gravitational-wave detection, in 2015, came from merging black holes; the achievement was recognized with the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

overview.text: Keratin is a group of fibrous structural proteins found in vertebrates, built from amino-acid chains that assemble into strong fibers. It matters because it reinforces and protects the epidermis and forms many structures made from skin, including human hair and nails and, in other animals, feathers, beaks, claws, horns, hooves, and scales. In skin, keratin-packed outer cells create a tough surface barrier; they are shed and replaced by cells from below. Keratins differ in structure: α-keratin chains coil into helices, while β-keratin has a pleated-sheet-like backbone. Chemical cross-links help stabilize keratin’s structure and make it resistant to ordinary physical and chemical damage.

key_facts.text: Keratin proteins are made from amino-acid building blocks linked into chains.
Cross-links between keratin chains help stabilize the structure and make it resistant to ordinary damage.
Keratin makes the epidermis’s outer surface mechanically tough; shedding those cells also removes microbes clinging to the surface.
α-keratin has a coiled-coil, alpha-helical structure; β-keratin has a zigzag or pleated-sheet-like structure.
Hair, nails, feathers, beaks, claws, horns, hooves, and scales are examples of specialized keratin-containing structures.

overview.text: Volume, commonly symbolized V, measures the three-dimensional space occupied by matter or bounded by a surface; unlike area, it is expressed in cubic units. Its SI unit is the cubic meter (m³), while a liter (L) equals a cubic decimeter and a milliliter equals a cubic centimeter, so the same unit system applies to solids, liquids, and gases. In thermodynamics, V describes the space occupied by a system such as a gas: it appears with pressure and temperature in the ideal-gas relation, and a change in gas volume can accompany pressure–volume work. Thus, volume connects everyday measurement with geometry and the analysis of physical systems.

key_facts.text: Volume measures three-dimensional space and is commonly represented by V.
The SI unit is the cubic meter (m³); it can express the volume of a solid, liquid, or gas.
One liter equals one cubic decimeter (1 L = 1 dm³), and one milliliter equals one cubic centimeter (1 mL = 1 cm³).
A cube measuring 10 cm on each side has a volume of 1 L.
For an ideal gas, pressure, volume, and temperature are related; changing a gas’s volume can also involve pressure–volume work.

overview.text: Young’s double-slit experiment is an optics demonstration associated with English physicist Thomas Young, who presented evidence for interference of light in 1801. In the familiar setup, light from one source reaches two narrow openings; each opening sends out spreading waves that overlap on a screen. Where waves arrive in step, they reinforce and make bright fringes; where they arrive out of step, they cancel and make dark fringes. The alternating pattern is a hallmark of interference and supported the wave description of light against the then-influential corpuscular view. Young’s first demonstration used a thin card to divide a beam, rather than two slits; the double-slit version appeared in his 1807 lectures. Modern physics describes light as having both wave-like and particle-like behavior.

key_facts.text: Thomas Young was an English physician and physicist who studied light and presented his ideas on optical interference in 1801.
In the familiar arrangement, two narrow openings act as coherent sources, and the overlapping light forms bright and dark fringes on a screen.
Bright fringes occur when waves arrive in phase; dark fringes occur when they arrive out of phase.
Young’s earliest demonstration used a thin card to split a beam; he published a double-slit version in 1807.
The experiment supported a wave description of light; modern physics describes light as having both wave-like and particle-like behavior.

overview.text: Fertilizer is a material added to soil or plants to supply nutrients and support growth, supplementing the nutrients already present in the soil. Many fertilizers provide nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), which have different roles in plant growth. Fertilizers can be packaged blends or materials such as manure and compost; their nutrient content and how quickly plants can use those nutrients vary. In agriculture, supplying nutrients helps produce crops for food, feed, fiber, and fuel. Too much fertilizer can waste resources and harm the environment when nutrients move into waterways, so application should match plant and soil needs.

key_facts.text: Fertilizer labels commonly list N-P-K in that order; the numbers indicate the proportions of those nutrients in the product.
Nitrogen supports leaf growth, phosphorus supports roots and fruiting, and potassium helps plants stay hardy and resist disease.
Manure and compost can supply nutrients; many organic nutrient sources must be broken down by soil organisms before plants can use them.
Commercial fertilizer is a major source of nutrients applied to crops, but manure and other organic materials can also contribute nutrients.
Applying more nutrients than plants need can harm the environment; fertilizer choices and amounts should be guided by soil and plant needs.

overview.text: In ecology, population size (often written N) is the number of individuals of one species within a defined area and at a particular time; the area chosen sets the population’s boundary. It is not the same as population density, which expresses individuals per unit area or volume. Ecologists track size to understand abundance and change, which can inform conservation and management. Because a complete count is often impractical, scientists estimate size from samples: quadrats suit plants and other less-mobile organisms, while mark-and-recapture can estimate mobile animals. Resource availability limits how large a population can grow; carrying capacity describes the maximum an environment can support.

key_facts.text: Population size is the total number of individuals; population density is the number per unit area or volume.
A population is defined by species and place; the area under study can have natural or human-made boundaries.
A complete count can be impractical, so researchers use samples: quadrats for plants and other less-mobile organisms, and mark-and-recapture for mobile animals.
Mark-and-recapture estimates population size from the proportion of marked individuals found in a later sample; the estimate can be affected if animals become easier or harder to recapture.
Carrying capacity is the maximum number of individuals an environment’s resources can support; it is not necessarily the population’s current size.

overview.text: Boyle’s law describes how pressure and volume change for a fixed amount of gas when temperature stays constant: increase the pressure and the volume decreases, and vice versa. Its defining feature is an inverse relationship, expressed as PV = constant; between two states, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. The law is named for Robert Boyle, the seventeenth-century natural philosopher whose work on gases helped establish the relationship experimentally. It is one of several gas laws that combine into the ideal gas law, PV = nRT. Breathing offers a familiar example: as the chest expands, lung pressure falls and air flows inward.

key_facts.text: The inverse relationship applies when both the gas’s temperature and amount remain constant.
At fixed temperature and amount, pressure multiplied by volume stays constant: PV = constant.
For two conditions of the same gas sample, the relationship can be written P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
OpenStax identifies Boyle’s law as one of four gas relationships combined in the ideal gas law, PV = nRT.
The Science Museum Group identifies Robert Boyle as an Irish natural philosopher and chemist (1627–1691), and notes that he and Robert Hooke devised an air-pump.
During inhalation, expanding the chest increases lung volume and lowers lung pressure, drawing air in—a familiar application of Boyle’s law.

overview.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS), also called disseminated sclerosis, is a chronic disease affecting the brain and spinal cord—the central nervous system. In MS, an abnormal immune response causes inflammation and damages myelin, the protective covering that helps nerve cells carry messages efficiently; resulting lesions can interrupt communication between the brain and body. The name “sclerosis” refers to scar tissue associated with this damage. Effects differ from person to person and may include vision problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness, stiffness, and balance difficulties. In relapsing-remitting MS, symptoms flare and improve or ease during remissions; progressive forms worsen gradually, either from the outset or after a relapsing course. The exact causes are not fully known, and genetic and environmental factors are thought to contribute.

key_facts.text: MS lesions affect the brain and spinal cord; MRI scans can show these damaged areas.
The three main patterns described by the NHS are relapsing-remitting, secondary progressive, and primary progressive MS.
There is no single test for diagnosing MS; assessment may include a neurological examination, MRI, blood tests, or spinal-fluid testing.
Symptoms and their effects vary; possible symptoms include fatigue, vision problems, tingling, muscle stiffness, and balance difficulties.

overview.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan (1866–1945) was an American zoologist and geneticist whose experiments with fruit flies helped make inheritance experimentally understandable. At Columbia University, where he joined the faculty in 1904, he and his students used Drosophila melanogaster to investigate inherited differences. Their results supported the chromosome theory: genes are carried on chromosomes. The group also advanced understanding of genetic linkage—genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together—and recombination. Morgan’s contribution was collaborative: students Calvin Bridges, Alfred Sturtevant, and Hermann Muller helped develop and extend this work. He received the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about chromosomes’ role in heredity.

key_facts.text: Morgan joined Columbia University in 1904, where his laboratory became known as the “Fly Room.”
Morgan and his research group used Drosophila melanogaster, the fruit fly, to study inheritance.
The group’s findings supported the idea that genes are carried on chromosomes and contributed to understanding genetic linkage and recombination.
His collaborators included Alfred Sturtevant, Calvin Bridges, and Hermann Muller; their work helped develop and extend the field’s understanding of heredity.
Morgan received the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning chromosomes’ role in heredity.

overview.text: A vacuum is a region with less matter and lower pressure than ordinary surroundings; in practical physics, the word often describes a space where gas pressure is below atmospheric pressure. A perfect vacuum, containing no matter, is an ideal limit: real vacuums still contain some particles. In quantum physics, “vacuum” has a second meaning—the lowest-energy state of a system—which is not simply empty space, because fields remain and can fluctuate. These meanings make vacuum useful both for describing low-pressure conditions in laboratories and for studying the basic behavior of matter and fields. The context determines whether “vacuum” means a nearly matter-free region or a quantum ground state.

key_facts.text: In ordinary use, a vacuum has pressure below atmospheric pressure; it need not be completely empty.
A perfect vacuum is an ideal case with no matter; real vacuums are not perfectly free of matter.
In quantum physics, the vacuum is the lowest-energy state, not necessarily a state with no fields or energy.
NASA defines vacuum for students as the absence of all matter, including air; this describes the idealized case.
CERN describes quantum-field fluctuations as part of the vacuum’s activity, distinguishing the quantum meaning from simply removing gas from a chamber.

overview.text: A donkey, also called an ass or burro, is a domesticated member of the horse family (Equidae), usually identified as Equus asinus. Its wild ancestry lies among African wild asses; genome evidence indicates donkeys were domesticated once in Africa around 5,000 BCE, then spread through Africa and Eurasia. Donkeys became important working animals because they carried loads over long distances, especially through semi-arid and upland regions, connecting people and communities. A large head, long mobile ears, erect mane, and tufted tail help distinguish a donkey from a horse; its well-supplied ears also aid cooling. A cautious response to danger is sometimes mislabeled as stubbornness.

key_facts.text: The Smithsonian identifies the domestic donkey as Equus asinus and notes that donkeys are also called asses.
Genomic research supports a single domestication in Africa around 5,000 BCE, followed by spread through Africa and Eurasia.
Donkeys helped carry people and goods across long distances, including in semi-arid and upland regions.
A donkey’s large head, long ears, erect mane, and tufted tail distinguish its appearance from a horse; its ears can help cool its body.
A donkey may pause or refuse when something seems threatening; the Smithsonian describes this cautious behavior as one reason people call donkeys stubborn.

overview.text: A familiar mouse is the house mouse, Mus musculus, a small mammal in the rodent order. It typically has brown-to-gray fur, a lighter belly, and a nearly hairless, scaled tail about as long as its head and body combined. House mice often live near people—in homes, barns, and food-storage areas—but also occur in fields and woodland. Usually active at night, they shelter in protected places and eat seeds and accessible human food. They are prey for small predators, may contaminate stored food, and are used in research because mice share important mammalian features and diseases with humans.

key_facts.text: The house mouse’s scientific name is Mus musculus; it belongs to class Mammalia and order Rodentia.
Its tail is nearly hairless and has visible scale rings; the tail is about as long as the head and body together.
House mice make nests in sheltered places near food, including hidden spots in buildings.
They are important prey for small predators, but can also consume or contaminate stored human food.
Laboratory mice help researchers study human physiology and disease; mouse models can be selectively bred or genetically engineered.

overview.text: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialized processor that accelerates the creation and processing of images by handling many data elements in parallel. Graphics work often involves repeating similar calculations across many vertices, fragments, or pixels; a GPU’s many computing units can work on those tasks at the same time. This design also makes GPUs useful beyond graphics: when a task can be divided into many similar calculations, a GPU can help speed video work, scientific computing, and machine-learning workloads. A GPU may be integrated alongside a CPU or installed as a discrete chip. A graphics card is a larger add-in board that contains a GPU and other supporting components. GPUs complement CPUs rather than simply replacing them.

key_facts.text: GPUs were originally designed to accelerate graphics rendering, including 3D images.
Parallel processing means working on multiple data elements at once; graphics calculations often suit this approach.
GPUs can accelerate some non-graphics tasks, including machine learning, video editing, and scientific computing.
A GPU may be integrated with a computer’s CPU or provided as a discrete chip.
A graphics card is an add-in board that contains a GPU and other components; the terms “GPU” and “graphics card” do not mean exactly the same thing.

overview.text: A neuron, or nerve cell, is a specialized cell that receives and sends information, making it a basic signaling unit of the nervous system. Its cell body contains the nucleus; branching dendrites receive signals, while an axon carries electrical impulses away from the cell body. Neurons vary in shape and role: sensory neurons convey information about stimuli, while motor neurons carry messages to muscles. Within a neuron, signals travel electrically along the axon. At many synapses, the axon terminal releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, which cross a small gap and affect a neighboring cell. This combination of electrical signaling within neurons and chemical signaling between cells helps connect neurons into circuits for sensation, movement, and communication between the brain and body.

key_facts.text: A typical neuron has a cell body with a nucleus, signal-receiving dendrites, and a message-carrying axon; neurons’ shapes can vary with their roles and locations.
Sensory neurons send information about stimuli toward the brain; motor neurons carry messages that help generate movement by activating muscles.
A neuron carries an electrical signal along its axon; at many synapses, chemical neurotransmitters carry the message across a small gap to another cell.
In most circuits, a synapse includes an axon ending, part of a neighboring neuron such as a dendrite, and the narrow gap between them.
Glia are nervous-system cells distinct from neurons; among their roles, they provide support and produce myelin insulation that helps nerve impulses travel.

overview.text: An optical lens is a shaped transparent element that refracts (bends) light as it enters and leaves, steering rays to form images. Lenses matter because this action helps magnifying glasses, cameras, eyeglasses, and the eye collect or redirect light. A converging lens bends parallel rays toward its optical axis so they meet at a real focal point; a diverging lens spreads rays as if they came from a virtual focal point. The distance from the lens to its focal point is its focal length, a key measure of how it handles light. Lens type and object position affect whether an image can be projected or is seen only by looking through the lens.

key_facts.text: Common converging lenses are thicker at the center than at the edges; common diverging lenses are thinner at the center.
A diverging lens’s focal point is virtual: the outgoing rays spread apart but appear to originate from that point when traced backward.
A converging lens can form a real image when the object is farther from the lens than its focal length, or an upright virtual image when the object is closer.
Lens power is the reciprocal of focal length in meters and is measured in diopters (D).
Light paths are reversible: a source placed at a converging lens’s focal point can emerge as a parallel beam.

overview.text: The spine, also called the vertebral or spinal column, is the flexible bony framework running from the neck to the tailbone. It supports the head and trunk, helps the body bend and move, and provides attachment points for muscles and ribs. Openings through the vertebrae line up to form the spinal canal, which protects and provides a passage for the spinal cord; the cord is not the same structure as the spine. In adults, the column has 24 separate vertebrae above the sacrum and coccyx, which form from fused vertebrae. Its natural curves and cushioning discs help combine support with movement.

key_facts.text: The 24 separate adult vertebrae are grouped as 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (rib-bearing), and 5 lumbar (lower-back) vertebrae.
The sacrum forms from five fused sacral vertebrae, and the coccyx (tailbone) typically forms from four fused coccygeal vertebrae.
A typical vertebra has a weight-bearing body and an arch; the aligned openings in the arches make the spinal canal.
Discs between neighboring vertebral bodies provide padding and allow movement; MedlinePlus also describes them as shock absorbers during activities such as walking and jumping.
The spine has four natural curves that contribute to its strength and flexibility; scoliosis refers to an abnormal sideways curve with twisting.

overview.text: A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field—a region where magnetic forces act. Most familiar magnets have north and south poles: opposite poles attract, while like poles repel. Their fields can pull on certain materials, especially iron, cobalt, and nickel; magnets can also influence a nearby compass needle, which turns to align with Earth’s magnetic field. Magnets matter both as simple tools and as part of electromagnetism: a current flowing through a wire coil creates a magnetic field, making an electromagnet. Magnetic compasses have helped people navigate for centuries, using a freely turning magnetized needle to indicate direction.

key_facts.text: Opposite magnetic poles attract; like poles repel.
Iron, cobalt, and nickel are examples of materials whose atoms can have strong magnetic properties.
A magnetic compass works because its magnetized needle turns to align with Earth’s magnetic field.
Electric current produces a magnetic field; a coil of wire can use this effect to act as an electromagnet.
People have used magnetic compasses for navigation for hundreds of years.

overview.text: Dinosaurs (Dinosauria) are a diverse branch of reptiles whose fossils reveal a remarkable range of sizes and forms. They flourished on land during the Mesozoic Era, which includes the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. A key feature distinguishing them from many other reptiles is their upright posture, with legs positioned beneath the body. Some walked on two legs and others on four. Pterosaurs and marine reptiles lived in the same ancient world but were not dinosaurs. Around 66 million years ago, non-bird dinosaurs disappeared in a mass extinction; birds are the surviving dinosaur lineage.

key_facts.text: Non-bird dinosaurs lived during the Mesozoic Era, from roughly 245 to 66 million years ago; its periods are the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous.
Their legs were positioned beneath their bodies; a distinctive hip-socket feature supported this upright stance.
Dinosaurs varied widely in size, and different kinds walked on two or four legs.
Pterosaurs, plesiosaurs, and mosasaurs were prehistoric reptiles, but they were not dinosaurs.
The end-Cretaceous mass extinction about 66 million years ago eliminated non-avian dinosaurs; birds are the surviving dinosaur group.

overview.text: Helium (He), atomic number 2, is a colorless, chemically unreactive gas and the lightest noble gas. Its name reflects an unusual history: astronomers identified it in sunlight in 1868, before it was confirmed on Earth in 1895. In stars, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy; later in some stars, helium can fuse into carbon. On Earth, helium’s low density lets it lift balloons, while its very low boiling point makes liquid helium useful for cooling superconducting magnets in MRI scanners. Helium–neon lasers also scan barcodes. These varied roles—from a product of stellar fusion to a specialized coolant—make helium important in astronomy, medicine, and technology.

key_facts.text: Helium is element 2 in Group 18; it is colorless and chemically unreactive.
Astronomers observed helium’s spectral signature in the Sun in 1868; it was confirmed on Earth in 1895.
Hydrogen fusion produces helium in stars. In later stages of some stars, helium fusion can produce carbon.
Liquid helium cools superconducting magnets in MRI scanners; helium–neon lasers are used to scan barcodes.
Because helium has low density, it is used to fill decorative and weather balloons.

overview.text: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the most advanced stage of infection with HIV, the virus that causes HIV infection; the terms are related but not interchangeable. HIV damages CD4 immune cells, weakening the body’s ability to fight infections and some cancers. In the United States, an AIDS diagnosis is made when a person’s CD4 count falls below 200 cells per cubic millimeter of blood or when certain AIDS-defining illnesses occur. Without effective treatment, HIV may progress to AIDS, sometimes after years. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can prevent or slow that progression and help the immune system recover. An AIDS diagnosis signals severe immune damage, but treatment can still help.

key_facts.text: AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
HIV is the virus; AIDS is an advanced stage of HIV infection, not a separate virus.
CD4 cells help the immune system fight infections; HIV attacks and destroys these cells.
In the United States, either a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or certain illnesses can qualify someone for an AIDS diagnosis.
ART does not cure HIV, but it can control the virus and help prevent progression to AIDS.

overview.text: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a virus that weakens the immune system by infecting CD4 T cells, white blood cells that help defend the body against infections. Its replication strategy is distinctive: after entering a CD4 cell, HIV uses reverse transcriptase to convert its RNA into DNA, then integrates viral DNA into the cell’s DNA so the cell can help make new viruses. Without treatment, loss of CD4 cells can leave the body vulnerable to serious infections and some cancers. This advanced stage of HIV infection is called acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), not a separate virus. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can suppress HIV and protect health, but it does not eliminate the virus.

key_facts.text: HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus; AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
HIV targets CD4 T cells, immune-system white blood cells that help protect the body from infection.
Reverse transcriptase converts HIV’s RNA into DNA; another enzyme, integrase, helps insert that DNA into a CD4 cell’s DNA.
AIDS is a late stage of HIV infection, not a separate virus; it occurs when the immune system is badly damaged.
ART can control HIV and lower its amount in the blood, but it is not a cure and the virus remains in the body.

overview.text: Plastic is not one chemical but a broad family of materials; most familiar examples are based on synthetic polymers, large molecules built from repeating monomer units. The polymer’s chain structure and chemistry help create different properties, so plastics can be flexible films, rigid containers, foams, or durable parts. Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped, while thermosetting plastics set into shapes that do not remelt reversibly. Their low weight, durability, and versatility make plastics useful in packaging, construction, transportation, and health care. But “plastic” does not name a single substance: products use many polymer types, and recycling systems may accept only some of them.

key_facts.text: Polymers are very large molecules made of repeating units called monomers; plastics are one group of polymeric materials.
Common plastic types include polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high- and low-density polyethylene (HDPE and LDPE), PVC, polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS).
Thermoplastics can be melted and reshaped with heat; thermosetting plastics set irreversibly and do not remelt in the same way.
Plastic products are used in packaging, construction, transportation, and health care, among other fields.
Different plastics have different resin types, and some recycling systems accept only certain types.

overview.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused mainly by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most often affects the lungs, but can also involve other parts of the body. TB spreads through the air when someone with infectious lung or throat TB releases bacteria by coughing, speaking, or singing—not through surface contact. Infection does not always cause illness: the immune system may keep the bacteria inactive, without symptoms or spread to others; active TB develops when the bacteria multiply. Historically, TB was called “consumption.” Today it is preventable and curable with appropriate treatment, although drug-resistant forms need different, more complex care.

key_facts.text: TB bacteria usually attack the lungs, but disease can also affect places such as the kidneys, brain, bones, or lymph nodes.
People with inactive (latent) TB infection do not have TB disease symptoms and cannot spread TB bacteria to others; infection can later progress to disease.
Infectious lung or laryngeal TB can spread through airborne particles released when a person coughs, speaks, or sings; TB is not transmitted by surface contact.
“Consumption” was a historical name for tuberculosis, associated with the dramatic weight loss seen in people with the disease.
TB disease is curable; drug-resistant TB can require longer and more complex treatment.

overview.text: Damping is the gradual decrease in an oscillator’s motion when forces such as friction or drag remove mechanical energy. It explains why real swings, spring systems, and plucked guitar strings do not keep moving forever without added energy. In lightly damped motion, the oscillator continues back and forth while its amplitude shrinks; the lost energy is often converted to heat. In a common mathematical model, drag is proportional to speed and the amplitude fades exponentially, though real damping forces do not always follow that simple rule. Stronger damping can stop the back-and-forth motion entirely, and controlled damping is useful in devices such as car shock absorbers.

key_facts.text: Damping forces oppose motion and reduce an oscillator’s mechanical energy; some of that energy is commonly transferred as heat.
With light damping, the amplitude decreases while the period and frequency remain nearly the same as in undamped motion.
For a common model where drag is proportional to speed, amplitude decays exponentially; actual damping forces do not always follow this model.
Underdamped systems keep oscillating as they settle; with sufficiently strong damping, a system moves toward equilibrium without oscillating.
Car shock absorbers use damping to reduce unwanted motion and help a vehicle’s suspension settle.

overview.text: The retina is the light-sensitive, layered neural tissue lining the back of the eyeball. The eye focuses light onto it, where rods and cones—its photoreceptor cells—begin the process of turning light into signals. Rods respond to dim light, while cones help detect color. Other retinal neurons process and relay this information; axons of retinal ganglion cells join to form the optic nerve, which carries signals to the brain. The macula, a central area of the retina, supports central vision, and its center, the fovea, provides the sharpest vision. The retina is essential to sight because it starts and organizes the eye’s visual signals.

key_facts.text: The retina lines the back of the eyeball and sends electrical impulses through the optic nerve to the brain.
Rods are specialized for dim light; cones are specialized for brighter light and color.
Retinal ganglion cell axons converge and leave the eye as the optic nerve.
The macula is a small retinal area needed for central vision; the fovea at its center is where vision is sharpest.
The retina is made up of interconnected neurons that encode light into signals the brain can understand.

overview.text: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into a gas, with molecules escaping from the liquid’s surface. It can happen below the liquid’s boiling point, so a puddle can slowly disappear without boiling. The change takes in energy, which can cool the nearby surface—as when sweat evaporates from skin. Evaporation is also a key route by which water moves from Earth’s surface into the atmosphere. There, water vapor may later cool and condense into liquid droplets, helping return water to the surface as part of the water cycle. Unlike evaporation, transpiration is water vapor released by plants.

key_facts.text: Evaporation occurs at a liquid’s surface; water can evaporate even below its boiling point.
Evaporation absorbs energy, and evaporating water can cool its surroundings; sweat cooling skin is one example.
In the water cycle, evaporation moves water from oceans, lakes, rivers, and other surfaces into the atmosphere.
Water vapor can condense back into liquid water; condensation is the reverse of evaporation.
Transpiration is distinct from evaporation: plants release water vapor through their leaves.

overview.text: Cilia (singular: cilium) are short, hairlike projections built from microtubules that extend from the surface of many eukaryotic cells. Motile cilia beat in coordinated patterns: they can move a single-celled organism such as Paramecium or push material across a cell surface. In human airways, cilia help sweep mucus and trapped particles toward the throat. Not all cilia propel things: primary cilia are typically non-motile and function as sensory and signaling structures, with receptors and ion channels in their membrane helping cells respond to outside cues. The common motile arrangement has nine outer microtubule pairs plus a central pair (9+2); primary cilia commonly have nine outer pairs and no central pair (9+0).

key_facts.text: Cilium is the singular form; cilia are microtubule-based, hairlike projections on some eukaryotic cells.
Cilia can propel Paramecium or move substances along a cell’s outer surface.
In the respiratory tract, beating cilia help carry mucus and trapped particles toward the throat.
Primary cilia are non-motile and use membrane receptors and ion channels to sense cues and support cell signaling.
The usual arrangements are 9+2 for motile cilia and 9+0 for primary cilia, though some motile cilia are exceptions.

overview.text: A chloroplast is a membrane-bound organelle found in plants and photosynthetic algae, where photosynthesis captures light energy and stores it as chemical energy. Its green pigment, chlorophyll, is embedded in internal membrane sacs called thylakoids; these are often stacked into grana. The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes, while the surrounding fluid, the stroma, is where carbon dioxide is used to build sugars. Chloroplasts have their own DNA and ribosomes. These features, along with other evidence, support the scientific explanation that chloroplasts evolved from cyanobacteria that entered an ancestral cell and became its long-term partners.

key_facts.text: Chloroplasts are the organelles where photosynthesis occurs in plants and photosynthetic algae.
A chloroplast has an outer and inner membrane, plus internal thylakoid membranes; stacks of thylakoids are called grana, and the surrounding fluid is the stroma.
Chlorophyll and other light-absorbing pigments are in the thylakoid membranes, where the light-dependent reactions begin photosynthesis.
The stroma is where energy from the light-dependent reactions helps convert carbon dioxide into sugars.
Chloroplasts contain their own DNA and ribosomes; evidence including these features supports their evolutionary origin from cyanobacteria through endosymbiosis.

overview.text: Dental enamel is the hard, mineral-rich outer covering of a tooth’s crown, the visible part above the gum, and is described as the hardest substance in the body. It consists of tightly arranged mineral rods, with calcium hydroxyapatite as its principal mineral. Despite its hardness, enamel can lose minerals: acids produced when mouth bacteria process sugars and starches dissolve its mineral structure. Saliva helps neutralize acids and supplies minerals for remineralization, while fluoride promotes that repair and makes enamel more resistant to acid. When mineral loss repeatedly exceeds repair, early weakened areas can progress toward cavities.

key_facts.text: Enamel covers the crown of a tooth; directly beneath it is dentin.
Enamel is described as the hardest substance in the body and is organized into tiny mineral rods.
Calcium hydroxyapatite is a principal mineral structure in enamel.
Acids made by oral bacteria can dissolve enamel minerals; repeated mineral loss can lead to cavities.
Saliva supports remineralization, and fluoride helps strengthen enamel’s resistance to acid.

overview.text: Biological fitness, also called evolutionary or Darwinian fitness, describes how much an organism or genotype contributes to future generations through reproduction. Biologists usually compare reproductive success with that of others in the same population, rather than treating fitness as a fixed personal score. It is not physical strength, health, or stamina: surviving matters evolutionarily when it helps an organism reproduce, and differences in offspring number can affect fitness even when survival is equal. Fitness depends on the environment, because traits that improve reproductive success in one setting may not do so in another. Natural selection can therefore favor heritable traits linked to greater reproductive contribution, shifting their frequency across generations.

key_facts.text: Relative fitness compares reproductive success with that of other organisms or genotypes in the population; in a common model, the highest value is set to 1.
Survival alone does not determine evolutionary fitness: it matters when it affects the number of offspring produced.
Fitness can reflect several routes to reproduction, including surviving to reproductive age, finding mates, and producing offspring.
A trait’s fitness effects depend on the environment; a trait advantageous under one set of conditions may not be advantageous under another.
When reproductive differences are linked to heritable traits, natural selection can change how common those traits are in a population over generations.

overview.text: Bosons are a major family of particles, distinguished from fermions by their intrinsic spin: a boson’s spin is zero or another whole-number multiple of the quantum unit of angular momentum. Unlike fermions, identical bosons are not barred by the Pauli exclusion principle from sharing a quantum state. This difference shapes how particles behave in groups. Many familiar elementary bosons—such as photons and W and Z bosons—carry fundamental forces, but bosons do not all serve the same role: the Higgs boson is associated with the Higgs field, whose discovery helped confirm an important part of the modern explanation of particle mass.

key_facts.text: Bosons have integer spin, including zero; fermions have half-integer spin.
Bosons do not obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so identical bosons can share a quantum state.
Photons carry the electromagnetic force; W and Z bosons carry the weak nuclear interaction.
The Higgs boson has spin zero and is associated with the Higgs field; CERN and ATLAS describe its discovery as evidence for the field and the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism.
ATLAS and CMS announced observation of a particle consistent with the Higgs boson on July 4, 2012.

overview.text: The Calvin cycle, also called the Calvin–Benson cycle, is a set of photosynthetic reactions in the chloroplast stroma that builds organic molecules from carbon dioxide. It is a key carbon-fixing pathway: carbon from CO₂ becomes part of a three-carbon sugar called G3P, which can contribute to making carbohydrates. The cycle has three stages—carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration. In fixation, the enzyme RuBisCO attaches CO₂ to the five-carbon molecule RuBP. The cycle then uses ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions to produce G3P and regenerate RuBP. “Light-independent” means light does not directly power these reactions; it does not mean they are independent of the light reactions’ products.

key_facts.text: The cycle takes place in the chloroplast stroma.
Its three stages are carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of RuBP.
RuBisCO joins CO₂ to RuBP; the resulting unstable compound splits into two 3-PGA molecules.
ATP supplies energy and NADPH supplies reducing power; both are produced in the light-dependent reactions.
The cycle’s net sugar output is G3P; some leaves the cycle while the rest helps regenerate RuBP.

overview.text: Corn, also called maize, is the annual grass Zea mays, native to Central and southwestern Mexico through western Guatemala according to Kew. Scientists generally identify the wild grass teosinte as its ancestor, although the University of Nebraska–Lincoln notes that the crop’s evolution remains debated. Corn’s structure is distinctive: pollen-producing tassels rise at the top of the stalk, while ears form lower down; silks on each ear receive pollen, and fertilized ovules develop into kernels. People eat corn kernels and process them into products such as flour, starch, sweeteners, and oil. In the United States, corn is also a major livestock-feed crop and an important source of fuel ethanol.

key_facts.text: Kew recognizes Zea mays as an accepted species and lists it as an annual grass native to Central and southwestern Mexico and western Guatemala.
Teosinte is widely considered corn’s wild ancestor, but the University of Nebraska–Lincoln notes that explanations of corn’s evolution remain debated.
The tassel at the top of a corn plant produces pollen; lower ears bear silks, and fertilized ovules develop into kernels.
Corn is processed into human foods and ingredients, including flour, meal, starch, sweeteners, and oil.
In the United States, corn is a major livestock-feed crop and is also used to produce fuel ethanol.

overview.text: Eyes are sensory organs that begin vision by collecting light; seeing also depends on the brain, which interprets signals sent from each retina. Light first passes through the clear cornea, which helps focus it; the pupil is the opening that admits light, while the iris adjusts its size. Behind it, the clear lens further focuses light onto the retina, a light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eyeball. Retinal photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals, carried along the optic nerve to the brain. The macula supports central vision, and its fovea is where vision is sharpest.

key_facts.text: The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped covering at the front of the eye and helps focus light.
The pupil is an opening in the iris; the iris changes its size to regulate how much light enters.
The lens sits behind the iris and focuses light on the retina, helping the eye focus on near and far objects.
Retinal receptor cells called rods and cones respond to light and send electrical impulses through the optic nerve to the brain.
The macula is a retinal area needed for central vision; its center, the fovea, is where vision is sharpest.

overview.text: The Van Allen radiation belts are two broad, doughnut-shaped zones of energetic charged particles held around Earth by its magnetic field. The particles follow magnetic field lines, bouncing between northern and southern regions; the belts are not solid rings but changing populations of trapped radiation. Typically there is an inner belt and a more variable outer belt, with protons and electrons present in different proportions. Explorer 1 and Explorer 3 detected trapped radiation in 1958, and follow-up spacecraft helped reveal the outer belt. The belts matter because energetic particles can disrupt or damage spacecraft electronics, so scientists study them to understand near-Earth space and protect satellites. Brief extra belts can sometimes appear during space-weather disturbances.

key_facts.text: Earth’s magnetic field traps charged particles in two belts that generally have a doughnut-like shape.
Particles travel along magnetic field lines, bouncing between polar regions.
Explorer 1 and Explorer 3 detected trapped radiation in 1958; later spacecraft helped identify the outer belt.
The belts’ energetic particles can damage spacecraft electronics, making the region important for satellite design and space research.
The two main belts are not the only possible arrangement: a temporary third ring was observed in 2012 and lasted about a month.

overview.text: A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy from one place to another; in many waves, the material involved oscillates around its usual position rather than traveling along with the disturbance. Waves include sound, ripples on water, earthquakes, and light. Mechanical waves, such as sound, need a substance called a medium to travel through, while electromagnetic waves, including light, can cross empty space. Waves are distinguished by how their disturbance moves: in a transverse wave it is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Some waves combine both kinds of motion.

key_facts.text: Waves transfer energy, but mechanical waves generally do not carry the medium’s material along with them; its particles oscillate around equilibrium.
Sound and water waves are mechanical waves that require a medium; electromagnetic waves such as light do not.
Transverse disturbances move perpendicular to wave travel; longitudinal disturbances move parallel to it. Sound in air is longitudinal.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium; wavelength is the distance between matching points, such as consecutive crests.
Frequency counts cycles passing a point per unit time; it is the inverse of period and is commonly measured in hertz (Hz).

overview.text: Aluminum (Al; aluminium is an alternate spelling) is chemical element 13, a silvery-white, lightweight metal and the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust. It is rarely found as a pure metal in nature, so industry obtains it from bauxite: the Bayer process refines the ore into alumina, then the Hall–Héroult process uses electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite to make aluminum. Its low density, ability to be shaped into thin sheets or wires, electrical conductivity, and resistance to corrosion make it useful in foil and cans, electrical lines, buildings, vehicles, and aircraft. Because pure aluminum is relatively soft, many structural parts use stronger aluminum alloys.

key_facts.text: Its chemical symbol is Al, and its atomic number is 13.
Aluminum is abundant in Earth’s crust but is usually bound in minerals rather than occurring as free metal.
Aluminum is malleable and ductile; its low density and corrosion resistance help make it useful in many applications.
Foil, cans, electrical transmission lines, building components, and aircraft parts are among its uses.
Primary production involves refining bauxite into alumina with the Bayer process, then using electrolysis in the Hall–Héroult process.

overview.text: Spiders are arachnids in the order Araneae. Unlike insects, they have eight legs, two main body regions, and no antennae. They are predators, but they do not all hunt alike: some wait in webs, while others ambush or chase prey. All spiders produce silk from spinnerets near the rear of the abdomen; webs are only one use, alongside egg coverings, shelters, and safety draglines. Orb webs, a familiar design, have radiating support threads and spiral capture threads, but spider webs take many forms. By capturing insects through varied hunting strategies, spiders play a useful role in ecosystems.

key_facts.text: Spiders belong to the arachnid order Araneae; arachnids also include mites, ticks, and scorpions.
A spider’s body has two main regions and eight legs; unlike insects, spiders have no antennae.
All spiders produce silk, but not all build webs to catch prey; jumping spiders can pursue prey, and crab spiders can ambush it.
Spinnerets on the abdomen produce silk, which can harden in air and serve uses such as egg cases, shelters, draglines, and webs.
Orb webs use radiating threads and spiral threads; other web designs include tangles, sheets, and spring traps.

overview.text: Velocity describes how an object's position changes over time. Average velocity is displacement—the vector from the starting position to the ending position—divided by elapsed time, not total path length divided by time. Because velocity is a vector, it includes both magnitude and direction; speed is its magnitude and does not specify direction. Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a particular moment. Along a curved path, its direction is tangent to the path. Velocity is commonly measured in meters per second (m/s), and a change in either speed or direction changes velocity.

key_facts.text: Average velocity equals displacement divided by elapsed time: v_avg = Δx/Δt.
Velocity is a vector, so a complete description includes direction; speed is scalar and gives only magnitude.
Average velocity can be zero on a round trip even when the traveler covers a nonzero distance, because the final position matches the starting position.
Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a specific moment; it equals average velocity over an interval when velocity is constant.
For motion along a curved path, the instantaneous velocity vector points tangent to the path.

overview.text: Mercury (Hg), atomic number 80, is a naturally occurring metal distinguished by being liquid at ordinary room temperatures: it freezes at about −38.8 °C, so it stays liquid around 20 °C. Its shiny silver appearance and high density (about 13.5 g/cm³) make it recognizable; its old name, quicksilver, reflects its silvery, flowing look. Mercury is historically important because its ability to form amalgams with gold helped recover gold from ores, and liquid mercury was used in thermometers and electrical devices. It is seldom found as free metal in nature; it is chiefly obtained from cinnabar ore. Elemental mercury can evaporate into harmful vapor, while methylmercury and other compounds are chemically different forms with distinct exposure risks.

key_facts.text: Mercury’s chemical symbol is Hg and its atomic number is 80.
It is a silvery liquid at 20 °C; its melting point is about −38.8 °C and its density is about 13.53 g/cm³.
Mercury rarely occurs uncombined in nature; cinnabar, or mercury sulfide, is a principal ore.
Mercury forms amalgams with metals such as gold; this property has been used to recover gold from ores.
Elemental mercury can evaporate into toxic vapor. Methylmercury is a different chemical form, so mercury’s health effects depend in part on which form is involved.

overview.text: Python is a general-purpose programming language: people use it to give computers instructions, build programs, and automate tasks. Guido van Rossum began creating it in December 1989 as a language influenced by ABC; he chose “Python” as a working title while a fan of the comedy show Monty Python’s Flying Circus. A defining feature is that indentation—the spaces at the start of a line—groups related statements into code blocks. Van Rossum said this design helps make programs more readable. Python is interpreted and has an extensive standard library, along with third-party modules, giving programmers ready-made tools for many kinds of projects.

key_facts.text: Python’s creator, Guido van Rossum, started the project in December 1989 and named it after Monty Python’s Flying Circus, not the snake.
Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language that supports several programming styles, including object-oriented, procedural, and functional programming.
Indentation determines how Python groups statements; inconsistent indentation can cause an error.
Python’s interpreter runs code, and the language’s extensive standard library supplies modules for common tasks; programmers can also use third-party modules.
Van Rossum said indentation reduces visual clutter and encourages a more uniform style, helping people read one another’s code.

overview.text: Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was an English theoretical physicist and cosmologist whose research explored gravity, black holes, and the universe. Working with Roger Penrose, he used mathematics and Einstein’s theory of general relativity to study singularities—points where that theory breaks down—and the implications for the universe’s beginning. In 1974, Hawking proposed that black holes emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation; over time, this process can make them lose energy. His 1988 book A Brief History of Time introduced questions about the universe’s origin and fate to a broad readership. After an operation took away his natural speaking voice, a computer speech synthesizer became his distinctive means of communication.

key_facts.text: With Roger Penrose, Hawking developed mathematical work on singularities in general relativity; their results connected the theory to the universe’s beginning.
Hawking radiation is a theoretical prediction: black holes can emit radiation and gradually lose energy.
Hawking’s book A Brief History of Time, published in 1988, explained cosmology—the study of the universe—to general readers.
He was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge from 1979 until 2009.
After a tracheotomy in 1985, Hawking lost his ability to speak; speech-synthesis software later enabled him to communicate with a computer-generated voice.

overview.text: Codebreaking, or cryptanalysis, analyzes codes and ciphers to defeat their protection and recover concealed information, sometimes without knowing the key. It is distinct from cryptography, which creates protective systems. Codebreakers may combine intercepted signals, clues about likely message wording, language skills, and tools for testing possible cipher settings. During World War II, teams at Britain’s Bletchley Park broke German, Italian, and Japanese ciphers, including German Enigma systems. The intelligence they produced contributed significantly to the Allied effort, showing how deciphering secret communications can affect military decisions.

key_facts.text: NIST describes cryptanalysis as attempting to defeat cryptographic protection without initially knowing the key.
Cryptography makes codes and ciphers; cryptanalysis attempts to break them.
Bletchley Park’s guide outlines steps including intercepting radio signals, working out how messages were encrypted, deciphering them, and using the results to build intelligence.
Bletchley Park codebreakers used clues about possible message wording to help machines check likely Enigma settings.
Bletchley Park’s wartime codebreaking grew into a large intelligence operation whose work provided vital intelligence and contributed significantly to Allied victory.

overview.text: Mass spectrometry (MS) is a family of analytical methods used to study what a sample contains. In a typical experiment, molecules are turned into gas-phase ions, separated according to their mass-to-charge ratios, and detected. The resulting mass spectrum displays signals from the detected ions; scientists use its peaks to investigate the masses and composition of substances. Different instruments and ionization methods suit different samples, so MS is not one single machine or procedure. It is significant in fields including chemistry and materials science, and can help identify components in complex mixtures. When paired with gas chromatography, it can analyze mixtures by separating their components before mass analysis.

key_facts.text: A mass spectrometer’s core tasks are creating ions, separating them by mass-to-charge ratio, and detecting them.
A basic mass spectrum plots detected-ion counts against mass-to-charge ratio.
Ionization methods include MALDI, which uses laser energy, and electrospray, which uses a strong electric field.
In gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, the mixture is separated into components before ions are analyzed; the resulting patterns can help identify its chemical makeup.
Early mass-spectrometry research provided the first evidence for stable, nonradioactive isotopes.
